chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
Just below the eutectoid line, with $C_\alpha = 0.022$, $C_E = 0.76$ and $C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = 6.67$ % C [Session 9 Slides 12-20].

| Steel | Microconstituents | Phases |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Eutectoid $C_0 = 0.76$ | 100 % pearlite | $\alpha$: $\dfrac{6.67 - 0.76}{6.648} = 0.889$; Fe$_3$C: $0.111$ |
| Hypoeutectoid $C_0 < 0.76$ | primary $\alpha$: $\dfrac{0.76 - C_0}{0.76 - 0.022}$; pearlite: $\dfrac{C_0 - 0.022}{0.76 - 0.022}$ | $\alpha$: $\dfrac{6.67 - C_0}{6.648}$; Fe$_3$C: $\dfrac{C_0 - 0.022}{6.648}$ |
| Hypereutectoid $C_0 > 0.76$ | primary Fe$_3$C: $\dfrac{C_0 - 0.76}{6.67 - 0.76}$; pearlite: $\dfrac{6.67 - C_0}{6.67 - 0.76}$ | $\alpha$: $\dfrac{6.67 - C_0}{6.648}$; Fe$_3$C: $\dfrac{C_0 - 0.022}{6.648}$ |

- **Every pearlite**, in any steel, is $88.9$ % ferrite and $11.1$ % cementite: it is a fixed mixture.
- Above 727 $^\circ$C (between $A_3$ and $A_1$) the two phases are $\alpha$ and $\gamma$: use the tie line from $0.022$ (or $0.02$) to the $A_3$ composition at that temperature.
- Ferrite of the pearlite: $W_{\alpha,\text{pearlite}} = W_{\text{pearlite}} \times 0.889$.
- Check, 0.3 % C steel: primary $\alpha = 0.623$, pearlite $= 0.377$, total $\alpha = 0.958$, Fe$_3$C $= 0.042$.
- Check, 1.2 % C steel: primary Fe$_3$C $= 0.074$, pearlite $= 0.926$, total Fe$_3$C $= 0.177$.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
Use the eutectic tie lines: $\gamma\,(2.14)$ to $L\,(4.30)$ for hypoeutectic and $L\,(4.30)$ to Fe$_3$C $(6.67)$ for hypereutectic alloys, at $1147\,^\circ$C $+\ \Delta T$.
- **Hypoeutectic ($2.14 < C_0 < 4.30$), just above 1147 $^\circ$C:** $W_{\gamma,p} = \dfrac{4.30 - C_0}{4.30 - 2.14}$, $W_L = \dfrac{C_0 - 2.14}{4.30 - 2.14}$.
- **Hypereutectic ($4.30 < C_0 < 6.67$), just above 1147 $^\circ$C:** $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},p} = \dfrac{C_0 - 4.30}{6.67 - 4.30}$, $W_L = \dfrac{6.67 - C_0}{6.67 - 4.30}$.
- **Just below 1147 $^\circ$C (phases):** $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = \dfrac{C_0 - 2.14}{6.67 - 2.14}$, $W_\gamma = \dfrac{6.67 - C_0}{6.67 - 2.14}$.
- **Ledeburite** (eutectic) is $52.3$ % austenite and $47.7$ % cementite; below 727 $^\circ$C its austenite becomes pearlite.
- Between 1147 and 727 $^\circ$C the austenite loses carbon along $A_{cm}$ and secondary cementite forms: use the tie line from $\gamma$ on $A_{cm}$ to $6.67$ (Problem T4-FC09: $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}(800) = \dfrac{3.0 - 1.0}{6.67 - 1.0}$).
- To find $C_0$ from a measured fraction, invert the lever rule (cards above): Problems T4-FC05 to FC07.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
With fast cooling the solid has no time to equalise: the **average** composition of the solid follows a **non-equilibrium solidus** to the right of the equilibrium one, so liquid is left below the equilibrium end of solidification [Session 7 Slides 23-24].
- The lever rule is the same, with the end of the tie line on the non-equilibrium solidus: Cu-35 Ni with $C_L = 24$ and average solid $38$ gives $W_L = \dfrac{38 - 35}{38 - 24} = 0.214$.
- **Homogenisation heat treatment:** hold below the solidus so solid-state diffusion (Unit 3) removes the composition gradient.
- Increasing the cooling rate in steels moves the eutectoid to lower T and lower %C: less primary ferrite and finer pearlite (harder) [Session 9 Slide 21].

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
- Corners are the pure components $A$, $B$, $C$; sides are binary alloys; the three percentages of a point add to $100$ %.
- **Reading a point:** the line of constant $\%A$ is parallel to the side opposite to $A$ (the side $B$-$C$), and so on for $B$ and $C$. Draw the three parallels, read each percentage on its own axis and check $\sum = 100$ [Session 10 Slide 5].
- Isotherms (horizontal sections), liquidus projections and solidus surfaces show the system (Ag-Cu-Zn, Fe-Cr-Ni at 650 $^\circ$C); phases of a point are the field where it falls (Slides 6-8).
- Example: $60$ % Cr, $20$ % Fe, $20$ % Ni lies in $\alpha + \gamma$; $74$ % Fe + $18$ % Cr + $8$ % Ni is a commercial stainless steel.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
- Al$_2$O$_3$-Cr$_2$O$_3$ has complete solid solubility: it is an isomorphous diagram and the lever rule is the same [Session 10 Slide 2].
- Al$_2$O$_3$-SiO$_2$ has the compound mullite $3\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\cdot2\text{SiO}_2$ (about $72$ wt% Al$_2$O$_3$), with the eutectic $L\,(7.7) \rightarrow \text{mullite} + \text{SiO}_2$ and the peritectic $L\,(77) + \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{mullite}$. Example: at $7.7$ % Al$_2$O$_3$, $W_{\text{mullite}} = \dfrac{7.7 - 0}{72 - 0} = 0.107$ [Session 10 Slides 3-4].
- Extension: the wt% of a compound $A_xB_y$ is $\dfrac{y\,M_B}{x\,M_A + y\,M_B}$ (mullite: $\dfrac{3 \times 101.96}{3\times101.96 + 2\times60.08} = 71.8$ %).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
- Using the arm **next to** the phase instead of the opposite one: the fraction of the phase closer to $C_0$ is the **larger**.
- Applying the whole $\alpha$-$\beta$ tie line to microconstituents (and the short one to phases): always ask first "phases or microconstituents?".
- Forgetting that pearlite is **two** phases (88.9 % $\alpha$ + 11.1 % Fe$_3$C) when counting total ferrite or cementite.
- Reading the tie line at the wrong temperature: it is horizontal and must be at the temperature asked, just above or just below an invariant line.
- Reading compositions in at% as wt% (check the axis label).
- Taking the primary phase of a hypereutectic alloy to be $\alpha$ (it is $\beta$) or of a hypereutectoid steel to be ferrite (it is cementite).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
$$\sigma_n = \frac{F}{A_0} \qquad \varepsilon_n = \frac{l - l_0}{l_0} = \frac{\Delta l}{l_0} \qquad A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4}$$
- $F$ is the load, $A_0$ the original cross-section, $l_0$ the original gauge length [Session 11 Slide 9]. Stress in MPa ($\text{N/mm}^2$) and strain with no units (never in % inside a formula).
- Shear: $\tau = F/A_0$, $\gamma = a/h = \tan\theta$, $\tau = G\gamma$ [Session 11 Slide 7].
- Three-point bend (modulus of rupture): $\text{MOR} = \dfrac{3FL}{2bh^2}$ [Session 11 Slide 6].

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Theorem: Hooke's law and elastic deformation
chunks.x:
$$\sigma = E\,\varepsilon \qquad \Delta l = \varepsilon\,l_0 = \frac{F\,l_0}{A_0\,E} \qquad l_0 = \frac{\Delta l\,A_0\,E}{F}$$
- $E$ is the slope of the straight part of the curve; it measures stiffness, depends on the bond strength, and $E_{\text{ceramics}} > E_{\text{metals}} > E_{\text{polymers}}$ [Session 11 Slides 12-13].
- Typical $E$: steel $207$ to $210$ GPa, aluminium $69$ to $70$ GPa, alumina $390$, silica $69$ [Session 11 Slides 13, 17]. Specific modulus: $E/\rho$.
- **Valid only in the elastic zone:** beyond the elastic limit read the table or the curve (Problems T5-01 item i, T5-07).
- **Largest elastic length:** from $\Delta l = F l_0/(A_0E)$ solved for $l_0$ with the largest elastic load (Problem T5-06).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Theorem: Poisson's ratio and the shear modulus
chunks.x:
$$
u = - rac{\varepsilon_{	ext{transverse}}}{\varepsilon_{	ext{longitudinal}}} \qquad \varepsilon_{	ext{transverse}} =  rac{\Delta d}{d_0} \qquad E = 2G\,(1 + 
u)$$
- Uniaxial tension: the width shrinks, $\Delta d = -
u\,\varepsilon_{ax}\,d_0 < 0$ [Session 11 Slide 19].
- Typical $
u$: metals $0.25$ to $0.4$, polymers $0.3$ to $0.45$, rubber $0.49$; the ideal incompressible limit is $
u = 0.5$.
- From a measured diameter change: $\varepsilon_{ax} = -\dfrac{\Delta d/d_0}{
u}$, then $\Delta l = \varepsilon_{ax}\,l_0$ and $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_{ax}$ (Problem T5-07).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Algorithm: Yield strength by the 0.2 percent offset
chunks.x:
1. Draw the elastic line $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ and its parallel through $\varepsilon = 0.002$: **offset line** $\sigma_{off}(\varepsilon) = E\,(\varepsilon - 0.002)$.
2. The yield strength $\sigma_y$ is the stress where the curve crosses the offset line [Session 11 Slide 28].
3. With a table: compute $g = \sigma_n - E(\varepsilon_n - 0.002)$ for each row; the crossing is on the segment where $g$ changes sign.
4. On that segment (rows $a$ and $b$), the curve is the line $\sigma = \sigma_a + m\,(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_a)$ with $m = \dfrac{\sigma_b - \sigma_a}{\varepsilon_b - \varepsilon_a}$. Equate it to the offset line and solve:
$$\varepsilon^* = \frac{\sigma_a - m\,\varepsilon_a + 0.002\,E}{E - m} \qquad \sigma_y = E\,(\varepsilon^* - 0.002)$$
5. Load and elongation at yield: $F_y = \sigma_y A_0$, $\Delta l_y = \varepsilon^* l_0$ (note: $\varepsilon^*$, the **total** strain, not $\varepsilon^* - 0.002$).
6. **Discontinuous yield** (low-carbon steels): $\sigma_y = \dfrac{\sigma_{max} + \sigma_{min}}{2}$ of the upper and lower yield points [Session 11 Slide 28].

Example (Problem T5-01, rows 7 and 8, $E = 196\,160$ MPa): $m = 29\,749$ MPa, $\varepsilon^* = 0.005786$, $\sigma_y = 742.6$ MPa.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
In short: put the straight segment of the table and the offset line equal and solve for the strain at the crossing.

| Step | Why |
| --- | --- |
| $\sigma_{off}(\varepsilon) = E\,(\varepsilon - 0.002)$ | line parallel to the elastic one, shifted by the plastic strain $0.002$ |
| $\sigma(\varepsilon) = \sigma_a + m\,(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_a)$ | between table rows the curve is taken as a straight segment (linear interpolation) |
| $\sigma_a + m(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_a) = E\,(\varepsilon - 0.002)$ | the yield point is on both lines |
| $\sigma_a - m\,\varepsilon_a + 0.002\,E = (E - m)\,\varepsilon$ | collect the terms in $\varepsilon$ |
| $\varepsilon^* = \dfrac{\sigma_a - m\,\varepsilon_a + 0.002\,E}{E - m}$ | solve; $E - m > 0$ because the segment is flatter than the elastic line |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Theorem: Strength, ductility, toughness and resilience
chunks.x:
$$\sigma_{UTS} = \frac{F_{max}}{A_0} \qquad EL\,(\%) = \frac{l_f - l_0}{l_0}\times100 \qquad RA\,(\%) = \frac{A_0 - A_f}{A_0}\times100$$
$$U_r = \int_0^{\varepsilon_y}\sigma\,d\varepsilon = \frac12\,\sigma_y\,\varepsilon_y = \frac{\sigma_y^2}{2E} \qquad \sigma_w = \frac{\sigma_y}{N} \qquad N_{eff} = \frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_{service}}$$
- **UTS:** maximum nominal stress; with constant $A_0$ it is at the maximum load. Necking follows [Session 11 Slide 30].
- **Elongation after fracture** is measured on the broken pieces: the elastic part is recovered. If the last record before fracture is $(\varepsilon_f,\ \sigma_f)$, then $\varepsilon_p = \varepsilon_f - \sigma_f/E$ and $EL = \varepsilon_p \times 100$ [Session 11 Slide 32].
- **Reduction in area** needs the final area: $A_f = \pi d_f^2/4$; in general $EL\,(\%) \neq RA\,(\%)$ [Session 11 Slide 33].
- **Toughness:** area under the whole curve (energy per volume, MPa $=$ MJ/m$^3$) [Session 11 Slide 34]. By trapezoids over a table: $U_t \approx \sum \tfrac12(\sigma_i + \sigma_{i+1})(\varepsilon_{i+1} - \varepsilon_i)$.
- **Resilience:** area under the elastic line up to $\sigma_y$; high $\sigma_y$ and low $E$ means high resilience (springs) [Session 11 Slide 35].
- **Working stress:** $N$ is between $1.2$ and $4$, usually $2$ when the statement gives none [Session 11 Slide 29]. A cable is safe if $N_{eff} \ge N$ (Problem T5-07).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Theorem: True stress and true strain
chunks.x:
$$\sigma_r = \frac{F}{A_i} = \sigma_n\,\frac{A_0}{A_i} \qquad \varepsilon_r = \int_{l_0}^{l}\frac{dl}{l} = \ln\frac{l}{l_0}$$
- **Before necking** (constant volume, $l_0A_0 = lA_i$): $\sigma_r = \sigma_n\,(1 + \varepsilon_n)$ and $\varepsilon_r = \ln(1 + \varepsilon_n)$ [Session 11 Slide 37].
- **After necking:** use the area, $\sigma_r = F/A_i$ and $\varepsilon_r = \ln\dfrac{A_0}{A_i} = 2\ln\dfrac{d_0}{d_i}$ [Session 11 Slide 38].
- True stress is larger than engineering stress, true strain is smaller than engineering strain, $\sigma_r > \sigma_n$ and $\varepsilon_r < \varepsilon_n$ (for tension).
- **From the reduction in area** (Problem T5-12): $\dfrac{A_f}{A_0} = 1 - \dfrac{RA}{100}$, then $\sigma_{f,r} = \dfrac{\sigma_f}{A_f/A_0}$ and $\varepsilon_r = \ln\dfrac{A_0}{A_f}$.
- The corrected curve after necking accounts for the triaxial stress in the neck.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Algorithm: Analysis of a tensile test from a load-elongation table
chunks.x:
1. **Area:** $A_0 = \pi d_0^2/4$ (mm$^2$). **Rows:** $\sigma_n = F/A_0$ (MPa) and $\varepsilon_n = \Delta L/l_0$ for every point; check the unit of the load column ("N/100" means hundreds of newtons).
2. **Young's modulus:** points that lie on the straight start, $E = \sum\sigma_i\varepsilon_i\big/\sum\varepsilon_i^2$ (least squares through the origin), or the secant $\sigma/\varepsilon$ of one early point.
3. **Yield strength:** offset construction above (algebraic on the sign-change segment).
4. **UTS:** $F_{max}/A_0$ with the largest load of the table.
5. **Ductility:** $\varepsilon_p = \varepsilon_f - \sigma_f/E$ (last row before fracture), $EL = \varepsilon_p\times100$.
6. **Resilience:** $U_r = \sigma_y^2/2E$.
7. **Load or elongation at yield:** $F_y = \sigma_y A_0$, $\Delta l_y = \varepsilon^* l_0$.
8. **Working stress:** $\sigma_w = \sigma_y/N$, $N = 2$ if no value is given.
9. **Load at a given elongation:** if $\Delta l$ is inside the elastic zone use Hooke; otherwise interpolate linearly between the two rows of the table (the interpolation card).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
All mechanisms work by **blocking the motion of dislocations**; the price is ductility and, in metals, conductivity [Session 12 Slides 4-14].

| Mechanism | What blocks the dislocations | Quantity | Effect on $\sigma_y$ and UTS | Effect on ductility and conductivity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Strain hardening (cold work) | tangles of new dislocations, $10^6$ to $10^{12}\ \text{m/m}^3$ | $\%\text{CW} = \dfrac{A_0 - A_d}{A_0}\times100$ | up | ductility down, conductivity down a little |
| Solid solution | strained lattice around solute atoms (smaller solute: tension; larger: compression) | solute content | up | ductility down, conductivity down a lot |
| Grain size reduction | grain boundaries (smaller $d$, more barriers) | $\sigma_y$ linear in $d^{-1/2}$ | up | ductility generally kept |
| Precipitation (age hardening) | dispersed particles of a second phase | smaller, denser, better dispersed | up (Al-Cu-Mg: UTS $469$ MPa against $45$ pure Al) | conductivity down |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
- Extension: the Hall-Petch relation $\sigma_y = \sigma_0 + k_y\,d^{-1/2}$ is the straight line of the slide ($\sigma_0$ and $k_y$ are constants of the material, not given in the slides).
- Extension: for a wire drawn from diameter $d_0$ to $d_d$, $\%\text{CW} = \bigl[1 - (d_d/d_0)^2\bigr]\times100$.
- Cold work produces texture; a recrystallisation anneal restores ductility (Unit 4 diagrams give the temperatures).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
Hardness is the resistance to a localised plastic indentation [Session 12 Slides 15-30].

| Test | Indenter | Formula | Units and notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Brinell HB (HBW) | ball of diameter $D$ (WC or steel) | $HB = \dfrac{2P}{\pi D\left(D - \sqrt{D^2 - D_i^2}\right)}$ | $P$ in kgf, $D$ and $D_i$ in mm, result in kgf/mm$^2$ |
| Brinell load | | $P = Q\,D^2$ | $Q = 30$ steels, $10$ bronze and brass, $5$ Al alloys, $2.5$ anti-friction alloys |
| Vickers HV | diamond pyramid, $136^\circ$ | $HV = \dfrac{2F\sin(136^\circ/2)}{d^2} = 1.854\,\dfrac{F}{d^2}$ | $F$ in kgf, $d$ the mean of the two diagonals in mm |
| Knoop KHN | diamond pyramid, $l/b = 7.11$ | $KHN = 14.2\,\dfrac{P}{l^2}$ | microhardness, load up to 1 kgf |
| Rockwell HR | diamond cone $120^\circ$ or steel ball | $HR = N - \dfrac{h}{S}$ | $h$ residual depth in mm; $S = 0.002$ mm; $N = 100$ for A, C, D; $N = 130$ for B, E, F, G, K; superficial $N$ and $T$ scales $S = 0.001$, $N = 100$ |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
- **Brinell inverse** (indentation diameter for a given $HB$): $k = D - \sqrt{D^2 - D_i^2} = \dfrac{2P}{\pi D\,HB}$, then $D_i^2 = k\,(2D - k)$ (Problem T5-15).
- **Rockwell in depth units:** $HRC = 100 - 500\,t$ and $HRB = 130 - 500\,t$ with $t$ in mm [Session 12 Slide 29].
- **Precautions:** distance to the edge above $4\varnothing$; thickness above $2\varnothing$ (Brinell, Rockwell) or $1.5$ times the diagonal (Vickers).
- **Hardness and strength** both measure plastic deformation, with a different line per material family (chart of Session 12 Slide 30). Extension, for steels only: $\sigma_{UTS}\,[\text{MPa}] \approx 3.45\,HB$.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Pattern: Thermal stress in a constrained bar (link with Unit 7)
chunks.x: Held at constant length, a bar heated by $\Delta T = T_f - T_0$ develops $\sigma = -E\alpha\,\Delta T$ (compression when heated, tension when cooled). If a load $F$ already acts, the wire stays stretched when $E\alpha\Delta T = F/A$, so $A = \dfrac{F}{E\,\alpha\,\Delta T}$ and $d = \sqrt{4A/\pi}$ (Problem T5-05: $d = 5.87$ mm). The full derivation is in Unit 7.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
- Taking the yield strength at the first row below the offset line instead of intersecting with it.
- Using $\varepsilon^* - 0.002$ as the strain at yield: the total strain is $\varepsilon^*$ (elastic plus the $0.002$ offset).
- Measuring ductility at the last point of the table without removing the elastic part $\sigma_f/E$.
- Using engineering values for fracture after necking, or $\ln(1+\varepsilon)$ after necking (it only holds before).
- Using the nominal diameter instead of the instantaneous one for true stress.
- Putting the load in kgf into formulas that need newtons (or the reverse): Brinell and Vickers use kgf.
- Dividing by $A_0$ in mm$^2$ and then treating the result as Pa: it is MPa.
- Confusing resilience (elastic area, $\sigma_y^2/2E$) with toughness (whole area).
- A statement that says "aluminium" with steel-like data: use the data of the statement and state the discrepancy.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Theorem: Ohm's law, conductivity and mobility
chunks.x:
$$V = I\,R \qquad R = \frac{\rho\,l}{A} \qquad \rho = \frac{1}{\sigma} \qquad J = \sigma E \qquad v_d = \mu\,E$$
$$\mu = \frac{\tau\,\lvert q_e\rvert}{m_e} \qquad \sigma = n\,\lvert q_e\rvert\,\mu$$
- $\sigma$ in $(\Omega\cdot\text{m})^{-1}$, $\rho$ in $\Omega\cdot\text{m}$, $\mu$ in m$^2$/(V$\cdot$s), $n$ in m$^{-3}$, $E$ in V/m [Session 13 Slides 10-13].
- Classes by conductivity: insulators $10^{-20}$ to $10^{-10}$, semiconductors $10^{-6}$ to $10^{4}$, conductors about $10^{7}$ $(\Omega\cdot\text{m})^{-1}$.
- Band gap: semiconductors $E_g < 2$ eV (Si $1.1$, Ge $0.67$), insulators $E_g > 2$ eV (diamond $6$ to $7$ eV). Conductors have a half-filled band or overlapping bands.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Derivation: Conductivity from the drift velocity
chunks.x:
In short: the charge crossing a unit area per second is $J = n\lvert q_e\rvert v_d$, and since $v_d = \mu E$ and $J = \sigma E$, the conductivity is $\sigma = n\lvert q_e\rvert\mu$.

| Step | Why |
| --- | --- |
| $a = \dfrac{q_eE}{m_e}$ | Newton's second law for one electron in the field $E$ |
| $v_d = \dfrac{\tau\lvert q_e\rvert E}{m_e} = \mu E$ | collisions with the ions (relaxation time $\tau$) stop the acceleration: constant drift velocity |
| $J = n\lvert q_e\rvert v_d = n\lvert q_e\rvert\mu E$ | charge per unit volume times velocity |
| $J = \sigma E \Rightarrow \sigma = n\lvert q_e\rvert\mu$ | microscopic form of Ohm's law |
| $E = V/l$ and $J = I/A \Rightarrow R = \rho\,l/A$ | link with the macroscopic Ohm's law (derived here) |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Theorem: Resistivity of metals, Matthiessen's rule
chunks.x:
$$\rho_{total} = \rho_T + \rho_r \qquad \rho_r = \rho_i + \rho_d \qquad \rho_T = \rho_0\,(1 + \alpha_T\,\Delta T)$$
- $\rho_T$ comes from the lattice vibrations and grows linearly with $T$; $\rho_r$ is the residual part from impurities ($\rho_i$) and deformation defects ($\rho_d$) and does **not** depend on temperature [Session 13 Slides 14-16].
- $\rho_0$ is the resistivity **at 0 $^\circ$C** and $\Delta T$ is the temperature in $^\circ$C.
- **Solve for a temperature:** $T = \dfrac{\rho_T - \rho_0}{\rho_0\,\alpha_T}$; two metals with the same resistivity: $\rho_{0,1}(1 + \alpha_1T_1) = \rho_{0,2}(1 + \alpha_2T_2)$.
- Example (Problem T6-01): $\rho_{Al,45} = 2.7\times10^{-6}(1 + 0.0039\times45) = 3.173\times10^{-6}\ \Omega\cdot\text{cm}$ and $T_{Ag} = (3.173 - 1.47)/(1.47\times0.0038) = 304.9\,^\circ$C with the rounded $3.173$ (the key gives $305\,^\circ$C).

| Metal | $\rho_0$ ($\mu\Omega\cdot\text{cm}$) | $\alpha_T$ ($^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Aluminium | 2.7 | 0.0039 |
| Copper | 1.6 | 0.0039 |
| Gold | 2.3 | 0.0034 |
| Iron | 9 | 0.0045 |
| Silver | 1.47 | 0.0038 |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Pattern: Effect of temperature, alloying and hardening on metals
chunks.x:
- Heating: $\rho$ rises (more phonon scattering); cooling: $\rho$ falls toward the constant $\rho_r$.
- Impurities, vacancies, dislocations and grain boundaries raise $\rho_r$ and lower $\sigma$.
- **Every strengthening method lowers conductivity** (the obstacles to dislocations also scatter electrons): cold work lowers it only slightly, solid solution (Zn in Cu) lowers it sharply, precipitates and fine grains in between [Session 13 Slides 18-19].
- Lightest wire with the same strength and conductivity: choose the method that raises the strength most per loss of conductivity (cold work or precipitates, not solid solution).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
$$\sigma = n_e\lvert q_e\rvert\mu_e + n_H\lvert q_e\rvert\mu_H = n_i\lvert q_e\rvert(\mu_e + \mu_H) \qquad n_i = \frac{\sigma}{\lvert q_e\rvert(\mu_e + \mu_H)}$$
$$\sigma = \sigma_0\exp\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT}\right) \qquad \ln\sigma = \ln\sigma_0 - \frac{E_g}{2k}\cdot\frac1T$$
- Electrons and holes come in pairs ($n_e = n_H = n_i$) and $\mu_e > \mu_H$; both $n_i$ and $\sigma$ **rise** with $T$ (the mobility loss is masked) [Session 13 Slides 27-29].
- **Ratio between two temperatures** ($\sigma_0$ cancels): $\sigma_2 = \sigma_1\exp\left[\dfrac{E_g}{2k}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)\right]$.
- **Band gap from two measurements:** $E_g = 2k\,\dfrac{\ln(\sigma_2/\sigma_1)}{1/T_1 - 1/T_2}$; on a plot of $\ln\sigma$ against $1/T$ the slope is $-E_g/2k$.
- $k = 8.62\times10^{-5}$ eV/K with $E_g$ in eV: the eV cancels. $T$ in kelvin.
- Example (Problem T6-07, Ge, $E_g = 0.67$ eV, $\sigma_{25} = 2.22$): $\sigma_{75} = 2.22\,e^{1.872} = 14.4\ (\Omega\cdot\text{m})^{-1}$.
- Example (Problem T6-08, Si, $\sigma = 4\times10^{-4}$, $\mu_e = 0.14$, $\mu_H = 0.048$): $n_i = 1.33\times10^{16}\ \text{m}^{-3}$.

| Property | Si | Ge |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| $E_g$ (eV) | 1.1 | 0.67 |
| $\mu_e$ (m$^2$/(V$\cdot$s)) | 0.135 | 0.39 |
| $\mu_H$ (m$^2$/(V$\cdot$s)) | 0.048 | 0.19 |
| $n_i$ (m$^{-3}$) | $1.5\times10^{16}$ | $2.4\times10^{19}$ |
| $\rho$ ($\Omega\cdot$m) | 2300 | 0.46 |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x: The slides print slightly different mobilities in two places (Si $0.14$ and $0.05$; Ge $0.38$ and $0.18$ on Slide 33): use the values given in the statement.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Pattern: Extrinsic semiconductors, n-type and p-type
chunks.x:
| | n-type | p-type |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Dopant | more valence electrons than the host: P, As, Sb (group VA) in Si and Ge | fewer valence electrons: B, Al, Ga, In (group IIIA) |
| Role | donor, level $E_d$ just under the conduction band | acceptor, level $E_a$ just above the valence band |
| Majority carriers | electrons, $\sigma \approx n_e\lvert q_e\rvert\mu_e$ | holes, $\sigma \cong p\lvert q_e\rvert\mu_H$ |
| Ionisation energy | $E_c - E_d$ | $E_a - E_v$ |
| Extrinsic range | $\sigma = \sigma_0\exp\left(-\dfrac{E_c - E_d}{2kT}\right)$ | $\sigma = \sigma_0\exp\left(-\dfrac{E_a - E_v}{2kT}\right)$ |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Pattern: Extrinsic semiconductors, n-type and p-type
chunks.x:
- Type: compare the group of the dopant with the group of the host ($Z_{\text{P}} - Z_{\text{Si}} = 5 - 4 = +1$ means donor, n-type).
- Doping distortion is negligible, so $\sigma$ is controlled by the **number of carriers**, and the majority carrier dominates: $\sigma \approx n_e\lvert q_e\rvert\mu_e$ (Problem T6-06: $n_e = 10^{23}\ \text{m}^{-3}$, $\mu_e = 0.14$ gives $\sigma = 2243\ (\Omega\cdot\text{m})^{-1}$).
- **Dopant concentration:** ppm times atoms per m$^3$ of host; for a host of density $\rho$ and atomic mass $M$, atoms per m$^3$ $= \rho N_A/M$ (extension).
- **Comparing dopants:** the smaller $E_d$ or $E_a$, the more carriers at a given $T$; concentrations are limited by the maximum solubility of the dopant.
- Low $T$ (extrinsic range): carriers come from ionised dopants. High $T$: the intrinsic law takes over.

| Dopant | Si $E_d$ (eV) | Si $E_a$ (eV) | Ge $E_d$ (eV) | Ge $E_a$ (eV) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| P | 0.045 | | 0.0120 | |
| As | 0.049 | | 0.0127 | |
| Sb | 0.039 | | 0.0096 | |
| B | | 0.045 | | 0.0104 |
| Al | | 0.057 | | 0.0102 |
| Ga | | 0.065 | | 0.0108 |
| In | | 0.160 | | 0.0112 |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
1. Decide intrinsic or extrinsic (pure material or doped).
2. **Intrinsic:** smaller $E_g$ gives larger $\sigma$ at the same $T$: InSb ($0.17$) > Ge ($0.67$) > Si ($1.11$) > GaAs ($1.42$) > AlP; $E_g$ grows and $\sigma$ falls as the bonding goes from covalent (group IV) to the III-V and II-VI compounds.
3. **Extrinsic:** compare $E_d$ or $E_a$ (smaller is better) and the dopant concentration (more carriers, higher $\sigma$), within the solubility limit.
4. State the temperature range: the criterion holds in the extrinsic range; at high $T$ the intrinsic law dominates.
5. With numbers: $\sigma = n\lvert q_e\rvert\mu$ for each case and compare.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
$$p = q\,d \qquad C = \varepsilon_r\,\varepsilon_0\,\frac{A}{d} = \varepsilon_r\,C_0 \qquad E_{break} = \frac{U_{break}}{d}$$
- A **dielectric** is an insulator ($E_g$ large) that polarises under a field, aligning its dipoles; it raises the capacitance by $\varepsilon_r$ [Session 13 Slides 51-52].
- An **insulator** should have: high $\rho$, high dielectric strength $E_{break}$, small loss factor $\tan\delta$ and low permittivity [Session 13 Slide 54].
- The **loss factor** is the energy lost as heat when the dipoles cannot follow the alternating field; it grows with moisture, temperature and frequency.
- **Ferroelectric** materials have spontaneous polarisation, a hysteresis loop and a Curie temperature; **piezoelectric** materials convert strain into voltage and the reverse [Session 13 Slides 55-60].
- Units: $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m, $C$ in F, $E_{break}$ in V/m (or kV/mm).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
- Using $\rho_0$ of the table with a temperature in kelvin: the table is at 0 $^\circ$C and $\Delta T$ is in $^\circ$C.
- Mixing $\mu\Omega\cdot$cm and $\Omega\cdot$m ($10^{-8}$) or conductivity against resistivity.
- Putting $T$ in $^\circ$C in $\exp(-E_g/2kT)$; forgetting the factor $2$ in the exponent.
- Using $E_g$ in joules with $k$ in eV/K (or the reverse): keep both in eV.
- Adding the hole term in an extrinsic semiconductor (negligible) or forgetting it in an intrinsic one.
- Calling a group IIIA dopant a donor (it is an acceptor) or a group VA dopant an acceptor.
- Believing that heating always lowers $\sigma$: it does for a metal ($\mu$ falls) and raises it for a semiconductor ($n$ rises).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Theorem: Magnetic field, induction and permeability
chunks.x:
$$B = \mu H \qquad B = \mu_0 H \ (\text{vacuum}) \qquad \mu_r = \frac{\mu}{\mu_0} \qquad B = \mu_0 H + \mu_0 M \qquad M = \chi_m H \qquad \mu_r = 1 + \chi_m$$
- $\mu_0 = 1.257\times10^{-6}$ H/m. The magnetic moment of an electron is measured in the Bohr magneton, $\mu_B = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2$ [Session 15 Slides 3-4].
- Moments of the transition metals in $\mu_B$: Sc 1, Ti 2, V 3, Cr 5, Mn 5, Fe 4, Co 3, Ni 2, Cu 0 (unpaired $3d$ electrons); metallic Fe $2.22$, Co $1.72$, Ni $0.60$, Gd $7.12$.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
| Type | Dipoles | $\mu_r$ and $\chi_m$ | Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Diamagnetic | induced, opposite to $H$, not permanent | $\mu_r < 1$, $\chi_m < 0$ (about $-10^{-5}$) | Au, Ag, Cu, Si, Zn, Al$_2$O$_3$ |
| Paramagnetic | permanent, random, aligned by $H$ | $\mu_r > 1$, $10^{-5} \le \chi_m < 10^{-2}$ | Al, Ti, Cr, Mo, Na, Zr |
| Ferromagnetic | permanent, parallel without a field | $\mu_r \gg 1$, $\chi_m$ up to $10^6$, $B \cong \mu_0 M$ | Fe, Co, Ni, Gd |
| Antiferromagnetic | permanent, antiparallel and equal | no net moment | Cr, Mn, MnO |
| Ferrimagnetic | permanent, antiparallel and unequal | $\mu_r \gg 1$, $\chi_m$ about $10^5$ to $10^6$ | ferrites, garnets, Fe$_3$O$_4$ |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Pattern: Domains, magnetisation curve and hysteresis
chunks.x:
- Domains are regions of aligned dipoles ($10$ to $100\ \mu$m) separated by **Bloch walls** (about $100$ nm). Magnetising means growth of favourable domains, then rotation, then saturation $M_s$ [Session 15 Slides 14-16].
- $\mu_i$ is the initial slope and $\mu_{max}$ the largest $B/H$ (tangent from the origin).
- **Hysteresis loop:** $B_r$ remanence (the induction left at $H = 0$), $H_c$ coercivity (the reverse field that brings $B$ to zero), $B_s$ saturation. The loop area is the energy lost per cycle [Session 15 Slide 17].
- Limit between soft and hard: $H_c = 10\,000$ A/m [Session 15 Slide 18].

| | Soft | Hard |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Bloch walls | easy to move | hard to move |
| Loop | narrow, high initial $\mu$, low $H_c$ | wide, high $B_r$, $B_s$ and $H_c$, low $\mu_i$ |
| Use | transformers, motors, alternating fields (low losses) | permanent magnets |

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Pattern: Domains, magnetisation curve and hysteresis
chunks.x:
- **Larger grains:** walls move more easily, so $\mu$ rises and $H_c$, $B_r$ fall. **More inclusions, dislocations, pores:** walls are pinned, so $\mu$ falls and $H_c$, $B_r$ rise [Session 15 Slide 21].
- **Temperature:** the loop shrinks ($M_s$, $B_r$, $H_c$ fall); above the **Curie temperature** $T_c$ a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic (Fe $1043$ K, Co $1404$, Ni $631$, Gd $289$); antiferromagnets have a Néel temperature (MnO $116$ K, Cr $310$, NiO $523$) [Session 15 Slides 22-24].
- **Superconductors:** zero resistivity below the critical temperature $T_c$, expulsion of the field (Meissner effect), limited by a critical field $H_c$ and a critical current density $J_c$ that fall as $T$ rises; Type I and Type II [Session 15 Slides 25-32].

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Theorem: Heat capacity and thermal expansion
chunks.x:
$$C = \frac{dQ}{dT} \qquad c_p = \frac{C}{\text{atomic weight}} \qquad C \approx 3R \ (T > \theta_D) \qquad \frac{\Delta l}{l_0} = \alpha\,\Delta T \quad \Delta T = T_f - T_0$$
- $C$ is per mole, J/(mol$\cdot$K); above the Debye temperature $\theta_D$ it is constant, $3R = 24.9$ J/(mol$\cdot$K) $\approx 6$ cal/(mol$\cdot$K) [Session 15 Slides 34-35]. Heat to warm a mass: $Q = m\,c_p\,\Delta T$ (extension).
- $\alpha$ in $^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$ or K$^{-1}$; typical $10^{-6}$: Al $23.6$, Cu $17.0$, steel about $12$; Invar $1.6$ [Session 15 Slides 36-38]. High melting temperature, strong bond, low $\alpha$.
- Final length $l_f = l_0\,(1 + \alpha\,\Delta T)$; extension: volume $\Delta V/V_0 \approx 3\alpha\Delta T$ for an isotropic solid.
- A **bimetal** bends toward the metal with the smaller $\alpha$ when heated [Session 15 Slide 39].

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
$$q = \frac{Q}{A} = -k\,\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x} \qquad k = k_e + k_{ph} \qquad L = \frac{k}{\sigma\,T} = 2.44\times10^{-8}\ \frac{\text{W}\cdot\Omega}{\text{K}^2} \qquad k_e = L\,\sigma\,T$$
- $q$ in W/m$^2$, $k$ in W/(m$\cdot$K); heat flows from hot to cold (minus sign). Same structure as Fick's first law [Session 15 Slide 40].
- Metals: $k \approx k_e$ (free electrons). Insulators and ceramics: $k \approx k_{ph}$ (phonons).
- Alloying, defects and porosity **lower** $k$ (they scatter electrons and phonons) [Session 15 Slide 43].
- Use: good electrical conductors are good thermal conductors; $k_e = L\sigma T$ links Unit 6 and Unit 7 (with $T$ in kelvin).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Derivation: Thermal stress in a constrained body
chunks.x:
In short: a body that cannot expand has zero total strain, so the elastic strain cancels the free thermal strain and the stress is $E\alpha(T_0 - T_f)$.

| Step | Why |
| --- | --- |
| $\varepsilon_{total} = \dfrac{\sigma}{E} + \alpha\,(T_f - T_0) = 0$ | elastic strain plus free thermal strain; the walls keep the length constant |
| $\sigma = -E\,\alpha\,(T_f - T_0)$ | solve for $\sigma$ |
| $\sigma = E\,\alpha\,(T_0 - T_f)$ | the form of the slides, with $\Delta T = T_0 - T_f$ [Session 15 Slide 45] |
| $T_f > T_0$ (heating): $\sigma < 0$, compression; $T_f < T_0$ (cooling): $\sigma > 0$, tension | signs of the slide |
| $[E\alpha\Delta T] = \text{MPa}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C} = \text{MPa}$ | dimensional check |

With a pre-existing load, add the stresses: $\sigma_2 = \sigma_F - E\alpha\Delta T$ for a stretched wire that is heated at constant length (Problem T5-05).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
$$TSR = \frac{\sigma_f\,k}{E\,\alpha_l}$$
- Thermal shock resistance rises with a **higher** fracture stress $\sigma_f$ and conductivity $k$, and with a **lower** modulus $E$ and expansion $\alpha_l$ [Session 15 Slides 47-48].
- Phase transformations with a dimensional change make the shock worse.
- Unit: W/m (check, extension).

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.x:
1. Name the quantity: expansion (free), stress (constrained), heat flow (gradient), magnetic response (type, loop).
2. Free expansion: $\Delta l = \alpha\,l_0\,\Delta T$. Constrained: $\sigma = E\alpha\Delta T$ and check against $\sigma_y$.
3. Heat flow: $Q = qA = kA\,\lvert\Delta T\rvert/\Delta x$.
4. Hysteresis loops: read $B_r$, $H_c$ and the area; soft or hard by $H_c$ against $10\,000$ A/m; explain the effect of grain size, impurities and porosity on the Bloch walls (Problems T7-11, T7-12).
5. Check units: kelvin differences equal $^\circ$C differences, but absolute temperatures in $\sigma = L$ formulas must be kelvin.

chunks.t: Formula Sheet - Aerospace Materials I
chunks.h: Trap: Mistakes in magnetic and thermal properties
chunks.x:
- The sign of the thermal stress: heating a constrained body gives compression, cooling gives tension.
- Using $\Delta T = T_f - T_0$ in the thermal-stress formula written as $E\alpha(T_0 - T_f)$ (double sign error).
- Mixing $\mu_r$ and $\chi_m$ ($\mu_r = 1 + \chi_m$) or $B$ and $H$ (a vacuum has $B = \mu_0H$).
- Taking a large grain size as harder to magnetise: it makes the walls move more easily (larger $\mu$, lower $H_c$).
- Using $C \approx 3R$ below the Debye temperature.
- Forgetting that alloying lowers thermal conductivity ($k$) as it lowers electrical conductivity.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 1 Metallic vs Covalent Bonding
chunks.x:
Compare and contrast metallic and covalent primary bonds in terms of (a) the nature of the bond, (b) the valence of the atoms involved, and (c) the ductility of the materials bonded in these ways.

Theory: Topic 1 - Bonding in Solids and Material Properties.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 1 Metallic vs Covalent Bonding
chunks.x:
- Both are **primary (strong) bonds**: covalent 125-300 kcal/mol, metallic 25-200 kcal/mol.
- The question asks for three comparisons: the nature of the bond, the role of valence, and ductility.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 1 Metallic vs Covalent Bonding
chunks.x:
| | Covalent | Metallic |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| How electrons are used | **Shared** between two atoms | Given up to an **electron sea** shared by all the atoms |
| Direction | **Highly directional**, no free electrons | **Non-directional** |
| Elements | Nonmetals, small electronegativity difference | Metals: cation cores + delocalized electrons |
| Valence | Outer s and p electrons shared to reach a noble-gas configuration; silicon (valence 4) must form 4 bonds | The valence electrons join the sea; more valence electrons → higher bonding energy (K +1: 89.6 kJ/mol; Ca +2: 177 kJ/mol) |
| Mechanical behaviour | Covalent solids are hard and incompressible; covalent lattices are very hard and brittle | Pure metals are much more malleable; metallic substances are ductile and workable |

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 1 Metallic vs Covalent Bonding
chunks.x:
**(a) Nature of the bond.** A covalent bond is a pair of electrons **shared between two specific atoms**, so it points in fixed directions (e.g. 109.5° in silicon). A metallic bond is the attraction between positive cores and a **sea of delocalized electrons** shared by all the atoms, so it has no direction.

**(b) Valence.** In covalent bonding the valence fixes **how many bonds** an atom must form: silicon, with valence 4, forms exactly four. In metallic bonding the valence fixes **how many electrons go to the sea**: the more valence electrons, the higher the bonding energy and the melting point (K → Ca).

**(c) Ductility.** Covalent materials are hard and brittle: their bonds have fixed directions. Metals are ductile, malleable and workable: their bonds are non-directional because the electron sea is shared by all the atoms.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 1 Metallic vs Covalent Bonding
chunks.x:
The two differences, **directional vs non-directional** and **localized vs delocalized** electrons, explain the rest: the same pair of ideas gives conduction in metals (the electron sea moves under a voltage) and its absence in covalent solids (no free electrons, non-conductive lattices).

**Back to:** Topic 1 - Bonding in Solids and Material Properties · Aerospace Materials I MOC

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 2 Potential Curves Titanium vs Aluminium
chunks.x:
Titanium is stiffer than aluminum, has a lower thermal expansion coefficient than aluminum, and has a higher melting temperature than aluminum. On the same graph, carefully and schematically draw the potential well curves for both metals and showing how the physical properties are manifested in these curves.

Theory: Topic 1 - Bonding in Solids and Material Properties.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 2 Potential Curves Titanium vs Aluminium
chunks.x:
- The statement gives three facts: Ti is **stiffer**, has a **lower thermal expansion coefficient** and a **higher melting temperature** than Al.
- The sketch is **schematic**: no numbers are asked for.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 2 Potential Curves Titanium vs Aluminium
chunks.x:
The energy curve has its minimum at the equilibrium distance $a_0$. Three features of it are linked to properties:

| Property | Feature of the curve |
| :--- | :--- |
| Melting temperature | **Depth** of the minimum (binding energy): high binding energy → high $T_m$ |
| Thermal expansion | **Width** of the trough: a deep, narrow trough (strong bonding) → low coefficient of thermal expansion |
| Stiffness (Young's modulus) | **Steepness** of the curve: a steep slope means more force is needed to stretch the bonds → higher modulus |

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 2 Potential Curves Titanium vs Aluminium
chunks.x:
Draw both curves on the same axes (energy vs distance), with their minima close to each other in distance:

- **Titanium:** a **deeper** minimum (higher melting temperature), a **narrower** trough (lower thermal expansion) and **steeper** walls around $a_0$ (stiffer).
- **Aluminium:** a **shallower** minimum, a **wider** trough and gentler walls.

How each property shows up:
1. **Melting temperature:** the Ti minimum lies lower; more energy is needed to break its bonds.
2. **Thermal expansion:** heating adds the same energy to both curves; in the narrow Ti trough the spacing between atoms grows less than in the wide Al trough.
3. **Stiffness:** around $a_0$ the Ti curve is steeper, so a larger force is needed to stretch the bonds.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 2 Potential Curves Titanium vs Aluminium
chunks.x:
All three facts point to the same thing: the bonds in titanium are **stronger** than in aluminium. One curve shape, deeper, narrower and steeper, carries the three properties at once.

**Back to:** Topic 1 - Bonding in Solids and Material Properties · Aerospace Materials I MOC

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 3 Elastic Modulus MgO vs Mg
chunks.x:
Would you expect MgO or magnesium to have the higher modulus of elasticity? Explain.

Theory: Topic 1 - Bonding in Solids and Material Properties.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 3 Elastic Modulus MgO vs Mg
chunks.x:
- **MgO** is an ionic compound: a metal (Mg) and a nonmetal (O).
- **Mg** is a pure metal: metallic bonding.
- No modulus values are needed: the answer follows from comparing the bonds.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 3 Elastic Modulus MgO vs Mg
chunks.x:
- A **high binding energy** (steep slope) means a greater force is needed to stretch the bonds, and so a **higher Young's modulus**.
- MgO has a very large lattice energy, 3932 kJ/mol, among the largest in the table, because its ions have valence +2 (valence ↑ → U ↑).
- Ionic compounds are **hard and brittle** with high melting points; MgO melts at 2800 °C and has a Mohs hardness of 6.5.
- Metals are **malleable**, ductile and workable; the metallic bond is the range of lowest energy among primary bonds (25-200 kcal/mol vs 150-370 kcal/mol for ionic).

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 3 Elastic Modulus MgO vs Mg
chunks.x: **MgO** should have the higher modulus of elasticity. Its ionic bond between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ has a very high binding (lattice) energy, so its energy curve is deep and steep and a greater force is needed to stretch the bonds. Metallic Mg has a weaker, non-directional bond to an electron sea, which gives a softer, more malleable material.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 3 Elastic Modulus MgO vs Mg
chunks.x:
The same strong ionic bonding that gives MgO its high melting point (2800 °C) and hardness also gives it its stiffness: all of them come from the deep, steep energy curve of a high-binding-energy bond.

**Back to:** Topic 1 - Bonding in Solids and Material Properties · Aerospace Materials I MOC

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 4 Elastic Modulus Aluminium vs Silicon
chunks.x:
Aluminum and silicon are side-by-side in the periodic table. Which would you expect to have the higher modulus of elasticity (E)? Explain.

Theory: Topic 1 - Bonding in Solids and Material Properties.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 4 Elastic Modulus Aluminium vs Silicon
chunks.x:
- **Aluminium** is a metal: metallic bonding.
- **Silicon** forms covalent bonds: with valence four it forms four directional covalent bonds in a tetrahedral structure (109.5°).
- Being neighbours in the periodic table, the difference comes from the **type of bond**, not from the position.
- No modulus values are needed: the answer follows from comparing the bonds.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 4 Elastic Modulus Aluminium vs Silicon
chunks.x:
- A high binding energy (steep slope) → greater force to stretch the bonds → **higher Young's modulus**.
- Covalent solids, formed by continuous covalent bonds (silicon carbide, quartz, diamond), are **hard and incompressible** with a **high $T_m$**; covalent lattices are **very hard** with **very high** melting points.
- Covalent bonds are **highly directional**.
- Metals are **malleable**, ductile and workable; metallic bonds are **non-directional**.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 4 Elastic Modulus Aluminium vs Silicon
chunks.x: **Silicon** should have the higher modulus of elasticity. It is held together by a continuous network of strong, **directional** covalent bonds, which makes it hard and incompressible: a greater force is needed to stretch the bonds, which is what a high modulus means. Aluminium is held by **non-directional** metallic bonds to an electron sea, which gives a malleable, workable material.

chunks.t: Problem - T1 Exam Question 4 Elastic Modulus Aluminium vs Silicon
chunks.x:
Two elements next to each other in the periodic table can behave very differently because they bond differently: covalent networks are very hard and brittle, metals are ductile and workable. Silicon's higher stiffness is the mechanical side of that difference.

**Back to:** Topic 1 - Bonding in Solids and Material Properties · Aerospace Materials I MOC

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
1. A composite material has an epoxy matrix reinforced with 68% in volume of unidirectional carbon fiber. The density of carbon fiber is 1.79 g/cm³ and of the epoxy resin is 1.20 g/cm³.
a) What's the percentage in weight of the carbon fibers and the epoxy resin?
b) What's the average density of the composite?
c) If the average density of the composite is 1.65 g/cm³, what's the percentage in volume of the carbon fibers inside the material?
d) Which of the two materials has a higher Elastic modulus? Calculate its value.
Data: E_FC = 400 GPa and E_epoxy = 3 GPa. Assume isostrain conditions.
*(Solution: a) 76%; b) 1.6 g/cm³; c) 76%; d) 304.7 GPa)*

"The two materials" of part d) are the two composites of the statement: the one with 68 vol% fibres (parts a and b) and the one whose density is 1.65 g/cm³ (part c).

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
1. **Two phases, no porosity.** The composite is fibre plus matrix only, so $V_f + V_m = 1$.
2. **Rule of mixtures.** A property of the composite is the volume-weighted sum of the properties of its phases, $P_{CM} = \sum_i f_i p_i$ with $\sum_i f_i = 1$ [Session 22 Slide 27]; for the density, $\rho_c = V_f\rho_f + V_m\rho_m$.
3. **Mass of a phase.** By the definition of density, the mass of each phase in a volume $V_c$ of composite is $m_i = \rho_i V_i = \rho_i f_i V_c$, so the weight fraction is $w_f = V_f\rho_f/\rho_c$.
4. **Isostrain.** Load along the continuous, aligned fibres with a perfect bond: $E_{1C} = V_f E_f + (1 - V_f)E_m$ [Session 22 Slide 22, Eq. 1].

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
| Quantity | Value |
| :--- | ---: |
| $V_f$ (parts a, b) | 0.68 |
| $\rho_f$ (carbon fibre) | 1.79 g/cm³ |
| $\rho_m$ (epoxy) | 1.20 g/cm³ |
| $\rho_c$ (part c) | 1.65 g/cm³ |
| $E_f$, $E_m$ | 400 GPa, 3 GPa |

**Unknowns:** (a) $w_f$, $w_m$; (b) $\rho_c$; (c) $V_f$ when $\rho_c = 1.65$ g/cm³; (d) which composite is stiffer and its $E_{1C}$.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
[Session 22 Slides 22, 27]:

$$\rho_c = V_f\rho_f + (1 - V_f)\rho_m \qquad w_f = \frac{V_f\rho_f}{\rho_c} \qquad E_{1C} = V_f E_f + (1 - V_f)E_m$$

**Strategy.**
1. Work with $1\ \text{cm}^3$ of composite: the mass of each phase is $\rho_i V_i$; their sum is $\rho_c$ (part b) and their ratio gives the weight fractions (part a).
2. Invert the density rule of mixtures for $V_f$ (part c).
3. Apply the isostrain rule to both composites and compare (part d).

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.h: 1. a) and b) Masses in 1 cm³ of composite [Session 22 Slide 27]
chunks.x:
In $1\ \text{cm}^3$ there are $0.68\ \text{cm}^3$ of fibre and $0.32\ \text{cm}^3$ of epoxy:

$$m_f = 0.68\ \text{cm}^3 \times 1.79\ \text{g/cm}^3 = 1.2172\ \text{g} \qquad m_m = 0.32\ \text{cm}^3 \times 1.20\ \text{g/cm}^3 = 0.3840\ \text{g}$$

Their sum is the mass of $1\ \text{cm}^3$ of composite, which is the density of part b):

$$\rho_c = 1.2172\ \text{g} + 0.3840\ \text{g} = 1.6012\ \text{g in } 1\ \text{cm}^3 \ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf{\rho_c = 1.60\ g/cm^3}$$

Weight fractions:

$$w_f = \frac{1.2172\ \text{g}}{1.6012\ \text{g}} = 0.760 \ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf{76.0\ \%\ \text{carbon fibre}} \qquad w_m = \frac{0.3840\ \text{g}}{1.6012\ \text{g}} = 0.240 \ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf{24.0\ \%\ \text{epoxy}}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.h: 2. c) Volume fraction from the density [Session 22 Slide 27]
chunks.x:
Writing $V_m = 1 - V_f$ in the density rule and solving for $V_f$:

$$\rho_c = V_f\rho_f + (1 - V_f)\rho_m = \rho_m + V_f(\rho_f - \rho_m) \ \Rightarrow\ V_f = \frac{\rho_c - \rho_m}{\rho_f - \rho_m}$$

$$V_f = \frac{1.65 - 1.20}{1.79 - 1.20} = \frac{0.45\ \text{g/cm}^3}{0.59\ \text{g/cm}^3} = 0.763 \ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf{76.3\ vol\%\ \text{carbon fibre}}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.h: 3. d) Isostrain modulus of the two composites [Session 22 Slide 22]
chunks.x:
Composite of parts a) and b), $V_f = 0.68$:

$$E_{1C} = 0.68 \times 400\ \text{GPa} + 0.32 \times 3\ \text{GPa} = 272.0 + 0.96 = 272.96\ \text{GPa}$$

Composite of part c), $V_f = 0.7627$:

$$E_{1C} = 0.7627 \times 400\ \text{GPa} + 0.2373 \times 3\ \text{GPa} = 305.08 + 0.71 = 305.8\ \text{GPa}$$

**Answer:** the composite of part c), with more fibre, is the stiffer one: $\mathbf{E_{1C} \approx 306\ GPa}$ (against 273 GPa for the 68 vol% composite).

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
- **Units.** $V_f$ and $w_f$ are dimensionless; $\rho_c$ is a volume-weighted sum of densities, in g/cm³; $E_{1C}$ is a sum of moduli, in GPa.
- **Bounds.** $1.20 < 1.60 < 1.79$ g/cm³ and $3 < 273 < 400$ GPa: each mixture value lies between those of its phases.
- **Weight against volume.** The fibre is the denser phase, so its weight fraction (76.0 %) is larger than its volume fraction (68 %).
- **Back-substitution.** $0.7627 \times 1.79 + 0.2373 \times 1.20 = 1.650$ g/cm³, the density given in c).
- **Limit.** For $V_f \to 1$ the modulus tends to $E_f = 400$ GPa; with $E_f \gg E_m$ the matrix adds less than 1 GPa, which is why $E_{1C} \approx V_f E_f$ [Session 22 Slide 22].

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x: Because the modulus along the fibres is almost proportional to $V_f$, the composite of part c), with 8 more volume percent of fibre, is 12 % stiffer and only 3 % denser. This is the reason aerospace laminates are made with as high a fibre fraction as processing allows.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-01 Weight Fractions Density and Modulus of a Carbon-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a) $w_f$ | 76% | 76.0 % fibre, 24.0 % epoxy | agrees |
| b) $\rho_c$ | 1.6 g/cm³ | 1.601 g/cm³ | agrees |
| c) $V_f$ | 76% | 76.3 vol% | agrees |
| d) $E$ | 304.7 GPa | 305.8 GPa (composite of part c) | agrees within rounding: the key uses $V_f = 0.76$, and $0.76 \times 400 + 0.24 \times 3 = 304.7$ GPa |

The key value 304.7 GPa is the modulus of the composite of part c) with $V_f$ rounded to 0.76, not the modulus of the 68 vol% composite (273.0 GPa); this is consistent with reading part d) as a comparison of the two composites of the statement.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-02 Choosing the Fibre for an Epoxy Composite with 40 Percent Fibres
chunks.x:
2. A composite material is planned to be manufactured using an epoxy matrix reinforced with continuous, longitudinally aligned fibers . The composite must contain a maximum fiber volume fraction of 40%,, and the minimum values for the elastic modulus and longitudinal tensile strength are set at 5.5·10⁴ and 1.2·10³ MPa respectively. he available candidate reinforcement materials include glass fibers, carbon fibers, and aramid fibers. Determine which reinforcement material is best suited to meet the specified requirements.
| Material | σ (MPa) | E (Gpa) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Epoxy Resin | 69 | 3.1 |
| Fiberglass | 2000 | 72 |
| Carbon Fiber | 3500 | 350 |
| Aramid Fiber | 3500 | 124 |
*(Solution: carbon fiber reinforced composite)*

The sheet prints "40%,," and "he available"; the requirement is $E_{1C} \ge 5.5\times10^4$ MPa = 55 GPa and $\sigma_{1C} \ge 1.2\times10^3$ MPa = 1200 MPa along the fibres.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-02 Choosing the Fibre for an Epoxy Composite with 40 Percent Fibres
chunks.x:
1. **Isostrain.** Continuous, aligned fibres loaded along their length with a perfect bond: $E_{1C} = V_f E_f + (1 - V_f)E_m$ [Session 22 Slide 22, Eq. 1].
2. **Longitudinal strength.** The strength follows the same rule of mixtures, $\sigma_C = \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_{y,m}(1 - V_f)$ [Session 22 Slide 26]. The table gives only one matrix stress (69 MPa), so it is used as the matrix term, as the key of the sheet does; the term is small next to the fibre term.
3. **Worst case.** Both properties grow with $V_f$, so if a fibre fails at the largest allowed fraction, $V_f = 0.40$, it fails at any lower fraction.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-02 Choosing the Fibre for an Epoxy Composite with 40 Percent Fibres
chunks.x:
| Constituent | $\sigma$ (MPa) | $E$ (GPa) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Epoxy (m) | 69 | 3.1 |
| Glass fibre | 2000 | 72 |
| Carbon fibre | 3500 | 350 |
| Aramid fibre | 3500 | 124 |

Limits: $V_f \le 0.40$, $E_{1C} \ge 55$ GPa, $\sigma_{1C} \ge 1200$ MPa.

**Unknown:** the fibre that meets both limits.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-02 Choosing the Fibre for an Epoxy Composite with 40 Percent Fibres
chunks.x:
[Session 22 Slides 22, 26]:

$$E_{1C} = V_f E_f + (1 - V_f)E_m \qquad \sigma_{1C} = V_f\sigma_f + (1 - V_f)\sigma_m$$

**Strategy.**
1. Evaluate both properties for each fibre at $V_f = 0.40$ and compare them with the limits.
2. As a second view, solve each rule for the smallest $V_f$ that reaches the limit and compare it with 0.40.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-02 Choosing the Fibre for an Epoxy Composite with 40 Percent Fibres
chunks.h: 1. Properties at the largest fraction, $V_f = 0.40$ [Session 22 Slides 22, 26]
chunks.x:
The matrix terms are common to the three candidates: $0.60 \times 3.1\ \text{GPa} = 1.86$ GPa and $0.60 \times 69\ \text{MPa} = 41.4$ MPa.

Glass:

$$E_{1C} = 0.40 \times 72 + 1.86 = 30.66\ \text{GPa} \qquad \sigma_{1C} = 0.40 \times 2000 + 41.4 = 841.4\ \text{MPa}$$

Carbon:

$$E_{1C} = 0.40 \times 350 + 1.86 = 141.86\ \text{GPa} \qquad \sigma_{1C} = 0.40 \times 3500 + 41.4 = 1441.4\ \text{MPa}$$

Aramid:

$$E_{1C} = 0.40 \times 124 + 1.86 = 51.46\ \text{GPa} \qquad \sigma_{1C} = 0.40 \times 3500 + 41.4 = 1441.4\ \text{MPa}$$

| Fibre | $E_{1C}$ (GPa) | $\ge 55$? | $\sigma_{1C}$ (MPa) | $\ge 1200$? |
| :--- | ---: | :---: | ---: | :---: |
| Glass | 30.7 | no | 841 | no |
| Carbon | 141.9 | yes | 1441 | yes |
| Aramid | 51.5 | no | 1441 | yes |

chunks.t: Problem - T10-02 Choosing the Fibre for an Epoxy Composite with 40 Percent Fibres
chunks.h: 2. Minimum fibre fraction for each limit
chunks.x:
Solving $E_{1C} = 55$ GPa and $\sigma_{1C} = 1200$ MPa for $V_f$:

$$V_{f,E} = \frac{E_{min} - E_m}{E_f - E_m} \qquad V_{f,\sigma} = \frac{\sigma_{min} - \sigma_m}{\sigma_f - \sigma_m}$$

| Fibre | $V_{f,E}$ | $V_{f,\sigma}$ | Needed $V_f$ | $\le 0.40$? |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | :---: |
| Glass | $(55 - 3.1)/(72 - 3.1) = 0.753$ | $(1200 - 69)/(2000 - 69) = 0.586$ | 0.753 | no |
| Carbon | $(55 - 3.1)/(350 - 3.1) = 0.150$ | $(1200 - 69)/(3500 - 69) = 0.330$ | 0.330 | yes |
| Aramid | $(55 - 3.1)/(124 - 3.1) = 0.429$ | $(1200 - 69)/(3500 - 69) = 0.330$ | 0.429 | no |

**Answer: carbon fibre.** It is the only candidate that meets both limits with at most 40 vol% fibre; it needs only 33 vol% (set by the strength). Aramid meets the strength but misses the modulus by a small margin (it would need 42.9 vol%), and glass misses both.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-02 Choosing the Fibre for an Epoxy Composite with 40 Percent Fibres
chunks.x:
- **Units.** Each term of $E_{1C}$ is a fraction times a modulus (GPa) and each term of $\sigma_{1C}$ a fraction times a stress (MPa); the limits were converted to the same units (55 GPa, 1200 MPa).
- **Consistency.** The two methods agree: a fibre passes at $V_f = 0.40$ exactly when its needed $V_f$ is below 0.40.
- **Limit.** For $V_f \to 0$ both rules return the epoxy (3.1 GPa, 69 MPa), far below the limits: the matrix alone cannot do the job.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-02 Choosing the Fibre for an Epoxy Composite with 40 Percent Fibres
chunks.x: Strength and stiffness select differently: aramid and carbon have the same tensile strength, but aramid is about three times less stiff, so the modulus limit is the one that rules it out. This matches the slides: glass fibres have a low modulus and aramid a lower modulus than carbon [Session 21 Slides 17, 30], and carbon fibres give the best combination of strength, stiffness and low weight [Session 21 Slide 21].

chunks.t: Problem - T10-02 Choosing the Fibre for an Epoxy Composite with 40 Percent Fibres
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Fibre | carbon fiber reinforced composite | carbon fibre ($E_{1C} = 141.9$ GPa, $\sigma_{1C} = 1441$ MPa at 40 vol%) | agrees |

chunks.t: Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
chunks.x:
3. A composite material has a 69.5% in weight of unidirectional graphite-HM fibers in an epoxy matrix.
a) Estimate the density and elastic modulus of the composite.
b) If a 50% of the graphite fibers are replaced with Kevlar fibers, estimate the specific elastic modulus and the specific tensile strength in the longitudinal direction in this new hybrid composite.
c) Calculate the minimum volumetric fraction of the graphite-HM fibers so that the initial composite has more strength than the hybrid composite of section b).
d) Do the same calculations as in (c) considering Kevlar fibers.
Data:
| Material | Density g/cm³ | Elastic modulus GPa | Tensile strength MPa |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Epoxy resin | 1.23 | 3.5 | 70 |
| Graphite-HM fiber | 1.86 | 390 | 2400 |
| Kevlar-49 fiber | 1.44 | 131 | 3700 |
*(Solution: a) 1.61 g/cm³, 235.4 GPa; b) 106.5×10⁶ m²/s², 1.24×10⁶ m²/s²; c) 0.77; d) 0.49)*

chunks.t: Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
chunks.x:
1. **Weight to volume.** The composition is given by weight. In 1 g of composite each phase occupies $w_i/\rho_i$; the sum of these volumes is $1/\rho_c$, and $V_i = (w_i/\rho_i)/\sum_j (w_j/\rho_j)$ (definition of density).
2. **Rule of mixtures** along the fibres, for the modulus, the strength and the density, extended term by term to three phases: $P_{CM} = \sum_i f_i p_i$ [Session 22 Slide 27]; isostrain modulus [Session 22 Slide 22]; strength $\sigma_C = \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_m(1 - V_f)$ [Session 22 Slide 26], with the tabulated matrix strength as the matrix term.
3. **Hybrid of part b).** Half of the graphite **volume** is replaced by the same volume of Kevlar, so $V_{gr} = V_K = V_f/2$ and $V_m$ is unchanged.
4. **Specific property** = property / density [Session 21 Slide 43]; in SI, Pa/(kg/m³) = m²/s².
5. **Parts c) and d).** "Initial composite" means the two-phase composite fibre + epoxy with the fibre of each part; its strength must exceed that of the hybrid.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
chunks.x:
| Constituent | $\rho$ (g/cm³) | $E$ (GPa) | $\sigma$ (MPa) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Epoxy (m) | 1.23 | 3.5 | 70 |
| Graphite-HM (gr) | 1.86 | 390 | 2400 |
| Kevlar 49 (K) | 1.44 | 131 | 3700 |

$w_{gr} = 0.695$, $w_m = 0.305$.

**Unknowns:** (a) $\rho_c$, $E_{1C}$; (b) $E/\rho$ and $\sigma/\rho$ of the hybrid; (c) minimum $V_{gr}$; (d) minimum $V_K$.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
chunks.x:
[Session 22 Slides 22, 26, 27]:

$$V_i = \frac{w_i/\rho_i}{\sum_j w_j/\rho_j} \qquad \rho_c = \sum_i V_i\rho_i \qquad E_{1C} = \sum_i V_i E_i \qquad \sigma_{1C} = \sum_i V_i\sigma_i$$

**Strategy.**
1. Convert the weight fractions to volume fractions; then density and modulus (a).
2. Split the fibre volume in two halves; density, modulus and strength of the hybrid; divide by the density (b).
3. Set the strength of a two-phase composite equal to the hybrid strength and solve for $V_f$ (c, d).

chunks.t: Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
chunks.h: 1. a) Volume fractions, density and modulus [Session 22 Slides 22, 27]
chunks.x:
Volumes of the phases in 1 g of composite:

$$\frac{w_{gr}}{\rho_{gr}} = \frac{0.695\ \text{g}}{1.86\ \text{g/cm}^3} = 0.37366\ \text{cm}^3 \qquad \frac{w_m}{\rho_m} = \frac{0.305\ \text{g}}{1.23\ \text{g/cm}^3} = 0.24797\ \text{cm}^3$$

Total volume $0.62163\ \text{cm}^3$, so

$$V_{gr} = \frac{0.37366}{0.62163} = 0.6011 \qquad V_m = 0.3989 \qquad \rho_c = \frac{1\ \text{g}}{0.62163\ \text{cm}^3} = \mathbf{1.609\ g/cm^3}$$

Isostrain modulus:

$$E_{1C} = 0.6011 \times 390\ \text{GPa} + 0.3989 \times 3.5\ \text{GPa} = 234.43 + 1.40 = \mathbf{235.8\ GPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
chunks.x:
Strength of a graphite-epoxy composite with fraction $V$, set greater than the hybrid strength:

$$2400\,V + 70\,(1 - V) > 1861.3 \ \Rightarrow\ 2330\,V > 1791.3 \ \Rightarrow\ V > \frac{1791.3}{2330} = 0.769$$

**$V_{gr,min} = 0.77$.** The initial composite of part a), with $V_{gr} = 0.60$, has $2400 \times 0.6011 + 70 \times 0.3989 = 1470.6$ MPa, weaker than the hybrid.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
chunks.x:
- **Units.** $\text{Pa}/(\text{kg/m}^3) = (\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2})/(\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-3}) = \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$, the unit of the key.
- **Fractions.** $0.30055 + 0.30055 + 0.3989 = 1.0000$.
- **Trends.** Kevlar is lighter, stronger and less stiff than graphite, so the hybrid is lighter (1.48 against 1.61 g/cm³), less stiff (158 against 236 GPa) and stronger (1861 against 1471 MPa) than the initial composite.
- **c) against d).** Kevlar is the stronger fibre, so it needs a smaller fraction (0.49) than graphite (0.77) to beat the hybrid; both are below 1, so both are possible in principle.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
chunks.x:
A hybrid trades stiffness for strength and lower density: replacing half the graphite by Kevlar lowers the specific modulus from $235.8\times10^9/1609 = 146.6\times10^6$ to $106.6\times10^6$ m²/s² but raises the strength by 27 %. To match the hybrid strength with graphite alone, more than 77 vol% of fibre would be needed, above the 50 to 60 % of typical fibre composites [Session 22 Slide 22].

Discrepancy with the official solution
The key gives $1.24\times10^6$ m²/s² for the specific strength of part b); the rule of mixtures gives $1.861\times10^9/1482.5 = 1.26\times10^6$ m²/s² (with $V_f$ rounded to 0.60: $1858/1.482 = 1.25\times10^6$). The key value is reproduced only if the matrix term is dropped, $(0.30055 \times 6100)/1482.5 = 1.24\times10^6$ m²/s², but parts c) and d) of the same key (0.77, 0.49) need the full hybrid strength of about 1860 MPa, so the computed $1.26\times10^6$ m²/s² is kept. The other key values agree after rounding ($E_{1C} = 235.4$ GPa is the result for $V_f = 0.60$).

chunks.t: Problem - T10-03 Graphite-Epoxy and Graphite-Kevlar Hybrid Composite
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a) $\rho_c$ | 1.61 g/cm³ | 1.609 g/cm³ | agrees |
| a) $E_{1C}$ | 235.4 GPa | 235.8 GPa | agrees within rounding (key uses $V_f = 0.60$) |
| b) $E/\rho$ | 106.5×10⁶ m²/s² | 106.6×10⁶ m²/s² | agrees |
| b) $\sigma/\rho$ | 1.24×10⁶ m²/s² | 1.26×10⁶ m²/s² | differs (see the warning) |
| c) $V_{gr,min}$ | 0.77 | 0.769 | agrees |
| d) $V_{K,min}$ | 0.49 | 0.493 | agrees |

chunks.t: Problem - T10-04 Modulus Strength and Load Fraction of a Kevlar 49-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
4. Calculate the elastic modulus of a unidirectional composite material with epoxy matrix and Kevlar 49 fibers, where 63% of its volume is fibers and is under isostrain conditions. If the tensile strength of Kevlar 49 fibers is 3700 MPa and the tensile strength of the epoxy resin is 70 MPa, calculate the tensile strength of the composite material. What fraction of load is carried by the Kevlar fibers?
Data: E_kevlar = 131 GPa; E_epoxy = 3.5 GPa.
*(Solution: a) 83.82 GPa; b) 2.36 GPa; c) 0.984)*

chunks.t: Problem - T10-04 Modulus Strength and Load Fraction of a Kevlar 49-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
1. **Isostrain.** Load along the aligned fibres, perfect bond: $\varepsilon_C = \varepsilon_f = \varepsilon_m$ and $E_{1C} = V_f E_f + (1 - V_f)E_m$ [Session 22 Slides 21-22].
2. **Strength.** $\sigma_C = \sigma_f V_f + \sigma_{y,m}(1 - V_f)$ [Session 22 Slide 26], with the given resin strength as the matrix term.
3. **Load sharing.** The total force is the sum of the forces in the phases, $F_C = F_f + F_m$, and $F_i = \sigma_i A_i$ [Session 22 Slide 21]. With a common strain, $\sigma_f = E_f\varepsilon$ and $\sigma_C = E_{1C}\varepsilon$, and $A_f/A_C = V_f$ for continuous fibres, so

$$\frac{F_f}{F_C} = \frac{\sigma_f A_f}{\sigma_C A_C} = \frac{E_f\varepsilon\,V_f}{E_{1C}\varepsilon} = \frac{V_f E_f}{E_{1C}}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T10-04 Modulus Strength and Load Fraction of a Kevlar 49-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
| Quantity | Value |
| :--- | ---: |
| $V_f$ | 0.63 |
| $E_f$, $E_m$ | 131 GPa, 3.5 GPa |
| $\sigma_f$, $\sigma_m$ | 3700 MPa, 70 MPa |

**Unknowns:** $E_{1C}$, $\sigma_C$, $F_f/F_C$.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-04 Modulus Strength and Load Fraction of a Kevlar 49-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
[Session 22 Slides 21, 22, 26]:

$$E_{1C} = V_f E_f + (1 - V_f)E_m \qquad \sigma_C = V_f\sigma_f + (1 - V_f)\sigma_m \qquad \frac{F_f}{F_C} = \frac{V_f E_f}{E_{1C}}$$

**Strategy.** Apply the three relations in order; the load fraction needs the modulus of the first step.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-04 Modulus Strength and Load Fraction of a Kevlar 49-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x: $$\sigma_C = 0.63 \times 3700\ \text{MPa} + 0.37 \times 70\ \text{MPa} = 2331 + 25.9 = 2356.9\ \text{MPa} = \mathbf{2.36\ GPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T10-04 Modulus Strength and Load Fraction of a Kevlar 49-Epoxy Composite
chunks.h: 3. Fraction of the load carried by the fibres [Session 22 Slide 21]
chunks.x:
$$\frac{F_f}{F_C} = \frac{0.63 \times 131\ \text{GPa}}{83.825\ \text{GPa}} = \frac{82.53}{83.825} = \mathbf{0.985}$$

The fibres carry 98.5 % of the load and the epoxy the remaining 1.5 %.

chunks.t: Problem - T10-04 Modulus Strength and Load Fraction of a Kevlar 49-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x:
- **Units.** GPa in the modulus, MPa in the strength; the load fraction is GPa/GPa, dimensionless.
- **Bounds.** $3.5 < 83.8 < 131$ GPa and $70 < 2357 < 3700$ MPa.
- **Approximation of the slides.** With $E_f \gg E_m$, $E_{1C} \approx V_f E_f = 82.5$ GPa, within 1.5 % of the full result [Session 22 Slide 22].
- **Limits.** $F_f/F_C \to 1$ when $E_m \to 0$, and $F_f/F_C = V_f$ when $E_f = E_m$ (a homogeneous material shares the load by area).

chunks.t: Problem - T10-04 Modulus Strength and Load Fraction of a Kevlar 49-Epoxy Composite
chunks.x: Under isostrain the stress in each phase is proportional to its modulus, so the fibre, 37 times stiffer than the epoxy, works at 37 times the stress. That is the "redistribution of the load" of Slide 22: the matrix holds the fibres in place and transfers the load, but almost all of it is carried by the fibres [Session 21 Slide 16].
