chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD12 Invariant Reactions and a Ni-40 Mo Alloy
chunks.x:
**12. According to the Ni-Mo phase, indicate: a. The equations that represent the invariant reactions, specifying the composition of the phases, temperature and type of reaction. b. The maximum solubility of Mo in Ni and at what temperature it is produced. c. The maximum solubility of Ni in Mo and at what temperature it is produced. d. Melting temperature of Ni and Mo. e. Present phases, their composition and amount for a Ni-40%Mo alloy at 1309 °C. f. Microconstituents and their amount for a Ni-40%Mo alloy at 1309 °C. Sketch the microstructure.**

*(Solution: a) eutectic reaction (1310 °C); peritectoid reaction (910 °C); peritectic reaction (1362 °C). b) 26% Mo. c) 4% Ni. d) 1455 °C; 2623 °C. e) $C_{NiMo}$ = 52%Mo; $C_\alpha$ = 27%Mo; $X_\alpha$ = 0.48; $X_{NiMo}$ = 0.52. f) $X_{NiMo,p}$ = 0.25; $X_E$ = 0.75)*

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD12 Invariant Reactions and a Ni-40 Mo Alloy
chunks.x:
1. **Equilibrium**, Ni-Mo diagram of the sheet. Its axis reads only "Mo (%)", but the compounds sit at their **atomic** compositions (Ni₄Mo ≈ 20, Ni₃Mo = 25, NiMo ≈ 52 % Mo; in wt% they would be at 29.0, 35.3 and 62.0), so the axis is in **atomic % Mo** (at.%), like the Ti-Si diagram of Problem 13. Printed temperatures: 1455, 2623, 1362, 1310, 910 and 870 °C. Compositions are **readings of the figure** (±1 at.%).
2. α is the Ni-rich solid solution and β the Mo-rich one; NiMo is an intermediate phase with a narrow composition range; Ni₃Mo and Ni₄Mo are compounds that form in the solid.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD12 Invariant Reactions and a Ni-40 Mo Alloy
chunks.x:

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1362 | $L\,(38) + \beta\,(96) \rightarrow \text{NiMo}\,(55)$ | peritectic |

At 870 °C the compound Ni₄Mo appears inside the α field (the small dome); only α and Ni₄Mo take part, so it is not a three-phase reaction.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD12 Invariant Reactions and a Ni-40 Mo Alloy
chunks.x:
- Maximum solubility of **Mo in Ni**: about **27 at.% Mo** (the key writes 26 %), at the eutectic temperature, **1310 °C**.
- Maximum solubility of **Ni in Mo**: about **4 at.% Ni** (β at 96 at.% Mo), at the peritectic temperature, **1362 °C**.
- Melting points: **Ni 1455 °C**, **Mo 2623 °C**.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD12 Invariant Reactions and a Ni-40 Mo Alloy
chunks.h: e) Phases of Ni-40 at.% Mo at 1309 °C
chunks.x:
Just below the eutectic: α (27) + NiMo (52), tie line length 25. On an at.% axis the lever rule gives **atom (mole) fractions** $X$, as the key writes them (the lever rule is a balance of whatever the axis counts; this remark is an extension, since the slides use wt% axes):
$$X_\alpha = \frac{C_{\text{NiMo}} - C_0}{C_{\text{NiMo}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{52 - 40}{52 - 27} = \frac{12}{25} = 0.48 \qquad X_{\text{NiMo}} = \frac{40 - 27}{25} = \frac{13}{25} = 0.52$$

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD12 Invariant Reactions and a Ni-40 Mo Alloy
chunks.x:
$36 < 40 < 52$: the alloy is **hypereutectic**, so primary NiMo forms first and the liquid of 36 at.% Mo becomes eutectic. Short tie line from 36 to 52 (length 16):
$$X_{\text{NiMo},p} = \frac{C_0 - C_e}{C_{\text{NiMo}} - C_e} = \frac{40 - 36}{52 - 36} = \frac{4}{16} = 0.25 \qquad X_E = \frac{52 - 40}{16} = \frac{12}{16} = 0.75$$

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD12 Invariant Reactions and a Ni-40 Mo Alloy
chunks.x:
- Atom balance at 1309 °C: $0.48 \times 27 + 0.52 \times 52 = 12.96 + 27.04 = 40.0$ at.% Mo.
- Phases inside the eutectic: all the α (0.48) and NiMo $0.52 - 0.25 = 0.27$; $0.48 + 0.27 = 0.75 = X_E$ ✓. The eutectic alone is $(52 - 36)/(52 - 27) = 16/25 = 0.64$ α, and $0.75 \times 0.64 = 0.48$ ✓.
- **Limiting cases** (atom fractions, dimensionless; compositions in at.% Mo): at $C_0 = 36$ the alloy would be all eutectic and at $C_0 = 52$ all primary NiMo; 40 at.% lies close to the eutectic end, hence three quarters eutectic.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD12 Invariant Reactions and a Ni-40 Mo Alloy
chunks.x: The alloy is three quarters eutectic (α + NiMo) with a quarter of primary NiMo crystals. On further cooling, the α and NiMo of this alloy reach the 910 °C peritectoid, where they react to form Ni₃Mo.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD13 Compounds and Cooling of a Ti-30 Si Alloy
chunks.x:
**13. Given the following Ti-Si phase diagram answer the next questions: a) Indicate the phases or compounds with incongruent and congruent melting. b) Write down the invariant reactions, specifying their name, temperature, and composition of the phases present. c) For an alloy with 30% Si describe the solidification and cooling sequence to 600 °C. Describe specifically the microstructure that can be expected at 1329 °C, 1169 °C, and 600 °C. d) For the same alloy of part c) and the temperatures of 1329 °C and 1169 °C indicate phase composition, phase fractions and quantity of microconstituents present.**

*(Solution: a) congruent melting: Ti₅Si₃ and TiSi₂; incongruent melting: Ti₃Si, Ti₅Si₄ and TiSi. b) Eutectic, T = 1330 °C; Eutectic, T = 1330 °C; Eutectic, T = 1480 °C; Peritectic, T = 1920 °C; Peritectic, T = 1570 °C; Peritectoid T = 1170 °C; Eutectoid, T = 865 °C. c) T = 1329 °C: $C_{\beta Ti}$ = 5.5% Si and $C_{Ti_5Si_3}$ = 35% Si, $x_{\beta Ti}$ = 0.17, $x_{Ti_5Si_3}$ = 0.83; T = 1169 °C: $C_{Ti_3Si}$ = 25% Si and $C_{Ti_5Si_3}$ = 35% Si, $x_{Ti_5Si_3}$ = 0.5, $x_{Ti_3Si}$ = 0.5. d) T = 1329 °C: $x_{eutectic}$ = 0.24, $x_{Ti_5Si_3,primary}$ = 0.76; T = 1169 °C phases and microconstituents are the same)*

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD13 Compounds and Cooling of a Ti-30 Si Alloy
chunks.x:
1. **Equilibrium**, Ti-Si diagram of the sheet. Printed temperatures: 1670, 1414, 2130, 1920, 1570, 1480, 1330 (twice), 1170 and 865 °C. Compositions are **readings of the figure** (±1 %), on the axis as printed.
2. The axis is labelled "% wt Silicon", but the compounds sit at 25 (Ti₃Si), 37.5 (Ti₅Si₃), 44.4 (Ti₅Si₄), 50 (TiSi) and 66.7 (TiSi₂), their **atomic** percentages of Si; the numbers below are read on the axis as printed, as the key does, so the fractions $x$ are **atom (mole) fractions** and the Phase 4 balances count Si atoms. Ti₅Si₃ has a composition range on the figure: about 35 on its Ti side (1330 and 1170 °C) and up to about 38 on its Si side (1920 °C).
3. Melting is congruent at a maximum of the liquidus and incongruent at a peritectic line [Session 8 Slide 17].

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD13 Compounds and Cooling of a Ti-30 Si Alloy
chunks.h: c) Cooling of Ti-30 % Si to 600 °C
chunks.x:
1. Liquid down to the liquidus of Ti₅Si₃ (roughly 1950 °C, a reading); there **primary Ti₅Si₃** starts to crystallise.
2. L + Ti₅Si₃ down to 1330 °C; the liquid becomes poorer in Si along the liquidus and reaches 14 % Si.
3. At 1330 °C the remaining liquid gives the **eutectic** βTi + Ti₅Si₃.
4. Between 1330 and 1170 °C: primary Ti₅Si₃ in a eutectic of βTi + Ti₅Si₃.
5. At 1170 °C the **peritectoid** βTi + Ti₅Si₃ → Ti₃Si uses up all the βTi (the alloy, 30 %, lies between Ti₃Si, 25 %, and Ti₅Si₃, 35 %), so below it the alloy is **Ti₃Si + Ti₅Si₃**.
6. No other line is crossed down to 600 °C; the boundaries of both compounds are vertical, so nothing changes.

**At 1329 °C** (βTi 5.5 / Ti₅Si₃ 35, length 29.5):
$$x_{\beta\text{Ti}} = \frac{35 - 30}{35 - 5.5} = \frac{5}{29.5} = 0.17 \qquad x_{\text{Ti}_5\text{Si}_3} = \frac{30 - 5.5}{29.5} = \frac{24.5}{29.5} = 0.83$$

**At 1169 °C and at 600 °C** (Ti₃Si 25 / Ti₅Si₃ 35, length 10):
$$x_{\text{Ti}_3\text{Si}} = \frac{35 - 30}{35 - 25} = \frac{5}{10} = 0.5 \qquad x_{\text{Ti}_5\text{Si}_3} = \frac{30 - 25}{10} = 0.5$$

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD13 Compounds and Cooling of a Ti-30 Si Alloy
chunks.x:
**At 1329 °C:** primary Ti₅Si₃ and eutectic. Short tie line from the eutectic liquid (14) to Ti₅Si₃ (35), length 21:
$$x_{\text{Ti}_5\text{Si}_3,p} = \frac{30 - 14}{35 - 14} = \frac{16}{21} = 0.76 \qquad x_E = \frac{35 - 30}{21} = \frac{5}{21} = 0.24$$

**At 1169 °C:** the peritectoid has turned the βTi (which was inside the eutectic) and part of the Ti₅Si₃ into Ti₃Si; the structure is Ti₃Si and Ti₅Si₃, in the same amounts as the phases, 0.5 and 0.5.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD13 Compounds and Cooling of a Ti-30 Si Alloy
chunks.x:
- 1329 °C: $0.17 \times 5.5 + 0.83 \times 35 = 0.94 + 29.06 = 30.0$ at.% Si (atom balance).
- 1169 °C: $0.5 \times 25 + 0.5 \times 35 = 30$ at.% Si.
- Eutectic at 1329 °C: it holds all the βTi (0.17) and Ti₅Si₃ $0.83 - 0.76 = 0.07$; $0.17 + 0.07 = 0.24 = x_E$ ✓.
- **Limiting cases** (atom fractions, dimensionless; compositions in at.% Si as printed): at 1329 °C, as $C_0 \to 14$ the primary Ti₅Si₃ tends to 0 and as $C_0 \to 35$ to 1; 30 lies close to the compound end, hence 0.76 of primary Ti₅Si₃.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD14 Reading a Hypothetical Diagram with Several Compounds
chunks.x:
**14. In the following graph, a hypothetical phase diagram is represented, identify and explain the following: a) The existing phases in each phase field of the diagram. b) The invariant reactions writing the temperature and the reaction's equation, the composition of each phase inside the reaction and its name. c) The congruent and incongruent fusion phases.**

*(Solution, from the annotated diagram of Solution problems Phase diagrams I.pdf, p. 37; the sheet prints none: β incongruent melting; γ congruent melting; δ incongruent melting; ε incongruent melting)*

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD14 Reading a Hypothetical Diagram with Several Compounds
chunks.x:
1. **Equilibrium**; the diagram has no printed values except the axes (wt% B; temperature assumed in °C, since the axis prints no unit), so every number below is a **reading of the figure**, to about ±1 wt% and ±10 °C.
2. Phases are named as in the official solution (p. 37): terminal solid solutions α (A side) and ζ (B side), intermediate phases β, γ (a vertical line: a compound of fixed composition at about 62 % B), δ and ε, and the liquid L.
3. Each horizontal line is an invariant reaction, named by its shape [Session 8 Slide 6]; melting is congruent at a maximum of the liquidus and incongruent at a peritectic line [Session 8 Slide 17].

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD14 Reading a Hypothetical Diagram with Several Compounds
chunks.h: 🧠 2. Phase 2: Frames and Change of Basis
chunks.x:
Frame: composition (wt% B) against temperature. The diagram is read on horizontal lines, from the top down and from left to right; no change of basis is involved.

**Method.** (a) Single-phase fields are the regions bounded by curved lines that touch the axis or a dome; each two-phase field takes the phases on its two sides along a horizontal tie line [Session 7 Slide 15]. (b) For each horizontal line: the three phases at its ends and middle point, and the shape. (c) Where each intermediate phase ends at the top.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD14 Reading a Hypothetical Diagram with Several Compounds
chunks.x:
- **γ melts congruently** at about 865 °C: it is at the maximum of its liquidus dome, and the liquid formed has its composition.
- **β, δ and ε melt incongruently**: each ends at a peritectic line (895, 660 and 595 °C), where on heating it gives a liquid plus a different solid (β → α + L, δ → γ + L, ε → δ + L).
- The pure components A (≈ 1200 °C) and B (≈ 695 °C) also melt congruently, like any pure metal [Session 8 Slide 17].

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD14 Reading a Hypothetical Diagram with Several Compounds
chunks.x:
- On every eutectic and eutectoid line the parent phase (L or δ) lies **between** the two products; on every peritectic line the product lies between the two reactants, with the liquid at one end [Session 8 Slide 6].
- Phase rule: three phases on each horizontal line, $F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$ [Session 7 Slide 13].
- δ is a closed field: it is created by a peritectic at 660 °C and destroyed by a eutectoid at 430 °C, so it exists only between those temperatures.
- **Limiting case**: an alloy with exactly the composition of a line compound (γ) is a single phase, with fractions 1 or 0 and no tie line; every two-phase reading above lies strictly between its tie-line ends.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD14 Reading a Hypothetical Diagram with Several Compounds
chunks.x: The diagram is a chain of simple diagrams joined at the compounds. A phase that touches the liquid only at a horizontal line cannot exist as a liquid of its own composition, which is the meaning of incongruent melting.

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD15 The Ti-B System and Ti-10 B and Ti-18 B Alloys
chunks.x:
**15. Given the phase diagram of the figure, answer the following questions: a. Write down the invariant reactions, indicating the name, temperature and composition of the phases involved. b. List the congruent and incongruent melting phases or compounds. c. For an alloy with 10% B, indicate the composition of the phases, the amount of phases and the amount of microconstituents at 1000 °C and 500 °C. d. Describe the solidification sequence of an alloy with 18% B at a very slow cooling from the liquid state up to 500 °C.**

*(Solution: a) peritectic (2200 °C); peritectic (2190 °C); eutectic (1540 °C); eutectic (2080 °C). b) Ti₃B₄ → L + TiB₂. c) 1000 °C: $C_{(\beta Ti)}$ = 0%B; $C_{TiB}$ = 18%B; $X_{(\beta Ti)}$ = 0.44; $X_{(TiB)}$ = 0.56; eutectic (x = 50%) and primary TiB (x = 50%). 500 °C: $C_{(\alpha Ti)}$ = 0%B; $C_{TiB}$ = 18%B; $X_{(\alpha Ti)}$ = 0.44; $X_{(TiB)}$ = 0.56; eutectic (x = 50%) and primary TiB (x = 50%))*

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD15 The Ti-B System and Ti-10 B and Ti-18 B Alloys
chunks.x:
- **TiB₂ melts congruently**, at the top of the liquidus, 3225 °C.
- **Ti₃B₄ melts incongruently** ($\text{Ti}_3\text{B}_4 \rightarrow L + \text{TiB}_2$ on heating at ~2200 °C), and so does **TiB** ($\text{TiB} \rightarrow L + \text{Ti}_3\text{B}_4$ at ~2190 °C): both end at peritectic lines [Session 8 Slide 17].

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD15 The Ti-B System and Ti-10 B and Ti-18 B Alloys
chunks.h: c) Ti-10 wt% B at 1000 °C and 500 °C
chunks.x:
**Phases** at 1000 °C: (βTi) 0 and TiB 18 (length 18):
$$X_{(\beta\text{Ti})} = \frac{18 - 10}{18 - 0} = \frac{8}{18} = 0.44 \qquad X_{\text{TiB}} = \frac{10 - 0}{18} = \frac{10}{18} = 0.56$$
At 500 °C the same, with (αTi) instead of (βTi): 0.44 and 0.56.

**Microconstituents.** $2 < 10 < 18$: hypereutectic, primary TiB and eutectic. Short tie line from the eutectic liquid (2) to TiB (18), length 16:
$$X_{\text{TiB},p} = \frac{10 - 2}{18 - 2} = \frac{8}{16} = 0.50 \qquad X_E = \frac{18 - 10}{16} = 0.50$$
The same at 1000 and 500 °C (the 884 °C change affects only the Ti inside the eutectic).

chunks.t: Problem - T4-PD15 The Ti-B System and Ti-10 B and Ti-18 B Alloys
chunks.h: d) Ti-18 wt% B, very slow cooling to 500 °C
chunks.x:
1. **Liquid**, down to the liquidus on the TiB₂ side of the dome (roughly 2500 °C at 18 wt% B, a reading).
2. **L + TiB₂**: primary TiB₂ crystallises; the liquid becomes poorer in B, down to 13 wt% at ~2200 °C.
3. **~2200 °C, peritectic** $L + \text{TiB}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ti}_3\text{B}_4$: since $13 < 18 < 24$, all the TiB₂ is used up and the alloy is L + Ti₃B₄.
4. **~2190 °C, peritectic** $L + \text{Ti}_3\text{B}_4 \rightarrow \text{TiB}$: the alloy has exactly the composition of TiB, so liquid and Ti₃B₄ are both used up: **100 % TiB**.
5. From ~2190 to 500 °C nothing changes: the alloy stays single-phase TiB.

chunks.x:
- (c): $0.44 \times 0 + 0.56 \times 18 = 10$ wt% B; the eutectic (0.50) contains all the Ti (0.44) and $0.56 - 0.50 = 0.06$ of TiB, $0.44 + 0.06 = 0.50$ ✓.
- (d): in equilibrium each peritectic is complete; with faster cooling the TiB would surround the Ti₃B₄ (and that the TiB₂) and the reactions would stay incomplete [Session 8 Slide 10].

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x:
1. **Uniaxial, uniform stress.** The load acts along the axis of the cylinder, and up to the necking the stress is the same on every cross-section of the gauge length. Under this hypothesis the engineering stress and strain are defined with the original area and length [Session 11 Slide 9].
2. **Linear elastic start.** For small loads the curve is a straight line through the origin, Hooke's law $\sigma = E\varepsilon$, and the slope of that line is the Young's modulus [Session 11 Slide 13].
3. **Conventional yield strength.** The yield strength is the stress at which the curve crosses the line drawn parallel to the elastic line from the residual strain $0.002$ (0.2 % offset), as the statement asks [Session 11 Slide 28].
4. **Between table rows the curve is a straight segment.** The table gives discrete points, so every reading between two of them is a linear interpolation.
5. **Elastic recovery.** When the sample breaks the load disappears and the elastic strain is recovered, so the ductility is the plastic strain at fracture [Session 11 Slide 32].
6. **Safety factor.** The statement gives none; the slide says that $N$ is usually 2, and that value is used for the working stress [Session 11 Slide 29].

| Elongation (table) | $\Delta L$ | see table | mm |
| Safety factor | $N$ | 2 | |

**Unknowns:** the curve (a), $E$ (b), $\sigma_y$ (c), $\sigma_{max}$ (d), the ductility (e), $U_r$ (f), $F_y$ and $\Delta l_y$ (g), $\sigma_w$ (h), and the load at $\Delta L = 0.1$ mm (i).

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x:
There is a single direction, the axis of the sample, and the stress state is uniaxial, so no change of basis and no rotation matrix are involved.

**Strategy.** Every item comes from the same table of engineering stress and strain, so the first thing to do is to build it:

$$\sigma_n = \frac{F}{A_0} \qquad \varepsilon_n = \frac{\Delta L}{l_0}$$

- The Young's modulus is the slope of the straight initial part (Hooke's law). A straight line through the origin is fitted by least squares: it minimises $\sum(\sigma_i - E\varepsilon_i)^2$, which gives $E = \sum\sigma_i\varepsilon_i / \sum\varepsilon_i^2$.
- The yield strength is found by the 0.2 % offset construction, solved algebraically on the segment of the table where the curve crosses the offset line.
- The tensile strength is the maximum nominal stress, and since $A_0$ is constant it corresponds to the maximum load.
- The ductility is the plastic strain at fracture, and the modulus of resilience is the area under the elastic line up to the yield point, $U_r = \sigma_y^2/(2E)$ [Session 11 Slide 35].
- For the load at a given elongation the table is used again: Hooke's law only holds in the elastic zone.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.h: 2. Engineering stress and strain of every point
chunks.x:
The load of the table is in hundreds of newtons, so $F = 100\times(F/100)$. For point 1:

$$F_1 = 100 \times 127 = 12\,700\ \text{N} \qquad \sigma_{n,1} = \frac{12\,700\ \text{N}}{128.68\ \text{mm}^2} = 98.69\ \text{MPa} \qquad \varepsilon_{n,1} = \frac{0.006\ \text{mm}}{12.5\ \text{mm}} = 4.80\times 10^{-4}$$

The same operation for all the points (the last column is the secant modulus, used in item b):

chunks.h: 2. Engineering stress and strain of every point

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x: The points of the table are plotted as they are, joined by straight segments. The right-hand panel enlarges the elastic part, where the Young's modulus line and the offset line of item c are drawn.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x:
The secant modulus $\sigma_n/\varepsilon_n$ of the last column is almost constant, 195 to 206 GPa, for points 1 to 5, and it drops to 170 GPa at point 6 and to 143 GPa at point 7: the specimen leaves the linear zone after point 5. The straight part is therefore made of points 1 to 5, and the fit through the origin is:

| Point | $\varepsilon_i$ | $\sigma_i$ (MPa) | $\sigma_i\varepsilon_i$ (MPa) | $\varepsilon_i^2$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0.00048 | 98.69 | 0.0474 | $2.304\times 10^{-7}$ |
| 2 | 0.00096 | 197.39 | 0.1895 | $9.216\times 10^{-7}$ |
| 3 | 0.00152 | 296.08 | 0.4500 | $2.310\times 10^{-6}$ |
| 4 | 0.00200 | 394.78 | 0.7896 | $4.000\times 10^{-6}$ |
| 5 | 0.00304 | 592.17 | 1.8002 | $9.242\times 10^{-6}$ |

$$\sum \sigma_i\varepsilon_i = 3.277\ \text{MPa} \qquad \sum \varepsilon_i^2 = 1.6704\times 10^{-5}$$

$$E = \frac{\sum \sigma_i\varepsilon_i}{\sum \varepsilon_i^2} = \frac{3.277}{1.6704\times 10^{-5}} = 196160\ \text{MPa} = \mathbf{196.2\ GPa} \approx 2.0\times10^{2}\ \text{GPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x:
The offset line starts at $\varepsilon = 0.002$ and is parallel to the elastic line:

$$\sigma_{off}(\varepsilon) = E\,(\varepsilon - 0.002)$$

The curve is above the line while $g = \sigma_n - E(\varepsilon_n - 0.002)$ is positive. The sign of $g$ changes between points 7 and 8, so the crossing is on that segment:

| Point | $\varepsilon_n$ | $\sigma_n$ (MPa) | $E(\varepsilon_n - 0.002)$ (MPa) | $g = \sigma_n - E(\varepsilon_n - 0.002)$ (MPa) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 6 | 0.00408 | 692.4 | 408.0 | 284.4 |
| 7 | 0.00504 | 720.4 | 596.3 | 124.1 |
| 8 | 0.00760 | 796.6 | 1098.5 | -301.9 |
| 9 | 0.01016 | 837.7 | 1600.7 | -762.9 |

The segment between the two points is the line

$$\sigma(\varepsilon) = \sigma_{7} + m\,(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_{7}) \qquad m = \frac{\sigma_{8} - \sigma_{7}}{\varepsilon_{8} - \varepsilon_{7}} = \frac{796.55 - 720.39}{0.00760 - 0.00504} = 29749.3\ \text{MPa}$$

Equating it to the offset line, $\sigma_{7} + m(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_{7}) = E(\varepsilon - 0.002)$, and solving for $\varepsilon$:

$$\varepsilon^* = \frac{\sigma_{7} - m\,\varepsilon_{7} + 0.002\,E}{E - m} = \frac{720.39 - 29749.3\times0.00504 + 0.002\times196160}{196160 - 29749.3} = \frac{962.778}{166411.2} = 0.0057855$$

$$\sigma_y = E\,(\varepsilon^* - 0.002) = 196160\times(0.0057855 - 0.002) = \mathbf{742.6\ MPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x:
The maximum load of the table is $F_{max} = 160\,400$ N at point 14. The nominal stress uses the original area, so the maximum load gives the maximum stress:

$$\sigma_{max} = \frac{F_{max}}{A_0} = \frac{160\,400\ \text{N}}{128.68\ \text{mm}^2} = \mathbf{1246.5\ MPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x:
The last record before the fracture is point 17: $\Delta L = 1.460$ mm and $F = 124\,700$ N, so

$$\varepsilon_f = \frac{1.460}{12.5} = 0.1168 \qquad \sigma_f = \frac{124\,700}{128.68} = 969.1\ \text{MPa}$$

At that moment the strain is the sum of an elastic and a plastic part, $\varepsilon_t = \varepsilon_e + \varepsilon_p$. After the fracture the load is zero and the elastic part is recovered along a line parallel to the elastic one, so what remains is $\varepsilon_p$ [Session 11 Slide 32]:

$$\varepsilon_e = \frac{\sigma_f}{E} = \frac{969.1}{196160} = 0.00494 \qquad \varepsilon_p = \varepsilon_f - \varepsilon_e = 0.1168 - 0.00494 = 0.1119$$

$$EL\,(\%) = \varepsilon_p \times 100 = \mathbf{11.2\ \%}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x:
The area under the elastic line up to the yield point is a triangle, $U_r = \tfrac12\sigma_y\varepsilon_{y}$ with $\varepsilon_{y} = \sigma_y/E$ [Session 11 Slide 35]:

$$U_r = \frac{\sigma_y^2}{2E} = \frac{(742.6\ \text{MPa})^2}{2\times196160\ \text{MPa}} = \mathbf{1.41\ MPa}$$

($1\ \text{MPa} = 1\ \text{MJ/m}^3$.)

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.h: g) Load and elongation at the yield point
chunks.x:
The load is the yield stress times the original area, and the elongation is the total strain of the yield point (the value $\varepsilon^*$ of item c) times the original length:

$$F_y = \sigma_y A_0 = 742.6\ \text{MPa}\times128.68\ \text{mm}^2 = 95\,554\ \text{N} = \mathbf{95.6\ kN}$$

$$\Delta l_y = \varepsilon^* l_0 = 0.0057855\times12.5\ \text{mm} = \mathbf{0.0723\ mm}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.h: i) Load for an elongation of 0.1 mm
chunks.x:
The elongation of the yield point is 0.0723 mm, so $0.1$ mm is in the plastic zone and the load is not proportional to the elongation. Using Hooke's law anyway, $F = E A_0\Delta l/l_0$, would give

$$F = \frac{196160\ \text{N/mm}^2\times128.68\ \text{mm}^2\times0.1\ \text{mm}}{12.5\ \text{mm}} = 201\,935\ \text{N} = 202\ \text{kN}$$

which is larger than the maximum load that the sample supports, 160 400 N: the answer is **not** possible with the values obtained. The alternative is the table itself. The elongation 0.1 mm is between points 8 ($\Delta L = 0.095$ mm, $F = 102\,500$ N) and 9 ($\Delta L = 0.127$ mm, $F = 107\,800$ N), and a linear interpolation on that segment gives

$$F = F_{8} + \frac{0.1 - 0.095}{0.127 - 0.095}\,(F_{9} - F_{8}) = 102\,500 + 0.15625\times(107\,800 - 102\,500) = \mathbf{103\,328\ N}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x:
- **Units.** $\sigma_n = F/A_0$ in N/mm² is MPa, $\varepsilon_n$ is a ratio of lengths and has no units, so $E = \sigma/\varepsilon$ is in MPa and $U_r = \sigma_y^2/2E$ is in MPa (energy per unit volume).
- **Order.** $\sigma_y = 742.6$ MPa $< \sigma_{max} = 1246.5$ MPa, and the fracture stress ($969.1$ MPa) is below the maximum, as in a ductile sample that necks.
- **The fit.** The secant moduli of points 1 to 5 are within 4.8 % of the fitted $E$, and the offset line crosses the curve between points 7 and 8, inside the segment used.
- **Item i.** The interpolated load, 103.3 kN, is between the loads of the two rows and below the maximum load; the Hooke value, 202 kN, is not.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-01 Complete Analysis of a Tensile Test from the Load-Elongation Table
chunks.x:
The sample is stiff ($E \approx 196$ GPa) and strong, and it yields at about 742.6 MPa, a strain of 0.579 %. From there to the maximum load the strain hardening raises the stress by 504 MPa, and the 11.2 % of plastic elongation at fracture shows that it is also ductile.

The data are not those of aluminium
The table of Session 11 gives $E = 69$ GPa for aluminium and 207 GPa for steel [Session 11 Slide 17]. The data of this problem give $E \approx 196$ GPa and a yield strength above 700 MPa, which are the values of a steel, not of aluminium. The statement says "aluminum"; the data are used as they are.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
2. A cylindrical sample made from a metallic material (assume a Poisson ratio of ν = 0.25) of 15 mm in diameter and a calibrated length of 50 mm was subjected to a tensile test, and the results are shown in the table below:
| Point | Force (kN) | ΔL (mm) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 70 | 0.25 |
| 2 | 120 | 0.40 |
| 3 | 150 | 0.50 |
| 4 | 160 | 0.60 |
| 5 | 170 | 0.75 |
| 6 | 200 | 1.75 |
| 7 | 220 | 3.00 |
| 8 | 233 | 5.00 |
| 9 | 233 | 6.50 |
| 10 | 220 | 8.00 |
The diameter of the sample after fracture was 12.45 mm. Calculate:
- a. The tensile strength.
- b. The Young's Modulus (or elastic modulus).
- c. The yield stress.
- d. The modulus of resilience.
- e. The real tension for an engineering deformation of 0.02.
- f. The percentage of deformation to fracture and percentage of area reduction.
*(The sheet prints the table in two rows; here each point has its own row.)*
*(Solution: a. $\sigma_{UTS} = 1319$ MPa; b. $E = 85$ GPa; c. $\sigma_y = 920$ MPa; d. $U_r = 4.98$ MPa; e. $\sigma_r = 1030$ MPa; f. 15 %, 7.3 %)*

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
1. **Uniaxial, uniform stress.** Up to the necking the stress is uniform along the gauge length, so the engineering quantities use the original area and length [Session 11 Slide 9].
2. **Linear elastic start.** Hooke's law $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ holds on the first points of the curve [Session 11 Slide 13].
3. **Yield strength by the 0.2 % offset.** The statement does not name a criterion; the conventional one for metals is the 0.2 % offset [Session 11 Slide 28].
4. **Straight segments between table rows**, so readings between two rows are linear interpolations.
5. **Uniform deformation before the necking.** The volume is constant, $A\,l = A_0 l_0$, until the maximum load, where the necking starts [Session 11 Slides 30 and 38]. The true stress of item e is computed in that range.
6. **Elastic recovery after the fracture.** The elastic strain disappears when the load does, and what is left is the plastic strain [Session 11 Slide 32]. The reduction of area uses the measured final diameter [Session 11 Slide 33].
7. **The Poisson ratio is not needed.** $\nu = 0.25$ is a datum of the statement, but none of the six items uses it: the only lateral information is the final diameter, which is measured.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
| Quantity | Symbol | Value | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Diameter | $d_0$ | 15 mm | $15\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Gauge length | $l_0$ | 50 mm | $50\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Diameter after fracture | $d_f$ | 12.45 mm | $12.45\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Poisson ratio (not used) | $\nu$ | 0.25 | |
| Load, elongation | $F$, $\Delta L$ | table | kN, mm |

**Unknowns:** $\sigma_{UTS}$ (a), $E$ (b), $\sigma_y$ (c), $U_r$ (d), $\sigma_r$ at $\varepsilon_n = 0.02$ (e), the elongation at fracture and the reduction of area (f).

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
The only direction is the axis of the cylinder and the stress is uniaxial, so there is no change of basis.

**Strategy.** As in any tensile test, the first step is to turn the table into engineering stress and strain,

$$\sigma_n = \frac{F}{A_0} \qquad \varepsilon_n = \frac{\Delta L}{l_0}$$

and then read each item from it: the maximum stress (a), the slope of the straight part by least squares through the origin (b), the offset construction solved on the crossing segment (c), $U_r = \sigma_y^2/2E$ (d) [Session 11 Slide 35].

**True stress (e).** With constant volume, $A\,l = A_0 l_0$, so $A = A_0 l_0/l = A_0/(1 + \varepsilon_n)$. The true stress is then

$$\sigma_r = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{F}{A_0}\,(1 + \varepsilon_n) = \sigma_n\,(1 + \varepsilon_n)$$

which is the relation of the slide for the uniform deformation [Session 11 Slide 38].

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
$$A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(15\ \text{mm})^2}{4}$$

The square is $15^2 = 225$, then $\pi\times225 = 706.86$ and dividing by 4:

$$A_0 = 176.71\ \text{mm}^2$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.h: 2. Engineering stress and strain of every point

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
The maximum load is $F_{max} = 233\,000$ N, reached at points 8 and 9 ($\varepsilon_n = 0.100$ and $0.130$: the load stays at its maximum while the sample elongates). The area $A_0$ is constant in the engineering stress, so

$$\sigma_{UTS} = \frac{F_{max}}{A_0} = \frac{233\,000\ \text{N}}{176.71\ \text{mm}^2} = \mathbf{1318.5\ MPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
The secant modulus is 79 to 85 GPa for points 1 to 3, and it drops to 75 GPa at point 4 and to 64 GPa at point 5: the linear zone ends after point 3. The fit through the origin with points 1 to 3 is:

| Point | $\varepsilon_i$ | $\sigma_i$ (MPa) | $\sigma_i\varepsilon_i$ (MPa) | $\varepsilon_i^2$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0.0050 | 396.1 | 1.9806 | $2.500\times 10^{-5}$ |
| 2 | 0.0080 | 679.1 | 5.4325 | $6.400\times 10^{-5}$ |
| 3 | 0.0100 | 848.8 | 8.4883 | $1.000\times 10^{-4}$ |

$$E = \frac{\sum \sigma_i\varepsilon_i}{\sum \varepsilon_i^2} = \frac{15.901}{1.8900\times 10^{-4}} = 84134\ \text{MPa} = \mathbf{84.1\ GPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
$$U_r = \frac{\sigma_y^2}{2E} = \frac{(923.9\ \text{MPa})^2}{2\times84134\ \text{MPa}} = \mathbf{5.07\ MPa}$$

($1\ \text{MPa} = 1\ \text{MJ/m}^3$.)

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
The elongation that corresponds to $\varepsilon_n = 0.02$ is $\Delta L = 0.02\times50 = 1.00$ mm, which is not a row of the table. It is between points 5 ($\Delta L = 0.75$ mm, $F = 170$ kN) and 6 ($\Delta L = 1.75$ mm, $F = 200$ kN):

$$F = F_{5} + \frac{1.00 - 0.75}{1.75 - 0.75}\,(F_{6} - F_{5}) = 170 + \frac{1.00 - 0.75}{1.75 - 0.75}\,(200 - 170) = 177.5\ \text{kN}$$

$$\sigma_n = \frac{177\,500\ \text{N}}{176.71\ \text{mm}^2} = 1004.4\ \text{MPa}$$

This strain is below the one of the maximum load ($\varepsilon_n = 0.100$), so the deformation is still uniform and the relation of section 2 applies:

$$\sigma_r = \sigma_n\,(1 + \varepsilon_n) = 1004.4\times(1 + 0.02) = \mathbf{1024.5\ MPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.h: f) Elongation at fracture and reduction of area
chunks.x:
The last row of the table is the fracture: $\Delta L = 8.00$ mm and $F = 220\,000$ N, so

$$\varepsilon_f = \frac{8.00}{50} = 0.160 \qquad \sigma_f = \frac{220\,000}{176.71} = 1244.9\ \text{MPa}$$

The elastic part of that strain is recovered when the sample breaks, $\varepsilon_e = \sigma_f/E$, and what is left is the plastic strain [Session 11 Slide 32]:

$$\varepsilon_e = \frac{1244.9}{84134} = 0.01480 \qquad \varepsilon_p = 0.160 - 0.01480 = 0.1452 \qquad EL = \mathbf{14.5\ \%}$$

For the reduction of area, the final area from the final diameter is

$$A_f = \frac{\pi\,(12.45\ \text{mm})^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\times155.0025}{4} = 121.74\ \text{mm}^2$$

$$RA\,(\%) = \frac{A_0 - A_f}{A_0}\times100 = \frac{176.71 - 121.74}{176.71}\times100 = \mathbf{31.1\ \%}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
- **Units.** Stresses in N/mm² = MPa, strains without units, $E$ and $U_r$ in MPa.
- **Order.** $\sigma_y = 923.9$ MPa $<\sigma_{UTS} = 1318.5$ MPa, and the stress rises 395 MPa between the yield and the maximum load.
- **True and engineering stress.** The true stress of item e, 1024.5 MPa, is 2 % above the engineering one, 1004.4 MPa, as the factor $1 + \varepsilon_n$ says.
- **Elongation against area reduction.** $RA = 31.1$ % is larger than $EL = 14.5$ %, as expected when a ductile sample necks: the section shrinks much more at the neck than the length grows over the whole gauge length.
- **Neck.** The stress that acts on the neck at the fracture is $F_f/A_f = 220\,000\ \text{N}/121.74\ \text{mm}^2 = 1807$ MPa, far above the engineering fracture stress of 1244.9 MPa because the area is much smaller than $A_0$.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x: The sample reaches 1.3 GPa with a plateau of maximum load, and it fails after a clear neck. The measured final diameter, not Poisson's ratio, gives the lateral information: Poisson's ratio only describes the elastic part of the deformation.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-02 Tensile Test of a 15 mm Cylinder Strength Resilience True Stress and Area Reduction
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a. $\sigma_{UTS}$ | 1319 MPa | 1318.5 MPa | agrees |
| b. $E$ | 85 GPa | 84.1 GPa | agrees (1 %); the key corresponds to the slope between points 2 and 3 |
| c. $\sigma_y$ | 920 MPa | 923.9 MPa | agrees (0.5 %) |
| d. $U_r$ | 4.98 MPa | 5.07 MPa | agrees (2 %); the key uses $E = 85$ GPa and $\sigma_y = 920$ MPa |
| e. $\sigma_r$ | 1030 MPa | 1024.5 MPa | agrees (0.5 %): the key reads $\sigma_n \approx 1010$ MPa at $\varepsilon_n = 0.02$ |
| f. elongation | 15 % | 14.5 % | agrees (rounded) |
| f. area reduction | 7.3 % | 31.1 % | **does not agree** |

Discrepancy with the official solution: area reduction
The official 7.3 % cannot be reproduced from the data of the statement. With $d_0 = 15$ mm and $d_f = 12.45$ mm the final area is $A_f = 121.74$ mm² and the reduction is $31.1$ %. A reduction of 7.3 % would need a final area of $0.927\,A_0$, that is, a final diameter of $15\sqrt{0.927} = 14.44$ mm. The computed value is kept.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-03 Tensile Test of a 13 mm Sample Modulus Cable Section and True Values
chunks.x:
1. **Uniaxial, uniform stress** up to the necking: engineering stress and strain with the original area and length [Session 11 Slide 9].
2. **Weight to force.** The loads are masses in kilograms; the force is $F = m\,g$ with $g = 9.81$ m/s².
3. **Linear elastic start** [Session 11 Slide 13] and **0.2 % offset yield strength** [Session 11 Slide 28].
4. **Calibrated length.** The first row ($m = 0$) gives the initial length $l_0 = 5.148$ mm and the other rows the current length. The strain is a ratio, so only the proportion matters.
5. **True quantities from the measured diameters** (item d). The true strain is $\varepsilon_r = \ln(A_0/A) = 2\ln(D_0/D)$ and the true stress is $\sigma_r = F/A$ with $A$ the instantaneous area [Session 11 Slide 38]. They are valid also after the necking, because they use the actual area at the neck.
6. **Design stress (item c).** The statement does not give a safety factor. The minimum section is the one for which the cable does not yield, $\sigma = F/A_0 \leq \sigma_y$; with the usual factor $N = 2$ it would be larger [Session 11 Slide 29].

**Strategy.** The table is converted into $\sigma_n = F/A_0$ and $\varepsilon_n = (l - l_0)/l_0$. Then:
- $E$ is the slope of the straight part (least squares through the origin), and the bar of item b is a direct application of Hooke's law, $\Delta l = (\sigma/E)\,l_b$.
- $\sigma_y$ by the 0.2 % offset is needed twice: for the cable (c) and for the resilience (e).
- The true values (d) are computed from the forces and the measured diameters, as the statement asks, and not from the engineering values.
- The elastic strain before the fracture (f) is $\sigma/E$ with the stress that acts at that moment [Session 11 Slide 32].

$$A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(13\ \text{mm})^2}{4}$$

With $13^2 = 169$ and $\pi\times169 = 530.93$:

$$A_0 = 132.73\ \text{mm}^2$$

For the first loaded point, $F_1 = 500\ \text{kg}\times9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 = 4\,905\ \text{N}$, so

chunks.t: Problem - T5-03 Tensile Test of a 13 mm Sample Modulus Cable Section and True Values
chunks.h: b) Young's modulus and the length of the bar
chunks.x:
The secant modulus of the last column grows from 63 to 74 GPa in points 1 to 4 and falls to 18 GPa at point 5: the linear zone ends after point 4. The first value is lower because a strain of 0.0006 comes from an elongation of only 0.003 mm, at the limit of the resolution of the table. The fit through the origin on points 1 to 4 is:

| Point | $\varepsilon_i$ | $\sigma_i$ (MPa) | $\sigma_i\varepsilon_i$ (MPa) | $\varepsilon_i^2$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0.00058 | 36.95 | 0.0215 | $3.396\times 10^{-7}$ |
| 2 | 0.00155 | 110.86 | 0.1723 | $2.415\times 10^{-6}$ |
| 3 | 0.00253 | 184.77 | 0.4666 | $6.377\times 10^{-6}$ |
| 4 | 0.00350 | 258.68 | 0.9045 | $1.223\times 10^{-5}$ |

$$E = \frac{\sum \sigma_i\varepsilon_i}{\sum \varepsilon_i^2} = \frac{1.565}{2.1357\times 10^{-5}} = 73273\ \text{MPa} = \mathbf{73.3\ GPa}$$

For the bar, the strain produced by $\sigma = 200$ MPa is $\varepsilon = \sigma/E$ and the elongation is $\Delta l = \varepsilon\,l_b$:

$$\varepsilon = \frac{200}{73273} = 0.002730 \qquad \Delta l = 0.002730\times130\ \text{mm} = 0.355\ \text{mm}$$

$$l = l_b + \Delta l = 130 + 0.355 = 130.355\ \text{mm} = \mathbf{13.04\ cm}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-03 Tensile Test of a 13 mm Sample Modulus Cable Section and True Values
chunks.x:
The yield strength is needed first. With the offset line $E(\varepsilon - 0.002)$ the sign of $g = \sigma_n - E(\varepsilon_n - 0.002)$ changes between points 4 and 5:

| Point | $\varepsilon_n$ | $\sigma_n$ (MPa) | $E(\varepsilon_n - 0.002)$ (MPa) | $g = \sigma_n - E(\varepsilon_n - 0.002)$ (MPa) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 3 | 0.00253 | 184.8 | 38.5 | 146.3 |
| 4 | 0.00350 | 258.7 | 109.7 | 149.0 |
| 5 | 0.01496 | 277.2 | 949.4 | -672.3 |
| 6 | 0.04002 | 291.9 | 2785.5 | -2493.6 |

$$m = \frac{277.16 - 258.68}{0.01496 - 0.00350} = 1612.2\ \text{MPa} \qquad \varepsilon^* = \frac{258.68 - 1612.2\times0.00350 + 0.002\times73273}{73273 - 1612.2} = \frac{399.587}{71660.3} = 0.0055761$$

$$\sigma_y = E\,(\varepsilon^* - 0.002) = 73273\times(0.0055761 - 0.002) = \mathbf{262.0\ MPa}$$

The weight of the elevator is $W = 450\times9.81 = 4414.5$ N. For the cable not to yield, $W/A_0 \leq \sigma_y$:

$$A_0 \geq \frac{W}{\sigma_y} = \frac{4414.5\ \text{N}}{262.0\ \text{N/mm}^2} = \mathbf{16.85\ mm^2}$$

If the usual safety factor $N = 2$ is also applied, the design stress is $\sigma_y/2$ and the section doubles, $A_0 \geq 33.7$ mm².

chunks.h: f) Elastic strain before the fracture
chunks.x:
The stress of the table at the fracture point (point 9) is $\sigma_n = 266.1$ MPa, and the elastic part of the strain is given by Hooke's law:

$$\varepsilon_e = \frac{\sigma_n}{E} = \frac{266.1}{73273} = \mathbf{3.63\times 10^{-3}}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-03 Tensile Test of a 13 mm Sample Modulus Cable Section and True Values
chunks.x:
- **Units.** Masses in kg and $g$ in m/s² give newtons, N/mm² is MPa, the strains have no units, and $A_0 \geq W/\sigma_y$ comes out in mm².
- **Order.** The true stress at maximum load (299.2 MPa) is above the engineering maximum (295.6 MPa) because the area has shrunk, and the true fracture stress (419.9 MPa) is much above the engineering one (266.1 MPa), while the engineering stress falls after the maximum.
- **Limit.** For $D = D_0$ the true strain $2\ln(D_0/D)$ is zero and the true stress is $F/A_0$, the engineering one.
- **Bar.** The elongation, 0.355 mm over 130 mm, is a strain of 0.27 %, well inside the elastic zone (the yield strain is 3.58 × 10⁻³ = 0.36 %).

chunks.t: Problem - T5-03 Tensile Test of a 13 mm Sample Modulus Cable Section and True Values
chunks.x:
The sample is a ductile metal with a clear yield at 262.0 MPa and a long hardening plateau up to 295.6 MPa; the neck makes the true stress at fracture 419.9 MPa. The cable needs at least 16.85 mm² to stay elastic under the elevator, and about twice as much with the usual safety factor.

Diameters and lengths of the table do not describe the same strain
At the maximum load the length of the table gives $\varepsilon_n = 0.0600$, that is, $\varepsilon_r = \ln(1+\varepsilon_n) = 0.0583$ with the uniform-deformation relation, and constant volume would give a diameter $13/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon_n} = 12.63$ mm. The statement gives $12.922$ mm, with $\varepsilon_r = 0.01204$. At the fracture, $A_0/A_f = 1.578$ while $l/l_0 = 1.1026$. The two sets of data do not describe the same deformation: the diameters measure the strain of the neck, the lengths the average over the calibrated length. The statement asks to compute the true values from the diameters, and that is what is done.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
chunks.x:
1. **Uniaxial, linear elastic wire.** The wire is loaded only along its axis and it stays elastic, so $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ [Session 11 Slide 13].
2. **Constant length while heating.** After the force is applied, the wire is held at a constant length: the total length, and therefore the total strain $\varepsilon$, does not change during the heating.
3. **Linear thermal expansion.** A temperature rise $\Delta T$ produces a free thermal strain $\varepsilon_T = \alpha_l\,\Delta T$. This law is not in the slides of Session 11 and 12 (it belongs to the thermal properties of Topic 7); it is given by the sheet through the datum $\alpha_l$.
4. **Strains add.** The total strain is the elastic (mechanical) strain plus the thermal strain, $\varepsilon = \sigma/E + \alpha_l\,\Delta T$, and $E$ and $\alpha_l$ are constant between 20 and 40 °C.
5. **"Compensates".** The thermal stress compensates the applied stress when the net stress of the wire after heating is zero.
6. **Circular, uniform section.** The area $A = \pi d^2/4$ is the same all along the wire and does not change with the temperature.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
chunks.x:

| Force | $F$ | 1400 N | 1400 N |
| Initial temperature, final temperature | $T_1$, $T_2$ | 20 °C, 40 °C | |
| Temperature rise | $\Delta T$ | 20 °C | 20 K |
| Young's modulus | $E$ | 207 GPa | $207\times10^{9}$ Pa = 207 000 N/mm² |
| Linear expansion coefficient | $\alpha_l$ | $12.5\times10^{-6}$ °C⁻¹ | $12.5\times10^{-6}$ K⁻¹ |
| Initial length | $l_0$ | 1 m | not needed |

chunks.t: Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
chunks.x:
There is a single direction, the axis of the wire; no change of basis is involved.

**Strategy.** The key is to follow the strain, because the length is the quantity that is fixed.

1. At 20 °C the force produces the stress $\sigma_F = F/A$ and the strain $\varepsilon_1 = \sigma_F/E$.
2. At 40 °C the strain is the same, $\varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon_1$, but it is now the sum of an elastic part $\sigma_2/E$ and a thermal part $\alpha_l\Delta T$. This gives the stress after the heating, $\sigma_2$.
3. The condition of the statement, $\sigma_2 = 0$, gives the area, and the area gives the diameter.

This is better than thinking in terms of forces, because the wire does not "know" about the force: it only keeps its length, and the stress is whatever is needed to keep it.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
chunks.h: 1. Stress after heating at constant length
chunks.x:
Before heating, the strain is $\varepsilon_1 = \sigma_F/E$ with $\sigma_F = F/A$. After heating, the strain is the same, and it is the sum of the elastic and the thermal strain:

$$\varepsilon_2 = \frac{\sigma_2}{E} + \alpha_l\,\Delta T = \varepsilon_1 = \frac{\sigma_F}{E}$$

Solving for the stress after the heating:

$$\sigma_2 = \sigma_F - E\,\alpha_l\,\Delta T$$

The second term is the thermal stress: heating at constant length lowers the tension by $E\alpha_l\Delta T$ (if it were larger than $\sigma_F$, $\sigma_2$ would be negative, a compression).

chunks.t: Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
chunks.x:
The thermal stress compensates the applied stress when the net stress vanishes, $\sigma_2 = 0$:

$$\frac{F}{A} = E\,\alpha_l\,\Delta T \quad\Rightarrow\quad A = \frac{F}{E\,\alpha_l\,\Delta T}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
chunks.h: 3. Numerical value of the thermal stress
chunks.x:
With $E = 207000$ N/mm²:

$$E\,\alpha_l = 207000\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{mm}^2}\times12.5\times10^{-6}\ \text{°C}^{-1} = 2.5875\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{mm}^2\,\text{°C}}$$

$$E\,\alpha_l\,\Delta T = 2.5875\times20\ \text{°C} = 51.75\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 51.75\ \text{MPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
chunks.x:
$$A = \frac{F}{E\alpha_l\Delta T} = \frac{1400\ \text{N}}{51.75\ \text{N/mm}^2} = 27.053\ \text{mm}^2$$

From $A = \pi d^2/4$, $d = \sqrt{4A/\pi}$:

$$4A = 108.21\ \text{mm}^2 \qquad \frac{4A}{\pi} = 34.445\ \text{mm}^2 \qquad d = \sqrt{34.445\ \text{mm}^2} = \mathbf{5.869\ mm}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
chunks.x:
- **Units.** $F/(E\alpha_l\Delta T)$: N divided by (N/mm² · °C⁻¹ · °C) = N/(N/mm²) = mm². The product $\alpha_l\Delta T$ has no units, so $E\alpha_l\Delta T$ is a stress.
- **Direct check.** With this area the applied stress is $F/A = 1400/27.053 = 51.75$ MPa, equal to the thermal stress 51.75 MPa, so $\sigma_2 = 0$.
- **Strains.** The thermal strain $\alpha_l\Delta T = 2.500\times 10^{-4}$ is the same as the elastic strain that the force produced, $\sigma_F/E = 2.500\times 10^{-4}$: heating gives back exactly the stretch that the force had imposed, and since the length cannot change the stress disappears.
- **Length not needed.** The initial length does not appear in the result. The free expansion of 1 m of wire would be $\alpha_l\Delta T\,l_0 = 0.25$ mm, the amount that the supports prevent.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-05 Thermal Stress in a Constrained Steel Wire
chunks.x: For a wire thinner than 5.87 mm the applied stress is larger than the thermal one, and some tension remains after the heating. For a thicker wire the applied stress is smaller, and the heating leaves the wire in compression (it could buckle). The result depends on $F/A$, not on the length, because only the strain matters. As $\Delta T \to 0$ the required area tends to infinity: without temperature rise the force cannot be compensated.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.x:
6. A sample made of a Ni alloy with an elastic modulus of 207 GPa and an initial diameter of 10.2 mm experiences an elastic deformation only when loads inferior to 8900 N are applied. Calculate the maximum length of the sample before the deformation if the maximum elongation allowed is 0.25 mm.
*(Solution: $l_0 = 475$ mm)*

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.x:
1. **Elastic up to 8900 N.** For loads below 8900 N the deformation is only elastic, so Hooke's law $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ holds [Session 11 Slide 13]. The load of 8900 N is therefore the largest load for which the sample is still elastic.
2. **Uniaxial, uniform stress** along the sample: $\sigma = F/A_0$ and $\varepsilon = \Delta l/l_0$ [Session 11 Slide 9].
3. **Worst case.** The elongation grows with the load and with the length. The longest sample that does not exceed the allowed elongation is found for the largest load that is applied, 8900 N.
4. The cross-section is a circle of 10.2 mm, and it does not change appreciably in the elastic range.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.x:
| Quantity | Symbol | Value | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Young's modulus | $E$ | 207 GPa | 207 000 N/mm² |
| Diameter | $d_0$ | 10.2 mm | $10.2\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Largest elastic load | $F$ | 8900 N | 8900 N |
| Maximum elongation allowed | $\Delta l_{max}$ | 0.25 mm | $0.25\times10^{-3}$ m |

**Unknown:** the maximum initial length $l_0$.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.x:
One direction (the axis of the sample), no change of basis.

**Strategy.** Hooke's law relates the stress produced by the load to the strain, and the strain relates the elongation to the length. Combining the three relations,

$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A_0} \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E} \qquad \Delta l = \varepsilon\,l_0$$

the elongation is proportional to the initial length. The condition $\Delta l \leq 0.25$ mm is then an upper bound for $l_0$, and the maximum length is the one for which $\Delta l = 0.25$ mm.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.x:
$$A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(10.2\ \text{mm})^2}{4}$$

The square is $10.2^2 = 104.04$, then $\pi\times104.04 = 326.85$ and dividing by 4:

$$A_0 = 81.71\ \text{mm}^2$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.h: 2. Stress and strain at the largest elastic load
chunks.x:
$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A_0} = \frac{8900\ \text{N}}{81.71\ \text{mm}^2} = 108.92\ \text{MPa}$$

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E} = \frac{108.92\ \text{N/mm}^2}{207000\ \text{N/mm}^2} = 5.2617\times 10^{-4}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.x:
From $\Delta l = \varepsilon\,l_0$ with $\Delta l = 0.25$ mm:

$$l_0 = \frac{\Delta l}{\varepsilon} = \frac{0.25\ \text{mm}}{5.2617\times 10^{-4}} = \mathbf{475.1\ mm}$$

The same result in one step, without the intermediate strain:

$$l_0 = \frac{\Delta l\,A_0\,E}{F} = \frac{0.25\ \text{mm}\times81.71\ \text{mm}^2\times207000\ \text{N/mm}^2}{8900\ \text{N}} = 475.1\ \text{mm}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.x:
- **Units.** $\Delta l\,A_0E/F$: mm · mm² · (N/mm²) / N = mm.
- **Back substitution.** For $l_0 = 475.1$ mm, $\Delta l = 5.2617\times 10^{-4}\times475.1 = 0.250$ mm, the allowed elongation.
- **Elastic range.** The strain, $5.2617\times 10^{-4}$, is of the order of $10^{-4}$, typical of the elastic deformation of a metal, so the use of Hooke's law is consistent with the statement.
- **Limit.** For a shorter sample the elongation is smaller (it is proportional to $l_0$) and the condition is satisfied with margin; for a longer one it is exceeded.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.x: The sample can be at most about 475 mm long. The limit is imposed by the stiffness $E$ (a stiff material elongates little) and by the section (a thicker sample has less stress for the same load); it is not imposed by the strength, because the stress stays elastic.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-06 Maximum Length of a Ni Alloy Sample for a Given Elongation
chunks.x:
* Topic 5 - Mechanical Properties
* Concept - Hooke's Law, Young's Modulus and Non-Linear Elasticity
* Concept - Uniaxial Tension Test and Engineering Stress-Strain

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.x:
7. In a construction site, a change in the diameter of one of the crane cables was detected. When the weight that the cable was withstanding was 48950 N, the change was 5.3 10⁻³ mm, and when the load was removed, the cable recovered its initial diameter of 15 mm. Considering that for this kind of steel the Poisson's ratio ν = 0.33 and according to the manufacturer data the initial length of the cable is 3 m.
- a. Calculate the length of the cable when it's holding the load mentioned above.
- b. If it has been detected that plastic deformation of the cable begins when it is holding a weight of 10000 kg, can it be considered that the cable is working under safe conditions? Assume a safety factor of 2.
- c. What is the value of the elastic modulus for this material?
- d. In order to prevent service problems the provider replaces the cable for a different one, which has a stress-strain curve represented below and an elastic modulus of E = 75 GPa. Can this material replace the previous one? Explain why.
- e. Calculate the final length of this new cable in case it is working under the same conditions (48950 N).

*(Solution: a. $l = 3003.2$ mm; b. yes; c. $E = 261.3$ GPa; d. no; e. $l = 3045$ mm)*

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.x:
1. **Elastic and isotropic cable under a uniaxial load.** When it holds the weight the cable is elastic (it recovers its diameter when the load is removed), the stress is uniform, and Hooke's law $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon_{lat} = -\nu\varepsilon_{ax}$ hold [Session 11 Slides 13 and 19].
2. **Lateral strain from the diameter.** The change of 5.3·10⁻³ mm is a decrease of the diameter ($\Delta d < 0$ under tension), and the strain is relative to the initial diameter, 15 mm.
3. **Yield load.** "Plastic deformation begins when it holds a weight of 10 000 kg" means that the yield strength is the stress that this weight produces; the weight in newtons is $m\,g$ with $g = 9.81$ m/s² [Session 11 Slide 28].
4. **Safety factor.** The working stress is $\sigma_w = \sigma_y/N$, and the cable works under safe conditions if the stress that it supports does not exceed $\sigma_w$ [Session 11 Slide 29].
5. **Replacement cable.** Its stress-strain curve is the one printed on the sheet (a chart of ten points), with the modulus given, $E = 75$ GPa. The yield strength of the new material is taken with the 0.2 % offset [Session 11 Slide 28], and the readings of the chart are the values of the markers.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.x:
| Quantity | Symbol | Value | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Load in service | $F$ | 48 950 N | 48 950 N |
| Initial diameter | $d_0$ | 15 mm | $15\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Change of diameter | $\Delta d$ | $-5.3\times10^{-3}$ mm | $-5.3\times10^{-6}$ m |
| Poisson's ratio | $\nu$ | 0.33 | dimensionless |
| Initial length | $l_0$ | 3 m | 3000 mm |
| Weight at which plastic deformation begins | $m$ | 10 000 kg | $98\,100$ N |
| Safety factor | $N$ | 2 | dimensionless |
| Modulus of the replacement cable | $E_{new}$ | 75 GPa | 75 000 N/mm² |

**Unknowns:** the length under load (a), whether the cable is safe (b), $E$ (c), whether the new cable can replace it (d), and its length under load (e).

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.x:
One direction (the axis of the cable) and the two equal transverse directions; no change of basis.

**Strategy.**
- (a) The measured change of the diameter gives the transverse strain; Poisson's ratio turns it into the axial strain, and the axial strain into the elongation.
- (c) Once the axial strain is known, the modulus is the stress divided by it. Item c is solved before b and d because $E$ is used in the discussion.
- (b) The weight of 10 000 kg gives the yield strength; the safety factor gives the working stress, which is compared with the stress in service.
- (d), (e) The new cable is compared with the old one through the yield strength of the curve of the sheet: if the service stress exceeds it, the cable deforms permanently. The length (e) is read on the curve at the service stress, which is the same, since the section and the load are the same.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.h: a) Length of the cable under the load
chunks.x:
The lateral strain is the change of the diameter over the initial diameter, negative because the diameter shrinks:

$$\varepsilon_{lat} = \frac{\Delta d}{d_0} = \frac{-5.3\times10^{-3}\ \text{mm}}{15\ \text{mm}} = -3.5333\times 10^{-4}$$

From $\nu = -\varepsilon_{lat}/\varepsilon_{ax}$ [Session 11 Slide 19], the axial strain is

$$\varepsilon_{ax} = -\frac{\varepsilon_{lat}}{\nu} = \frac{3.5333\times 10^{-4}}{0.33} = 1.0707\times 10^{-3}$$

and the elongation and the length are

$$\Delta l = \varepsilon_{ax}\,l_0 = 1.0707\times 10^{-3}\times3000\ \text{mm} = 3.212\ \text{mm} \qquad l = l_0 + \Delta l = 3000 + 3.212 = \mathbf{3003.2\ mm}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.x: $$E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{ax}} = \frac{277.00\ \text{N/mm}^2}{1.0707\times 10^{-3}} = 258708\ \text{MPa} = \mathbf{258.7\ GPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.h: b) Is the cable working under safe conditions?
chunks.x:
The weight at which the plastic deformation begins is $W_y = 10\,000\times9.81 = 98\,100$ N, so the yield strength is

$$\sigma_y = \frac{W_y}{A_0} = \frac{98\,100\ \text{N}}{176.71\ \text{mm}^2} = 555.1\ \text{MPa}$$

With the safety factor of 2 the working stress, and the corresponding load, are

$$\sigma_w = \frac{\sigma_y}{N} = \frac{555.1}{2} = 277.6\ \text{MPa} \qquad F_w = \frac{W_y}{N} = \frac{98\,100}{2} = 49\,050\ \text{N}$$

The stress in service, 277.00 MPa, is not larger than $\sigma_w = 277.6$ MPa (equivalently, $48 950\ \text{N} < 49\,050\ \text{N}$), so the cable **works under safe conditions**: the safety factor really available is

$$N_{eff} = \frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma} = \frac{555.1}{277.00} = 2.004 \geq 2$$

The margin is very small, 0.20 % of the permitted load.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.h: d) Can the new cable replace the previous one?
chunks.x:
The curve of the sheet is a chart of ten points. Its markers are at the strains and stresses of the table of Problem 3 (for example, the point at $\varepsilon = 0.0035$ and $\sigma \approx 259$ MPa, and the maximum at $\approx 296$ MPa), and those values are used as readings.

The yield strength of the new material, with the offset line $E_{new}(\varepsilon - 0.002)$ and $E_{new} = 75\,000$ MPa, changes sign of $g = \sigma - E_{new}(\varepsilon - 0.002)$ between the points 4 and 5:

| Point | $\varepsilon_n$ | $\sigma_n$ (MPa) | $E(\varepsilon_n - 0.002)$ (MPa) | $g = \sigma_n - E(\varepsilon_n - 0.002)$ (MPa) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 3 | 0.00253 | 184.8 | 39.4 | 145.4 |
| 4 | 0.00350 | 258.7 | 112.2 | 146.4 |
| 5 | 0.01496 | 277.2 | 971.8 | -694.6 |
| 6 | 0.04002 | 291.9 | 2851.2 | -2559.2 |

$$m = \frac{277.16 - 258.68}{0.01496 - 0.00350} = 1612.2\ \text{MPa} \qquad \varepsilon^* = \frac{258.68 - 1612.2\times0.00350 + 0.002\times75\,000}{75\,000 - 1612.2} = \frac{403.042}{73387.8} = 0.0054919$$

$$\sigma_{y,new} = E_{new}\,(\varepsilon^* - 0.002) = 75\,000\times(0.0054919 - 0.002) = 261.9\ \text{MPa}$$

The stress that the new cable would carry is the same, 277.00 MPa, since the load and the section are the same. It is **larger** than its yield strength, $277.00 > 261.9$ MPa:

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.h: d) Can the new cable replace the previous one?
chunks.x:
$$N_{eff,new} = \frac{\sigma_{y,new}}{\sigma} = \frac{261.9}{277.00} = 0.945 < 1 \quad (\text{the old cable has } 2.004)$$

Equivalently, the yield load of the new cable is $\sigma_{y,new}A_0 = 46.3$ kN, below the 48 950 N of service. The new cable would deform plastically and permanently under the same load, with no safety margin: the answer is **no**.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.h: e) Length of the new cable under the same conditions
chunks.x:
The strain is read on the curve at the service stress $\sigma = 277.00$ MPa, which is between the points 4 and 5 ($\sigma = 258.68$ MPa at $\varepsilon = 0.00350$ and $\sigma = 277.16$ MPa at $\varepsilon = 0.01496$). By linear interpolation:

$$\varepsilon = 0.00350 + \frac{277.00 - 258.68}{277.16 - 258.68}\,(0.01496 - 0.00350) = 0.01486$$

$$\Delta l = \varepsilon\,l_0 = 0.01486\times3000\ \text{mm} = 44.6\ \text{mm} \qquad l = 3000 + 44.6 = \mathbf{3044.6\ mm}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.x:
- **Units.** $\Delta d/d_0$ and the strains have no units; N/mm² is MPa; $m\,g$ in kg·m/s² is N.
- **Poisson.** $\varepsilon_{lat}$ is negative and $\varepsilon_{ax}$ positive, and $|\varepsilon_{lat}| = 0.33\,\varepsilon_{ax}$, as the definition of $\nu$ demands.
- **Elastic range of the old cable.** The strain, $1.0707\times 10^{-3}$, is a small fraction of the one at which it yields, $\sigma_y/E = 555.1/258708 = 2.1\times10^{-3}$ (it works at about half of it, as the safety factor 2 says).
- **Consistency of $E$.** The modulus 258.7 GPa is larger than the one of steel in the table of the slide, 207 GPa [Session 11 Slide 17], by about 25 %. The text of the sheet speaks of "this kind of steel", so the value is plausible within the data of the problem.
- **New cable.** Its length under load, 3044.6 mm, is 14 times the elongation of the old one (3.2 mm against 44.6 mm), and permanent: on unloading it recovers $\sigma/E_{new} = 277.00/75\,000$ and keeps $\varepsilon_p = 0.01117$, that is, about 33.5 mm of permanent elongation.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.x:
The two cables have the same section and carry the same load, but the old one works at 50 % of its yield strength and the new one above 100 %. A cable is not defined by its stiffness but by its yield strength: the new one is also much more flexible ($E = 75$ GPa against 259 GPa) and elongates by about 14 times as much. To keep the safety factor of 2 with the new material the section should be at least $A \geq N F/\sigma_{y,new} = 2\times48 950/261.9 = 373.8$ mm², that is, a diameter of 21.8 mm instead of 15 mm.

The last item of the sheet
The statement prints a "f." after item e, followed only by the chart of the stress-strain curve. There is no item f: the chart is the one that item d refers to ("a stress-strain curve represented below").

chunks.t: Problem - T5-07 Crane Cable Poisson Ratio Safety Factor and Replacement Cable
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a. length | 3003.2 mm | 3003.2 mm | agrees |
| b. safe? | yes | yes ($N_{eff} = 2.004$) | agrees, with a margin of 0.20 % |
| c. $E$ | 261.3 GPa | 258.7 GPa | differs 1 % |
| d. can replace? | no | no ($N_{eff,new} = 0.945$) | agrees |
| e. length | 3045 mm | 3044.6 mm | agrees |

Discrepancy with the official solution: modulus of the cable
The key gives $E = 261.3$ GPa. The data of the statement give 258.7 GPa from the unrounded strain, and 259.7 GPa if the elongation is rounded to 3.2 mm. The 261.3 GPa of the key is not reproduced by either value (it needs an axial strain of $1.060\times10^{-3}$); the difference is 1 % and it does not affect the other answers. The computed value is kept.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-08 Elastic Limits of a Brass Sample
chunks.x:
8. For a particular kind of brass, plastic deformation begins at 345 MPa, and its elastic modulus is 103 GPa.
- a. What is the value of the yield stress?
- b. What is the maximum stress that can be applied to a sample of this brass with a cross-section 130 mm² without plastic deformation taking place? And the maximum load?
- c. If the initial length of the sample is 76 mm, what is the maximum length that it can reach without plastic deformation?
*(Solution: a. $\sigma_y = 345$ MPa; b. $\sigma_{max} = 345$ MPa, $F_{max} = 44850$ N; c. $l = 76.25$ mm)*

chunks.t: Problem - T5-08 Elastic Limits of a Brass Sample
chunks.x:
1. **Yield strength.** "Plastic deformation begins at 345 MPa" means that 345 MPa is the yield strength of the brass: below it the deformation is only elastic, above it part of it is permanent [Session 11 Slide 28].
2. **Linear elastic below the yield strength**, $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ [Session 11 Slide 13], with the given modulus.
3. **Uniaxial, uniform stress**: $\sigma = F/A_0$ and $\varepsilon = \Delta l/l_0$ [Session 11 Slide 9]. The maximum values without plastic deformation are those that correspond to the stress $\sigma_y$.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-08 Elastic Limits of a Brass Sample
chunks.x:
| Quantity | Symbol | Value | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Stress at which plastic deformation begins | $\sigma_y$ | 345 MPa | $345\times10^{6}$ Pa |
| Young's modulus | $E$ | 103 GPa | 103 000 N/mm² |
| Cross-section (item b) | $A_0$ | 130 mm² | $130\times10^{-6}$ m² |
| Initial length (item c) | $l_0$ | 76 mm | $76\times10^{-3}$ m |

**Unknowns:** $\sigma_y$ (a), the maximum stress and load (b), the maximum length (c).

chunks.t: Problem - T5-08 Elastic Limits of a Brass Sample
chunks.x:
One direction (the axis of the sample), no change of basis.

**Strategy.** The three items are the same limit seen from three sides. The largest stress that does not cause plastic deformation is the yield strength (a, b). The largest load is that stress times the area, $F = \sigma_y A_0$ (b). The largest length is the initial length plus the elongation at the yield strength, and that elongation comes from Hooke's law, $\varepsilon_y = \sigma_y/E$ and $\Delta l = \varepsilon_y\,l_0$ (c).

chunks.t: Problem - T5-08 Elastic Limits of a Brass Sample
chunks.h: b) Maximum stress and maximum load
chunks.x:
Without plastic deformation the stress cannot be larger than the yield strength, so

$$\sigma_{max} = \sigma_y = \mathbf{345\ MPa}$$

The load that produces that stress in a section of 130 mm² follows from $\sigma = F/A_0$:

$$F_{max} = \sigma_{max}\,A_0 = 345\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{mm}^2}\times130\ \text{mm}^2 = 44\,850\ \text{N} = \mathbf{44.85\ kN}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-08 Elastic Limits of a Brass Sample
chunks.h: c) Maximum length without plastic deformation
chunks.x:
The strain at the yield strength comes from Hooke's law:

$$\varepsilon_y = \frac{\sigma_y}{E} = \frac{345\ \text{N/mm}^2}{103000\ \text{N/mm}^2} = 3.3495\times 10^{-3}$$

The elongation of a sample of 76 mm is

$$\Delta l = \varepsilon_y\,l_0 = 3.3495\times 10^{-3}\times76\ \text{mm} = 0.2546\ \text{mm}$$

and the maximum length that it can reach without plastic deformation is

$$l = l_0 + \Delta l = 76 + 0.2546 = \mathbf{76.255\ mm}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-08 Elastic Limits of a Brass Sample
chunks.x:
- **Units.** (N/mm²)·mm² = N for the load; (N/mm²)/(N/mm²) has no units for the strain; strain × mm = mm for the elongation.
- **Order of magnitude.** $\varepsilon_y = 0.335$ %, a few tenths of a percent, the order of magnitude of the elastic strain of a metal.
- **Limit.** If the load were zero, $l = l_0 = 76$ mm. At the yield load, the sample is only 0.25 mm longer, that is, 0.33 % of its length.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-08 Elastic Limits of a Brass Sample
chunks.x: Up to $44.85$ kN the sample returns to 76 mm when unloaded. Beyond that load part of the elongation is permanent. The brass elongates very little (a quarter of a millimetre) before it yields: the yield strength is a stress limit, but it translates into a small strain because $E$ is large.

chunks.x:

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a. $\sigma_y$ | 345 MPa | 345 MPa | agrees |
| b. $\sigma_{max}$, $F_{max}$ | 345 MPa, 44 850 N | 345 MPa, 44\,850 N | agrees |
| c. $l$ | 76.25 mm | 76.25 mm | agrees |

chunks.t: Problem - T5-09 Elongation and Diameter Change of a Steel Sample under Load
chunks.x:
9. A load of 48900 N produces elastic deformation in a cylindrical sample of 15.2 mm in diameter and a length of 254 mm. Considering that for this kind of steel E = 207 GPa and ν = 0.27, determine the elongation in the direction of the applied force and the change in diameter of the sample.
*(Solution: $\Delta l = 0.33$ mm, $\Delta\phi = -0.0053$ mm)*

chunks.t: Problem - T5-09 Elongation and Diameter Change of a Steel Sample under Load
chunks.x:
1. **Elastic deformation.** The statement says that the load produces only elastic deformation, so Hooke's law holds, $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ [Session 11 Slide 13].
2. **Uniaxial, uniform stress** along the axis of the cylinder: $\sigma = F/A_0$ and $\varepsilon = \Delta l/l_0$ [Session 11 Slide 9].
3. **Isotropic material.** With a uniaxial stress, the transverse strain is $\varepsilon_{lat} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{ax}$, equal in the two transverse directions [Session 11 Slide 19].
4. The cross-section is circular and uniform, so that the diameter changes in the same proportion in every direction of the section.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-09 Elongation and Diameter Change of a Steel Sample under Load
chunks.x:
| Quantity | Symbol | Value | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Load | $F$ | 48 900 N | 48 900 N |
| Diameter | $d_0$ | 15.2 mm | $15.2\times10^{-3}$ m |

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
10. Plastic deformation in a copper wire of 200 cm in length and a diameter of 1 mm begins when it is loaded with 15.3 kg. If the elastic modulus for copper is 110 GPa.
- a. Calculate its yield strength.
- b. Considering that when it is loaded with 29.6 kg the strain is 0.011, calculate the final length of the wire once it has been unloaded.
- c. Calculate the resilience modulus.
*(Solution: a. $\sigma_y = 190.9$ MPa; b. $l = 201.85$ cm; c. $U_r = 0.165$ MPa)*

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
1. **Uniaxial, uniform stress** in the wire: $\sigma = F/A_0$ [Session 11 Slide 9]. The weight of a mass $m$ is $F = m\,g$ with $g = 9.81$ m/s².
2. **Yield strength.** "Plastic deformation begins when it is loaded with 15.3 kg" gives the yield strength, $\sigma_y = F_y/A_0$ [Session 11 Slide 28].
3. **Total strain under load.** The strain 0.011 of item b is the total strain (elastic plus plastic) measured while the load of 29.6 kg is applied, relative to the initial length: $\varepsilon = \Delta l/l_0$ [Session 11 Slide 9].
4. **Unloading is elastic.** When the load is removed the elastic strain is recovered along a line of slope $E$, parallel to the elastic line, starting from the stress that the wire carried; what remains is the plastic strain [Session 11 Slides 21 and 32].
5. **Resilience** of the elastic range: $U_r = \sigma_y^2/(2E)$ [Session 11 Slide 35].

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
| Quantity | Symbol | Value | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Length | $l_0$ | 200 cm | 2.000 m = 2000 mm |
| Diameter | $d_0$ | 1 mm | $1\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Young's modulus | $E$ | 110 GPa | 110 000 N/mm² |
| Mass at which plastic deformation begins | $m_1$ | 15.3 kg | $F_1 = 15.3\times9.81 = 150.09$ N |
| Mass of item b | $m_2$ | 29.6 kg | $F_2 = 29.6\times9.81 = 290.38$ N |
| Total strain under $m_2$ | $\varepsilon$ | 0.011 | 0.011 (dimensionless) |

**Unknowns:** $\sigma_y$ (a), the final length after unloading (b), $U_r$ (c).

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
One direction (the axis of the wire); no change of basis.

**Strategy.** (a) is a stress: weight over area. (c) follows from (a) and $E$. Item (b) is the delicate one, and it is solved by following the strain along the load path:

1. The wire is loaded up to $\sigma_2 = F_2/A_0$, above the yield strength, and the total strain there is 0.011.
2. It is unloaded along a straight line of slope $E$: the strain recovered is $\sigma_2/E$ (the stress that it carried, not the yield strength).
3. The strain that remains is permanent, and it gives the final length.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
The force at which the plastic deformation begins is

$$F_1 = m_1\,g = 15.3\ \text{kg}\times9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 = 150.09\ \text{N}$$

$$\sigma_y = \frac{F_1}{A_0} = \frac{150.09\ \text{N}}{0.7854\ \text{mm}^2} = \mathbf{191.1\ MPa}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
The stress under the load of 29.6 kg is

$$F_2 = 29.6\times9.81 = 290.38\ \text{N} \qquad \sigma_2 = \frac{290.38}{0.7854} = 369.7\ \text{MPa}$$

which is above the yield strength (93 % higher), so the wire is in the plastic zone and the total strain, $\varepsilon = 0.011$, is the sum of an elastic part and a plastic part, $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_e + \varepsilon_p$. On unloading, the elastic part is recovered along the line of slope $E$ that starts at $\sigma_2$:

$$\varepsilon_e = \frac{\sigma_2}{E} = \frac{369.7\ \text{N/mm}^2}{110000\ \text{N/mm}^2} = 3.3611\times 10^{-3}$$

The strain that remains is

$$\varepsilon_p = \varepsilon - \varepsilon_e = 0.011 - 3.3611\times 10^{-3} = 0.007639$$

and the final length, once unloaded, is

$$l_f = l_0\,(1 + \varepsilon_p) = 200\ \text{cm}\times(1 + 0.007639) = \mathbf{201.53\ cm}$$

(that is, the wire is left 1.53 cm longer than at the beginning).

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
$$U_r = \frac{\sigma_y^2}{2E} = \frac{(191.1\ \text{MPa})^2}{2\times110000\ \text{MPa}} = \mathbf{0.166\ MPa}$$

($1\ \text{MPa} = 1\ \text{MJ/m}^3$.)

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
- **Units.** kg·m/s² = N; N/mm² = MPa; the strains have no units; $l_f$ in the unit of $l_0$ (cm).
- **Order.** $\varepsilon_e = 3.3611\times 10^{-3} < \varepsilon = 0.011$, and $\varepsilon_p > 0$: the wire does not return to 200 cm. If the load were removed from the yield point, the permanent strain would be zero; here the wire has gone beyond it.
- **Elastic strain at yield.** The strain of the yield point, $\sigma_y/E = 0.001737$, is smaller than the elastic strain recovered from $\sigma_2$ ($3.3611\times 10^{-3}$): the unloading starts from a higher stress, and the recovery is larger.
- **Limits.** If $\sigma_2 = \sigma_y$ the wire would be exactly at the yield point and $\varepsilon_p$ would be (almost) zero; the larger the stress reached, the larger the elastic recovery and the permanent strain.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
The copper wire yields at about 191.1 MPa, and after being loaded to 369.7 MPa it keeps a permanent elongation of 1.53 cm in 200 cm. A load that goes beyond the yield strength leaves a trace: the length after unloading depends on how far the stress went.

Value of $g$
The key is consistent with $g = 9.8$ m/s², which gives $\sigma_y = 190.9$ MPa instead of 191.1 MPa ($0.1$ % difference) and $U_r = 0.1657$ MPa. The result here uses $g = 9.81$ m/s² throughout the sheet.

chunks.t: Problem - T5-10 Copper Wire Yield Strength Permanent Elongation and Resilience
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a. $\sigma_y$ | 190.9 MPa | 191.1 MPa | agrees (the key uses $g = 9.8$ m/s²) |
| b. final length | 201.85 cm | 201.53 cm | **does not agree**, see below |
| c. $U_r$ | 0.165 MPa | 0.166 MPa | agrees |

Discrepancy with the official solution: length after unloading
The key, 201.85 cm, is obtained by recovering only the elastic strain of the yield point, $\sigma_y/E = 1.7373\times 10^{-3}$: $l = 200\,(1 + 0.011 - 1.7373\times 10^{-3}) = 201.85$ cm. That is the unloading of a wire that had been stressed to $\sigma_y$. But the wire of item b carried $\sigma_2 = 369.7$ MPa, and on unloading it recovers $\sigma_2/E = 3.3611\times 10^{-3}$. The correct permanent strain is therefore $0.007639$ and the length 201.53 cm. The key therefore recovers less elastic strain than the wire really does. The computed value is kept.
