| (b) Chains in 1 g | $2.408\times10^{18}$ | $2.4088\times10^{18}$ | agrees; the key truncates the last digit |

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.x:
2. Describe for each of the following polymer pairs, which one is more likely to crystallize? Explain your answer.
a) Branched Polyethylene vs linear polyethylene.
b) Polyethylene vs polyethylene-polypropylene co-polymer.
c) Isotactic Polypropylene vs Atactic polypropylene.
*(Solution: a) Liner PE, b) PE, c) Isostatic PP)*

The key prints "Liner" and "Isostatic"; they mean linear and isotactic.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.x:
1. **What crystallinity needs.** The crystallinity of a polymer is the degree to which there are regions where the chains are aligned with one another [Session 19 Slide 23]; in the crystalline lamellae the chains fold back and forth in an ordered way [Session 19 Slide 25]. A chain crystallizes easily when it is **regular** along its length, so that neighbouring segments fit next to each other.
2. **Factors of the slides.** Linear polymers pack best and are the most crystalline, branched ones less; symmetric and simple monomers favour crystallinity, complex ones lower it; random and graft copolymers are amorphous and alternating and block copolymers have some crystallinity; atactic polymers are amorphous, isotactic and syndiotactic ones probably crystalline [Session 19 Slides 26-27].
3. **Same conditions.** Within each pair the cooling rate and the molecular weight are taken as equal, so only the structure of the chain decides.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.x:
| Pair | Structural difference |
| :--- | :--- |
| a) | branched against linear chain of the same polymer |
| b) | homopolymer against copolymer with a second monomer |
| c) | regular (isotactic) against random (atactic) side groups |

**Unknown:** in each pair, the polymer that is more likely to crystallize, and why.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.x:
Each pair differs in only one structural feature, so each answer follows from one of the factors of Slides 26 and 27: the molecular structure (a), the copolymer sequence and the simplicity of the monomer (b), and the tacticity (c).

**Strategy.** For each pair, name the feature, say how it changes the regularity of the chain, and apply the rule of the slides.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.h: 1. a) Branched polyethylene against linear polyethylene [Session 19 Slides 22, 26-27]
chunks.x:
The branches are side chains that stick out of the backbone at irregular places. They keep the backbones apart and prevent them from lying side by side in the folded lamellae, so the packing is poorer. Slide 26 states that linear polymers have a higher amount of packing and a higher degree of crystallinity, and branched polymers a lower one; the table of Slide 27 gives "most probable" for linear and "sometimes" for branched.

**Answer: linear polyethylene.**

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.h: 2. b) Polyethylene against a polyethylene-polypropylene copolymer [Session 19 Slides 20, 27]
chunks.x:
Polyethylene, $\mathrm{-[CH_2{-}CH_2]_n-}$, is the example of a symmetric and simple monomer ("Simple, YES" on Slide 27): every unit is the same and the chain is perfectly regular. In the copolymer, propylene units with a $\mathrm{CH_3}$ side group are inserted among the ethylene units. The statement does not say the type of copolymer; for a random sequence (the usual one) the $\mathrm{CH_3}$ groups appear at random places and the chain is irregular, so the copolymer is amorphous (Slide 27: random and graft copolymers are amorphous). Even an alternating or block copolymer has only "some crystallinity" according to the same slide, less than the regular homopolymer.

**Answer: polyethylene.**

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.h: 3. c) Isotactic polypropylene against atactic polypropylene [Session 19 Slides 18-19, 26]
chunks.x:
In polypropylene, $\mathrm{-[CH_2{-}CH(CH_3)]_n-}$, the $\mathrm{CH_3}$ groups can be all on the same side (isotactic), alternating (syndiotactic) or at random (atactic) [Session 19 Slide 18]. The isotactic chain repeats the same arrangement all along, so its segments fit together; the atactic chain has no pattern and cannot pack. Slide 26 states that atactic polymers are amorphous and isotactic or syndiotactic ones are probably crystalline, and Slide 19 adds that atactic polypropylene is a wax-type material with very bad mechanical properties.

**Answer: isotactic polypropylene.**

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.x:
- **One rule behind the three answers.** In every pair the polymer chosen is the more regular one: no branches, one kind of unit, one arrangement of the side groups. Regularity is what lets chains fold into lamellae.
- **Consistency with the density.** The crystalline polymer is denser than the amorphous one [Session 19 Slide 24], so in each pair the chosen polymer would show the higher density for the same cooling, which is how the difference would be measured (the formula of Slide 25).
- **Limit cases.** A crosslinked polymer is the extreme of irregular packing: "almost never" crystalline [Session 19 Slide 27]. At the other extreme, a linear, isotactic homopolymer of a simple monomer is the most likely to crystallize.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.x: Crystallinity is a question of geometry: chains crystallize when they can lie parallel and close together. Branches, foreign units and random side groups all break that order. The practical consequence is that the more crystalline member of each pair is also the denser, stiffer and stronger one with the higher melting temperature [Session 19 Slides 27, 43], which is why linear high-density polyethylene and isotactic polypropylene are the grades used for structural plastic parts.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-02 Which Polymer Crystallizes More Easily
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a) | linear PE (printed "Liner PE") | linear PE | agrees |
| b) | PE | PE | agrees |
| c) | isotactic PP (printed "Isostatic PP") | isotactic PP | agrees |

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x:
3. Assuming that a thermoplastic polymer can be produced by rolling (deformation) and casting (with fast cooling). Which one of the two methods will produce a polymer with higher strength? Explain your answer.
*(Solution: polymer produced by rolling)*

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x:
1. **Same polymer.** Both routes use the same thermoplastic (same chains, same molecular weight); only the processing differs.
2. **Rolling.** Rolling deforms the solid polymer, stretching it in the rolling direction.
3. **Casting with fast cooling.** The polymer is poured as a melt into a mould and cooled quickly, so the chains solidify in the arrangement they had in the liquid.
4. **What the slides say about strength.** Deforming a polymer can increase its strength, because the chains become oriented and interact more effectively; the strength also increases with the degree of crystallinity [Session 19 Slide 43]. An oriented polymer is significantly stronger and stiffer than an isotropic one [Session 19 Slide 39].

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x:
| Route | State of the chains |
| :--- | :--- |
| Rolling | chains aligned by the deformation |
| Fast-cooled casting | chains frozen as random coils, little time to crystallize |

**Unknown:** the route that gives the higher strength, and why.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x:
The strength of a thermoplastic is set by how the chains resist sliding past each other: aligned, well-packed chains share the load through many secondary bonds along their length, while random coils carry it through few contacts and entanglements. The cold-drawing and strain-hardening stages of the tensile test show the same mechanism inside one specimen [Session 19 Slides 38-39].

**Strategy.**
1. Describe the chain arrangement after each route.
2. Compare the two with the factors of Slide 43.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x: The deformation unravels the coiled chains and aligns them parallel to the rolling direction, as in the cold drawing of the tensile test (Slide 38: the chains unravel, aligning themselves parallel to the direction of the applied stress). The aligned chains lie closer and interact more effectively, so more secondary bonds must be broken for them to slide; in a semicrystalline polymer the lamellae are also tilted and their block segments aligned with the axis (Slide 41). This is the strain hardening of Slide 39: the oriented polymer is significantly stronger and stiffer.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x: In the melt the chains are random coils. Fast cooling gives them little time to fold into lamellae before the temperature drops below $T_g$ and the segments freeze (Slide 28): a faster cooling gives smaller crystals (Slide 26), and the chains that have not crystallized stay as an amorphous, isotropic tangle. That the fast cooling also lowers the degree of crystallinity is the author's reading of Slides 26 and 28 (the slides state the effect on the crystal size).

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x:
| | Rolling | Fast-cooled casting |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Chain orientation | aligned (anisotropic) | random (isotropic) |
| Interaction between chains | more effective | less effective |
| Crystallinity | kept or increased by alignment | reduced by the fast cooling |
| Strength | higher | lower |

**Answer: the polymer produced by rolling.**

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x:
- **Direction.** The gain in strength is in the direction of the orientation. Crystallization and orientation raise the anisotropy [Session 19 Slides 23-24], so a rolled sheet is strongest along the rolling direction; in the transverse direction the gain is smaller (extension).
- **Limit of the deformation.** Orientation can only be pushed until no further chain alignment is possible; then the polymer fractures [Session 19 Slide 40]. Rolling is therefore applied with a moderate reduction, not to failure.
- **Same mechanism in fibres.** Fibres are made with linear, oriented, crystalline chains and are the strongest form of a polymer [Session 20 Slide 16], which confirms the role of orientation.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x: In metals cold work raises the strength by multiplying dislocations; in a thermoplastic the deformation raises it by aligning the chains. The cast and quenched polymer is the opposite case: its chains are frozen as a disordered tangle, with the least effective interaction between them. Drawing and rolling are the reason why stretched films and fibres are much stronger than moulded blocks of the same polymer.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-03 Rolling or Fast-Cooled Casting for Higher Strength
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Stronger route | polymer produced by rolling | rolling | agrees; chain orientation, Session 19 Slides 39 and 43 |

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.x:
4. Which of the following polymer pairs has higher melting temperature? Why?
a) Branched PE with <Mn> = 850 000 g/mol; Linear PE with <Mn> = 850 000 g/mol
b) PTFE with density equal to 2.14 g/cm³ and <Mw> = 600 000 g/mol; PTFE with density equal to 2.20 g/cm³ and <Mw> = 600 000 g/mol.
c) Syndiotactic PVC with <Mn> = 500 000 g/mol; Linear PE with <Mn> = 225 000 g/mol.
d) Linear and syndiotactic PP with <Mw> = 750 000 g/mol; Atactic and linear PP with <Mw> = 500 000 g/mol.
*(Solution: a) Linear PE > Branched PE; b) PTFE 2.20 > PTFE 2.14; c) PVC > PE; d) Syndiotactic PP > Atactic PP)*

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.x:
1. **Where $T_m$ comes from.** $T_m$ is the transition of the **crystalline** regions [Session 19 Slide 28]: it is the temperature at which the ordered, folded chains of the lamellae come apart. A polymer with no crystalline regions has no melting temperature, only a glass transition [Session 19 Slide 23].
2. **Factors that raise $T_m$.** More crystallinity raises $T_m$ [Session 19 Slide 27]; $T_m$ rises with the molecular weight and levels off for long chains [Session 19 Slide 30]; polar groups increase the intermolecular forces [Session 19 Slide 43] and the ordering [Session 19 Slide 27].
3. **Crystallinity and structure.** Linear and regular (isotactic or syndiotactic) chains crystallize, branched chains less, atactic chains not at all [Session 19 Slides 26-27]; the crystalline polymer is denser than the amorphous one [Session 19 Slide 24].
4. **Reference values.** Melting points printed on Session 20 Slide 8: polyethylene 110 – 137 °C, polyvinyl chloride about 204 °C, polypropylene 165 – 177 °C.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.x:
| Pair | Same in both | Different |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a) PE | $M_n = 850\,000$ g/mol | branched against linear |
| b) PTFE | $M_w = 600\,000$ g/mol | density 2.14 against 2.20 g/cm³ |
| c) | (different polymers) | syndiotactic PVC, $M_n = 500\,000$ g/mol, against linear PE, $M_n = 225\,000$ g/mol |
| d) PP | linear | syndiotactic, $M_w = 750\,000$ g/mol, against atactic, $M_w = 500\,000$ g/mol |

**Unknown:** in each pair, the polymer with the higher $T_m$, and why.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.x:
In each pair, find which polymer has more (or better) crystalline regions and stronger forces between its chains: that one needs more thermal energy to break up its crystals. The molecular weight acts in the same direction when it differs, but all the weights here are far above the range where Slide 30 shows a strong effect.

**Strategy.** For each pair: identify the controlling factor, apply the rule of the slides, and compare with the printed melting points where they exist.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.h: 1. a) Branched PE against linear PE, same $M_n$
chunks.x:
The molecular weights are equal, so only the structure differs. The branches keep the chains from packing, so the branched PE has a lower degree of crystallinity and less perfect crystals [Session 19 Slides 26-27]; more crystallinity means a higher $T_m$ [Session 19 Slide 27].

**Answer: the linear PE.** (The range 110 – 137 °C printed for polyethylene on Session 20 Slide 8 covers both kinds; that the low end belongs to the branched, low-density PE and the high end to the linear, high-density PE is an extension.)

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.h: 2. b) PTFE of density 2.14 against 2.20 g/cm³, same $M_w$
chunks.x:
Same polymer and same molecular weight, so the density measures the crystallinity: the crystalline regions are denser than the amorphous ones [Session 19 Slide 24], and by the formula of Slide 25 the degree of crystallinity grows with the actual density $\rho_s$ for fixed $\rho_c$ and $\rho_a$:

$$X_c = \frac{\rho_c(\rho_s - \rho_a)}{\rho_s(\rho_c - \rho_a)} \qquad \frac{dX_c}{d\rho_s} = \frac{\rho_c\,\rho_a}{\rho_s^{2}(\rho_c - \rho_a)} > 0$$

(the derivative, by the quotient rule on $(\rho_s - \rho_a)/\rho_s = 1 - \rho_a/\rho_s$, is an extension). The denser PTFE is more crystalline and therefore has the higher $T_m$ [Session 19 Slide 27].

**Answer: the PTFE of density 2.20 g/cm³.**

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.h: 3. c) Syndiotactic PVC against linear PE
chunks.x:
Three factors point the same way:
- **Polarity.** PVC carries a polar C-Cl bond in every unit, $\mathrm{-[CH_2{-}CHCl]_n-}$; polar groups increase the intermolecular forces [Session 19 Slide 43] and the ordering [Session 19 Slide 27], so more energy is needed to separate the chains. PE has only C-H bonds and van der Waals forces.
- **Regularity.** The PVC is syndiotactic, so it can crystallize [Session 19 Slide 26].
- **Molecular weight.** $500\,000 > 225\,000$ g/mol, and $T_m$ rises with $M$ [Session 19 Slide 30], although at these weights the effect is small.

The printed melting points confirm it: about 204 °C for PVC against 110 – 137 °C for PE [Session 20 Slide 8]. The same side group raises $T_g$ from $-110$ °C (HDPE) to 87 °C (PVC) [Session 19 Slide 29].

**Answer: the syndiotactic PVC.**

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.h: 4. d) Linear syndiotactic PP against linear atactic PP
chunks.x:
The syndiotactic chain has its $\mathrm{CH_3}$ groups in a regular alternating pattern and can crystallize; the atactic chain has them at random and is amorphous [Session 19 Slides 18, 26]. An amorphous polymer has no crystalline regions, so it has no true melting temperature, only $T_g$ [Session 19 Slides 23, 28]: Slide 19 describes atactic PP as a wax-type material. The higher molecular weight of the syndiotactic PP (750 000 against 500 000 g/mol) adds in the same direction [Session 19 Slide 30].

**Answer: the syndiotactic PP.**

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.x:
- **Units of the derivative in b).** $[\rho_c\rho_a/(\rho_s^2(\rho_c - \rho_a))] = (\text{g/cm}^3)^2/(\text{g/cm}^3)^3 = \text{cm}^3/\text{g}$, so $dX_c = (\text{cm}^3/\text{g})\,d\rho_s$ is dimensionless, as a fraction must be.
- **Molecular weight.** In pairs a) and b) the weights are equal, so they cannot be the reason; in c) and d) the weight differs but in the same direction as the structural factor, so the answers do not depend on how large its effect is.
- **Limit.** A fully amorphous polymer ($X_c = 0$, case of the atactic PP) has no $T_m$ at all; its stiffness falls at $T_g$ and it softens progressively [Session 19 Slide 45].

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.x: The melting temperature measures how well the chains are packed in crystals and how strongly they attract each other. Linear, regular, polar chains pack well and attract each other strongly; branched, random or non-polar chains do not. This is why the polymers chosen for parts that must work hot are the linear, regular and polar ones, such as the engineering thermoplastics of Session 20 Slide 9 (nylon 6,6, polycarbonate, polysulfone, with melting points of 250 to 315 °C).

chunks.t: Problem - T9-04 Which Polymer Has the Higher Melting Temperature
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a) | linear PE > branched PE | linear PE | agrees |
| b) | PTFE 2.20 > PTFE 2.14 | PTFE 2.20 g/cm³ | agrees |
| c) | PVC > PE | syndiotactic PVC | agrees; about 204 °C against 110 – 137 °C on Session 20 Slide 8 |
| d) | syndiotactic PP > atactic PP | syndiotactic PP | agrees |

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.x:
5. Draw three representations of the logarithm of the Young's modulus versus temperature for an amorphous polymer.
a) In one of those show how the behavior changes when the molecular weight increases.
b) In another diagram, show the behavior changes when crosslinking increases.
c) If this polymer is processed so that it has some crystallinity, show how the Young's modulus changes with temperature.

The sheet prints no solution for this problem.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.x:
1. **The base curve.** An amorphous polymer has only a glass transition [Session 19 Slide 23]. Its modulus (measured, for example, as the relaxation modulus $E_r(10)$ at 10 s) goes through five regions as the temperature rises: **glassy**, about $10^3$ MPa, below $T_g$; **leathery**, the steep drop of about three decades around $T_g$; **rubbery**, a plateau; **rubbery flow**; and **viscous flow** (liquid) [Session 19 Slide 49].
2. **Log scale.** The modulus changes by several orders of magnitude, so it is plotted as $\log E$; the drop at $T_g$ is then a step and the plateaus are horizontal lines [Session 19 Slides 45-46].
3. **What changes each curve.** Higher molecular weight means more entanglements [Session 19 Slide 43]; crosslinks are covalent bonds between chains [Session 19 Slide 22]; crystalline regions melt only at $T_m$ [Session 19 Slide 28].
4. **Sketches.** The statement asks for qualitative drawings; the figures of the slides are used as the drawings, and no numbers are needed.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.x:
| Diagram | Parameter that changes |
| :--- | :--- |
| a) | molecular weight (entanglement density) |
| b) | degree of crosslinking |
| c) | degree of crystallinity |

**Unknown:** the three diagrams of $\log E$ against $T$ and the explanation of each change.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.x:
The modulus of a polymer is high when the chain segments cannot move (glass) and low when they can (rubber, liquid). Each structural change of the statement adds a different kind of obstacle to that motion above $T_g$, so each one acts on a different part of the base curve.

**Strategy.**
1. Draw the base curve of the amorphous polymer and name its regions.
2. For each case, say which region changes, in which direction and why, and give the diagram of the slides.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.h: 1. Base curve of the amorphous polymer [Session 19 Slide 49]
chunks.x: Below $T_g$ the segments are frozen and the modulus is high and nearly flat (glassy region). At $T_g$ the segments of the amorphous regions start to move [Session 19 Slide 28] and the modulus drops by about three orders of magnitude (leathery region). Above it the entanglements hold the chains together for a while, which gives the rubbery plateau; at higher temperatures whole chains slide past each other (rubbery flow) and finally the polymer flows as a viscous liquid.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.x: The glassy region and the position of the drop hardly change ($T_g$ rises only slightly with $M$ and levels off for long chains, Slide 30). The change is **above $T_g$**: longer chains have more entanglements (Slide 43), which act as temporary links, so the rubbery plateau is **longer** and the flow region moves to **higher temperatures**. The slide draws it as curves that stay higher and fall later for higher entanglement density and increasing molecular weight.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.x: Crosslinks are permanent covalent bonds, so the chains can never slide past each other: the **flow regions disappear**, and the plateau above $T_g$ stays up to the temperature at which the polymer degrades. The more crosslinks, the **higher the plateau** and the **smaller the drop** at $T_g$; with heavy crosslinking (a thermoset) the modulus hardly falls at all and $T_g$ moves up. Slide 46 draws no, slight, increasing and heavy crosslinking; curve B of Slide 49 (lightly crosslinked atactic polystyrene) shows the flat rubbery plateau with no flow.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.x:
- **Order of magnitude.** On the log scale the glassy modulus of polystyrene is about $10^3$ MPa, about 1 GPa, inside the range 0.007 – 4 GPa of polymers [Session 19 Slides 32, 49]. The plateau is about three decades lower, about 1 MPa, the modulus of a rubber.
- **Limit cases.** No crosslinks and no crystals: the base curve, which flows. Infinite crosslinking: a rigid network with no drop. 100 % crystallinity: no glass transition, one drop at $T_m$. The three diagrams go continuously from the base curve to these limits.
- **Time and rate.** The modulus is measured at a fixed time; at a higher strain rate the whole curve moves to higher temperatures, because a higher rate has the same effect as a lower temperature [Session 19 Slide 48].

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.x: The three changes act on different parts of the curve: the molecular weight only delays the flow, the crosslinks remove the flow and lift the plateau, and the crystallinity props the modulus up between $T_g$ and $T_m$. In use this decides the working temperature: an amorphous thermoplastic must work below $T_g$, a semicrystalline one can work up to near $T_m$, an elastomer works on its rubbery plateau and a thermoset keeps its stiffness until it degrades.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-05 Log Modulus Against Temperature for an Amorphous Polymer
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a) Molecular weight | not printed on the sheet | longer rubbery plateau, flow at higher $T$ | consistent with Session 19 Slides 30, 43 and 45 |
| b) Crosslinking | not printed on the sheet | higher plateau, smaller drop, no flow | consistent with Session 19 Slides 46 and 49 |
| c) Crystallinity | not printed on the sheet | smaller drop at $T_g$, plateau up to $T_m$ | consistent with Session 19 Slides 45 and 49 |

chunks.t: Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
chunks.x:
6. Determine the degree of crystallinity of polypropylene with density 0.853g/cm³, given that the densities of amorphous and totally crystalline polypropylene are 0.83 and 0.947 g/cm³ respectively. Represent the change in the elastic modulus with temperature for this polymer, a completely amorphous polymer and a completely crystalline polymer.
*(Solution: 21.8%)*

chunks.t: Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
chunks.x:
1. **Two-phase sample.** The polypropylene is a mixture of crystalline regions of density $\rho_c$ and amorphous regions of density $\rho_a$ [Session 19 Slide 24], and the degree of crystallinity is the mass fraction of crystalline polymer, given by the formula of Session 19 Slide 25 (its derivation from the additive volumes is in the theory note, Section 10.3).
2. **Modulus curves.** The modulus against temperature for 100 % amorphous, 50 % / 50 % and 100 % crystalline polymers is the figure of Session 19 Slide 45.
3. **Temperatures of polypropylene.** $T_g = -20$ °C (table of Session 19 Slide 29; the panel of the same slide prints $-15$ °C) and $T_m = 165$ – $177$ °C [Session 20 Slide 8].

chunks.t: Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
chunks.x:
| Quantity | Symbol | Value |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| Density of the sample | $\rho_s$ | 0.853 g/cm³ |
| Density of amorphous PP | $\rho_a$ | 0.83 g/cm³ |
| Density of totally crystalline PP | $\rho_c$ | 0.947 g/cm³ |

**Unknowns:** the degree of crystallinity, and the modulus-temperature curves of this PP, of an amorphous polymer and of a crystalline polymer.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
chunks.x:
[Session 19 Slide 25]:

$$\%\ \text{crystallinity} = \frac{\rho_c(\rho_s - \rho_a)}{\rho_s(\rho_c - \rho_a)} \times 100$$

The sample density lies between $\rho_a$ and $\rho_c$, and the formula places it on the scale between the two in terms of mass.

**Strategy.**
1. Check that $\rho_a < \rho_s < \rho_c$.
2. Evaluate the numerator and the denominator separately and divide.
3. Place the result among the curves of Slide 45.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
chunks.x:
$$\rho_a = 0.83 < \rho_s = 0.853 < \rho_c = 0.947\ \text{g/cm}^3$$

so the result must lie between 0 and 100 %, and since $\rho_s$ is much closer to $\rho_a$, near the amorphous end.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
chunks.x:
- **Completely amorphous polymer:** high glassy modulus below $T_g$, a drop of several decades at $T_g$, a short plateau and the fall to flow; there is no $T_m$.
- **Completely crystalline polymer:** no glass transition; the modulus stays high and falls only at $T_m$.
- **This polypropylene, 21.8 % crystalline:** its curve lies between the amorphous curve and the 50 % / 50 % curve of the slide. At $T_g$ (about $-20$ °C) it drops, but less than the amorphous polymer, because 21.8 % of its mass stays crystalline; between $T_g$ and $T_m$ it keeps an intermediate plateau held by the crystallites; at $T_m$ (165 – 177 °C) the crystals melt and the modulus falls to the flow region.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
chunks.x:
- **Units.** Numerator and denominator are both products of two densities, $(\text{g/cm}^3)^2$, so the ratio is dimensionless.
- **Limits.** $\rho_s = \rho_a$ gives $0$ and $\rho_s = \rho_c$ gives $\rho_c(\rho_c - \rho_a)/[\rho_c(\rho_c - \rho_a)] = 1$, that is 100 %.
- **Mass against volume fraction.** The volume fraction would be $(\rho_s - \rho_a)/(\rho_c - \rho_a) = 0.023/0.117 = 19.7\ \%$; the mass fraction is larger, $\times\rho_c/\rho_s = 0.947/0.853 = 1.110$, because the crystalline regions are denser (extension).

chunks.t: Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
chunks.x: Only about one fifth of this polypropylene is crystalline. Room temperature lies above its $T_g$, so the amorphous four fifths are rubbery and the stiffness at room temperature comes from the crystalline fifth: a polymer with this low crystallinity is soft and tough rather than stiff. A more crystalline grade (isotactic PP, slowly cooled) would have a higher density and a higher plateau, closer to the crystalline curve.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-06 Degree of Crystallinity of Polypropylene from Its Density
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Degree of crystallinity | 21.8 % | 21.824 % | agrees |
| Modulus curves | not printed on the sheet | between the amorphous and the 50 % / 50 % curves of Slide 45 | consistent with Session 19 Slide 45 |

chunks.t: Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
chunks.x:
7. A thermoplastic polymer has been analyzed, obtaining the following fractions of weight wᵢ shown in the table for the following ranges of molecular weight in the table:
a) Calculate the weight-average molecular weight
b) Calculate de polydispersity assuming that the number average molecular weight is 12880 g/mol.
c) If the polymerization degree is 230 and assuming that the polymer is an alkene (CₙH₂ₙ) with the general formula shown below, determine the value of X in the structural formula below. (Atomic mass: H = 1, C = 12).
d) Explain if the crystallinity of the polymer should be higher or lower than the crystallinity of polyethylene.

*(Solution: a) Mw = 15500 g/mol; b) PDI = 1.2; c) X = 1, polybutadiene; d) lower)*

The sheet prints "Calculate de polydispersity". The structural formula is a repeat unit $\mathrm{-CH_2{-}CH-}$ with the side chain $\mathrm{(CH_2)_X{-}CH_3}$ hanging from the CH, in brackets with subscript $n$.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
chunks.x:
1. **Mean of each range.** Each range is represented by its midpoint $M_i$, as in the example of Session 19 Slides 14-15.
2. **Averages.** $M_w = \sum w_i M_i$ and the index of polydispersion $I = M_w/M_n$ [Session 19 Slide 13]; the sheet calls it PDI.
3. **Degree of polymerization.** The polymerization degree 230 is the number average $X_n = M_n/M_0$ [Session 19 Slide 12], with $M_n = 12\,880$ g/mol from part b).
4. **Repeat unit.** Counting the atoms of the drawn unit: $\mathrm{CH_2}$, $\mathrm{CH}$, $X$ groups $\mathrm{CH_2}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3}$.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
chunks.x:
[Session 19 Slides 12-13]:

$$M_w = \sum w_i M_i \qquad I = \frac{M_w}{M_n} \qquad M_0 = \frac{M_n}{X_n}$$

**Strategy.**
1. Weight each midpoint by its weight fraction and add.
2. Divide by the given $M_n$.
3. Get $M_0$ from $M_n$ and $X_n$, write $M_0$ of the drawn unit as a function of $X$ and solve.
4. Compare the chain with polyethylene using the factors of crystallinity of Slides 26-27.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
chunks.x:
Molecular weight of the repeat unit from the degree of polymerization:

$$M_0 = \frac{M_n}{X_n} = \frac{12\,880\ \text{g/mol}}{230} = 56.0\ \text{g/mol}$$

Atoms of the drawn unit: carbon, $1\ (\mathrm{CH_2}) + 1\ (\mathrm{CH}) + X\ (\mathrm{CH_2}\ \text{groups}) + 1\ (\mathrm{CH_3}) = X + 3$; hydrogen, $2 + 1 + 2X + 3 = 2X + 6$. The unit is $\mathrm{C}_{X+3}\mathrm{H}_{2X+6}$, that is $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}$ with $n = X + 3$, an alkene formula as the statement says. Its molecular weight:

$$M_0 = 12(X + 3) + 1(2X + 6) = 14X + 42\ \text{g/mol}$$

Setting it equal to 56.0 g/mol:

$$14X + 42 = 56 \ \Rightarrow\ 14X = 14 \ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf{X = 1}$$

The repeat unit is $\mathrm{-CH_2{-}CH(CH_2CH_3)-}$, $\mathrm{C_4H_8}$ (56 g/mol): a vinyl polymer with an ethyl side group, the polymer of 1-butene, usually called poly(1-butene) or polybutene (the name is an extension; it is not on the slides).

chunks.t: Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
chunks.h: 4. d) Crystallinity compared with polyethylene [Session 19 Slides 26-27]
chunks.x:
Polyethylene, $\mathrm{-[CH_2{-}CH_2]_n-}$, is the example of a simple, symmetric monomer that crystallizes easily (Slide 27). This polymer has an ethyl side group on every second carbon:
- the side group is bulkier and makes the unit more complex, and complex monomeric structures lower the degree of crystallinity (Slide 26);
- the CH carbon carries two different groups, so the polymer can be atactic, and atactic polymers are amorphous (Slide 26); only an isotactic or syndiotactic grade could crystallize, and still with more difficulty than PE.

**Answer: lower than polyethylene.**

chunks.t: Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
chunks.x:
- **Units.** $w_i$ is dimensionless, so $M_w$ is in g/mol; $I$ and $X_n$ are pure numbers; $M_0 = M_n/X_n$ is in g/mol.
- **$M_w \ge M_n$.** $15\,500 > 12\,880$ g/mol, so $I = 1.203 > 1$, as it must be for a polymer with a distribution of lengths.
- **Back-substitution.** $230\times56\ \text{g/mol} = 12\,880$ g/mol, exactly the given $M_n$.
- **Limit.** $X = 0$ would give $\mathrm{C_3H_6}$ (42 g/mol), polypropylene; each extra $\mathrm{CH_2}$ adds 14 g/mol, so only $X = 1$ matches 56 g/mol.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
chunks.x:
The data describe a moderately polydisperse polymer ($I = 1.2$) of about 230 units per chain, whose unit is polypropylene with one more $\mathrm{CH_2}$ in the side group. The longer side group makes the chain less regular than polyethylene and polypropylene, so it packs less well and is less crystalline, which also means a lower density, stiffness and melting point than polyethylene of similar chain length.

Discrepancy with the official solution
The key gives "X = 1, polybutadiene". The value $X = 1$ agrees, but the drawn unit with $X = 1$ is $\mathrm{C_4H_8}$, a saturated unit with an ethyl side group (the polymer of 1-butene), not polybutadiene. Polybutadiene is made from 1,3-butadiene, $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}CH{=}CH_2}$ [Session 20 Slide 15]; its repeat unit keeps one double bond, $\mathrm{C_4H_6}$ = 54 g/mol, does not follow the $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}$ formula of the statement, and $230\times54 = 12\,420$ g/mol does not give the stated $M_n = 12\,880$ g/mol. The name in the key is therefore not consistent with the statement; the computed polymer is the polymer of 1-butene.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-07 Weight Average Polydispersity and Repeat Unit of a Polyalkene
chunks.x:
| Item | Official | Computed | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a) $M_w$ | 15 500 g/mol | 15 500 g/mol | agrees |
| b) PDI | 1.2 | 1.203 | agrees |
| c) $X$ | 1, polybutadiene | 1, unit $\mathrm{C_4H_8}$ (polymer of 1-butene) | $X$ agrees; the name does not (see the warning) |
| d) Crystallinity | lower | lower than PE | agrees |

chunks.t: Problem - T9-08 Number and Weight Averages and Monomer of an Unknown Polymer
chunks.x:
8. A polymer sample with unknown molecular weight has been analyzed and the following results were obtained.
a) Calculate the number-average and weight-average molecular weight.
b) If the number average degree of polymerization is 211, calculate the molecular weight of the monomeric unit.
c) Which of these polymers correspond to: PE, PVC, PTFE, PP, PS, PMMA, Nylon 66, PC.
d) What is the weight-average degree of polymerization?

*(Solution: a) Mn = 47720, Mw = 53720; b) M0 = 226.2; c) Nylon 66; d) Xw = 238)*

chunks.t: Problem - T9-08 Number and Weight Averages and Monomer of an Unknown Polymer
chunks.x:
1. **Mean of each range.** Each range is represented by its midpoint $M_i$ [Session 19 Slides 14-15].
2. **Averages.** $M_n = \sum x_i M_i$, $M_w = \sum w_i M_i$ [Session 19 Slide 13], and $X_n = M_n/M_0$ [Session 19 Slide 12].
3. **Weight-average degree of polymerization.** By analogy with $X_n$, $X_w = M_w/M_0$ (this definition is an extension; the slides define only $X_n$).
4. **Repeat units of the candidates.** From Session 19 Slide 50 and Session 20 Slides 8-9: PE $\mathrm{C_2H_4}$, PVC $\mathrm{C_2H_3Cl}$, PTFE $\mathrm{C_2F_4}$, PP $\mathrm{C_3H_6}$, PS $\mathrm{C_8H_8}$, PMMA $\mathrm{C_5H_8O_2}$, nylon 6,6 $\mathrm{-[NH{-}(CH_2)_6{-}NH{-}CO{-}(CH_2)_4{-}CO]-}$ = $\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}N_2O_2}$, and polycarbonate $\mathrm{-[O{-}CO{-}O{-}C_6H_4{-}C(CH_3)_2{-}C_6H_4]-}$ = $\mathrm{C_{16}H_{14}O_3}$. Atomic masses C = 12, H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, F = 19, Cl = 35.5 g/mol (the sheet gives none for this problem; standard values).

chunks.t: Problem - T9-08 Number and Weight Averages and Monomer of an Unknown Polymer
Problem - T9-08 Number and Weight Averages and Monomer of an Unknown Polymer
chunks.x:
[Session 19 Slides 12-13]:

$$M_n = \sum x_i M_i \qquad M_w = \sum w_i M_i \qquad M_0 = \frac{M_n}{X_n}$$

**Strategy.**
1. Compute the two weighted sums.
2. Divide $M_n$ by $X_n$ to get the molecular weight of the repeat unit.
3. Compute $M_0$ of every candidate and pick the one that matches.
4. Divide $M_w$ by $M_0$.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-08 Number and Weight Averages and Monomer of an Unknown Polymer
chunks.h: 1. a) Number-average and weight-average molecular weights [Session 19 Slide 13]

chunks.t: Problem - T9-08 Number and Weight Averages and Monomer of an Unknown Polymer
Problem - T9-08 Number and Weight Averages and Monomer of an Unknown Polymer

$$X_w = \frac{M_w}{M_0} = \frac{53\,720\ \text{g/mol}}{226.16\ \text{g/mol}} = 237.5 \approx \mathbf{238}$$

(with the rounded $M_0 = 226$ g/mol of nylon 6,6, $X_w = 237.7$, also 238).

chunks.t: Problem - T9-08 Number and Weight Averages and Monomer of an Unknown Polymer
chunks.x:
- **Units.** $x_i$ and $w_i$ are dimensionless, so $M_n$ and $M_w$ are in g/mol; $X_n$ and $X_w$ are pure numbers.
- **$M_w \ge M_n$.** $53\,720 > 47\,720$ g/mol; the index of polydispersion is $I = 53\,720/47\,720 = 1.126$, a narrow distribution.
- **Consistency of the two columns (extension).** The weight fraction of a range follows from its number fraction as $w_i = x_i M_i/M_n$: for 44 000 – 56 000 g/mol, $0.28\times50\,000/47\,720 = 0.293$, against 0.29 in the table. Computed in the same way from the $x_i$, $M_w = \sum x_i M_i^2/\sum x_i M_i = 53\,978$ g/mol, 0.5 % above the 53 720 g/mol of the $w_i$ column, so the two columns describe the same sample within the rounding of the table.
- **Second candidate.** The closest other candidate, polycarbonate (254 g/mol), would need $X_n = 47\,720/254 = 188$, not 211.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-09 Densities of Crystalline and Amorphous Polypropylene
chunks.x:
9.- The densities of amorphous and totally crystalline polypropylene are given in the table below.
a) Write the formula of polypropylene and justify whether it can present tacticity.
b) Calculate the density of completely crystalline and completely amorphous polypropylene.
c) Deterrmine the density of a sample that is 74.6% crystalline.

*(Solution: b) ρa = 0.84 g/cm³, ρc = 0.946 g/cm³; c) ρ = 0.917 g/cm³)*

The sheet prints "Deterrmine". The first sentence says that the table gives the densities of amorphous and totally crystalline polypropylene, but the table gives the density and the crystallinity of two samples, and part b) asks for the two densities: they are the unknowns.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-09 Densities of Crystalline and Amorphous Polypropylene
chunks.x:
1. **Same polypropylene.** Both samples are the same polymer, so they share the same $\rho_c$ and $\rho_a$ and differ only in their degree of crystallinity.
2. **Crystallinity formula.** The degree of crystallinity (mass fraction) is $X_c = \rho_c(\rho_s - \rho_a)/[\rho_s(\rho_c - \rho_a)]$ [Session 19 Slide 25].
3. **Repeat unit.** Polypropylene is $\mathrm{-[CH_2{-}CH(CH_3)]_n-}$ [Session 19 Slide 50].

chunks.t: Problem - T9-09 Densities of Crystalline and Amorphous Polypropylene
chunks.x:
| Sample | $\rho_s$ (g/cm³) | $X_c$ |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0.904 | 0.628 |
| 2 | 0.895 | 0.544 |
| 3 (part c) | unknown | 0.746 |

**Unknowns:** (a) the formula and its tacticity; (b) $\rho_c$ and $\rho_a$; (c) $\rho_s$ for $X_c = 0.746$.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-09 Densities of Crystalline and Amorphous Polypropylene
chunks.x:
The formula of Slide 25 has two unknowns, $\rho_c$ and $\rho_a$, and each sample gives one equation, so two samples fix both. The formula is not linear in the densities, but it becomes linear in the specific volumes $1/\rho$. Multiply both sides by $\rho_s(\rho_c - \rho_a)$ and divide by $\rho_s\rho_c\rho_a$:

$$X_c\left(\frac{1}{\rho_a} - \frac{1}{\rho_c}\right) = \frac{1}{\rho_a} - \frac{1}{\rho_s} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{\rho_s} = \frac{X_c}{\rho_c} + \frac{1 - X_c}{\rho_a}$$

which says that the specific volume of the sample is the mass-weighted mean of the specific volumes of its crystalline and amorphous parts. With $u = 1/\rho_c$ and $v = 1/\rho_a$ each sample gives a linear equation.

**Strategy.**
1. Write the formula of polypropylene and look at its asymmetric carbon.
2. Write the two linear equations in $u$ and $v$ and solve them.
3. Use the same relation with $X_c = 0.746$.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-09 Densities of Crystalline and Amorphous Polypropylene
chunks.x:
$$\mathrm{-[CH_2{-}CH(CH_3)]_n-}$$

Every second carbon of the chain carries a $\mathrm{CH_3}$ side group and an H, so it has four different neighbours (H, $\mathrm{CH_3}$ and the two chain segments). The $\mathrm{CH_3}$ group can be placed on one side or the other of the chain each time a unit is added: polypropylene is a vinyl polymer $\mathrm{H_2C{=}CH{-}R}$ with R = $\mathrm{CH_3}$, so **it can present tacticity**: isotactic, syndiotactic or atactic, as drawn on Slide 19.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-09 Densities of Crystalline and Amorphous Polypropylene
chunks.h: 2. b) Densities of crystalline and amorphous polypropylene
chunks.x:
Specific volumes of the samples:

$$\frac{1}{\rho_1} = \frac{1}{0.904\ \text{g/cm}^3} = 1.106195\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g} \qquad \frac{1}{\rho_2} = \frac{1}{0.895\ \text{g/cm}^3} = 1.117318\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g}$$

The two equations:

$$0.628\,u + 0.372\,v = 1.106195\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g} \qquad 0.544\,u + 0.456\,v = 1.117318\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g}$$

Subtracting the second from the first:

$$0.084\,u - 0.084\,v = -0.011124\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = u + 0.132426\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g}$$

Substituting in the first:

$$0.628\,u + 0.372\,(u + 0.132426) = u + 0.049262 = 1.106195 \quad\Rightarrow\quad u = 1.056932\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g}$$

$$v = 1.056932 + 0.132426 = 1.189358\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g}$$

Densities:

$$\rho_c = \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{1.056932\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g}} = \mathbf{0.9461\ g/cm^3} \qquad \rho_a = \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{1.189358\ \text{cm}^3/\text{g}} = \mathbf{0.8408\ g/cm^3}$$

chunks.t: Problem - T9-09 Densities of Crystalline and Amorphous Polypropylene
chunks.h: 3. c) Density of a 74.6 % crystalline sample

chunks.t: Problem - T9-09 Densities of Crystalline and Amorphous Polypropylene
chunks.x:
- **Back-substitution in the formula of Slide 25.** With $\rho_c = 0.94613$ and $\rho_a = 0.84079$ g/cm³: sample 1, $0.94613(0.904 - 0.84079)/[0.904(0.94613 - 0.84079)] = 0.628$; sample 2, $0.544$. Both data are recovered.
- **Order.** $\rho_a = 0.841 < 0.895 < 0.904 < 0.917 < \rho_c = 0.946$ g/cm³: the samples lie between the two limits, and the more crystalline the sample, the denser it is [Session 19 Slide 24].
- **Units.** $u$ and $v$ are specific volumes in cm³/g, the coefficients $X_c$ are dimensionless, and every term of the equations is in cm³/g.
- **Comparison with Problem T9-06.** That problem gives $\rho_a = 0.83$ and $\rho_c = 0.947$ g/cm³ for polypropylene; the values found here are close to them.

chunks.t: Problem - T9-09 Densities of Crystalline and Amorphous Polypropylene
chunks.x:
Two density measurements of samples of known crystallinity are enough to find the densities of the pure phases, which cannot be measured directly (a fully crystalline polypropylene cannot be made). The crystalline phase is about 12.5 % denser than the amorphous one, because the folded chains of the lamellae pack more closely than the random coils. Once $\rho_c$ and $\rho_a$ are known, the density of any sample gives its crystallinity, which is how the crystallinity of a polymer part is checked in practice.

Sensitivity of the result to rounding
The key rounds the densities to $\rho_a = 0.84$ and $\rho_c = 0.946$ g/cm³. Putting these rounded values back into the formula of Slide 25 gives 63.2 % and 54.8 % instead of the 62.8 % and 54.4 % of the table. This is not an error of the key: the two samples are close in density, so the system is ill-conditioned (determinant $0.628\times0.456 - 0.372\times0.544 = 0.084$), and the change of $0.0008$ g/cm³ in $\rho_a$ alone moves the crystallinity of sample 1 by 0.3 points (from 62.8 % to 63.1 %). With the unrounded $\rho_a = 0.8408$ g/cm³ the table is recovered exactly, and the density of part c) is 0.917 g/cm³ with either set.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.h: Bank P01 — Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the Part II problem of the 2019 Assessment Test II (Ni-Nb) and of the final of January 2017 (Ag-Sn). The A-B system is hypothetical. Method: Session 7, Slides 15-21 and 30-32; Session 8, Slides 6, 14-15 and 17. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
The figure shows the equilibrium phase diagram of a hypothetical binary system A-B (composition in wt% B). Every invariant temperature and the compositions of the phases on each invariant line are printed on the diagram.

a) Determine all the invariant reactions: type of reaction, temperature and composition of every phase involved.

b) For an alloy A-50 wt% B at 700 − ΔT °C, give the phases present with their compositions and amounts, and the microconstituents present with their amounts.

c) Sketch the microstructure of an alloy A-20 wt% B at 700 + ΔT °C and at 700 − ΔT °C, labelling every microconstituent and giving its amount.

d) Indicate whether the intermetallic compound γ melts congruently or incongruently, and give the maximum solubility of B in A and of A in B, with the temperature at which each is observed.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
#### Data read on the diagram

| Item | Value read on the figure |
| :--- | :--- |
| Melting point of A | 900 °C (left axis) |
| Melting point of B | 1050 °C (right axis) |
| Compound γ | vertical line at 60 wt% B, top of the liquidus at 1150 °C |
| Invariant line at 700 °C | α 10 wt% B, L 35 wt% B, γ 60 wt% B |
| Invariant line at 850 °C | γ 60 wt% B, L 78 wt% B, β 92 wt% B |
| Alloys | $C_0$ = 50 wt% B (part b), $C_0$ = 20 wt% B (part c) |

Unit conversion: a composition in wt% is a mass fraction times 100, so 50 wt% B means 0.50 kg of B per kg of alloy. The lever rule uses the ratio of two differences of compositions, so the fractions it gives are dimensionless mass fractions whether the compositions are written in wt% or as fractions. No formula of this problem needs kelvin, so the temperatures stay in °C.

#### Model

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
- **Invariant reactions** [Session 8 Slide 6]: three phases coexist on a horizontal line at a fixed temperature. On cooling, eutectic $L \rightarrow \alpha + \beta$ (a liquid field ends in a V on the line), peritectic $\alpha + L \rightarrow \beta$ (a solid field ends in an inverted V below the line), eutectoid $\gamma \rightarrow \alpha + \beta$ and peritectoid $\alpha + \beta \rightarrow \gamma$ in the solid state.
- **Tie line and lever rule** [Session 7 Slides 15-16]: in a two-phase field, the horizontal line through the alloy point gives the compositions of the two phases at its ends; each phase takes the arm on the side of the other phase, divided by the length of the tie line.
- **Microconstituents** [Session 7 Slides 30-32]: the primary (proeutectic) constituent is counted on the tie line just above the eutectic temperature, where the remaining liquid has the eutectic composition and becomes the eutectic; the total phases are counted on the tie line just below it.
- **Intermetallic compounds and melting** [Session 8 Slides 14-15, 17]: a stoichiometric compound is a vertical line; it melts congruently when it sits at a maximum of the liquidus (the liquid keeps its composition) and incongruently when it ends at a peritectic line.
- Hypotheses: equilibrium cooling, pressure fixed at 1 atm, values read on the figure as printed.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x: Look for the horizontal lines: each one joins three phases. Decide the type from the field that lies above the line and the shape of the boundaries that meet it.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
- 700 °C, eutectic: L (35 wt% B) → α (10 wt% B) + γ (60 wt% B).
- 850 °C, eutectic: L (78 wt% B) → γ (60 wt% B) + β (92 wt% B).
- The maximum of γ at 1150 °C is a congruent melting point, not a three-phase reaction.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
#### Find the three-phase lines on the diagram

The diagram has two horizontal lines, at 700 °C (from 10 to 60 wt% B) and at 850 °C (from 60 to 92 wt% B). By the Gibbs phase rule at constant pressure, $F = C - P + 1$ [Session 7 Slide 13], three phases in a two-component system leave $F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$, so a three-phase equilibrium can only appear as a horizontal line at one temperature with three fixed compositions. Those are the invariant reactions [Session 8 Slide 6].

#### Classify the line at 700 °C

Above the line, between 10 and 60 wt% B, there are two fields, α + L and γ + L, whose liquidus branches fall from 900 °C (pure A) and from 1150 °C (γ) and meet in a V at 35 wt% B on the line. Below the line there is the single two-solid field α + γ. A liquid that ends in a V on the line and gives two solids below it is a **eutectic** [Session 8 Slide 6]. Reading the three points on the figure, on cooling:

$$L\,(35\ \text{wt\% B}) \;\xrightarrow{\;700\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \alpha\,(10\ \text{wt\% B}) + \gamma\,(60\ \text{wt\% B}) \qquad \text{eutectic}$$

#### Classify the line at 850 °C

Between 60 and 92 wt% B the liquidus falls from the maximum of γ (1150 °C) and from the melting point of B (1050 °C) to a V at 78 wt% B on the line; below the line lies γ + β. Again a liquid gives two solids, so this is a second **eutectic**:

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
$$L\,(78\ \text{wt\% B}) \;\xrightarrow{\;850\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \gamma\,(60\ \text{wt\% B}) + \beta\,(92\ \text{wt\% B}) \qquad \text{eutectic}$$

#### Check that no other point is invariant

The melting points of A (900 °C) and B (1050 °C) and the maximum of γ (1150 °C) are points where one solid melts to a liquid of its own composition; they behave as one-component transformations ($F = 1 - 2 + 1 = 0$ with the composition fixed) and involve two phases, not three, so they are not invariant reactions of the binary system. Each eutectic temperature lies below the melting points of its two neighbouring solids (700 < 900 and 700 < 1150; 850 < 1150 and 850 < 1050), as a eutectic must.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x: Phases: tie line just below 700 °C, from α to γ. Microconstituents: tie line just above 700 °C, from the eutectic liquid to γ, because the primary γ forms before the eutectic.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
- Phases at 700 − ΔT °C: α (10 wt% B) 0.200 and γ (60 wt% B) 0.800.
- Microconstituents: primary γ 0.600 and eutectic (α + γ) 0.400.
- Inside the eutectic: eutectic α 0.200 and eutectic γ 0.200 of the alloy.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
#### Locate the alloy and derive the lever rule

The alloy, 50 wt% B, lies between the eutectic composition (35) and γ (60), so on cooling it first crosses the γ liquidus and forms primary γ. Just below 700 °C it lies in the α + γ field. On a tie line with phases α and γ the two mass balances are, for the alloy and for B [Session 7 Slide 16]:

$$W_\alpha + W_\gamma = 1 \qquad W_\alpha C_\alpha + W_\gamma C_\gamma = C_0$$

Substituting $W_\gamma = 1 - W_\alpha$ in the second balance:

$$W_\alpha C_\alpha + (1 - W_\alpha) C_\gamma = C_0$$

$$W_\alpha (C_\alpha - C_\gamma) = C_0 - C_\gamma$$

Dividing by $(C_\alpha - C_\gamma)$ and changing the sign of numerator and denominator:

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_\gamma - C_0}{C_\gamma - C_\alpha} \qquad W_\gamma = 1 - W_\alpha = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_\gamma - C_\alpha}$$

This is the lever rule: each phase takes the arm on the side of the other phase.

#### Apply it to the phases just below 700 °C

Tie line read on the figure: $C_\alpha$ = 10 wt% B, $C_\gamma$ = 60 wt% B, length 60 − 10 = 50 wt% B.

$$W_\alpha = \frac{60 - 50}{60 - 10} = \frac{10}{50} = 0.200 \qquad W_\gamma = \frac{50 - 10}{60 - 10} = \frac{40}{50} = 0.800$$

#### Count the microconstituents on the tie line just above 700 °C

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
Just above 700 °C the alloy is γ (60 wt% B) + liquid that has reached the eutectic composition, 35 wt% B. All that liquid becomes eutectic at 700 °C, and the γ already present stays as primary γ. The same lever rule on the tie line from L (35) to γ (60), length 25 wt% B:

$$W_{\gamma,\text{primary}} = \frac{C_0 - C_E}{C_\gamma - C_E} = \frac{50 - 35}{60 - 35} = \frac{15}{25} = 0.600 \qquad W_{E} = W_{L}(700 + \Delta T) = \frac{60 - 50}{60 - 35} = \frac{10}{25} = 0.400$$

#### Split the eutectic into its phases

All the α of the alloy is inside the eutectic (there is no primary α), so eutectic α = $W_\alpha$ = 0.200. The γ inside the eutectic is the total γ minus the primary γ:

$$W_{\gamma,\text{eutectic}} = W_\gamma - W_{\gamma,\text{primary}} = 0.800 - 0.600 = 0.200$$

Check: $0.200 + 0.200 = 0.400 = W_E$. The eutectic itself has the composition 35 wt% B, so inside it the fraction of α is $(60 - 35)/(60 - 10) = 25/50 = 0.500$, and $0.500 \times 0.400 = 0.200$, the same eutectic α.

#### Answer and checks

At 700 − ΔT °C: phases α (10 wt% B, 20.0 %) and γ (60 wt% B, 80.0 %); microconstituents primary γ (60.0 %) and eutectic α + γ (40.0 %). B balance: $0.200 \times 10 + 0.800 \times 60 = 2 + 48 = 50$ wt% B $= C_0$.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x: 20 wt% B is hypoeutectic (between 10 and 35): primary α forms first. Above the line the second constituent is still liquid; below it, that liquid has become eutectic.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
- 700 + ΔT °C: primary α (10 wt% B) 0.600 in liquid (35 wt% B) 0.400.
- 700 − ΔT °C: primary α 0.600 in eutectic α + γ 0.400; total phases α 0.800 and γ 0.200.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
#### Follow the cooling path to the eutectic line

The vertical line of 20 wt% B crosses the α liquidus (at about 800 °C, a reading of the figure): grains of primary α nucleate and grow, while the liquid becomes richer in B along the liquidus. Just above 700 °C the α has 10 wt% B and the liquid 35 wt% B, the eutectic composition [Session 7 Slides 30-31].

#### Amounts at 700 + ΔT °C

Lever rule derived in part (b), on the tie line from α (10) to L (35), length 25 wt% B:

$$W_\alpha = \frac{35 - 20}{35 - 10} = \frac{15}{25} = 0.600 \qquad W_L = \frac{20 - 10}{35 - 10} = \frac{10}{25} = 0.400$$

#### Amounts at 700 − ΔT °C

At 700 °C the liquid (0.400) transforms at constant temperature into the eutectic $L \rightarrow \alpha + \gamma$; the primary α (0.600) does not change. The total phases come from the tie line from α (10) to γ (60), length 50:

$$W_\alpha = \frac{60 - 20}{60 - 10} = \frac{40}{50} = 0.800 \qquad W_\gamma = \frac{20 - 10}{60 - 10} = \frac{10}{50} = 0.200$$

The eutectic holds all the γ (0.200) and $0.800 - 0.600 = 0.200$ of α, and $0.200 + 0.200 = 0.400$, the eutectic fraction.

#### The sketches

Left: rounded grains of primary α (60 %) surrounded by liquid. Right: the same α grains, now surrounded by a lamellar eutectic of alternating α and γ layers (40 %).

chunks.x: A compound at the top of a liquidus dome melts like a pure metal. The maximum solubility of a terminal solid solution is the end of its field on an invariant line.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
- γ melts congruently at 1150 °C (maximum of the liquidus).
- Maximum solubility of B in A (α): 10 wt% B at 700 °C.
- Maximum solubility of A in B (β): 100 − 92 = 8 wt% A at 850 °C.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x:
#### Classify the melting of γ

The vertical line of γ (60 wt% B) reaches the liquidus at its maximum, 1150 °C: heated to that point, γ gives a liquid of 60 wt% B, its own composition, and no other solid appears. By Session 8 Slide 17 that is **congruent melting**. Had γ ended at a horizontal peritectic line below the liquidus, it would decompose into a liquid plus another solid (incongruent melting); this diagram has no peritectic line.

#### Maximum solubility of B in A

The α field is bounded by the solidus (from 900 °C) and the solvus (down to 200 °C); both meet the eutectic line at 10 wt% B, the widest point of the field. So α dissolves at most **10 wt% B, at 700 °C**; below 700 °C the solvus moves back towards A and the solubility falls.

#### Maximum solubility of A in B

The β field is widest where its boundaries meet the 850 °C line, at 92 wt% B, so β holds at most

$$100 - 92 = 8\ \text{wt\% A}$$

at **850 °C**.

chunks.t: Two eutectics around a congruently melting compound in a hypothetical A-B system
chunks.x: The compound γ splits the diagram into two simple eutectic sub-systems, A-γ and γ-B, each read exactly like Pb-Sn: a hypoeutectic alloy of the A-γ side (20 wt% B) gives primary α in an α + γ eutectic, a hypereutectic one (50 wt% B) gives primary γ. Control cases of the lever rule: as $C_0 \to 35$ wt% B the primary γ of part (b) tends to $(35-35)/25 = 0$ and the alloy becomes 100 % eutectic; as $C_0 \to 60$ it tends to 1. All fractions lie between 0 and 1 and add up to 1. Dimensions: the lever rule is a ratio of compositions (wt% over wt%), so every fraction is dimensionless, as a mass fraction must be. A common exam mistake is to give the primary γ from the tie line below 700 °C ($W_\gamma$ = 0.800): that number is the total γ, which also contains the γ inside the eutectic.

Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the Al-Ni problem of January 2014 (diagram in atomic percent) and of the finals that ask for a composition worked backwards from a microstructure. The M-N system is hypothetical. Method: Session 7, Slides 13-16 and 30-32; Session 8, Slides 6, 8-9, 14-15 and 17. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
The figure shows the equilibrium phase diagram of a hypothetical binary system M-N, with the composition in **atomic percent** of N. The intermediate phase δ is the stoichiometric compound MN₂.

a) Write all the invariant reactions: type, temperature and composition (at% N) of every phase involved.

b) Does δ melt congruently or incongruently? Give the phases and their amounts when δ is heated to 1000 + ΔT °C, and the maximum solubility of N in M and of M in N, with their temperatures.

c) A slowly cooled M-N alloy, examined just below 600 °C, shows grains of primary δ surrounded by 30.0 % of eutectic microconstituent (atom fraction 0.300). Find the composition of the alloy.

d) For the alloy of part (c), give the phases present, their compositions and their amounts at 1000 + ΔT °C, at 1000 − ΔT °C and at 600 − ΔT °C.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
#### Data read on the diagram

| Item | Value read on the figure |
| :--- | :--- |
| Melting points | M 1400 °C, N 700 °C |
| Compound δ = MN₂ | vertical line at 66.7 at% N, from the 1000 °C line down |
| Invariant line at 1000 °C | α 25 at% N, δ 66.7 at% N, L 78 at% N |
| Invariant line at 600 °C | δ 66.7 at% N, L 92 at% N, β 98 at% N |
| Microstructure of part (c) | primary δ + eutectic, $x_E$ = 0.300 just below 600 °C |

Units: the axis is in at% N, so a composition of 66.7 at% N means 0.667 mol of N atoms per mol of atoms. The lever rule is a ratio of composition differences, so on an atomic axis it gives **atom (mole) fractions** $x$ of each phase or constituent; this reading of the lever rule on an at% axis is an **extension** of Session 7 Slide 16, where the axis is in wt% and the fractions are mass fractions $W$ (the same construction, with the balance written for atoms instead of mass). The value 66.7 is $2/3 \times 100$, the N content of MN₂ (two N atoms out of three).

#### Model

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
- **Invariant reactions** [Session 8 Slide 6]: eutectic $L \rightarrow \alpha + \beta$; peritectic $\alpha + L \rightarrow \beta$, where a solid field ends in an inverted V below the line [Session 8 Slides 8-9].
- **Gibbs phase rule** at constant pressure, $F = C - P + 1$ [Session 7 Slide 13]: three phases of two components give $F = 0$, a horizontal line.
- **Lever rule** on a tie line [Session 7 Slides 15-16]; **microconstituents** counted on the tie line just above the eutectic line [Session 7 Slides 30-32].
- **Congruent and incongruent melting** [Session 8 Slide 17]: a compound at a maximum of the liquidus melts congruently; one ending at a peritectic line melts incongruently (liquid plus another solid).
- Hypotheses: equilibrium cooling (complete peritectic reaction, no coring), 1 atm, compositions read on the figure as printed.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x: Two horizontal lines. For each, look at what lies above it: a liquid that ends in a V (eutectic) or a solid plus liquid that meet a new solid in an inverted V (peritectic).

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
- 1000 °C, peritectic: α (25 at% N) + L (78 at% N) → δ (66.7 at% N).
- 600 °C, eutectic: L (92 at% N) → δ (66.7 at% N) + β (98 at% N).

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
#### Why horizontal lines are the invariant reactions

With $C = 2$ and $P = 3$ the phase rule gives $F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$ [Session 7 Slide 13]: temperature and the three compositions are fixed, so every three-phase equilibrium is one horizontal line. The diagram has two of them.

#### Classify the line at 1000 °C

The line runs from α (25) to L (78). Above it lies the two-phase field α + L. Below it, the vertical line of δ (66.7) starts at the line and splits it into α + δ (left) and δ + L (right): a new solid appears below the line between the two phases above it, the inverted V of a **peritectic** [Session 8 Slides 8-9]. On cooling:

$$\alpha\,(25\ \text{at\% N}) + L\,(78\ \text{at\% N}) \;\xrightarrow{\;1000\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \delta\,(66.7\ \text{at\% N}) \qquad \text{peritectic}$$

#### Classify the line at 600 °C

The liquidus of δ falls from 78 at% N at 1000 °C and the liquidus of β falls from 700 °C (pure N); they meet in a V at 92 at% N on the line, and below it lies δ + β. A liquid that gives two solids is a **eutectic**:

$$L\,(92\ \text{at\% N}) \;\xrightarrow{\;600\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \delta\,(66.7\ \text{at\% N}) + \beta\,(98\ \text{at\% N}) \qquad \text{eutectic}$$

#### Check

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x: Each reaction has the composition of the product (or the liquid of the eutectic) between the other two: $25 < 66.7 < 78$ and $66.7 < 92 < 98$. The eutectic temperature, 600 °C, is below the melting point of N (700 °C) and below the temperature at which δ stops existing (1000 °C).

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x: δ does not reach the liquidus: follow its vertical line up to the 1000 °C line and read the tie line just above it. The lever rule is derived here from the two atom balances.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
- δ melts incongruently (it ends at the peritectic line, 1000 °C).
- At 1000 + ΔT °C, δ has become α (25 at% N) 0.213 + L (78 at% N) 0.787.
- Maximum solubility of N in M: 25 at% N at 1000 °C; of M in N: 2 at% M at 600 °C.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
#### Classify the melting of δ

The δ line stops at 1000 °C, on the peritectic line, well below the liquidus. Heating δ through 1000 °C runs the peritectic backwards, $\delta \rightarrow \alpha + L$: the compound gives a liquid of a different composition (78 at% N) plus another solid (α). By Session 8 Slide 17 this is **incongruent melting**.

#### Derive the lever rule for atom fractions

Just above 1000 °C the δ composition, $C_0$ = 66.7 at% N, lies in α + L on the tie line from α (25) to L (78). The atoms of the alloy are shared by the two phases, and so are the N atoms:

$$x_\alpha + x_L = 1 \qquad x_\alpha C_\alpha + x_L C_L = C_0$$

Substituting $x_L = 1 - x_\alpha$:

$$x_\alpha C_\alpha + (1 - x_\alpha) C_L = C_0$$

$$x_\alpha (C_\alpha - C_L) = C_0 - C_L$$

$$x_\alpha = \frac{C_L - C_0}{C_L - C_\alpha} \qquad x_L = 1 - x_\alpha = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_L - C_\alpha}$$

#### Amounts at 1000 + ΔT °C

Tie line length $78 - 25 = 53$ at% N:

$$x_\alpha = \frac{78 - 66.7}{78 - 25} = \frac{11.3}{53} = 0.213 \qquad x_L = \frac{66.7 - 25}{78 - 25} = \frac{41.7}{53} = 0.787$$

Most of the compound turns into liquid, and about a fifth of its atoms stay as solid α.

#### Maximum solubilities

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
The α field is widest where it touches the peritectic line, at 25 at% N: N dissolves in M up to **25 at% N at 1000 °C**. The β field touches the eutectic line at 98 at% N, so M dissolves in N up to

$$100 - 98 = 2\ \text{at\% M}$$

at **600 °C**.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x: Write the eutectic fraction with the lever rule on the tie line just above 600 °C (from δ to the eutectic liquid) and solve it for $C_0$. Check which side of the eutectic point the alloy must be on.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
- The alloy is between δ (66.7) and the eutectic point (92), because its primary constituent is δ.
- $C_0$ = 74.29 at% N (about 74.3 at% N).

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
#### Choose the side of the eutectic

The eutectic microconstituent at 600 °C forms from alloys between 66.7 and 98 at% N. Those between 66.7 and 92 at% N reach 600 °C with primary δ, those between 92 and 98 at% N with primary β. The alloy shows primary δ, so $66.7 < C_0 < 92$.

#### Write the eutectic fraction with the lever rule

Just above 600 °C the alloy is δ (66.7) + liquid of eutectic composition (92). All that liquid becomes eutectic, so the eutectic fraction is the liquid fraction on this tie line (lever rule of part b):

$$x_E = x_L(600 + \Delta T) = \frac{C_0 - C_\delta}{C_E - C_\delta}$$

#### Isolate the composition

Multiply both sides by $(C_E - C_\delta)$:

$$x_E\,(C_E - C_\delta) = C_0 - C_\delta$$

Add $C_\delta$ to both sides:

$$C_0 = C_\delta + x_E\,(C_E - C_\delta)$$

Substitute $x_E$ = 0.300, $C_\delta$ = 66.7 and $C_E$ = 92 at% N:

$$C_0 = 66.7 + 0.300 \times (92 - 66.7) = 66.7 + 0.300 \times 25.3 = 66.7 + 7.59 = 74.29\ \text{at\% N}$$

#### Check

$66.7 < 74.29 < 92$, as required. Back-substitution: $(74.29 - 66.7)/(92 - 66.7) = 7.59/25.3 = 0.300$. The primary δ is $1 - 0.300 = 0.700$. The other root, from the hypereutectic side, $x_E = (98 - C_0)/(98 - 92)$, would give $C_0 = 98 - 0.300 \times 6 = 96.2$ at% N, but that alloy has primary β, not δ, so it is rejected.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x: At 1000 + ΔT the alloy (74.29) lies between α (25) and L (78). After the peritectic it lies between δ (66.7) and L (78), because it has more N than δ. Below 600 °C the tie line runs from δ to β.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x:
#### Just above the peritectic line

The alloy, 74.29 at% N, lies on the tie line from α (25) to L (78), length 53:

$$x_\alpha = \frac{78 - 74.29}{78 - 25} = \frac{3.71}{53} = 0.0700 \qquad x_L = \frac{74.29 - 25}{78 - 25} = \frac{49.29}{53} = 0.930$$

#### Just below the peritectic line

At 1000 °C all the α reacts with part of the liquid to form δ. Since $C_0 = 74.29 > 66.7$, the α runs out first and liquid is left over (as for alloy 2 of Session 8 Slide 9). Tie line from δ (66.7) to L (78), length 11.3:

$$x_\delta = \frac{78 - 74.29}{78 - 66.7} = \frac{3.71}{11.3} = 0.328 \qquad x_L = \frac{74.29 - 66.7}{78 - 66.7} = \frac{7.59}{11.3} = 0.672$$

#### Just below the eutectic line

Between 1000 and 600 °C more δ grows from the liquid, which follows the liquidus to 92 at% N; at 600 °C the remaining liquid (0.300, part c) becomes eutectic δ + β. Tie line from δ (66.7) to β (98), length 31.3:

$$x_\delta = \frac{98 - 74.29}{98 - 66.7} = \frac{23.71}{31.3} = 0.758 \qquad x_\beta = \frac{74.29 - 66.7}{98 - 66.7} = \frac{7.59}{31.3} = 0.242$$

#### Check with the microconstituents

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x: The δ total (0.758) is primary δ (0.700) plus eutectic δ, so the eutectic δ is 0.0575 and the eutectic β 0.242; together $0.0575 + 0.242 = 0.300 = x_E$. N balance at 600 − ΔT: $0.758 \times 66.7 + 0.242 \times 98 = 50.56 + 23.72 = 74.28$ at% N, equal to $C_0$ = 74.29 within the rounding of the fractions.

chunks.t: Alloy composition from the eutectic fraction in an M-N system with an incongruent compound (at%)
chunks.x: δ cannot be melted as a single liquid of its own composition: it decomposes at 1000 °C into a liquid and the M-rich α, which is why it ends in a peritectic and not at a maximum of the liquidus. The fraction of eutectic is a fingerprint of the composition: on the δ side it grows linearly from 0 at 66.7 at% N to 1 at 92 at% N, so a measured eutectic fraction fixes $C_0$ uniquely once the primary constituent is known. Limiting cases: $x_E \to 0$ gives $C_0 \to 66.7$ (pure δ) and $x_E \to 1$ gives $C_0 \to 92$ (fully eutectic). Dimensions: every fraction is at% over at%, dimensionless, and every composition stays between the ends of its tie line. Common mistake: using mass fractions or quoting the result in wt%; on an at% diagram the lever rule gives atom fractions, and converting to wt% would need the atomic masses of M and N, which the problem does not give.
