Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the cooling-sequence problems of the Unit 4 sheet and of the final of January 2016. The X-Y system is hypothetical. Method: Session 7, Slides 13-16 and 30-32; Session 8, Slides 6-11 and 17. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
The figure shows the equilibrium phase diagram of a hypothetical binary system X-Y (composition in wt% Y). γ is an intermetallic compound of 55 wt% Y; β is an intermediate solid solution that exists only between 1100 and 600 °C.

a) Write all the invariant reactions with their type, temperature and the composition of the three phases, and say how γ melts.

b) Apply the Gibbs phase rule (pressure constant) at the point of 25 wt% Y and 600 °C, inside the β + L field and inside the β field, and explain what each result means.

c) An alloy X-40 wt% Y is cooled slowly from the liquid. Describe its solidification down to 900 °C, giving the phases, their compositions and their amounts at 1100 + ΔT, 1100 − ΔT, 900 + ΔT and 900 − ΔT °C.

d) Continue the cooling to 600 − ΔT °C: give the phases and the microconstituents with their amounts, and sketch the microstructure at 1100 + ΔT, 900 − ΔT and 600 − ΔT °C.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
#### Data read on the diagram

| Item | Value read on the figure |
| :--- | :--- |
| Melting points | X 1300 °C, Y 800 °C, γ 1000 °C (top of its liquidus) |
| Line at 1100 °C | α 15, β 30, L 45 wt% Y |
| Line at 900 °C | β 38, L 50, γ 55 wt% Y |
| Line at 650 °C | γ 55, L 80, δ 95 wt% Y |
| Line at 600 °C | α 10, β 25, γ 55 wt% Y |
| Alloy | $C_0$ = 40 wt% Y |

Units: 40 wt% Y is a mass fraction of 0.40 kg of Y per kg of alloy; the lever rule divides two composition differences, so the fractions it gives are dimensionless mass fractions. Temperatures stay in °C because no formula here needs kelvin.

#### Model

- **Invariant reactions** [Session 8 Slide 6]: eutectic $L \rightarrow \alpha + \beta$, peritectic $\alpha + L \rightarrow \beta$ [Session 8 Slides 8-9], eutectoid $\gamma \rightarrow \alpha + \beta$ in the solid state [Session 8 Slide 7], peritectoid $\alpha + \beta \rightarrow \gamma$ [Session 8 Slide 11].
- **Gibbs phase rule** $F = C - P + N$, with $N = 1$ at constant pressure [Session 7 Slide 13].
- **Lever rule** on the tie line [Session 7 Slides 15-16]; primary constituents counted just above an invariant line, total phases just below it [Session 7 Slides 30-32].
- **Congruent melting** at a maximum of the liquidus [Session 8 Slide 17].
- Hypotheses: equilibrium cooling (the peritectic reaction and the solid-state diffusion are complete), 1 atm, values as printed.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x: There are four horizontal lines. Two of them have a liquid whose composition lies between the two solids (a V-shaped meeting of the liquidus), one has a solid field closing in a V from above (no liquid at all), and one has a new solid appearing below the line between a solid and a liquid above it.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
- 1100 °C, peritectic: α (15) + L (45) → β (30).
- 900 °C, eutectic: L (50) → β (38) + γ (55).
- 650 °C, eutectic: L (80) → γ (55) + δ (95).
- 600 °C, eutectoid: β (25) → α (10) + γ (55). All in wt% Y.
- γ melts congruently at 1000 °C.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
#### Why each horizontal line is an invariant reaction

Three phases of a two-component system at constant pressure leave $F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$ [Session 7 Slide 13], so each three-phase equilibrium is one horizontal line with three fixed compositions. The diagram has four.

#### The line at 1100 °C

Above it lies α + L, from α (15) to L (45). Below it the field of β starts at 30 wt% Y, between the two: a new solid forms from a solid and a liquid, the inverted V of a **peritectic** [Session 8 Slides 8-9]:

$$\alpha\,(15) + L\,(45) \;\xrightarrow{\;1100\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \beta\,(30) \qquad \text{peritectic, wt\% Y}$$

#### The lines at 900 and 650 °C

At 900 °C the liquidus of β (falling from 45 at 1100 °C) and the left branch of the liquidus of γ (falling from 1000 °C) meet in a V at 50 wt% Y; below lies β + γ. At 650 °C the right branch of the γ liquidus and the liquidus of δ (from 800 °C, pure Y) meet in a V at 80 wt% Y; below lies γ + δ. Both are **eutectics**:

$$L\,(50) \;\xrightarrow{\;900\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \beta\,(38) + \gamma\,(55) \qquad L\,(80) \;\xrightarrow{\;650\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \gamma\,(55) + \delta\,(95)$$

#### The line at 600 °C

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
No liquid reaches this line. The single-phase field β narrows downwards between its two solvus lines and closes in a V at 25 wt% Y on the line; below it lies α + γ. A solid that transforms into two other solids is a **eutectoid** [Session 8 Slide 7]:

$$\beta\,(25) \;\xrightarrow{\;600\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \alpha\,(10) + \gamma\,(55) \qquad \text{eutectoid}$$

#### Melting of γ

The vertical line of γ reaches the liquidus at its maximum, 1000 °C, where γ gives a liquid of its own composition (55 wt% Y): **congruent melting** [Session 8 Slide 17].

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
#### State the rule and why N = 1

The phase rule is $F = C - P + N$ [Session 7 Slide 13]. Pressure is fixed at 1 atm in a phase diagram of this kind, so only temperature is a non-compositional variable, $N = 1$, and $F = C - P + 1$. The system has two components, X and Y, so $C = 2$.

#### At the eutectoid point

Three phases coexist, β, α and γ, so $P = 3$:

$$F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$$

Nothing can be changed: the transformation happens only at 600 °C, with β of 25, α of 10 and γ of 55 wt% Y. On a cooling curve it gives a plateau, like the eutectic.

#### Inside β + L

Two phases, $P = 2$:

$$F = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$$

Choosing the temperature uses the only degree of freedom: the compositions of β and L are then fixed by the ends of the tie line, and the alloy composition only changes their amounts.

#### Inside β

One phase, $P = 1$:

$$F = 2 - 1 + 1 = 2$$

Temperature and composition can both change (within the field) without a new phase appearing.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x: The 40 wt% Y vertical first meets the α liquidus. At 1100 °C, 40 lies between β (30) and L (45), so the peritectic uses up all the α and leaves liquid. Then β grows from the liquid down to the eutectic at 900 °C.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
#### First solid: primary α

The 40 wt% Y vertical crosses the liquidus of α just above 1100 °C (the liquidus reaches 45 wt% Y at 1100 °C, so for 40 wt% Y it is a few tens of degrees higher; a reading of the figure). Crystals of α start to grow, and the liquid becomes richer in Y along the liquidus.

#### Derive the lever rule and apply it at 1100 + ΔT

On a tie line with phases α and L the alloy and the element Y must both be conserved:

$$W_\alpha + W_L = 1 \qquad W_\alpha C_\alpha + W_L C_L = C_0$$

Substituting $W_L = 1 - W_\alpha$ in the balance of Y:

$$W_\alpha C_\alpha + (1 - W_\alpha) C_L = C_0$$

Expanding the bracket:

$$W_\alpha C_\alpha + C_L - W_\alpha C_L = C_0$$

Grouping the terms in $W_\alpha$ and moving $C_L$ to the right-hand side:

$$W_\alpha (C_\alpha - C_L) = C_0 - C_L$$

Dividing by $(C_\alpha - C_L)$ and changing the sign of numerator and denominator:

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_L - C_0}{C_L - C_\alpha} \qquad W_L = 1 - W_\alpha = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_L - C_\alpha}$$

Just above 1100 °C, α has 15 and L has 45 wt% Y (length 30):

$$W_\alpha = \frac{45 - 40}{45 - 15} = \frac{5}{30} = 0.167 \qquad W_L = \frac{40 - 15}{45 - 15} = \frac{25}{30} = 0.833$$

#### The peritectic reaction at 1100 °C

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
At 1100 °C, α (15) reacts with L (45) to give β (30). The alloy (40) lies to the right of β, between β and L, so the α runs out before the liquid. Just below 1100 °C the tie line runs from β (30) to L (45), length 15:

$$W_\beta = \frac{45 - 40}{45 - 30} = \frac{5}{15} = 0.333 \qquad W_L = \frac{40 - 30}{45 - 30} = \frac{10}{15} = 0.667$$

#### From 1100 to 900 °C: β grows from the liquid

In β + L the liquid follows the β liquidus from 45 to 50 wt% Y and β follows its solidus from 30 to 38 wt% Y; the amount of β grows. Just above 900 °C (β 38, L 50, length 12):

$$W_\beta = \frac{50 - 40}{50 - 38} = \frac{10}{12} = 0.833 \qquad W_L = \frac{40 - 38}{50 - 38} = \frac{2}{12} = 0.167$$

This β, formed partly by the peritectic and partly from the liquid, is the **primary β** (0.833), and the liquid, now of eutectic composition, is the future eutectic (0.167).

#### The eutectic at 900 °C

The remaining liquid transforms at 900 °C into β (38) + γ (55). Just below the line, the total phases on the tie line from β (38) to γ (55), length 17:

$$W_\beta = \frac{55 - 40}{55 - 38} = \frac{15}{17} = 0.882 \qquad W_\gamma = \frac{40 - 38}{55 - 38} = \frac{2}{17} = 0.118$$

Microconstituents: primary β 0.833 and eutectic (β + γ) 0.167. All the γ is in the eutectic, and the eutectic β is $0.882 - 0.833 = 0.049$; $0.049 + 0.118 = 0.167$.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x: Between 900 and 600 °C the β follows its solvus from 38 to 25 wt% Y and rejects γ. At 600 °C every grain of β, primary or eutectic, transforms into the eutectoid α + γ.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
- 600 + ΔT: β (25) 0.500, γ (55) 0.500.
- 600 − ΔT: α (10) 0.333, γ (55) 0.667.
- Microconstituents at 600 − ΔT: eutectoid (α + γ) 0.500 and γ outside the eutectoid 0.500 (eutectic γ 0.118 plus γ precipitated in the solid 0.382).

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x:
#### From 900 to 600 °C: precipitation of γ

In β + γ the boundary of β moves from 38 to 25 wt% Y as the temperature falls, so the β loses Y and γ precipitates from it in the solid state (Session 8 Slides 2-4 call this solid-state precipitation). Just above 600 °C (β 25, γ 55, length 30):

$$W_\beta = \frac{55 - 40}{55 - 25} = \frac{15}{30} = 0.500 \qquad W_\gamma = \frac{40 - 25}{55 - 25} = \frac{15}{30} = 0.500$$

The γ grew from 0.118 to 0.500, so $0.500 - 0.118 = 0.382$ of γ precipitated between 900 and 600 °C.

#### The eutectoid at 600 °C

All the β (0.500), which now has the eutectoid composition 25 wt% Y, transforms into the fine eutectoid α + γ. Below the line the total phases on the tie line from α (10) to γ (55), length 45:

$$W_\alpha = \frac{55 - 40}{55 - 10} = \frac{15}{45} = 0.333 \qquad W_\gamma = \frac{40 - 10}{55 - 10} = \frac{30}{45} = 0.667$$

The microconstituents are counted just above the line, like a primary constituent above a eutectic: eutectoid = $W_\beta(600 + \Delta T)$ = 0.500, and γ outside it = 0.500. Check: inside the eutectoid (25 wt% Y) the fraction of α is $(55 - 25)/(55 - 10) = 30/45 = 0.667$, and $0.667 \times 0.500 = 0.333$, all the α of the alloy.

#### The three sketches

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x: At 1100 + ΔT: a few rounded grains of primary α in a large amount of liquid. At 900 − ΔT: large grains of primary β (the α has disappeared in the peritectic) in a lamellar eutectic β + γ. At 600 − ΔT: every former β region, primary and inside the eutectic, is now a fine eutectoid α + γ, with films of γ precipitated on the boundaries of the former β grains.

chunks.t: Cooling an X-40 wt% Y alloy through a peritectic, a eutectic and a eutectoid
chunks.x: The alloy passes through three invariant reactions, but none of the original microconstituents survives unchanged: the primary α is consumed by the peritectic, and the primary β disappears in the eutectoid, leaving only a trace of its shape. This is the solid-state counterpart of the eutectic: like a eutectic liquid, the β of 25 wt% Y transforms at one temperature into two phases ($F = 0$). Checks: every fraction lies between 0 and 1, each pair adds up to 1, and the Y balance at 600 − ΔT is $0.333 \times 10 + 0.667 \times 55 = 3.33 + 36.67 = 40.0$ wt% Y. Limiting case: an alloy of exactly 30 wt% Y would leave neither α nor liquid after the peritectic and be 100 % β just below 1100 °C. Dimensions: all fractions are wt% over wt%, dimensionless. Common mistake: taking the eutectoid fraction from the tie line below 600 °C ($W_\alpha$ = 0.333, a phase) instead of from the β just above it (0.500, a microconstituent).

chunks.h: Bank P04 — Building a diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the June 2014 final (draw a diagram from its features) and of the Part II problem of the 2019 Assessment Test II. The G-H system is hypothetical. Method: Session 7, Slides 15-16 and 26-32; Session 8, Slides 6, 8-9, 14-15 and 17. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
A laboratory has measured the following features of a hypothetical binary system G-H (compositions in wt% H). No diagram is given.

| Feature | Measured data |
| :--- | :--- |
| Pure G | melts at 1500 °C; forms the terminal solid solution α |
| Pure H | melts at 1350 °C; forms the terminal solid solution β |
| Compound θ (stoichiometric, 30 wt% H) | melts at 1400 °C to a liquid of 30 wt% H |
| Compound η (stoichiometric, 60 wt% H) | stable only below 1150 °C |
| Three-phase equilibrium at 1250 °C | α (6 wt% H), L (15 wt% H), θ (30 wt% H) |
| Three-phase equilibrium at 1150 °C | L (50 wt% H), η (60 wt% H), β (88 wt% H) |
| Three-phase equilibrium at 1000 °C | θ (30 wt% H), L (40 wt% H), η (60 wt% H) |
| Solvus lines | α holds 3 wt% H and β 92 wt% H at 700 °C |

a) Draw the phase diagram between 700 and 1600 °C to scale and label every phase field.

b) Name each invariant reaction, writing it on cooling with the compositions of the three phases, say which compound melts congruently and which incongruently, and give the maximum solubility of H in G and of G in H with their temperatures.

c) A casting of 2.00 kg of G-55 wt% H is cooled slowly. Give the mass and composition of each phase at 1150 + ΔT °C and at 1150 − ΔT °C, and the mass of β used up by the reaction at 1150 °C.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x: d) For the same casting at 1000 − ΔT °C, give the mass of each microconstituent and of each phase, and the masses of θ and η inside the eutectic.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $T_G$, $T_H$ | melting points of G and H | 1500 °C, 1350 °C |
| $C_\theta$, $C_\eta$ | compositions of the compounds | 30, 60 wt% H |
| 1250 °C | α, L, θ | 6, 15, 30 wt% H |
| 1150 °C | L, η, β | 50, 60, 88 wt% H |
| 1000 °C | θ, L, η | 30, 40, 60 wt% H |
| $m_0$, $C_0$ | mass and composition of the casting | 2.00 kg, 55 wt% H |

Unit conversions: 55 wt% H is a mass fraction of 0.55, so the casting contains $0.55 \times 2.00\ \text{kg} = 1.10$ kg of H and 0.90 kg of G. The lever rule gives mass fractions $W$ (dimensionless); the mass of a phase is $m_i = W_i\,m_0$ in kg.

#### Model

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
- **Phase fields** [Session 7 Slides 26-27]: liquidus, solidus and solvus bound the fields; single-phase and two-phase fields alternate across every boundary, and three phases meet only on a horizontal invariant line ($F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0$, Session 7 Slide 13).
- **Invariant reactions** [Session 8 Slide 6]: eutectic $L \rightarrow \alpha + \beta$ (the liquid lies between the two solids on the line), peritectic $\alpha + L \rightarrow \beta$ (the new solid lies between the solid and the liquid) [Session 8 Slides 8-9].
- **Compounds** [Session 8 Slides 14-15, 17]: a stoichiometric compound is a vertical line; congruent melting at a maximum of the liquidus, incongruent melting at a peritectic line.
- **Lever rule** [Session 7 Slides 15-16]; primary constituent counted just above the eutectic line [Session 7 Slides 30-32].
- Hypotheses: equilibrium cooling (complete peritectic reaction), 1 atm, the boundaries between the given points drawn as smooth curves (their exact shape is not measured, only their end points).

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x: Start with the fixed points: the two melting points, the top of θ, the three horizontal lines and the two vertical compound lines. Then join each liquid point to the next with the liquidus, and each solid end to its melting point or to the bottom of the diagram.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
- Liquidus: 1500 °C (0) → 1250 °C (15) → 1400 °C (30) → 1000 °C (40) → 1150 °C (50) → 1350 °C (100).
- Vertical lines: θ at 30 wt% H up to 1400 °C, η at 60 wt% H up to 1150 °C.
- Fields: L; α; α + L; α + θ; θ + L on both sides of θ; θ + η; η + L; η + β; β + L; β.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
#### Place the fixed points

On axes of 0 to 100 wt% H and 700 to 1600 °C: the melting points (0, 1500) and (100, 1350); the top of θ (30, 1400), because θ gives a liquid of its own composition there; the three horizontal lines at 1250 °C (6 to 30), 1150 °C (50 to 88) and 1000 °C (30 to 60), each with its three points marked; the vertical line of θ at 30 wt% H from 700 to 1400 °C, and that of η at 60 wt% H from 700 °C up to 1150 °C only, because η exists only below that temperature.

#### Draw the liquidus

The liquidus must pass through every liquid point of the table, in order of composition: from G (1500 °C) down to the liquid of the 1250 °C line (15), up to the maximum of θ (1400 °C at 30), down to the liquid of the 1000 °C line (40), up to the liquid of the 1150 °C line (50), and up to H (1350 °C). Above it everything is liquid.

#### Draw the solid boundaries

α: solidus from (0, 1500) to (6, 1250) and solvus from (6, 1250) to (3, 700). β: solidus from (100, 1350) to (88, 1150) and solvus from (88, 1150) to (92, 700).

#### Label the fields

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x: Two-phase fields fill the gaps between neighbouring single-phase regions: α + L (between the α solidus and the liquidus), θ + L on each side of θ above 1250 and 1000 °C, α + θ (below 1250 °C between α and θ), θ + η (below 1000 °C), η + L (between 1000 and 1150 °C, left of η), η + β (below 1150 °C), and β + L (above 1150 °C, between the liquidus and the β solidus). Each boundary crossed horizontally changes the number of phases by one (one, two, one, two), as required.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x: For each line, ask which phase lies between the other two: if it is the liquid, the line is a eutectic; if it is a solid that exists only below the line, it is a peritectic.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
- 1250 °C, eutectic: L (15) → α (6) + θ (30).
- 1150 °C, peritectic: L (50) + β (88) → η (60).
- 1000 °C, eutectic: L (40) → θ (30) + η (60).
- θ melts congruently (1400 °C); η melts incongruently (1150 °C).
- Maximum solubility: 6 wt% H in G at 1250 °C; 100 − 88 = 12 wt% G in H at 1150 °C.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
#### The line at 1250 °C

The liquid (15) lies between α (6) and θ (30), with α + L and θ + L above and α + θ below: the liquid gives two solids, a **eutectic** [Session 8 Slide 6]:

$$L\,(15) \;\xrightarrow{\;1250\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \alpha\,(6) + \theta\,(30) \qquad \text{eutectic, wt\% H}$$

#### The line at 1150 °C

Here the solid η (60) lies between the liquid (50) and β (88), and η exists only below the line. Above the line there is β + L; below it η + L and η + β. A liquid and a solid combine into a new solid: a **peritectic** [Session 8 Slides 8-9]:

$$L\,(50) + \beta\,(88) \;\xrightarrow{\;1150\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \eta\,(60) \qquad \text{peritectic}$$

#### The line at 1000 °C

The liquid (40) lies between θ (30) and η (60), with θ + L and η + L above and θ + η below: a second **eutectic**:

$$L\,(40) \;\xrightarrow{\;1000\ ^\circ\text{C}\;}\; \theta\,(30) + \eta\,(60) \qquad \text{eutectic}$$

#### Melting of the compounds

θ melts at 1400 °C to a liquid of 30 wt% H, its own composition, at the top of the liquidus: **congruent melting** [Session 8 Slide 17]. η ends at the peritectic line: heated above 1150 °C it decomposes into L (50) + β (88), a liquid of another composition plus another solid, so it melts **incongruently**.

#### Maximum solubilities

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
α is widest on the 1250 °C line: **6 wt% H in G at 1250 °C**. β is widest on the 1150 °C line, at 88 wt% H, so it holds

$$100 - 88 = 12\ \text{wt\% G}$$

at **1150 °C**. Both solubilities fall on cooling, along the solvus lines (to 3 wt% H and 8 wt% G at 700 °C).

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x: 55 lies on the 1150 °C line between L (50) and β (88), and below it between L (50) and η (60). Find the fractions with the lever rule, then multiply by 2.00 kg.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
- 1150 + ΔT: L (50 wt% H) 1.737 kg, β (88 wt% H) 0.263 kg.
- 1150 − ΔT: η (60 wt% H) 1.000 kg, L (50 wt% H) 1.000 kg.
- All the β, 0.263 kg, is used up by the peritectic.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
#### Derive the lever rule

On a tie line with phases L and β the mass of the alloy and the mass of H are conserved:

$$W_L + W_\beta = 1 \qquad W_L C_L + W_\beta C_\beta = C_0$$

Substituting $W_\beta = 1 - W_L$:

$$W_L C_L + (1 - W_L) C_\beta = C_0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad W_L (C_L - C_\beta) = C_0 - C_\beta$$

$$W_L = \frac{C_\beta - C_0}{C_\beta - C_L} \qquad W_\beta = \frac{C_0 - C_L}{C_\beta - C_L}$$

#### Just above 1150 °C

The alloy lies in β + L on the tie line from L (50) to β (88), length 38 wt% H:

$$W_L = \frac{88 - 55}{88 - 50} = \frac{33}{38} = 0.8684 \qquad W_\beta = \frac{55 - 50}{88 - 50} = \frac{5}{38} = 0.1316$$

Masses, with $m_i = W_i\,m_0$:

$$m_L = 0.8684 \times 2.00\ \text{kg} = 1.737\ \text{kg} \qquad m_\beta = 0.1316 \times 2.00\ \text{kg} = 0.263\ \text{kg}$$

#### Just below 1150 °C

At 1150 °C, L (50) and β (88) react to form η (60). The alloy (55) lies left of η, between L and η, so the β runs out first and liquid remains. Tie line from L (50) to η (60), length 10:

$$W_\eta = \frac{55 - 50}{60 - 50} = \frac{5}{10} = 0.500 \qquad W_L = \frac{60 - 55}{60 - 50} = \frac{5}{10} = 0.500$$

$$m_\eta = 0.500 \times 2.00\ \text{kg} = 1.000\ \text{kg} \qquad m_L = 0.500 \times 2.00\ \text{kg} = 1.000\ \text{kg}$$

#### Mass balance of the reaction

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x: All 0.263 kg of β disappear. The η formed (1.000 kg) comes from that β and from $1.000 - 0.263 = 0.737$ kg of liquid, which is exactly the drop of the liquid from 1.737 to 1.000 kg. H check: $0.263 \times 0.88 + 0.737 \times 0.50 = 0.2316 + 0.3684 = 0.600$ kg of H in 1.000 kg of η, that is 60 wt% H, the composition of η.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x: Between 1150 and 1000 °C η grows from the liquid, which moves along the liquidus to 40 wt% H. The η present just above 1000 °C is primary η; the liquid left becomes the eutectic θ + η.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
- Primary η 1.500 kg; eutectic (θ + η) 0.500 kg.
- Phases: θ (30 wt% H) 0.333 kg, η (60 wt% H) 1.667 kg.
- Inside the eutectic: θ 0.333 kg and η 0.167 kg.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x:
#### Primary η just above 1000 °C

The tie line runs from the eutectic liquid (40) to η (60), length 20 wt% H. The η is primary and the liquid will become eutectic:

$$W_{\eta,\text{primary}} = \frac{55 - 40}{60 - 40} = \frac{15}{20} = 0.750 \qquad W_E = \frac{60 - 55}{60 - 40} = \frac{5}{20} = 0.250$$

$$m_{\eta,\text{primary}} = 0.750 \times 2.00 = 1.500\ \text{kg} \qquad m_E = 0.250 \times 2.00 = 0.500\ \text{kg}$$

#### Phases just below 1000 °C

Tie line from θ (30) to η (60), length 30:

$$W_\theta = \frac{60 - 55}{60 - 30} = \frac{5}{30} = 0.1667 \qquad W_\eta = \frac{55 - 30}{60 - 30} = \frac{25}{30} = 0.8333$$

$$m_\theta = 0.1667 \times 2.00 = 0.333\ \text{kg} \qquad m_\eta = 0.8333 \times 2.00 = 1.667\ \text{kg}$$

#### Split the eutectic

All the θ is in the eutectic (there is no primary θ), so eutectic θ = 0.333 kg. The eutectic η is the total η minus the primary η:

$$m_{\eta,E} = 1.667 - 1.500 = 0.167\ \text{kg}$$

Check: $0.333 + 0.167 = 0.500$ kg, the mass of eutectic. The eutectic has 40 wt% H, so inside it the θ fraction is $(60 - 40)/(60 - 30) = 20/30 = 0.667$, and $0.667 \times 0.500 = 0.333$ kg, as found.

chunks.t: Building a G-H diagram with a congruent and an incongruent compound from a table of equilibria
chunks.x: The two compounds split the diagram into three simpler parts: G-θ (a simple eutectic), θ-η (a simple eutectic) and η-H (a peritectic). θ behaves like a pure metal because it melts at a maximum of the liquidus; η cannot be melted as a single liquid. The casting of 55 wt% H shows the peritectic in action: the 0.263 kg of β formed first is completely consumed at 1150 °C, so the final microstructure has no trace of β, only primary η in a θ + η eutectic. Checks: every pair of fractions adds up to 1 and the masses add up to 2.00 kg; H balance at 1000 − ΔT: $0.333 \times 0.30 + 1.667 \times 0.60 = 0.100 + 1.000 = 1.100$ kg of H $= 0.55 \times 2.00$ kg. Limiting case: a casting of exactly 60 wt% H would leave no liquid after the peritectic and be 100 % η. Dimensions: $W$ is wt% over wt%, dimensionless, and $m = W\,m_0$ has units of kg. Common mistake: drawing η up to the liquidus as if it melted congruently; the table says η exists only below 1150 °C, which is the signature of a peritectic.

Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.h: Bank P05 — Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the Pb-Sn problems of Problems T4_PhaseDiagrams I.pdf, with the values of Session 7 Slide 32. Method: tie line and lever rule [Session 7 Slides 15-16], eutectic microconstituents [Session 7 Slides 30, 32], precipitation below the solvus [Session 8 Slides 3-4]. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
The figure shows the Pb-Sn phase diagram with the values of Session 7 Slide 32. A Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy is cooled slowly (equilibrium) from 300 °C to 100 °C. The readings needed are printed on the figure: the alloy meets the liquidus at 215 °C; at 200 °C the tie line through the alloy ends at 16.7 and 55.7 wt% Sn; at 100 °C it ends at 4.8 and 99.8 wt% Sn.

(a) Write the invariant reaction of the diagram (name, temperature, compositions of the three phases). Classify the alloy and say at which temperatures its solidification starts and ends, and which phase forms first.

(b) At 200 °C, give the phases present, their compositions and their mass fractions.

(c) Just above (183 + ΔT) and just below (183 − ΔT) the eutectic temperature, give the phases with their compositions and mass fractions, and the microconstituents with their mass fractions. What fraction of all the α of the alloy is inside the eutectic?

(d) At 100 °C, give the phases, their compositions and mass fractions. Explain where the extra β comes from.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value | Where it is read |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Alloy composition | $C_0$ | 50 wt% Sn (mass fraction 0.50 of Sn) | statement |
| Melting points | $T_{Pb}$, $T_{Sn}$ | 327 °C, 232 °C | ends of the liquidus |
| Eutectic point | $T_E$, $C_E$ | 183 °C, 61.9 wt% Sn | point E |
| Ends of the eutectic line | $C_\alpha$, $C_\beta$ | 18.3 and 97.8 wt% Sn | ends of the horizontal line at 183 °C |
| Liquidus of the alloy | $T_L$ | 215 °C | the dashed alloy line meets the liquidus |
| Tie line at 200 °C | $C_\alpha$, $C_L$ | 16.7 and 55.7 wt% Sn | solidus and liquidus at 200 °C |
| Tie line at 100 °C | $C_\alpha$, $C_\beta$ | 4.8 and 99.8 wt% Sn | the two solvus lines at 100 °C |

The compositions are mass percentages; the lever rule only uses differences and ratios of them, so they can stay in wt% (the conversion to mass fractions, dividing by 100, cancels in every ratio).

#### Model

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
- Gibbs phase rule at constant pressure for two components, $F = C - P + 1 = 3 - P$ [Session 7 Slide 13]: in a two-phase field $F = 1$, so once the temperature is fixed the compositions of both phases are fixed; they are the ends of the horizontal tie line [Session 7 Slide 15].
- Lever rule [Session 7 Slides 15-16]: on a tie line from $C_1$ to $C_2$, $W_1 = \dfrac{C_2 - C_0}{C_2 - C_1}$ and $W_2 = \dfrac{C_0 - C_1}{C_2 - C_1}$ (derived in part (b)).
- Microconstituents of a hypoeutectic alloy [Session 7 Slides 30, 32]: the α present just above 183 °C is the primary α; the liquid present then (of 61.9 wt% Sn) becomes the eutectic. Hypotheses: equilibrium cooling, closed system (no loss of mass).

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x: Look for the point where the liquidus has its minimum and the horizontal line that passes through it. Compare $C_0$ with the three compositions of that line.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
- Eutectic at 183 °C: L (61.9 wt% Sn) → α (18.3 wt% Sn) + β (97.8 wt% Sn) on cooling.
- $18.3 < 50 < 61.9$: hypoeutectic alloy; the primary phase is α.
- Solidification starts at 215 °C (first solid α) and ends at 183 °C.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
#### Identify the invariant reaction at point E

The only horizontal line of the diagram is at 183 °C. It touches three phase fields from above and below: the liquid meets it at a single point E (the minimum of the liquidus), α ends at its left end and β at its right end. A liquid that turns into two solids at a fixed temperature and composition is a eutectic reaction [Session 7 Slides 26-27]. Reading the three compositions on the line:

$$\text{cooling: } L\ (61.9\ \text{wt\% Sn}) \rightarrow \alpha\ (18.3\ \text{wt\% Sn}) + \beta\ (97.8\ \text{wt\% Sn}) \quad \text{at } 183\ ^\circ\text{C (eutectic)}$$

It is invariant: with three phases, $F = 3 - P = 3 - 3 = 0$, so neither the temperature nor any composition can change while the reaction proceeds [Session 7 Slide 13].

#### Classify the alloy

The eutectic line runs from 18.3 to 97.8 wt% Sn, and the eutectic point is at 61.9 wt% Sn. An alloy between the α end and E is hypoeutectic, and its primary (proeutectic) phase is α [Session 7 Slide 30]:

$$C_\alpha = 18.3 < C_0 = 50 < C_E = 61.9 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{hypoeutectic alloy, primary phase } \alpha$$

#### Read the start and the end of solidification

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x: Following the dashed vertical line $C_0 = 50$ from above: it stays in L down to the liquidus, which it meets at **215 °C** (printed on the figure). Below that the alloy is in the α + L field, so the first solid is α, the phase on the left boundary of that field. The liquid keeps changing its composition along the liquidus until it reaches E; the last liquid, of 61.9 wt% Sn, solidifies as eutectic at **183 °C**, where solidification ends. Solidification therefore takes place over the interval $215 - 183 = 32$ °C.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
#### Place the point and read the tie line

At 200 °C the alloy point (50, 200) is in the α + L field. The horizontal tie line through it meets the α solidus at $C_\alpha = 16.7$ wt% Sn and the liquidus at $C_L = 55.7$ wt% Sn (printed on the figure). These are the compositions of the two phases [Session 7 Slide 15].

#### Derive the lever rule from two mass balances

Take a mass of alloy as the unit. The alloy is made only of α and L, so their mass fractions add up to one (total mass balance); the tin in the alloy is the tin in α plus the tin in L (mass balance of Sn):

$$W_\alpha + W_L = 1$$

$$W_\alpha C_\alpha + W_L C_L = C_0$$

From the first equation, $W_\alpha = 1 - W_L$. Substituting into the second:

$$(1 - W_L)\,C_\alpha + W_L C_L = C_0$$

$$C_\alpha + W_L\,(C_L - C_\alpha) = C_0$$

$$W_L = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_L - C_\alpha}$$

and then $W_\alpha = 1 - W_L = \dfrac{C_L - C_\alpha - C_0 + C_\alpha}{C_L - C_\alpha} = \dfrac{C_L - C_0}{C_L - C_\alpha}$. Each phase is given by the arm of the lever on the side of the **other** phase, divided by the length of the tie line [Session 7 Slide 16].

#### Substitute the readings at 200 °C

The tie line has length $C_L - C_\alpha = 55.7 - 16.7 = 39.0$ wt% Sn:

$$W_L = \frac{50 - 16.7}{55.7 - 16.7} = \frac{33.3}{39.0} = 0.854$$

$$W_\alpha = \frac{55.7 - 50}{55.7 - 16.7} = \frac{5.7}{39.0} = 0.146$$

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x: Check: $0.854 + 0.146 = 1.000$, and the Sn balance $0.1462 \times 16.7 + 0.8538 \times 55.7 = 2.44 + 47.56 = 50.0$ wt% Sn returns $C_0$. The alloy is still mostly liquid, because 200 °C is only 15 °C below its liquidus.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x: Above 183 °C use the tie line from α to the eutectic liquid; below it, the full eutectic line from α to β. The liquid of 61.9 wt% Sn present just above becomes the eutectic just below.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
- 183 + ΔT: α (18.3) and L (61.9 wt% Sn); $W_\alpha = 0.273$, $W_L = 0.727$.
- 183 − ΔT: α (18.3) and β (97.8 wt% Sn); $W_\alpha = 0.601$, $W_\beta = 0.399$.
- Microconstituents: primary α $W_{\alpha'} = 0.273$, eutectic $W_E = 0.727$; α inside the eutectic 0.328 of the alloy; 54.6 % of all the α is eutectic α.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
#### Lever rule just above 183 °C

At 183 + ΔT the alloy is still in α + L; the tie line ends at the two ends of the left part of the eutectic line, $C_\alpha = 18.3$ and $C_L = C_E = 61.9$ wt% Sn (length $61.9 - 18.3 = 43.6$). With the lever rule of part (b):

$$W_L = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_E - C_\alpha} = \frac{50 - 18.3}{61.9 - 18.3} = \frac{31.7}{43.6} = 0.727$$

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_E - C_0}{C_E - C_\alpha} = \frac{61.9 - 50}{43.6} = \frac{11.9}{43.6} = 0.273$$

#### Lever rule just below 183 °C (total phases)

At 183 − ΔT the eutectic reaction has consumed all the liquid and the alloy is in α + β. The tie line is the whole eutectic line, from $C_\alpha = 18.3$ to $C_\beta = 97.8$ wt% Sn (length $97.8 - 18.3 = 79.5$) [Session 7 Slide 32]:

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_\beta - C_0}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{97.8 - 50}{79.5} = \frac{47.8}{79.5} = 0.601$$

$$W_\beta = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{50 - 18.3}{79.5} = \frac{31.7}{79.5} = 0.399$$

#### Microconstituents just below 183 °C

The α that existed at 183 + ΔT does not take part in the reaction: it stays as **primary α**. The liquid, which has exactly the eutectic composition, becomes the **eutectic** microconstituent (alternating α and β) [Session 7 Slides 30, 32]. Therefore the microconstituent fractions are the phase fractions just above the eutectic temperature:

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
$$W_{\alpha'} = W_\alpha(183 + \Delta T) = 0.273 \qquad W_E = W_L(183 + \Delta T) = 0.727$$

#### Split the α between primary and eutectic

All the β is inside the eutectic (the primary phase is α). The α inside the eutectic is the total α minus the primary α; with four significant figures, $W_\alpha = 47.8/79.5 = 0.6013$ and $W_{\alpha'} = 11.9/43.6 = 0.2729$:

$$W_{\alpha,E} = W_\alpha - W_{\alpha'} = 0.6013 - 0.2729 = 0.328$$

$$\frac{W_{\alpha,E}}{W_\alpha} = \frac{0.3283}{0.6013} = 0.546$$

So **54.6 %** of all the α of the alloy is eutectic α. Check: the eutectic is $W_{\alpha,E} + W_{\beta,E} = 0.328 + 0.399 = 0.727 = W_E$, and its own make-up is $(97.8 - 61.9)/79.5 = 0.452$ α, so $0.727 \times 0.452 = 0.328$ (checked).

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x: Below 183 °C the ends of the tie line move along the two solvus lines. Compare the β fraction at 100 °C with the one just below 183 °C.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
- α (4.8 wt% Sn) and β (99.8 wt% Sn); $W_\alpha = 0.524$, $W_\beta = 0.476$.
- β grows by 0.077 of the alloy between 183 − ΔT and 100 °C: it precipitates from the α, whose Sn solubility falls from 18.3 to 4.8 wt%.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
#### Lever rule at 100 °C

The alloy is still in α + β; the tie line now ends on the α solvus at 4.8 and on the β solvus at 99.8 wt% Sn (length $99.8 - 4.8 = 95.0$):

$$W_\alpha = \frac{99.8 - 50}{99.8 - 4.8} = \frac{49.8}{95.0} = 0.524$$

$$W_\beta = \frac{50 - 4.8}{99.8 - 4.8} = \frac{45.2}{95.0} = 0.476$$

#### Explain the change with the solvus

The α solvus slopes to the left: the solubility of Sn in α falls from 18.3 wt% at 183 °C to 4.8 wt% at 100 °C. The α of the alloy (primary and eutectic) is therefore supersaturated as it cools and rejects the excess Sn as small particles of β inside its grains: this is precipitation in the solid state, which grows as the temperature decreases [Session 8 Slides 3-4]. The amount of β gained is

$$\Delta W_\beta = W_\beta(100\ ^\circ\text{C}) - W_\beta(183 - \Delta T) = 0.4758 - 0.3987 = 0.077$$

that is, 7.7 % of the mass of the alloy. The β side changes little (97.8 → 99.8 wt% Sn), so almost all the change comes from the α side. The microconstituents keep their names: primary α (now with fine β precipitates) and eutectic.

chunks.t: Cooling of a Pb-50 wt% Sn alloy read from the Pb-Sn diagram
chunks.x:
On cooling, the Pb-50 Sn alloy starts to solidify at 215 °C with α, holds 14.6 % α at 200 °C and 27.3 % just above 183 °C; the remaining 72.7 % of liquid, now of eutectic composition, solidifies at 183 °C as eutectic. Because 50 wt% Sn is close to E (61.9), the eutectic dominates the microstructure, and more than half of the α (54.6 %) is eutectic α.

Control cases: as $C_0 \to 18.3$ the eutectic fraction $W_E = (C_0 - 18.3)/43.6 \to 0$ (all primary α), and as $C_0 \to 61.9$, $W_E \to 1$ (fully eutectic). All fractions lie between 0 and 1, and each pair adds up to 1. Dimensional check: the lever rule is a ratio of two composition differences, (wt% Sn)/(wt% Sn), so the fractions are dimensionless, as they must be.

Common exam mistake: taking the primary α from the long tie line below 183 °C (0.601). That number is the total α (primary plus eutectic); the primary α must be read on the short tie line just above 183 °C, which ends at the eutectic liquid.

chunks.h: Bank P06 — Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the final of June 2014 (question 3), where the diagram is built from a list of features, and of Problem 8 of the Unit 4 sheet. Method: binary eutectic systems [Session 7 Slides 26-27], tie line and lever rule [Session 7 Slides 15-16], microconstituents [Session 7 Slides 31-32], solvus and precipitation [Session 8 Slides 2-4]. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
Two metals A and B are completely soluble in the liquid state and partially soluble in the solid state, where they form a solid solution α rich in A and a solid solution β rich in B. Metal A melts at 900 °C and metal B at 700 °C. The system has a single invariant point, a eutectic at 550 °C, where the liquid contains 70 wt% B. At that temperature α can dissolve at most 20 wt% B and β at most 8 wt% A. At room temperature (20 °C) the solubilities fall to 5 wt% B in α and 3 wt% A in β. Assume that every boundary of the diagram is a straight line between the points given, and that cooling is slow (equilibrium).

(a) Draw the phase diagram (temperature against wt% B), label every region and write the invariant reaction.

(b) For an alloy of 85 wt% B: at which temperature does it start to solidify and what is the composition of the first solid? Give the phases, their compositions and their mass fractions at 600 °C.

(c) For the same alloy, give the microconstituents and their mass fractions just below 550 °C, and the mass fraction of each phase inside the eutectic.

(d) Which alloys of the system contain eutectic at room temperature? An alloy of 12 wt% B contains none: at which temperature does β appear in it, and how much β is there at 20 °C?

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Feature of the statement | Point of the diagram (wt% B, °C) | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A melts at 900 °C | (0, 900) | top of the liquidus and of the α solidus |
| B melts at 700 °C | (100, 700) | top of the liquidus and of the β solidus |
| Eutectic, liquid of 70 wt% B at 550 °C | E = (70, 550) | lowest point of the liquidus |
| α holds at most 20 wt% B at 550 °C | (20, 550) | α end of the eutectic line |
| β holds at most 8 wt% A at 550 °C | (100 − 8, 550) = (92, 550) | β end of the eutectic line |
| α holds 5 wt% B at 20 °C | (5, 20) | lower end of the α solvus |
| β holds 3 wt% A at 20 °C | (100 − 3, 20) = (97, 20) | lower end of the β solvus |
| Alloys | $C_0$ = 85 and 12 wt% B | parts (b) to (d) |

The composition axis is wt% B, so a content of A is turned into a content of B with $C_B = 100 - C_A$: 8 wt% A is 92 wt% B, and 3 wt% A is 97 wt% B. The lever rule uses ratios of composition differences, so the wt% can be used directly (the factor 1/100 that turns them into mass fractions cancels).

#### Model

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
- Binary eutectic system with partial solid solubility [Session 7 Slides 26-27]: liquidus from each melting point down to E; solidus from each melting point to the end of the eutectic line; solvus from each end of the eutectic line down to room temperature.
- Straight boundary through $(C_1, T_1)$ and $(C_2, T_2)$, as the statement imposes: $C = C_1 + (T - T_1)\dfrac{C_2 - C_1}{T_2 - T_1}$ (linear interpolation).
- Lever rule on a horizontal tie line [Session 7 Slides 15-16]; microconstituents of a hypereutectic alloy: primary β and eutectic [Session 7 Slides 31-32]; precipitation of β when an alloy crosses the solvus [Session 8 Slides 3-4].

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x: Place the seven points first. Each melting point is the common top of a liquidus and a solidus; each end of the eutectic line is the common top of a solidus end and a solvus.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
#### Draw the boundaries from the points

The liquidus is the line above which only liquid exists; in a eutectic system it falls from the melting point of each metal to the eutectic point, so it is made of the two segments (0, 900)–(70, 550) and (70, 550)–(100, 700). The solidus is the line below which there is no liquid; it falls from each melting point to the corresponding end of the eutectic line: (0, 900)–(20, 550) for α and (100, 700)–(92, 550) for β. The horizontal eutectic line joins (20, 550) and (92, 550). Below it, the solvus lines give the limit of solubility in each solid solution: (20, 550)–(5, 20) for α and (92, 550)–(97, 20) for β [Session 7 Slides 26-27].

#### Label the regions

Above the liquidus: L. Between the A-side liquidus and the α solidus: α + L. Between the B-side liquidus and the β solidus: β + L. Left of the α solidus and α solvus: α. Right of the β solidus and β solvus: β. Below the eutectic line, between the two solvus lines: α + β. Every two-phase field lies between two one-phase fields of the phases it contains, as it must in a binary diagram.

#### Write the invariant reaction

At 550 °C a liquid of fixed composition gives two solids of fixed compositions; this is a eutectic reaction, and with three phases it has $F = 3 - P = 0$ degrees of freedom [Session 7 Slide 13]:

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
$$\text{cooling: } L\ (70\ \text{wt\% B}) \rightarrow \alpha\ (20\ \text{wt\% B}) + \beta\ (92\ \text{wt\% B}) \quad \text{at } 550\ ^\circ\text{C (eutectic)}$$

The diagram is thermodynamically sensible: both liquidus branches fall towards E, each solid solution is richest in solute at the eutectic temperature, and the eutectic composition lies between those of α and β.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
- Liquidus temperature 625 °C; first solid β of 96 wt% B.
- At 600 °C: L of 80 wt% B and β of 94.7 wt% B; $W_L = 0.659$, $W_\beta = 0.341$.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
#### Liquidus temperature of the alloy

On the straight B-side liquidus from (70, 550) to (100, 700), the temperature rises by $(700 - 550)/(100 - 70) = 150/30 = 5$ °C per wt% B. Writing the line and putting $C = 85$:

$$T = 550 + 5\,(C - 70) = 550 + 5\,(85 - 70) = 550 + 75 = 625\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

#### Composition of the first solid

At 625 °C the first crystal is the solid in equilibrium with the liquid, at the other end of the tie line, on the β solidus from (92, 550) to (100, 700). On that line the composition grows by $(100 - 92)/(700 - 550) = 8/150$ wt% B per °C:

$$C_\beta = 92 + (T - 550)\,\frac{8}{150} = 92 + (625 - 550)\,\frac{8}{150} = 92 + 4.0 = 96.0\ \text{wt\% B}$$

The first solid (β of 96 wt% B) is richer in B than the alloy, as the tie line requires.

#### Ends of the tie line at 600 °C

At 600 °C the alloy (85, 600) lies between the liquidus and the β solidus: β + L. The liquid end is found by isolating $C$ in the liquidus equation:

$$600 = 550 + 5\,(C_L - 70) \quad\Rightarrow\quad C_L - 70 = \frac{600 - 550}{5} = 10 \quad\Rightarrow\quad C_L = 80\ \text{wt\% B}$$

$$C_\beta = 92 + (600 - 550)\,\frac{8}{150} = 92 + 2.667 = 94.67\ \text{wt\% B}$$

#### Derive the lever rule and apply it

With W the mass fractions of the two phases, the total mass balance and the mass balance of B are

$$W_L + W_\beta = 1$$

$$W_L C_L + W_\beta C_\beta = C_0$$

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
Putting $W_L = 1 - W_\beta$ into the second equation and expanding:

$$(1 - W_\beta)\,C_L + W_\beta C_\beta = C_0$$

$$C_L + W_\beta\,(C_\beta - C_L) = C_0$$

so

$$W_\beta = \frac{C_0 - C_L}{C_\beta - C_L} \qquad W_L = 1 - W_\beta = \frac{C_\beta - C_0}{C_\beta - C_L}$$

With a tie line of length $94.67 - 80 = 14.67$ wt% B [Session 7 Slide 16]:

$$W_\beta = \frac{85 - 80}{94.67 - 80} = \frac{5}{14.67} = 0.341$$

$$W_L = \frac{94.67 - 85}{94.67 - 80} = \frac{9.667}{14.67} = 0.659$$

Check of the B balance: $0.659 \times 80 + 0.341 \times 94.67 = 52.73 + 32.27 = 85.0$ wt% B.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x: The β present just above 550 °C is the primary β; the remaining liquid has the eutectic composition. Below 550 °C the tie line spans the whole eutectic line.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
- Primary β $W_{\beta'} = 0.682$; eutectic $W_E = 0.318$.
- Total phases: $W_\alpha = 0.0972$, $W_\beta = 0.903$.
- Inside the eutectic: α 0.0972 and β 0.221 of the alloy.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
#### Phases just above 550 °C

The tie line now runs from the eutectic liquid ($C_E = 70$) to the β end of the eutectic line ($C_\beta = 92$), length 22 wt% B:

$$W_{\beta}(550 + \Delta T) = \frac{C_0 - C_E}{C_\beta - C_E} = \frac{85 - 70}{92 - 70} = \frac{15}{22} = 0.682$$

$$W_{L}(550 + \Delta T) = \frac{92 - 85}{22} = \frac{7}{22} = 0.318$$

#### Microconstituents just below 550 °C

The alloy is hypereutectic ($70 < 85 < 92$), so its primary phase is β [Session 7 Slide 31]. The β formed above 550 °C remains as **primary β**, and the liquid of 70 wt% B turns entirely into the **eutectic** microconstituent [Session 7 Slide 32]:

$$W_{\beta'} = 0.682 \qquad W_E = 0.318$$

#### Total phases just below 550 °C

Now α + β, on the tie line from 20 to 92 wt% B (length 72):

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_\beta - C_0}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{92 - 85}{92 - 20} = \frac{7}{72} = 0.0972$$

$$W_\beta = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{85 - 20}{72} = \frac{65}{72} = 0.903$$

#### Phases inside the eutectic

The primary constituent is β, so every bit of α is in the eutectic: $W_{\alpha,E} = W_\alpha = 0.0972$. The β of the eutectic is the total β minus the primary β, with four figures:

$$W_{\beta,E} = W_\beta - W_{\beta'} = 0.9028 - 0.6818 = 0.221$$

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x: Check with the make-up of the eutectic, which is $(92 - 70)/72 = 0.3056$ α: $0.3182 \times 0.3056 = 0.0972$ α, and $0.0972 + 0.221 = 0.318 = W_E$.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x: Eutectic can only form from liquid that reaches E. For 12 wt% B, find where the alloy line meets the α solvus, then use the tie line at 20 °C.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
- Eutectic at room temperature for $20 < C_0 < 92$ wt% B.
- The 12 wt% B alloy crosses the α solvus at 267.3 °C; at 20 °C it holds $W_\beta = 0.0761$ of precipitated β.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
#### Range of alloys with eutectic

An alloy contains eutectic only if some of its liquid reaches the eutectic point at 550 °C, that is, if its vertical line crosses the eutectic line. The line runs from 20 to 92 wt% B, so the alloys with eutectic are those with $20 < C_0 < 92$ wt% B. An alloy of 12 wt% B solidifies completely as α before reaching 550 °C (it crosses the α solidus), so it has no eutectic.

#### Temperature at which β appears

Below its solidus the 12 wt% B alloy is single-phase α, until its vertical line meets the α solvus, the straight line from (20, 550) to (5, 20). Writing that line as temperature against composition and putting $C = 12$:

$$T = 20 + (C - 5)\,\frac{550 - 20}{20 - 5} = 20 + (12 - 5)\,\frac{530}{15} = 20 + 7 \times 35.33 = 267.3\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

Below 267.3 °C α cannot hold all its B, and β precipitates as fine particles inside the α grains and on their boundaries [Session 8 Slides 3-4].

#### Amount of β at 20 °C

At 20 °C the tie line runs from the α solvus (5 wt% B) to the β solvus (97 wt% B), length 92:

$$W_\beta = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{12 - 5}{97 - 5} = \frac{7}{92} = 0.0761$$

$$W_\alpha = \frac{97 - 12}{92} = \frac{85}{92} = 0.924$$

All this β (7.61 % of the alloy) is precipitated β; none of it is eutectic.

chunks.t: Building a eutectic diagram from a description and using it
chunks.x:
The description fixes the diagram completely once straight lines are assumed: seven points, six boundaries and six regions. The 85 wt% B alloy starts to solidify at 625 °C with β of 96 wt% B, is two-thirds primary β at 550 °C, and the last 31.8 % of liquid becomes a eutectic that holds all the α of the alloy (9.72 %). The 12 wt% B alloy shows that a two-phase structure does not need a eutectic: it appears by precipitation when the solvus is crossed at 267.3 °C.

Control cases: for $C_0 \to 70$ the primary β $W_{\beta'} = (C_0 - 70)/22 \to 0$ and the alloy is all eutectic; for $C_0 \to 92$, $W_{\beta'} \to 1$. For $C_0 \to 5$ the solvus temperature tends to 20 °C, and for $C_0 \to 20$ to 550 °C. Dimensional check: interpolation slopes are in °C per wt% B (5 °C/wt%, 530/15 = 35.33 °C/wt%) or wt% B per °C (8/150), so every interpolated temperature is in °C and every composition in wt% B; the fractions are ratios of compositions and are dimensionless.

Common exam mistake: writing the β end of the eutectic line at 8 wt% B instead of 92 wt% B; the statement gives the solubility of A in β, and the axis is wt% B.

Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.h: Bank P07 — Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the problems that deduce a composition from a microstructure (Problem 2 of the Unit 4 sheet; the 2016 and 2017 extraordinary finals), with the Ag-Cu values printed on the diagram of Problems T4_PhaseDiagrams I.pdf, p. 2. Method: lever rule [Session 7 Slides 15-16] and microconstituents of hypo- and hypereutectic alloys [Session 7 Slides 30-32]. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
A casting of 3.0 kg of an Ag-Cu alloy of unknown composition was cooled slowly. Its micrograph (sketch below) shows rounded, dendritic grains of a primary constituent in a fine lamellar matrix. Image analysis gives 55 % of the section as lamellar matrix and 45 % as primary grains; take these area fractions as mass fractions. Microanalysis shows that the primary grains are the Cu-rich solid solution (Cu).

The Ag-Cu diagram of the problem sheet has a single eutectic at 779.1 °C, where the liquid contains 28.1 wt% Cu; at that temperature the Ag-rich solid solution (Ag) holds 8.8 wt% Cu and the Cu-rich solid solution (Cu) holds 92 wt% Cu.

(a) Show that the eutectic fraction alone allows two compositions of the alloy, compute both, and use the micrograph to choose the right one.

(b) Just below 779.1 °C, give the phases with their compositions and mass fractions, and the mass fraction of each phase inside the eutectic.

(c) For the 3.0 kg casting, give the mass in kg of every microconstituent and of every phase just below 779.1 °C, and the mass and composition of the liquid just above 779.1 °C. How many kg of Cu does that liquid hold?

(d) The supplier's certificate states Ag-50 wt% Cu. What eutectic fraction would that alloy show? Is the certificate consistent with the micrograph?

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Eutectic temperature | $T_E$ | 779.1 °C |
| Eutectic liquid | $C_E$ | 28.1 wt% Cu |
| (Ag) at $T_E$ | $C_\alpha$ | 8.8 wt% Cu |
| (Cu) at $T_E$ | $C_\beta$ | 92 wt% Cu |
| Eutectic fraction (lamellar matrix) | $W_E$ | 0.55 |
| Primary fraction (grains) | $W_{\beta'}$ | 0.45, identified as (Cu) |
| Mass of the casting | $m$ | 3.0 kg |
| Certificate | $C_{cert}$ | 50 wt% Cu |

In what follows α is (Ag) and β is (Cu). Compositions are mass percentages of Cu; in a ratio of composition differences the factor 1/100 that turns them into mass fractions cancels, but in a mass of Cu it does not: 28.1 wt% is a mass fraction of 0.281.

#### Model

- Lever rule on a horizontal tie line [Session 7 Slides 15-16], derived in part (a) from the two mass balances.
- Microconstituents [Session 7 Slides 30-32]: just below $T_E$ the primary phase is the solid present just above $T_E$, and the eutectic is the liquid of composition $C_E$ present just above $T_E$. A hypoeutectic alloy ($C_\alpha < C_0 < C_E$) has primary α; a hypereutectic one ($C_E < C_0 < C_\beta$) has primary β.
- Hypotheses: equilibrium cooling; area fraction equal to mass fraction (as the statement imposes); closed system.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x: Write the eutectic fraction with the lever rule twice: once on the tie line α–E (hypoeutectic) and once on E–β (hypereutectic). Then solve each for $C_0$.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
- Hypoeutectic candidate: $C_0 = 19.4$ wt% Cu (primary would be (Ag)).
- Hypereutectic candidate: $C_0 = 56.86$ wt% Cu (primary would be (Cu)).
- The primary grains are (Cu): the alloy is Ag-56.86 wt% Cu.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
#### Derive the lever rule for the eutectic fraction

Just above $T_E$ the alloy holds a primary solid and liquid of composition $C_E$; that liquid becomes the eutectic, so $W_E = W_L(T_E + \Delta T)$. For a tie line from a solid of composition $C_s$ to the liquid $C_E$, the total mass balance and the Cu balance are

$$W_s + W_L = 1$$

$$W_s C_s + W_L C_E = C_0$$

Putting $W_s = 1 - W_L$ in the second equation and expanding:

$$(1 - W_L)\,C_s + W_L C_E = C_0$$

$$C_s + W_L\,(C_E - C_s) = C_0$$

hence

$$W_E = W_L = \frac{C_0 - C_s}{C_E - C_s}$$

#### Hypoeutectic candidate (solid α, $C_s = 8.8$)

$$0.55 = \frac{C_0 - 8.8}{28.1 - 8.8} = \frac{C_0 - 8.8}{19.3}$$

$$C_0 - 8.8 = 0.55 \times 19.3 = 10.615 \quad\Rightarrow\quad C_0 = 8.8 + 10.615 = 19.4\ \text{wt\% Cu}$$

#### Hypereutectic candidate (solid β, $C_s = 92$)

With $C_s = 92$ the same formula reads $W_E = (C_0 - 92)/(28.1 - 92) = (92 - C_0)/(92 - 28.1)$:

$$0.55 = \frac{92 - C_0}{92 - 28.1} = \frac{92 - C_0}{63.9}$$

$$92 - C_0 = 0.55 \times 63.9 = 35.145 \quad\Rightarrow\quad C_0 = 92 - 35.145 = 56.86\ \text{wt\% Cu}$$

#### Choose with the primary constituent

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
The eutectic fraction is the same function of $C_0$ on both sides of E, rising from 0 at an end of the eutectic line to 1 at E, so one value of $W_E$ always corresponds to two alloys. The primary constituent tells them apart: a hypoeutectic Ag-Cu alloy would show primary (Ag), a hypereutectic one primary (Cu) [Session 7 Slides 30-31]. The microanalysis finds (Cu) grains, so

$$C_0 = 56.86\ \text{wt\% Cu} \qquad (28.1 < 56.86 < 92\text{, hypereutectic})$$

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x: The tie line now spans the whole eutectic line, from 8.8 to 92 wt% Cu. The primary constituent is β, so all the α is in the eutectic.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
- α (8.8 wt% Cu) $W_\alpha = 0.422$; β (92 wt% Cu) $W_\beta = 0.578$.
- Inside the eutectic: α 0.422 and β 0.128 of the alloy; the eutectic itself is 76.8 % α.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
#### Total phases with the lever rule

Below $T_E$ the liquid has gone and the alloy is α + β. With the lever rule of part (a) on the tie line from $C_\alpha = 8.8$ to $C_\beta = 92$ (length 83.2), carrying $C_0 = 56.855$:

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_\beta - C_0}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{92 - 56.855}{92 - 8.8} = \frac{35.145}{83.2} = 0.422$$

$$W_\beta = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{56.855 - 8.8}{83.2} = \frac{48.055}{83.2} = 0.578$$

#### Split the β between primary and eutectic

The primary β is 0.45 of the alloy (data). The rest of the β, and all of the α, are inside the eutectic:

$$W_{\beta,E} = W_\beta - W_{\beta'} = 0.5776 - 0.45 = 0.128$$

$$W_{\alpha,E} = W_\alpha = 0.422$$

Check: $W_{\alpha,E} + W_{\beta,E} = 0.422 + 0.128 = 0.550 = W_E$.

#### Make-up of the eutectic

The eutectic is the liquid of 28.1 wt% Cu split on the tie line 8.8–92; its α fraction is

$$\frac{C_\beta - C_E}{C_\beta - C_\alpha} = \frac{92 - 28.1}{83.2} = \frac{63.9}{83.2} = 0.768$$

so the eutectic is 76.8 % α and 23.2 % β whatever the alloy, and $0.55 \times 0.768 = 0.422$ reproduces $W_{\alpha,E}$. The lamellar matrix is mostly the Ag-rich phase.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
- Primary β 1.35 kg, eutectic 1.65 kg; α 1.267 kg, β 1.733 kg (of which 0.383 kg in the eutectic).
- Just above 779.1 °C: 1.65 kg of liquid of 28.1 wt% Cu, holding 0.464 kg of Cu.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
#### Microconstituents and phases just below 779.1 °C

The mass of each constituent is its mass fraction times the mass of the casting, $m_i = W_i\,m$:

$$m_{\beta'} = 0.45 \times 3.0\ \text{kg} = 1.35\ \text{kg} \qquad m_E = 0.55 \times 3.0\ \text{kg} = 1.65\ \text{kg}$$

$$m_\alpha = 0.4224 \times 3.0\ \text{kg} = 1.267\ \text{kg} \qquad m_\beta = 0.5776 \times 3.0\ \text{kg} = 1.733\ \text{kg}$$

$$m_{\beta,E} = 0.1276 \times 3.0\ \text{kg} = 0.383\ \text{kg}$$

Check: $1.35 + 1.65 = 3.00$ kg and $1.267 + 1.733 = 3.000$ kg.

#### The liquid just above 779.1 °C

Just above $T_E$ the alloy is β + L; the liquid has the eutectic composition, 28.1 wt% Cu, and its mass is the future eutectic, 1.65 kg. Converting the composition to a mass fraction, $28.1\ \text{wt\%} \rightarrow 0.281$:

$$m_{Cu,L} = 0.281 \times 1.65\ \text{kg} = 0.464\ \text{kg}$$

#### Cu balance of the casting

The Cu of the primary β is $0.92 \times 1.35\ \text{kg} = 1.242$ kg, so the casting holds $1.242 + 0.464 = 1.706$ kg of Cu, which is $1.706/3.0 = 0.5686$ of its mass: 56.86 wt% Cu, the composition found in part (a).

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
- Ag-50 wt% Cu would show $W_E = 0.657$ eutectic and 0.343 primary (Cu).
- Measured 0.55: the certificate overstates the Ag content of the alloy (or understates its Cu); the micrograph points to 56.86 wt% Cu.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
#### Eutectic fraction of the certified alloy

Ag-50 wt% Cu is also hypereutectic ($28.1 < 50 < 92$), so its eutectic is

$$W_E(50) = \frac{92 - 50}{92 - 28.1} = \frac{42}{63.9} = 0.657$$

and its primary (Cu) is $1 - 0.657 = 0.343$.

#### Compare with the measurement

The micrograph shows 0.55 eutectic, not 0.657: about 11 points less eutectic and therefore more primary (Cu) than the certified alloy would have. Because $W_E$ falls as $C_0$ moves from E towards β, less eutectic means more Cu: the measurement corresponds to 56.86 wt% Cu, not 50. Within the hypotheses of the problem (equilibrium cooling, area fraction equal to mass fraction), the certificate is not consistent with the micrograph. The two alloys would also differ in their total phase fractions: α would be $42/83.2 = 0.505$ for the certified alloy, against 0.422 for the alloy of the micrograph.

chunks.t: Composition of an Ag-Cu alloy worked backwards from its micrograph
chunks.x:
A eutectic fraction alone never fixes the composition: it gives one hypoeutectic and one hypereutectic alloy, here 19.4 and 56.86 wt% Cu, and the nature of the primary grains decides between them. The alloy is hypereutectic: 45 % primary (Cu) dendrites in a matrix that, although it is 55 % of the alloy, is three-quarters Ag-rich α.

Control cases: with $W_E \to 1$ both candidates tend to $C_E = 28.1$ (fully eutectic), and with $W_E \to 0$ they tend to the ends of the eutectic line, 8.8 and 92 wt% Cu. All fractions lie between 0 and 1 and the masses add up to 3.0 kg. Dimensional check: the lever rule is a ratio of composition differences, (wt% Cu)/(wt% Cu), so it is dimensionless; a mass is a dimensionless fraction times kg, so it is in kg; and a mass of Cu needs the composition as a fraction (0.281), not as 28.1.

Common exam mistake (the trap of this problem): solving only on the side of the eutectic point one is used to (the hypoeutectic one) and answering 19.4 wt% Cu, an alloy that would show primary (Ag), not the (Cu) grains of the micrograph.

chunks.h: Bank P08 — Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of Session 7 Slide 23, where the compositions of the liquid and the solid are tabulated along the cooling of one alloy, and of the finals that ask for kilograms of each constituent. Method: tie line and lever rule [Session 7 Slides 15-16], eutectic microconstituents [Session 7 Slides 30, 32], precipitation below the solvus [Session 8 Slides 3-4]. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
In a hypothetical A-B system, A melts at 1000 °C and forms with B a eutectic at 800 °C. Instead of the diagram, the laboratory gives the compositions (wt% B) of the phases that are in equilibrium at several temperatures:

| T (°C) | Liquid in equilibrium with α | α (on the solidus or solvus) | β (on the solvus) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1000 | 0 (pure A melts) | 0 | — |
| 950 | 12 | 4 | — |
| 900 | 24 | 8 | — |
| 850 | 36 | 12 | — |
| 800 (eutectic) | 48 | 16 | 85 |
| 600 | — | 10 | 88 |
| 400 | — | 6 | 91 |
| 20 | — | 3 | 94 |

Between two rows every boundary may be taken as straight (linear interpolation). A casting of 50 kg of an A-30 wt% B alloy is cooled slowly from 1050 °C to 20 °C.

(a) At which temperature does the casting start to solidify, and what is the composition of the first solid? At which temperature does it finish, and what is the composition of the last liquid?

(b) At 850 °C, give the phases, their compositions and their masses in kg.

(c) Just above and just below 800 °C, give the phases and the microconstituents with their masses in kg, and the mass of α inside the eutectic.

(d) At 20 °C, give the masses of α and β. How many kg of β form below 800 °C, from which constituent, and why?

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Alloy | $C_0$ | 30 wt% B |
| Mass of the casting | $m$ | 50 kg |
| Eutectic | $T_E$, $C_E$ | 800 °C, 48 wt% B |
| Ends of the eutectic line | $C_\alpha$, $C_\beta$ | 16 and 85 wt% B |
| Tie lines | rows of the table | liquid and α from 950 to 800 °C; α and β from 800 to 20 °C |

The first column of compositions lies on the liquidus, the second on the α solidus (above 800 °C) or on the α solvus (below), the third on the β solvus. The table is the diagram: plotting its points and joining them gives the figure of part (a). The lever rule uses ratios of compositions in wt% B, where the factor 1/100 cancels; a mass is a fraction times 50 kg.

#### Model

- Tie line at temperature $T$: its ends are the two compositions in the row of $T$ [Session 7 Slide 15]; between rows, linear interpolation, $C(T) = C_1 + (T - T_1)\dfrac{C_2 - C_1}{T_2 - T_1}$.
- Lever rule [Session 7 Slides 15-16], derived in part (b).
- Microconstituents of a hypoeutectic alloy [Session 7 Slides 30, 32]; precipitation below the solvus [Session 8 Slides 3-4]. Hypotheses: equilibrium cooling, closed system.

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x: Find between which rows the liquid column passes 30 wt% B, and interpolate both columns at that temperature. Then compare 30 with the eutectic line 16–85.

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
- Solidification starts at 875 °C; the first solid is α of 10 wt% B.
- It ends at 800 °C with the eutectic reaction; the last liquid has 48 wt% B.

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
#### Place the alloy against the liquidus

On cooling, the alloy stays liquid until the liquid column of the table reaches its own composition: that point is on the liquidus. The liquid column goes from 24 wt% B at 900 °C to 36 wt% B at 850 °C, so 30 wt% B is reached between those two rows. Writing the liquidus between them as a straight line and isolating $T$:

$$C_L = 24 + (900 - T)\,\frac{36 - 24}{900 - 850} = 24 + 0.24\,(900 - T)$$

$$30 = 24 + 0.24\,(900 - T) \quad\Rightarrow\quad 900 - T = \frac{30 - 24}{0.24} = 25 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T = 875\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

#### Composition of the first solid

At 875 °C the first crystals are the α at the other end of the tie line, on the α solidus, interpolated between 8 wt% B (900 °C) and 12 wt% B (850 °C):

$$C_\alpha(875) = 8 + (900 - 875)\,\frac{12 - 8}{900 - 850} = 8 + 25 \times 0.08 = 10\ \text{wt\% B}$$

The first solid is much poorer in B than the alloy (10 against 30 wt% B), so the liquid left behind gets richer in B as α grows.

#### End of solidification

The alloy lies on the eutectic line, $16 < 30 < 48$, so it is hypoeutectic: its liquid keeps enriching along the liquidus until it reaches the eutectic point, 48 wt% B at 800 °C, and that last liquid turns into α + β at constant temperature [Session 7 Slides 30, 32]:

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x: $$\text{cooling: } L\ (48\ \text{wt\% B}) \rightarrow \alpha\ (16\ \text{wt\% B}) + \beta\ (85\ \text{wt\% B}) \quad \text{at } 800\ ^\circ\text{C (eutectic)}$$

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
#### Read the tie line

850 °C lies between 875 °C and 800 °C, so the alloy is in α + L. The row of 850 °C gives the ends of the tie line: $C_\alpha = 12$ and $C_L = 36$ wt% B.

#### Derive the lever rule

The two phases make up the whole alloy (total mass balance), and the B of the alloy is the B of α plus the B of the liquid (mass balance of B):

$$W_\alpha + W_L = 1$$

$$W_\alpha C_\alpha + W_L C_L = C_0$$

Replacing $W_\alpha = 1 - W_L$ and expanding:

$$(1 - W_L)\,C_\alpha + W_L C_L = C_0$$

$$C_\alpha + W_L\,(C_L - C_\alpha) = C_0$$

so

$$W_L = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_L - C_\alpha} \qquad W_\alpha = 1 - W_L = \frac{C_L - C_0}{C_L - C_\alpha}$$

#### Substitute and convert to kg

$$W_L = \frac{30 - 12}{36 - 12} = \frac{18}{24} = 0.75 \qquad W_\alpha = \frac{36 - 30}{24} = \frac{6}{24} = 0.25$$

$$m_L = 0.75 \times 50\ \text{kg} = 37.5\ \text{kg} \qquad m_\alpha = 0.25 \times 50\ \text{kg} = 12.5\ \text{kg}$$

Check of the B balance: $12.5 \times 0.12 + 37.5 \times 0.36 = 1.5 + 13.5 = 15.0$ kg of B, which is $0.30 \times 50$ kg.

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x: Above 800 °C the tie line runs from α (16) to the eutectic liquid (48); below it, from α (16) to β (85). The liquid of 48 wt% B becomes the eutectic.

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
- 800 + ΔT: α 28.125 kg, L 21.875 kg.
- 800 − ΔT: α 39.86 kg (16 wt% B), β 10.14 kg (85 wt% B).
- Primary α 28.125 kg, eutectic 21.875 kg; α inside the eutectic 11.73 kg.

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
#### Just above 800 °C

The row of 800 °C gives $C_\alpha = 16$ and $C_L = C_E = 48$ wt% B (length 32):

$$W_\alpha = \frac{48 - 30}{48 - 16} = \frac{18}{32} = 0.5625 \qquad W_L = \frac{30 - 16}{32} = \frac{14}{32} = 0.4375$$

$$m_\alpha = 0.5625 \times 50 = 28.125\ \text{kg} \qquad m_L = 0.4375 \times 50 = 21.875\ \text{kg}$$

#### Just below 800 °C: phases

The eutectic reaction has used up the liquid. The tie line is the whole eutectic line, $C_\alpha = 16$ to $C_\beta = 85$ wt% B (length 69):

$$W_\alpha = \frac{85 - 30}{85 - 16} = \frac{55}{69} = 0.7971 \qquad W_\beta = \frac{30 - 16}{69} = \frac{14}{69} = 0.2029$$

$$m_\alpha = 0.7971 \times 50 = 39.86\ \text{kg} \qquad m_\beta = 0.2029 \times 50 = 10.14\ \text{kg}$$

#### Just below 800 °C: microconstituents

The α formed above 800 °C stays as **primary α**, and the liquid of eutectic composition becomes the **eutectic** [Session 7 Slide 32]:

$$m_{\alpha'} = 28.125\ \text{kg} \qquad m_E = 21.875\ \text{kg}$$

All the β is in the eutectic (the primary phase is α); the α of the eutectic is the total α minus the primary α:

$$m_{\alpha,E} = 39.86 - 28.125 = 11.73\ \text{kg}$$

Check with the make-up of the eutectic, $(85 - 48)/69 = 0.5362$ α: $0.5362 \times 21.875 = 11.73$ kg, and $11.73 + 10.14 = 21.87$ kg $= m_E$.

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
- α (3 wt% B) 35.16 kg; β (94 wt% B) 14.84 kg.
- 4.69 kg of β precipitate below 800 °C, from the α (primary and eutectic).

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
#### Phases at 20 °C

Below 800 °C the ends of the tie line follow the two solvus columns; at 20 °C they are $C_\alpha = 3$ and $C_\beta = 94$ wt% B (length 91):

$$W_\alpha = \frac{94 - 30}{94 - 3} = \frac{64}{91} = 0.7033 \qquad W_\beta = \frac{30 - 3}{91} = \frac{27}{91} = 0.2967$$

$$m_\alpha = 0.7033 \times 50 = 35.16\ \text{kg} \qquad m_\beta = 0.2967 \times 50 = 14.84\ \text{kg}$$

#### β formed in the solid state

$$\Delta m_\beta = m_\beta(20\ ^\circ\text{C}) - m_\beta(800 - \Delta T) = 14.835 - 10.145 = 4.69\ \text{kg}$$

(with the unrounded masses $50 \times 27/91 = 14.835$ kg and $50 \times 14/69 = 10.145$ kg). The α column falls from 16 wt% B at 800 °C to 3 wt% B at 20 °C: α can hold less and less B, so the α of the casting (primary α and the α of the eutectic) becomes supersaturated and rejects the excess as small β particles, which grow as the temperature falls [Session 8 Slides 3-4]. The β column also moves (85 → 94 wt% B), so the β already present gets slightly richer in B too. The microconstituents keep their names; the primary α now holds fine β precipitates.

chunks.t: Cooling history of a 50 kg casting from a table of tie-line compositions
chunks.x:
The table is enough to follow the whole cooling: the casting starts to solidify at 875 °C with α of 10 wt% B, is three-quarters liquid at 850 °C, reaches 800 °C with 28.1 kg of primary α and 21.9 kg of liquid of 48 wt% B, and that liquid becomes eutectic. In the solid, another 4.69 kg of β precipitate down to room temperature.

Control cases: for $C_0 \to 16$ the eutectic vanishes and for $C_0 \to 48$ the casting is all eutectic; at the liquidus temperature (875 °C) the lever rule gives $W_L = (30 - 10)/(30 - 10) = 1$, all liquid, as it must. Every pair of masses adds up to 50 kg. Dimensional check: the lever rule is (wt% B)/(wt% B), dimensionless; the interpolation slopes are 0.24 and 0.08 wt% B per °C, so $(T_1 - T)$ in °C times them gives wt% B; masses are fractions times kg.

Common exam mistake: taking the first solid to have the alloy composition (30 wt% B). The first solid sits at the other end of the tie line, on the solidus, and is much poorer in B (10 wt% B).
