chunks.h: Bank P09 — Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the Fe-C questions of the finals (a bar of steel in kg, phases just above and just below 727 °C, proeutectoid and eutectoid ferrite). Method: Session 9, Slides 4, 10 and 14-18; lever rule of Session 7, Slides 15-21. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
A bar of plain carbon steel with a mass of 8.0 kg and a carbon content of 0.45 wt% C is fully austenitised and then cooled slowly enough to stay at equilibrium. Use the metastable Fe-Fe₃C diagram of the course.

(a) Just above the eutectoid temperature (727 + ΔT °C), name the phases present and give their chemical composition and mass fraction.

(b) Just below the eutectoid temperature (727 − ΔT °C), name the phases and the microconstituents present and give the mass fraction of each.

(c) Calculate the mass, in kg, of proeutectoid ferrite, of eutectoid ferrite (the ferrite inside the pearlite) and of cementite in the bar at 727 − ΔT °C.

(d) Draw a schematic sketch of the microstructure at 727 − ΔT °C, and explain how the amount of proeutectoid ferrite and the pearlite would change if the bar were cooled faster.

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value | As a fraction or in SI |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Mass of the bar | $m$ | 8.0 kg | 8.0 kg |
| Carbon content of the steel | $C_0$ | 0.45 wt% C | 0.0045 |
| Carbon in ferrite at 727 °C (maximum solubility) | $C_\alpha$ | 0.022 wt% C | Session 9, Slides 5 and 10 |
| Eutectoid composition (austenite at 727 °C) | $C_E$ | 0.76 wt% C | Session 9, Slide 10 |
| Carbon in cementite, Fe₃C | $C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}$ | 6.67 wt% C | Session 9, Slides 4 and 8 |
| Eutectoid temperature | $T_E$ | 727 °C | Session 9, Slide 10 |

The lever rule uses ratios of compositions, so the wt% values can be used directly: the factor 1/100 that turns wt% into a mass fraction cancels between numerator and denominator.

#### Model

- Metastable Fe-Fe₃C diagram, Session 9, Slide 4. Eutectoid reaction on cooling, Session 9, Slide 10: γ (0.76 wt% C) → α (0.022 wt% C) + Fe₃C (6.67 wt% C) at 727 °C; its product is pearlite.
- Since $C_0 = 0.45 < C_E = 0.76$, the steel is **hypoeutectoid** (Session 9, Slide 4): its microconstituents below 727 °C are proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite (Session 9, Slide 14).
- Lever rule on a tie line (Session 7, Slides 15-21), derived in part (a).
- Hypothesis: slow (equilibrium) cooling, so the compositions of the phases are those read on the diagram.

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x: At 727 + ΔT °C the point (0.45 wt% C, 727 °C) lies in the α + γ field; the ends of the tie line are the ferrite and austenite boundaries at that temperature.

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
- Phases: ferrite α with 0.022 wt% C and austenite γ with 0.76 wt% C
- $W_\alpha = 0.4201$ (42.0 %), $W_\gamma = 0.5799$ (58.0 %)

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
#### Locate the alloy on the diagram and read the ends of the tie line

On cooling, the 0.45 wt% C austenite crosses the A3 line and ferrite starts to form at the austenite grain boundaries (Session 9, Slide 15). Just above 727 °C the point lies in the two-phase field α + γ. The horizontal tie line at 727 + ΔT °C ends on the ferrite boundary at $C_\alpha = 0.022$ wt% C and on the A3 line at the eutectoid point, $C_\gamma = C_E = 0.76$ wt% C (Session 9, Slides 4 and 17).

#### Derive the lever rule from the two mass balances

The phases are the only two places where the mass of the alloy can be, so the mass fractions add up to one (mass balance of the alloy):

$$W_\alpha + W_\gamma = 1$$

The carbon of the alloy is shared between the two phases (mass balance of carbon):

$$W_\alpha C_\alpha + W_\gamma C_\gamma = C_0$$

Substitute $W_\gamma = 1 - W_\alpha$ from the first balance into the second:

$$W_\alpha C_\alpha + (1 - W_\alpha) C_\gamma = C_0$$

Expand and group the terms in $W_\alpha$:

$$W_\alpha (C_\alpha - C_\gamma) = C_0 - C_\gamma$$

Divide by $(C_\alpha - C_\gamma)$ and change the sign of numerator and denominator:

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_\gamma - C_0}{C_\gamma - C_\alpha}, \qquad W_\gamma = 1 - W_\alpha = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_\gamma - C_\alpha}$$

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
This is the lever rule of Session 7, Slides 15-21: each phase is weighted by the segment of the tie line on the **opposite** side of $C_0$.

#### Substitute the compositions

Tie line length: $C_\gamma - C_\alpha = 0.76 - 0.022 = 0.738$ wt% C.

$$W_\alpha = \frac{0.76 - 0.45}{0.76 - 0.022} = \frac{0.31}{0.738} = 0.4201$$

$$W_\gamma = \frac{0.45 - 0.022}{0.76 - 0.022} = \frac{0.428}{0.738} = 0.5799$$

**Result:** 42.0 % ferrite with 0.022 wt% C and 58.0 % austenite with 0.76 wt% C.

**Checks:** $0.4201 + 0.5799 = 1$. Carbon balance: $0.4201 \times 0.022 + 0.5799 \times 0.76 = 0.0092 + 0.4407 = 0.450$ wt% C $= C_0$.

chunks.x: The phases come from the long tie line α - Fe₃C at 727 − ΔT; the microconstituents come from the austenite that existed at 727 + ΔT, because all of it becomes pearlite.

chunks.x:

- Microconstituents: proeutectoid ferrite $W_{\alpha_p} = 0.4201$; pearlite $W_P = 0.5799$ (0.76 wt% C)

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
#### Phases: lever rule on the tie line from ferrite to cementite

Below 727 °C the point lies in the α + Fe₃C field (Session 9, Slide 9). The tie line at 727 − ΔT runs from $C_\alpha = 0.022$ to $C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = 6.67$ wt% C, length $6.67 - 0.022 = 6.648$. With the lever rule of part (a), written for the pair α, Fe₃C (Session 9, Slide 18):

$$W_\alpha = \frac{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_0}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{6.67 - 0.45}{6.67 - 0.022} = \frac{6.22}{6.648} = 0.9356$$

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{0.45 - 0.022}{6.648} = \frac{0.428}{6.648} = 0.0644$$

#### Microconstituents: the austenite of 727 + ΔT becomes pearlite

The proeutectoid (primary) ferrite formed above 727 °C does not change when the steel crosses the eutectoid line. The austenite present at 727 + ΔT has exactly the eutectoid composition, 0.76 wt% C, so all of it undergoes the eutectoid reaction γ (0.76) → α (0.022) + Fe₃C (6.67) and becomes pearlite (Session 9, Slides 10 and 18). The fractions are therefore those of part (a), which is the lever rule on the short tie line from $C_\alpha$ to $C_E$:

$$W_{\alpha_p} = \frac{C_E - C_0}{C_E - C_\alpha} = \frac{0.76 - 0.45}{0.738} = 0.4201, \qquad W_P = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_E - C_\alpha} = \frac{0.428}{0.738} = 0.5799$$

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
**Result:** two phases, ferrite (93.6 %, 0.022 wt% C) and cementite (6.4 %, 6.67 wt% C); two microconstituents, proeutectoid ferrite (42.0 %) and pearlite (58.0 %, overall 0.76 wt% C).

**Checks:** each pair adds up to 1. The ferrite phase (93.6 %) is larger than the proeutectoid ferrite (42.0 %) because the pearlite also contains ferrite; part (c) separates the two.

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
- Proeutectoid ferrite: 3.360 kg
- Eutectoid ferrite (inside the pearlite): 4.125 kg
- Cementite: 0.515 kg (all of it inside the pearlite)

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
#### Split the ferrite phase into proeutectoid and eutectoid ferrite

The ferrite phase of part (b) is the sum of the proeutectoid ferrite and the ferrite of the pearlite lamellae (Session 9, Slide 18):

$$W_{\alpha} = W_{\alpha_p} + W_{\alpha_E}$$

Isolate the eutectoid ferrite:

$$W_{\alpha_E} = W_\alpha - W_{\alpha_p} = \frac{6.22}{6.648} - \frac{0.31}{0.738} = 0.9356 - 0.4201 = 0.5156$$

#### Convert mass fractions into masses

A mass fraction is the mass of the constituent divided by the mass of the bar, $W_i = m_i / m$, so $m_i = W_i\, m$ with $m = 8.0$ kg:

$$m_{\alpha_p} = 0.4201 \times 8.0\ \text{kg} = 3.360\ \text{kg}$$

$$m_{\alpha_E} = 0.5156 \times 8.0\ \text{kg} = 4.125\ \text{kg}$$

$$m_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = 0.0644 \times 8.0\ \text{kg} = 0.515\ \text{kg}$$

(The products are computed with the unrounded fractions, 0.420054, 0.515566 and 0.064380.)

#### Check with the make-up of pearlite

Every pearlite has the make-up of the eutectoid steel, $W_\alpha = (6.67 - 0.76)/(6.67 - 0.022) = 5.91/6.648 = 0.8890$ ferrite and 0.1110 cementite (Session 9, Slide 13). The pearlite of the bar weighs $0.5799 \times 8.0 = 4.640$ kg, so it holds $0.8890 \times 4.640 = 4.125$ kg of ferrite and $0.1110 \times 4.640 = 0.515$ kg of cementite, the values above. Mass check: $3.360 + 4.125 + 0.515 = 8.000$ kg.

chunks.x: Draw two kinds of grains in the proportion of part (b). For the cooling rate, recall where the eutectoid point moves on Session 9, Slide 21.

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
- Sketch: light grains of proeutectoid ferrite (about 42 % of the area) and lamellar pearlite colonies (about 58 %)
- Faster cooling: the eutectoid point moves to lower temperature and lower %C, so less proeutectoid ferrite, more pearlite and finer (harder) pearlite

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
#### Draw the two microconstituents in their proportions

The proeutectoid ferrite nucleated at the austenite grain boundaries between the A3 line and 727 °C and grew into equiaxed, light grains; the remaining austenite became pearlite, alternating lamellae of ferrite and cementite (Session 9, Slides 12 and 14). As an approximation (not stated on the slides), the densities of ferrite and pearlite are taken as close, so the mass fractions are drawn as area fractions on the section: about 42 % of light ferrite grains and 58 % of lamellar colonies.

#### Faster cooling: displacement of the eutectoid point

Session 9, Slide 21: if the cooling rate increases, the eutectoid point moves towards lower temperatures and lower carbon contents. The tie line used for the microconstituents then ends at a value $C_E' < 0.76$ wt% C, and the proeutectoid ferrite fraction $(C_E' - C_0)/(C_E' - C_\alpha)$ falls because its numerator shrinks faster than its denominator. So the bar would show **less proeutectoid ferrite and more pearlite**, and the pearlite lamellae would be **closer together (fine pearlite)**, which raises its hardness (Session 9, Slides 12 and 21). The number 0.4201 is valid only for equilibrium cooling.

chunks.t: Hypoeutectoid steel bar above and below the eutectoid temperature
chunks.x:
The steel spends its last moments above 727 °C as a 42/58 mixture of ferrite and eutectoid austenite; the eutectoid reaction turns all of that austenite into pearlite without touching the ferrite, which is why the microconstituent fractions below 727 °C equal the phase fractions above it. Most of the bar is ferrite (93.6 % by mass), and the 6.4 % of hard cementite is entirely inside the pearlite.

**Limiting cases:** with $C_0 \to C_\alpha = 0.022$ the lever rule gives $W_{\alpha_p} \to 1$ (all ferrite); with $C_0 \to C_E = 0.76$ it gives $W_{\alpha_p} \to 0$ (all pearlite, the eutectoid steel of Session 9, Slide 13).

**Dimensional check:** the lever rule is a ratio of two compositions, (wt%)/(wt%), so it is dimensionless; a mass is a dimensionless fraction times kg, so it is in kg.

**Common exam mistake:** giving the 0.9356 of the long tie line as the "proeutectoid ferrite". That is the whole ferrite phase; the proeutectoid ferrite comes from the short tie line ending at 0.76 wt% C.

Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the Fe-C questions of the finals (cementite in each microconstituent, phases at a second temperature). The data are given as a narrative and read from the figure. Method: Session 9, Slides 4, 10, 13 and 19-20; lever rule of Session 7, Slides 15-21. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
A 2.5 kg forging of a tool steel with 1.10 wt% C is held at 950 °C (point a of the figure) until it is completely austenitic. It is then cooled slowly to room temperature, so the steel follows the equilibrium diagram. At point b the first new constituent appears at the grain boundaries; the steel goes on cooling through 780 °C, reaches the eutectoid line and ends at room temperature. The figure is the steel corner of the metastable Fe-Fe₃C diagram drawn with the values of the course; the Acm line is drawn as a straight segment between its two printed ends.

(a) Read the temperature of point b on the diagram. Which constituent starts to form there, and where? Give the phases, their compositions and their mass fractions at 780 °C.

(b) Write the reaction that takes place at 727 °C and calculate the mass, in kg, of proeutectoid cementite and of pearlite in the forging at 727 − ΔT °C.

(c) Calculate the mass of the ferrite and cementite phases in the forging at 727 − ΔT °C.

(d) How much of the cementite is inside the pearlite? Check it in two independent ways, and explain where the proeutectoid cementite sits and what that means for the toughness of the steel.

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Mass of the forging | $m$ | 2.5 kg | statement |
| Carbon content | $C_0$ | 1.10 wt% C | statement |
| Eutectoid point | $(C_E, T_E)$ | (0.76 wt% C, 727 °C) | figure; Session 9, Slide 10 |
| Upper end of Acm (maximum solubility of C in γ) | $(C_{\gamma,\max}, T_{eu})$ | (2.14 wt% C, 1147 °C) | figure; Session 9, Slides 6 and 10 |
| Carbon in ferrite at 727 °C | $C_\alpha$ | 0.022 wt% C | figure; Session 9, Slides 5 and 10 |
| Carbon in cementite | $C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}$ | 6.67 wt% C | Session 9, Slides 4 and 8 |

Compositions enter only as ratios in the lever rule, so they are used in wt% (the factor 1/100 that turns wt% into a fraction cancels). Masses stay in kg.

#### Model

- Since $0.76 < C_0 = 1.10 < 2.14$ wt% C, the steel is **hypereutectoid** (Session 9, Slide 4): its microconstituents below 727 °C are proeutectoid cementite and pearlite (Session 9, Slide 19).
- Lever rule, from the mass balances $W_1 + W_2 = 1$ and $W_1 C_1 + W_2 C_2 = C_0$ (Session 7, Slides 15-21); derived in part (a).
- The straight Acm segment of the figure, through $(0.76, 727)$ and $(2.14, 1147)$, gives the boundary γ / γ + Fe₃C: $T_{Acm}(C) = 727 + (C - 0.76)\,\dfrac{1147 - 727}{2.14 - 0.76}$ °C.
- Hypothesis: equilibrium (slow) cooling.

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x: Point b is where the vertical line of the steel meets Acm. At 780 °C the tie line goes from the Acm line to the cementite line at 6.67 wt% C.

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
- Point b: about 830 °C (830.5 °C on the straight Acm); proeutectoid cementite starts to form at the austenite grain boundaries
- At 780 °C: γ with 0.934 wt% C, $W_\gamma = 0.9711$; Fe₃C with 6.67 wt% C, $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = 0.0289$

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
#### Read point b on the Acm line

From a (950 °C) down to b the steel is single-phase austenite with 1.10 wt% C ($W_\gamma = 1$). Point b lies on the straight Acm segment. Between its printed ends, the temperature grows linearly with the composition: the slope is $(1147 - 727)/(2.14 - 0.76) = 420/1.38 = 304.3$ °C per wt% C. At $C_0 = 1.10$:

$$T_b = 727 + (1.10 - 0.76) \times \frac{420}{1.38} = 727 + 0.34 \times 304.3 = 727 + 103.5 = 830.5\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

On the dashed 50 °C grid of the figure, b lies three fifths of the way from the 800 °C line to the 850 °C line: about 830 °C, in agreement.

#### Constituent that forms at b

Below Acm the solubility of carbon in austenite is lower than 1.10 wt% C, so the excess carbon leaves the austenite as **proeutectoid cementite**, Fe₃C, which forms along the boundaries of the austenite grains (Session 9, Slide 19). The austenite that remains becomes poorer in carbon, following the Acm line down towards 0.76 wt% C.

#### Composition of the austenite at 780 °C

At 780 °C the tie line starts on Acm. Invert the straight line $T = 727 + (C - 0.76)\times 420/1.38$ for $C$: subtract 727, multiply by $1.38/420$, add 0.76:

$$C_\gamma(780) = 0.76 + (780 - 727) \times \frac{1.38}{420} = 0.76 + 53 \times 0.003286 = 0.76 + 0.1741 = 0.934\ \text{wt\% C}$$

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
The other end of the tie line is cementite, $C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = 6.67$ wt% C (a vertical line on the diagram, Session 9, Slide 4).

#### Lever rule, derived from the mass balances

Mass of the alloy: $W_\gamma + W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = 1$. Carbon: $W_\gamma C_\gamma + W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = C_0$. Put $W_\gamma = 1 - W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}$ into the carbon balance:

$$C_\gamma + W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}(C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\gamma) = C_0$$

Subtract $C_\gamma$ and divide by $(C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\gamma)$:

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = \frac{C_0 - C_\gamma}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\gamma}, \qquad W_\gamma = \frac{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_0}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\gamma}$$

#### Substitute at 780 °C

Tie line length: $6.67 - 0.934 = 5.736$ wt% C.

$$W_\gamma = \frac{6.67 - 1.10}{6.67 - 0.934} = \frac{5.57}{5.736} = 0.9711, \qquad W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = \frac{1.10 - 0.934}{5.736} = \frac{0.166}{5.736} = 0.0289$$

**Result:** at 780 °C, 97.1 % austenite with 0.934 wt% C and 2.9 % cementite with 6.67 wt% C. **Check:** $0.9711 \times 0.934 + 0.0289 \times 6.67 = 0.907 + 0.193 = 1.10$ wt% C.

chunks.x: Just above 727 °C the austenite has reached 0.76 wt% C. All of it becomes pearlite; the cementite formed above 727 °C stays as proeutectoid cementite.

chunks.x:
- Reaction on cooling at 727 °C: γ (0.76) → α (0.022) + Fe₃C (6.67), eutectoid, product pearlite
- $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},p} = 0.0575$ → 0.1438 kg; $W_P = 0.9425$ → 2.356 kg

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
#### The eutectoid reaction

Cooling: γ (0.76 wt% C) → α (0.022 wt% C) + Fe₃C (6.67 wt% C) at 727 °C, **eutectoid** reaction; the lamellar product is pearlite (Session 9, Slides 10 and 12).

#### Tie line just above 727 °C

At 727 + ΔT the tie line runs from the eutectoid austenite, $C_E = 0.76$, to cementite, 6.67 wt% C; length $6.67 - 0.76 = 5.91$. With the lever rule of part (a):

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},p} = \frac{C_0 - C_E}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_E} = \frac{1.10 - 0.76}{5.91} = \frac{0.34}{5.91} = 0.0575$$

$$W_\gamma(727 + \Delta T) = \frac{6.67 - 1.10}{5.91} = \frac{5.57}{5.91} = 0.9425$$

#### Microconstituents at 727 − ΔT and their masses

The proeutectoid cementite does not take part in the reaction, and all the austenite of 0.76 wt% C becomes pearlite, so $W_P = 0.9425$ (Session 9, Slide 20). With $m_i = W_i\,m$ and $m = 2.5$ kg:

$$m_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},p} = 0.05753 \times 2.5\ \text{kg} = 0.1438\ \text{kg}, \qquad m_P = 0.9425 \times 2.5\ \text{kg} = 2.356\ \text{kg}$$

**Checks:** $0.1438 + 2.356 = 2.500$ kg. Between 780 °C (2.9 % cementite) and 727 °C (5.75 %) the proeutectoid cementite has kept growing, as expected while the austenite moves down Acm.

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
#### Lever rule on the tie line α - Fe₃C

Below 727 °C the steel lies in the α + Fe₃C field (Session 9, Slide 9); the tie line runs from $C_\alpha = 0.022$ to 6.67 wt% C, length $6.67 - 0.022 = 6.648$:

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{1.10 - 0.022}{6.648} = \frac{1.078}{6.648} = 0.1622, \qquad W_\alpha = \frac{6.67 - 1.10}{6.648} = \frac{5.57}{6.648} = 0.8378$$

#### Masses

$$m_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = 0.16215 \times 2.5\ \text{kg} = 0.4054\ \text{kg}, \qquad m_\alpha = 0.83785 \times 2.5\ \text{kg} = 2.095\ \text{kg}$$

**Check:** $0.4054 + 2.095 = 2.500$ kg. Even this hard tool steel is about 84 % ferrite by mass.

chunks.x: Total cementite = proeutectoid cementite + eutectoid cementite. The second way uses the make-up of any pearlite (Session 9, Slide 13).

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
- Eutectoid cementite: $W = 0.1046$ → 0.2616 kg (both ways)
- Proeutectoid cementite: a continuous network along the former austenite grain boundaries; hard and brittle, it lowers the toughness

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
#### First way: subtract the proeutectoid cementite from the total

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},E} = W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},p} = \frac{1.078}{6.648} - \frac{0.34}{5.91} = 0.16215 - 0.05753 = 0.1046$$

$$m_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},E} = 0.10462 \times 2.5\ \text{kg} = 0.2616\ \text{kg}$$

#### Second way: the make-up of pearlite

Every pearlite has the composition of the eutectoid, 0.76 wt% C, so its cementite fraction is the lever rule of the eutectoid steel (Session 9, Slide 13):

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}^{(P)} = \frac{0.76 - 0.022}{6.67 - 0.022} = \frac{0.738}{6.648} = 0.1110$$

The pearlite of the forging is 2.356 kg (part b), so its cementite is $0.1110 \times 2.356 = 0.2616$ kg, the same value.

#### Where the proeutectoid cementite sits

The proeutectoid cementite forms between b and 727 °C at the boundaries of the austenite grains, so after cooling it is a thin, continuous network around the pearlite colonies (Session 9, Slide 19). Cementite is hard and brittle (Session 9, Slide 8), and a continuous brittle film along the grain boundaries gives a crack an easy path: the 0.1438 kg network makes the forging hard but lowers its toughness.

chunks.t: Slow cooling of a hypereutectoid tool steel read on the Fe-Fe3C diagram
chunks.x:
Of the 0.4054 kg of cementite in the forging, about one third (0.1438 kg) formed above 727 °C as a grain-boundary network and two thirds (0.2616 kg) formed at 727 °C inside the pearlite lamellae. The transformation starts about 103 °C above the eutectoid line because 1.10 wt% C exceeds what austenite can hold below 830 °C.

**Limiting cases:** $C_0 \to 0.76$ makes point b fall to 727 °C and $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},p} \to 0$ (all pearlite); $C_0 \to 2.14$ moves b to 1147 °C and gives the largest proeutectoid cementite of a steel, $(2.14 - 0.76)/5.91 = 0.234$.

**Dimensional check:** a temperature on Acm is °C + (wt%)·(°C/wt%) = °C; every lever rule is (wt%)/(wt%), dimensionless; a mass is a fraction times kg.

**Common exam mistake:** using the long tie line (0.022 to 6.67) for the proeutectoid cementite. That gives the total cementite, 0.1622; the proeutectoid part needs the short tie line from 0.76 wt% C.

chunks.t: Carbon content of an unknown steel worked back from its micrograph
chunks.x:
A bar of plain carbon steel of unknown composition (less than 2.14 wt% C) has been cooled slowly from the austenite field. A polished and etched section shows the structure of the figure. Point counting gives **88.0 % of lamellar colonies**; the remaining 12.0 % is a constituent X that forms a **thin, continuous network along the former austenite grain boundaries**, around the colonies. Microhardness indentations show that X is **much harder** than the lamellar colonies. Take the area fractions as mass fractions; they are the fractions formed just below 727 °C, which the slow cooling to room temperature keeps.

(a) Identify the lamellar constituent. Show that a fraction of 88.0 % of it is compatible with two different carbon contents, one on each side of the eutectoid, and calculate both.

(b) Use the description of X to decide which of the two carbon contents is the right one, and justify it. For that steel, estimate the lowest temperature at which it is fully austenitic.

(c) Calculate the mass fractions of the ferrite and cementite phases of the steel just below 727 °C, and how the cementite is shared between X and the colonies.

(d) Give the phases present at 800 °C, their compositions and their mass fractions.

chunks.x: Write the pearlite fraction with the lever rule twice: once for a hypoeutectoid steel and once for a hypereutectoid one. Each equation is linear in $C_0$.

chunks.t: Carbon content of an unknown steel worked back from its micrograph
chunks.x:
- Lamellar colonies: pearlite (α + Fe₃C lamellae, 0.76 wt% C overall)

chunks.t: Carbon content of an unknown steel worked back from its micrograph
chunks.x:
#### The lamellar constituent

Alternating lamellae of ferrite and cementite are **pearlite**, the product of the eutectoid reaction γ (0.76) → α (0.022) + Fe₃C (6.67) at 727 °C (Session 9, Slides 10 and 12). Pearlite always has the eutectoid composition, 0.76 wt% C, but it appears in both hypo- and hypereutectoid steels, so 88.0 % of pearlite alone does not tell on which side of 0.76 the steel lies.

#### Lever rule for the pearlite, derived once

Just above 727 °C the pearlite is still austenite of $C_E = 0.76$ wt% C, in equilibrium with a proeutectoid phase of composition $C_p$ ($C_\alpha$ or $C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}$). Mass balance: $W_P + W_p = 1$. Carbon balance: $W_P C_E + W_p C_p = C_0$. Substitute $W_p = 1 - W_P$:

$$W_P C_E + (1 - W_P) C_p = C_0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad W_P (C_E - C_p) = C_0 - C_p \quad\Rightarrow\quad W_P = \frac{C_0 - C_p}{C_E - C_p}$$

#### Hypoeutectoid candidate ($C_p = C_\alpha$)

$$W_P = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_E - C_\alpha}$$

Multiply both sides by $(C_E - C_\alpha)$ and add $C_\alpha$:

$$C_0 = C_\alpha + W_P (C_E - C_\alpha) = 0.022 + 0.880 \times (0.76 - 0.022) = 0.022 + 0.880 \times 0.738 = 0.022 + 0.6494 = 0.671\ \text{wt\% C}$$

#### Hypereutectoid candidate ($C_p = C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}$)

$$W_P = \frac{C_0 - C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}}{C_E - C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}} = \frac{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_0}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_E}$$

chunks.t: Carbon content of an unknown steel worked back from its micrograph
chunks.x:
Multiply by $(C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_E)$ and isolate $C_0$:

$$C_0 = C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - W_P (C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_E) = 6.67 - 0.880 \times 5.91 = 6.67 - 5.2008 = 1.469\ \text{wt\% C}$$

**Result:** both 0.671 wt% C (hypoeutectoid, $0.671 < 0.76$) and 1.469 wt% C (hypereutectoid, $0.76 < 1.469 < 2.14$) are steels with 88.0 % pearlite. **Check:** both lie inside their ranges, so both are physically possible.

chunks.x:
- X is much harder than the pearlite, so it is proeutectoid cementite (not ferrite): the steel is hypereutectoid, $C_0 = 1.469$ wt% C
- Fully austenitic above about 943 °C (Acm line)

chunks.t: Carbon content of an unknown steel worked back from its micrograph
chunks.x:
#### What X is

In a hypoeutectoid steel the proeutectoid constituent is ferrite, which forms **equiaxed grains** of its own between the pearlite colonies (Session 9, Slide 14). In a hypereutectoid steel it is cementite, which forms a **thin network along the boundaries of the former austenite grains** around the pearlite (Session 9, Slide 19). The grain-boundary position alone does not decide, because proeutectoid ferrite also nucleates on the austenite grain boundaries (Session 9, Slide 15; Topic 4, section 14.2), and a large amount of it can outline them too. The hardness does decide: ferrite is a soft phase (Session 9, Slide 5) and would be softer than the pearlite, which contains 11 % of cementite, whereas cementite is hard and brittle (Session 9, Slide 8) and is harder than the pearlite. X is much harder than the colonies, so X is **proeutectoid cementite**, and its thin continuous network is the shape Slide 19 shows for it. The steel is hypereutectoid and

$$C_0 = 1.469\ \text{wt\% C}$$

The other candidate, 0.671 wt% C, would show 12.0 % of ferrite grains, not a grain-boundary network, and is rejected.

#### Lowest temperature of the single-phase austenite field

chunks.t: Carbon content of an unknown steel worked back from its micrograph
chunks.x:
A hypereutectoid steel is fully austenitic above the Acm line (Session 9, Slides 4 and 11). On the straight Acm segment the temperature grows by $(1147 - 727)/(2.14 - 0.76) = 420/1.38 = 304.3$ °C per wt% C above the eutectoid point:

$$T_{Acm} = 727 + (1.469 - 0.76) \times 304.3 = 727 + 0.709 \times 304.3 = 727 + 215.8 = 942.8\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

**Result:** the bar must have been above about 943 °C to be entirely austenite. (Had the steel been the 0.671 wt% C candidate, it would have been fully austenitic above the A3 line, which at 0.671 wt% C lies only some 5 to 20 °C above 727 °C, depending on how its curve is read: the slides do not give A3 in numbers.)

- Cementite in X (proeutectoid): 0.120; cementite in the pearlite: 0.0977

chunks.t: Carbon content of an unknown steel worked back from its micrograph
chunks.x:
#### Phases: lever rule on the tie line from 0.022 to 6.67 wt% C

Length $6.67 - 0.022 = 6.648$ (Session 9, Slide 9 for the α + Fe₃C field):

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{1.469 - 0.022}{6.648} = \frac{1.447}{6.648} = 0.2177, \qquad W_\alpha = 1 - 0.2177 = 0.7823$$

#### Cementite inside the pearlite

The pearlite is the eutectoid steel, whose cementite fraction is (Session 9, Slide 13)

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}^{(P)} = \frac{C_E - C_\alpha}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\alpha} = \frac{0.738}{6.648} = 0.1110$$

so the cementite of the colonies, per unit mass of steel, is $W_P \times 0.1110 = 0.880 \times 0.1110 = 0.0977$. The rest of the cementite is X, the proeutectoid cementite, $W_X = 0.120$.

**Check:** $0.120 + 0.0977 = 0.2177 = W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}$, the value of the long tie line: the two independent routes agree. The ferrite is all inside the pearlite: $0.880 \times (1 - 0.1110) = 0.7823 = W_\alpha$.

chunks.x: 800 °C is between 727 °C and the Acm temperature of part (b): the steel is in the γ + Fe₃C field. Read the austenite composition on Acm at 800 °C.

chunks.t: Carbon content of an unknown steel worked back from its micrograph
chunks.x:
#### Field and ends of the tie line

Since $727 < 800 < 942.8$ °C, the point (1.469 wt% C, 800 °C) lies in the γ + Fe₃C field (Session 9, Slide 9). The tie line ends on Acm and on the cementite line. Inverting the straight Acm, $C = 0.76 + (T - 727)\times 1.38/420$:

$$C_\gamma(800) = 0.76 + (800 - 727) \times \frac{1.38}{420} = 0.76 + 73 \times 0.003286 = 0.76 + 0.2399 = 1.000\ \text{wt\% C}$$

#### Lever rule

Tie line length $6.67 - 1.000 = 5.670$:

$$W_\gamma = \frac{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_0}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\gamma} = \frac{6.67 - 1.469}{5.670} = \frac{5.201}{5.670} = 0.9172, \qquad W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = 1 - 0.9172 = 0.0828$$

**Result:** 91.7 % austenite with 1.000 wt% C and 8.3 % proeutectoid cementite with 6.67 wt% C. **Check:** the proeutectoid cementite grows from 8.3 % at 800 °C to 12.0 % at 727 + ΔT, as it must while the austenite slides down Acm towards 0.76 wt% C; carbon balance $0.9172 \times 1.000 + 0.0828 \times 6.67 = 0.917 + 0.552 = 1.469$ wt% C.

chunks.t: Carbon content of an unknown steel worked back from its micrograph
chunks.x:
A pearlite fraction measured on a micrograph fixes the distance of the steel from the eutectoid, not the side: the same 88.0 % lies 0.089 wt% C below 0.76 (on the short ferrite side of the diagram) and 0.709 wt% C above it (on the long cementite side). The shape of the proeutectoid constituent, grains of ferrite or a network of cementite, is the second datum that removes the ambiguity, exactly as Slides 14 and 19 of Session 9 show it.

**Limiting cases:** $W_P \to 1$ makes both candidates collapse to $C_E = 0.76$ wt% C (the eutectoid steel); $W_P \to 0$ gives $C_\alpha = 0.022$ on one side and 6.67 wt% C on the other, which is outside the steels: below 2.14 wt% C the pearlite of a hypereutectoid steel never falls below $(6.67 - 2.14)/5.91 = 0.7665$.

**Dimensional check:** $C_0 = C_\alpha + W_P (C_E - C_\alpha)$ is wt% + (dimensionless)(wt%) = wt%; $T_{Acm}$ is °C + (wt%)(°C/wt%) = °C.

**Common exam mistake:** stopping at the first root, 0.671 wt% C, without asking which proeutectoid phase the micrograph shows.

Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the Fe-C questions of the finals (amounts of each microconstituent, effect of an alloying element on the eutectoid point). The data are a table of three steels, and the question asks for a comparison and a design limit. Method: Session 9, Slides 4, 8, 10, 12-14, 18-20 and 22-23; lever rule of Session 7, Slides 15-21. chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
A supplier offers three plain carbon steels, all slowly cooled from the austenite field:

| Steel | Carbon content (wt% C) |
| :--- | :--- |
| S1 | 0.25 |
| S2 | 0.60 |
| S3 | 1.35 |

(a) Classify each steel and calculate the mass fraction of each of its microconstituents just below 727 °C.

(b) Calculate the mass fractions of the ferrite and cementite phases of each steel just below 727 °C. Rank the three steels by hardness and justify the ranking.

(c) A designer wants a plain carbon hypoeutectoid steel with at least 50 % pearlite. What is the lowest carbon content that meets the requirement? Is there any hypereutectoid steel that does not meet it?

(d) Steel S2 is now alloyed in one version with chromium and in another with manganese. State how each element changes the eutectoid temperature and the eutectoid composition, and how the microconstituents of S2 change. What would S2 look like if the eutectoid composition fell below 0.60 wt% C?

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Carbon contents | $C_0$ | 0.25, 0.60, 1.35 wt% C | statement |
| Carbon in ferrite at 727 °C | $C_\alpha$ | 0.022 wt% C | Session 9, Slides 5 and 10 |
| Eutectoid composition | $C_E$ | 0.76 wt% C | Session 9, Slide 10 |
| Carbon in cementite | $C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}$ | 6.67 wt% C | Session 9, Slides 4 and 8 |
| Upper limit of steels | $C_{\gamma,\max}$ | 2.14 wt% C | Session 9, Slide 4 |
| Eutectoid temperature | $T_E$ | 727 °C | Session 9, Slide 10 |

Compositions enter only as ratios in the lever rule, so the wt% values are used directly (the factor 1/100 cancels). Percentages of the answers are fractions times 100.

#### Model

- Classification by carbon content: hypoeutectoid below 0.76, hypereutectoid from 0.76 to 2.14 wt% C (Session 9, Slide 4).
- Lever rule from the mass balances $W_1 + W_2 = 1$ and $W_1 C_1 + W_2 C_2 = C_0$ (Session 7, Slides 15-21), derived in part (a).
- Cementite is hard and brittle, ferrite is soft (Session 9, Slides 5 and 8).
- Alloying elements (Session 9, Slides 22-23): α-stabilisers move the eutectoid to higher temperature and lower %C; γ-stabilisers move it to lower temperature and lower %C.

- S2 (hypoeutectoid): $W_{\alpha_p} = 0.2168$, $W_P = 0.7832$
- S3 (hypereutectoid): $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},p} = 0.0998$, $W_P = 0.9002$

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
#### Classify the three steels

S1 (0.25) and S2 (0.60) are below 0.76 wt% C: **hypoeutectoid**, with proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite (Session 9, Slide 14). S3 (1.35) lies between 0.76 and 2.14 wt% C: **hypereutectoid**, with proeutectoid cementite and pearlite (Session 9, Slide 19).

#### Derive the lever rule once

At 727 + ΔT the steel is a proeutectoid phase of composition $C_p$ plus austenite of $C_E = 0.76$. Mass balance: $W_p + W_\gamma = 1$. Carbon balance: $W_p C_p + W_\gamma C_E = C_0$. Substitute $W_\gamma = 1 - W_p$ into the carbon balance:

$$W_p C_p + (1 - W_p) C_E = C_0$$

Expand, subtract $C_E$ and group the terms in $W_p$:

$$W_p (C_p - C_E) = C_0 - C_E \quad\Rightarrow\quad W_p = \frac{C_0 - C_E}{C_p - C_E} = \frac{C_E - C_0}{C_E - C_p}$$

All that austenite becomes pearlite at 727 °C, and the proeutectoid phase does not change, so just below 727 °C $W_P = 1 - W_p$ (Session 9, Slides 18 and 20).

#### S1 and S2: proeutectoid ferrite ($C_p = C_\alpha = 0.022$, tie line length $0.76 - 0.022 = 0.738$)

$$W_{\alpha_p}(S1) = \frac{0.76 - 0.25}{0.738} = \frac{0.51}{0.738} = 0.6911, \qquad W_P(S1) = 1 - 0.6911 = 0.3089$$

$$W_{\alpha_p}(S2) = \frac{0.76 - 0.60}{0.738} = \frac{0.16}{0.738} = 0.2168, \qquad W_P(S2) = 1 - 0.2168 = 0.7832$$

#### S3: proeutectoid cementite ($C_p = 6.67$, tie line length $6.67 - 0.76 = 5.91$)

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C},p}(S3) = \frac{1.35 - 0.76}{5.91} = \frac{0.59}{5.91} = 0.0998, \qquad W_P(S3) = \frac{6.67 - 1.35}{5.91} = \frac{5.32}{5.91} = 0.9002$$

**Checks:** each pair adds up to 1; the pearlite grows from S1 to S2 as $C_0$ approaches 0.76, and in S3 it falls again as $C_0$ moves away on the cementite side.

chunks.x:
- $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}$: S1 0.0343, S2 0.0869, S3 0.1998 (ferrite: 0.9657, 0.9131, 0.8002)
- Hardness: S3 > S2 > S1, in the order of the cementite fraction

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
#### Lever rule on the tie line from 0.022 to 6.67 wt% C

Below 727 °C every steel lies in the α + Fe₃C field (Session 9, Slide 9). Tie line length $6.67 - 0.022 = 6.648$; with the lever rule of part (a) written for α and Fe₃C:

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} - C_\alpha}, \qquad W_\alpha = 1 - W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}$$

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}(S1) = \frac{0.25 - 0.022}{6.648} = \frac{0.228}{6.648} = 0.0343, \qquad W_\alpha(S1) = 0.9657$$

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}(S2) = \frac{0.60 - 0.022}{6.648} = \frac{0.578}{6.648} = 0.0869, \qquad W_\alpha(S2) = 0.9131$$

$$W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}}(S3) = \frac{1.35 - 0.022}{6.648} = \frac{1.328}{6.648} = 0.1998, \qquad W_\alpha(S3) = 0.8002$$

#### Ranking by hardness

Ferrite is a soft phase and cementite is hard and brittle (Session 9, Slides 5 and 8), so at the same (slow) cooling the hardness grows with the fraction of cementite: **S3 (20.0 % Fe₃C) > S2 (8.7 %) > S1 (3.4 %)**. The fraction of cementite grows linearly with $C_0$, which is why harder steels are those with more carbon. S3 pays for its hardness with a brittle network of proeutectoid cementite at the grain boundaries (Session 9, Slide 19).

chunks.x: **Check:** the cementite of S3 splits into 0.0998 proeutectoid and $0.9002 \times 0.1110 = 0.0999$ inside the pearlite (0.1110 is the cementite of any pearlite, Session 9, Slide 13); $0.09983 + 0.09993 = 0.1998$.

chunks.x: Write $W_P \geq 0.50$ with the hypoeutectoid lever rule and solve the inequality for $C_0$. For hypereutectoid steels, look at the end of the steel range.

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
- Hypoeutectoid: $C_0 \geq 0.391$ wt% C (S1 fails, S2 meets it)
- Every hypereutectoid steel meets it: the least pearlite, at 2.14 wt% C, is 0.7665

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
#### Set up the inequality

For a hypoeutectoid steel the pearlite fraction is the lever rule of part (a):

$$W_P = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_E - C_\alpha} \geq 0.50$$

Multiply both sides by the positive length $(C_E - C_\alpha) = 0.738$ (the sense of the inequality is kept) and add $C_\alpha$:

$$C_0 \geq C_\alpha + 0.50\,(C_E - C_\alpha) = 0.022 + 0.50 \times 0.738 = 0.022 + 0.369 = 0.391\ \text{wt\% C}$$

**Result:** the hypoeutectoid steel needs at least 0.391 wt% C. S1 (0.25, 30.9 % pearlite) fails; S2 (0.60, 78.3 %) passes.

#### Hypereutectoid steels

For $C_0 > 0.76$, $W_P = (6.67 - C_0)/5.91$ decreases as $C_0$ grows, so its smallest value in the steel range is at $C_0 = 2.14$ wt% C (Session 9, Slide 4):

$$W_P(2.14) = \frac{6.67 - 2.14}{5.91} = \frac{4.53}{5.91} = 0.7665$$

That is above 0.50, so **every hypereutectoid steel** has more than 50 % pearlite.

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
- Cr (favours α): eutectoid at higher temperature and lower %C
- Mn (favours γ): eutectoid at lower temperature and lower %C
- In both cases S2 is closer to the eutectoid: less proeutectoid ferrite, more pearlite, and the pearlite has less than 0.76 wt% C
- If the eutectoid composition fell below 0.60 wt% C, S2 would behave as hypereutectoid: proeutectoid cementite + pearlite

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
#### Direction of the shift for each element

Session 9, Slide 22: elements that favour α (Si, P, Al, Be, Sn, Sb, As, Ti, Nb, V, Ta, Mo, W, **Cr**) stabilise ferrite and displace the eutectoid to **higher temperature and lower %C**; elements that favour γ (**Mn**, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Au) stabilise austenite and displace it to **lower temperature and lower %C**. Slide 23 gives the size of the shifts against the alloy content; the statement gives no content, so only the direction is asked.

| Version of S2 | Eutectoid temperature | Eutectoid composition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| S2 + Cr (α-stabiliser) | above 727 °C | below 0.76 wt% C |
| S2 + Mn (γ-stabiliser) | below 727 °C | below 0.76 wt% C |

#### Consequence for the microconstituents of S2

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
In both versions the eutectoid composition $C_E'$ is lower than 0.76, so the pearlite (which always has the eutectoid composition) carries less than 0.76 wt% C. The proeutectoid ferrite is $W_{\alpha_p} = (C_E' - C_0)/(C_E' - C_\alpha)$: a smaller $C_E'$ shrinks the numerator, so S2 has **less proeutectoid ferrite and more pearlite** than the plain 0.60 wt% C steel of part (a). Its total cementite fraction (the long tie line from ferrite to cementite) does not change when the eutectoid point moves; what changes is how the cementite is distributed: more of the soft proeutectoid ferrite is replaced by pearlite, which is harder than ferrite (it contains the hard cementite lamellae, Session 9, Slides 8 and 12).

#### If the eutectoid composition fell below 0.60 wt% C

Then $C_0 = 0.60 > C_E'$ and S2 would sit on the cementite side of the new eutectoid: on slow cooling it would form **proeutectoid cementite** at the austenite grain boundaries, followed by pearlite, like a hypereutectoid plain steel (Session 9, Slide 19).

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements
chunks.x:
The three steels show the whole story of the Fe-Fe₃C steel corner: the pearlite fraction peaks at the eutectoid and falls on both sides, but the cementite fraction, which sets the hardness, grows steadily with the carbon content. S1 is a soft, mostly ferritic steel; S2 is mostly pearlite; S3 is the hardest and the least tough, because of its 10 % grain-boundary cementite network. Alloying moves the eutectoid point, so "hypo" and "hyper" are relative to the eutectoid of the actual alloy, not always to 0.76 wt% C.

**Limiting cases:** $C_0 \to 0.022$ gives $W_{\alpha_p} \to 1$ and $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} \to 0$; $C_0 \to 0.76$ gives $W_P \to 1$ from both sides; $C_0 \to 6.67$ would give $W_{\text{Fe}_3\text{C}} \to 1$ (outside the steels).

**Dimensional check:** every lever rule is (wt%)/(wt%), dimensionless; the bound of part (c) is wt% + (dimensionless)(wt%) = wt%.

**Common exam mistake:** saying that a γ-stabiliser such as Mn raises the eutectoid carbon content because it "stabilises austenite". Session 9, Slide 22 states that both kinds of element lower the eutectoid %C; they differ only in the direction of the temperature shift.

chunks.t: Three steels compared: microconstituents, hardness and alloying elements

chunks.h: Bank P13 — Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the load and gauge-length tables of the finals of January 2013 and January 2014 (magnesium). Here the data are a table of raw readings, and the path is: table of engineering stress and strain, slope of the straight rows, 0.2 % offset line solved by linear interpolation between two rows, maximum load. Method: Session 11, Slides 9, 12, 28 and 30. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
A round specimen of a titanium alloy with a diameter of 10.0 mm and an initial gauge length of 50.000 mm is pulled in a uniaxial tension test. The machine records the load and the distance between the gauge marks:

| Row | Load $F$ (N) | Gauge length $l$ (mm) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 0 | 50.000 |
| 1 | 15 000 | 50.089 |
| 2 | 30 000 | 50.179 |
| 3 | 45 000 | 50.268 |
| 4 | 60 000 | 50.357 |
| 5 | 63 000 | 50.420 |
| 6 | 66 000 | 50.500 |
| 7 | 69 000 | 50.900 |
| 8 | 72 000 | 51.750 |
| 9 | 74 000 (maximum load) | 53.000 |
| 10 | 71 000 (fracture) | 54.600 |

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Initial diameter | $d_0$ | 10.0 mm | $10.0\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Initial gauge length | $l_0$ | 50.000 mm | $5.0000\times10^{-2}$ m |
| Loads of the table | $F$ | 15 000 to 74 000 N | N |
| Offset of the conventional yield strength | $\varepsilon_{\text{off}}$ | 0.002 | (dimensionless) |

Initial cross-section, with the conversion to SI written out:

$$A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(10.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m})^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\times1.000\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2}{4} = 7.854\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2 = 78.54\ \text{mm}^2$$

Since $1\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 10^6\ \text{N/m}^2 = 1\ \text{MPa}$, a load in N divided by an area in mm² gives the stress directly in MPa.

#### Model

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
- Engineering stress and strain, defined with the original area and length [Session 11 Slide 9]: $\sigma = F/A_0$ and $\varepsilon = (l - l_0)/l_0$.
- Hooke's law in the elastic zone, $\sigma = E\,\varepsilon$; the Young's modulus $E$ is the slope of the straight part of the curve [Session 11 Slide 12].
- Conventional yield strength: the stress where the curve meets the line parallel to the elastic line drawn from $\varepsilon = 0.002$ [Session 11 Slide 28].
- Tensile strength: the maximum engineering stress the specimen supports [Session 11 Slide 30].
- Hypotheses: uniaxial stress, uniform over the gauge length up to the maximum load; between two rows of the table the curve is taken as a straight segment (linear interpolation).

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
- $A_0 = 78.54\ \text{mm}^2$
- Row 4: $\sigma = 763.9$ MPa, $\varepsilon = 0.00714$
- $E = 107.0$ GPa (rows 1 to 4 are the straight part)

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
#### Engineering stress and strain of one row, written out

The idea is to remove the size of the specimen from the readings: the load per unit of original area and the elongation per unit of original length [Session 11 Slide 9]. For row 4:

$$\sigma_4 = \frac{F_4}{A_0} = \frac{60\,000\ \text{N}}{78.54\ \text{mm}^2} = 763.9\ \text{MPa}$$

$$\varepsilon_4 = \frac{l_4 - l_0}{l_0} = \frac{50.357\ \text{mm} - 50.000\ \text{mm}}{50.000\ \text{mm}} = \frac{0.357\ \text{mm}}{50.000\ \text{mm}} = 0.00714$$

#### The same operation for every row

The last column is the secant ratio $\sigma/\varepsilon$, which is constant only while Hooke's law holds:

| Row | $F$ (N) | $l - l_0$ (mm) | $\sigma$ (MPa) | $\varepsilon$ | $\sigma/\varepsilon$ (GPa) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 15 000 | 0.089 | 191.0 | 0.00178 | 107.3 |
| 2 | 30 000 | 0.179 | 382.0 | 0.00358 | 106.7 |
| 3 | 45 000 | 0.268 | 573.0 | 0.00536 | 106.9 |
| 4 | 60 000 | 0.357 | 763.9 | 0.00714 | 107.0 |
| 5 | 63 000 | 0.420 | 802.1 | 0.00840 | 95.5 |
| 6 | 66 000 | 0.500 | 840.3 | 0.01000 | 84.0 |
| 7 | 69 000 | 0.900 | 878.5 | 0.01800 | 48.8 |
| 8 | 72 000 | 1.750 | 916.7 | 0.03500 | 26.2 |
| 9 | 74 000 | 3.000 | 942.2 | 0.06000 | 15.7 |
| 10 | 71 000 | 4.600 | 904.0 | 0.09200 | 9.8 |

#### Pick the straight rows and average their slope

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
Rows 1 to 4 give the same ratio within the reading error of the last digit of $l$ (106.7 to 107.3 GPa); from row 5 on the ratio falls (95.5, 84.0 GPa), so the curve has left the straight line. The modulus is the slope of the straight part through the origin [Session 11 Slide 12], taken as the mean of the four secant ratios:

$$E = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{\sigma_1}{\varepsilon_1} + \frac{\sigma_2}{\varepsilon_2} + \frac{\sigma_3}{\varepsilon_3} + \frac{\sigma_4}{\varepsilon_4}\right) = \frac{107.3 + 106.7 + 106.9 + 107.0}{4}\ \text{GPa} = 106\,970\ \text{MPa} \approx 107.0\ \text{GPa}$$

(The sum is formed with the unrounded ratios.) Check: the slide's table gives $E = 107$ GPa for titanium [Session 11 Slide 17], so the readings are consistent with a titanium alloy.

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x: Write the offset line as $\sigma = E(\varepsilon - 0.002)$, find the two rows between which the curve passes from above it to below it, and intersect the offset line with the straight segment that joins those two rows.

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
- The crossing lies between rows 5 and 6
- Slope of that segment $m = 23\,873$ MPa
- $\varepsilon^* = 0.009814$, $\sigma_y = 835.9$ MPa

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
#### Equation of the offset line

The conventional yield strength is read where the curve meets the line parallel to the elastic one, shifted to a plastic strain of 0.002 [Session 11 Slide 28]. Parallel means the same slope $E$; passing through $(0.002, 0)$ gives

$$\sigma_{\text{off}}(\varepsilon) = E\,(\varepsilon - 0.002)$$

#### Locate the crossing between two rows

The curve is above the offset line while $g = \sigma - E(\varepsilon - 0.002)$ is positive:

| Row | $\varepsilon$ | $\sigma$ (MPa) | $E(\varepsilon - 0.002)$ (MPa) | $g$ (MPa) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 | 0.00714 | 763.9 | 549.8 | 214.1 |
| 5 | 0.00840 | 802.1 | 684.6 | 117.5 |
| 6 | 0.01000 | 840.3 | 855.8 | -15.4 |

$g$ changes sign between rows 5 and 6, so the yield point lies on the segment that joins them.

#### Equation of the segment between rows 5 and 6

Its slope is the rise over the run of the two rows:

$$m = \frac{\sigma_6 - \sigma_5}{\varepsilon_6 - \varepsilon_5} = \frac{840.34 - 802.14}{0.01000 - 0.00840}\ \text{MPa} = \frac{38.20}{0.00160}\ \text{MPa} = 23\,873\ \text{MPa}$$

and the segment is $\sigma(\varepsilon) = \sigma_5 + m\,(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_5)$.

#### Intersect the two lines

At the crossing $\varepsilon = \varepsilon^*$ both lines give the same stress:

$$\sigma_5 + m\,(\varepsilon^* - \varepsilon_5) = E\,(\varepsilon^* - 0.002)$$

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
Expanding both sides and moving the terms in $\varepsilon^*$ to the right:

$$\sigma_5 - m\,\varepsilon_5 + 0.002\,E = (E - m)\,\varepsilon^*$$

Dividing by $(E - m)$:

$$\varepsilon^* = \frac{\sigma_5 - m\,\varepsilon_5 + 0.002\,E}{E - m} = \frac{802.14 - 200.54 + 213.94}{106\,970 - 23\,873} = \frac{815.55}{83\,097} = 0.009814$$

#### Yield strength

Substituting $\varepsilon^*$ in the offset line:

$$\sigma_y = E\,(\varepsilon^* - 0.002) = 106\,970\ \text{MPa}\times(0.009814 - 0.002) = 106\,970\ \text{MPa}\times0.007814 = 835.9\ \text{MPa}$$

Check on the other line: $\sigma_5 + m(\varepsilon^* - \varepsilon_5) = 802.14 + 23\,873\times0.001414 = 835.9$ MPa, the same value, and it lies between $\sigma_5 = 802.1$ and $\sigma_6 = 840.3$ MPa, as it must.

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
#### Maximum engineering stress

The tensile strength is the maximum nominal stress the specimen supports [Session 11 Slide 30]. With $A_0$ fixed, the maximum of $F/A_0$ is at the maximum load, row 9:

$$\sigma_{TS} = \frac{F_{\max}}{A_0} = \frac{74\,000\ \text{N}}{78.54\ \text{mm}^2} = 942.2\ \text{MPa}$$

#### Comparison with the yield strength

$$\frac{\sigma_{TS}}{\sigma_y} = \frac{942.2\ \text{MPa}}{835.9\ \text{MPa}} = 1.127$$

The alloy hardens only about 13 % between yielding and the maximum load: a high-strength alloy with little strain hardening. After row 9 the load falls (row 10, 71 000 N) because the specimen necks [Session 11 Slide 30], so row 10 is not the tensile strength even though the specimen is longer.

chunks.t: Titanium alloy tensile test from a load and gauge length table
chunks.x:
- **Order of magnitude.** $E = 107.0$ GPa matches the titanium value of the slide's table (107 GPa) [Session 11 Slide 17]; $\sigma_y$ of about 840 MPa and $\sigma_{TS}$ of about 940 MPa are those of a high-strength titanium alloy, far above an aluminium alloy.
- **Control checks.** The yield point lies after the last straight row (row 4) and before the maximum (row 9): $\varepsilon_4 = 0.00714 < \varepsilon^* = 0.009814 < \varepsilon_9 = 0.060$; and $\sigma_y < \sigma_{TS}$. If the offset were zero, the line would be the elastic line itself and the crossing would move back to the end of the straight part (about row 4): the offset is what makes the reading reproducible.
- **Dimensions.** $\sigma = F/A_0$ is N/m² = Pa; $\varepsilon$ is m/m, dimensionless; $E = \sigma/\varepsilon$ and $m$ are in Pa; in $\varepsilon^* = (\sigma_5 - m\varepsilon_5 + 0.002E)/(E - m)$ the numerator and denominator are both in Pa, so $\varepsilon^*$ is dimensionless, as a strain must be.
- **Common exam mistake.** Taking the yield strength as the stress of the last straight row (763.9 MPa) or as the stress at a total strain of 0.002 (on the elastic line, 214 MPa): the 0.2 % is a plastic strain, measured from the offset line, not from the origin.

Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.h: Bank P14 — Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of parts (c) to (e) of the magnesium problems of the finals of January 2013 and January 2014. The data come as a narrative with no table: two loads and the measurements of the broken specimen. The path is: engineering stresses, %EL and %RA, then the true stress and true strain in the neck with the measured area, and why the constant-volume formulas would fail there. Method: Session 11, Slides 9, 30-33, 37-38. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.x: A round specimen of an aluminium alloy, 8.00 mm in diameter, with gauge marks 40.00 mm apart, is pulled to fracture. The highest load recorded during the test is 21.5 kN, and the load at the instant of fracture is 17.8 kN. After the test the two halves are fitted together: the gauge marks are then 45.60 mm apart, and the diameter of the neck at the fracture surface is 6.10 mm.

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Initial diameter | $d_0$ | 8.00 mm | $8.00\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Initial gauge length | $l_0$ | 40.00 mm | $4.000\times10^{-2}$ m |
| Maximum load | $F_{\max}$ | 21.5 kN | $2.15\times10^{4}$ N |
| Load at fracture | $F_f$ | 17.8 kN | $1.78\times10^{4}$ N |
| Gauge length after fracture | $l_f$ | 45.60 mm | $4.560\times10^{-2}$ m |
| Neck diameter after fracture | $d_f$ | 6.10 mm | $6.10\times10^{-3}$ m |

Areas, with the conversions written out ($1\ \text{mm}^2 = 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2$):

$$A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(8.00\ \text{mm})^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\times64.00\ \text{mm}^2}{4} = 50.27\ \text{mm}^2 = 5.027\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2$$

$$A_f = \frac{\pi d_f^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(6.10\ \text{mm})^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\times37.21\ \text{mm}^2}{4} = 29.22\ \text{mm}^2 = 2.922\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2$$

A load in N over an area in mm² gives MPa, because $1\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 10^{6}\ \text{N/m}^2$.

#### Model

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.x:
- Engineering stress $\sigma = F/A_0$ [Session 11 Slide 9]; tensile strength = maximum engineering stress [Session 11 Slide 30]; fracture stress = stress at fracture [Session 11 Slide 31].
- Percent elongation after failure $EL\,(\%) = \dfrac{l_f - l_0}{l_0}\times100$ [Session 11 Slide 32]; percent reduction in area $RA\,(\%) = \dfrac{A_0 - A_f}{A_0}\times100$ [Session 11 Slide 33].
- True stress $\sigma_T = F/A_i$ with the instantaneous area; true strain $\varepsilon_T = \int dl/l$; after necking $\varepsilon_T = \ln(A_0/A) = 2\ln(D_0/D)$ [Session 11 Slides 37-38].
- Hypotheses: uniaxial load; the measurements after fracture are made with the load removed, so the elastic strain has been recovered [Session 11 Slide 32].

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.x:
#### Tensile strength and engineering fracture stress

The tensile strength is the largest engineering stress [Session 11 Slide 30]; with $A_0$ fixed it corresponds to the largest load:

$$\sigma_{TS} = \frac{F_{\max}}{A_0} = \frac{21\,500\ \text{N}}{50.27\ \text{mm}^2} = 427.7\ \text{MPa}$$

The engineering fracture stress is the load at fracture over the same original area [Session 11 Slide 31]:

$$\sigma_f = \frac{F_f}{A_0} = \frac{17\,800\ \text{N}}{50.27\ \text{mm}^2} = 354.1\ \text{MPa}$$

$\sigma_f < \sigma_{TS}$: after the maximum the load falls because the specimen necks.

#### Percent elongation

The marks are measured on the broken, unloaded specimen, so the elastic strain has been recovered and $l_f - l_0$ is the plastic elongation [Session 11 Slide 32]:

$$EL\,(\%) = \frac{l_f - l_0}{l_0}\times100 = \frac{45.60\ \text{mm} - 40.00\ \text{mm}}{40.00\ \text{mm}}\times100 = \frac{5.60}{40.00}\times100 = 14.0\ \%$$

#### Percent reduction in area

The final area is the area of the fracture surface in the neck [Session 11 Slide 33]:

$$RA\,(\%) = \frac{A_0 - A_f}{A_0}\times100 = \frac{50.265 - 29.225}{50.265}\times100 = \frac{21.040}{50.265}\times100 = 41.9\ \%$$

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.x: The circle areas share the factor $\pi/4$, so the same number comes from the diameters alone: $RA = \left(1 - d_f^2/d_0^2\right)\times100 = (1 - 37.21/64.00)\times100 = 41.9$ %. As the slide warns, $EL\,(\%) \neq RA\,(\%)$ [Session 11 Slide 33].

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.x:
- $\sigma_{T,f} = 609.1$ MPa
- $\varepsilon_{T,f} = 0.542$
- $\sigma_f(1 + EL/100) = 403.7$ MPa underestimates it by about a third

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.x:
#### True stress at fracture with the measured area

The true stress is the load over the area that actually carries it at that instant [Session 11 Slide 37]. At fracture that area is the neck, $A_f$:

$$\sigma_{T,f} = \frac{F_f}{A_f} = \frac{17\,800\ \text{N}}{29.22\ \text{mm}^2} = 609.1\ \text{MPa}$$

Equivalently $\sigma_{T,f} = \sigma_f\,A_0/A_f = 354.1\ \text{MPa}\times1.720 = 609.1$ MPa [Session 11 Slide 38].

#### True strain at fracture: derivation from constant volume in the neck

The true strain adds each small elongation $dl$ divided by the current length $l$ [Session 11 Slide 37]. An antiderivative of $1/l$ is $\ln l$, and Barrow's rule with the limits substituted gives

$$\varepsilon_T = \int_{l_0}^{l}\frac{dl}{l} = \left[\ln l\right]_{l_0}^{l} = \ln l - \ln l_0 = \ln\frac{l}{l_0}$$

After necking the length between the marks no longer describes the strain of the neck, so the integral is applied to a thin slice of the neck itself. Plastic deformation keeps the volume of that slice constant: its initial length $l_0$ and area $A_0$ become $l$ and $A$ with $A_0 l_0 = A l$. Dividing both sides by $A\,l_0$:

$$\frac{l}{l_0} = \frac{A_0}{A} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \varepsilon_T = \ln\frac{A_0}{A}$$

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.x:
which is the expression of the slide for the necked region [Session 11 Slide 38]. At the fracture surface $A = A_f$. With $A = \pi D^2/4$ the factor $\pi/4$ cancels in the ratio, and the logarithm of a square is twice the logarithm:

$$\varepsilon_{T,f} = \ln\frac{A_0}{A_f} = \ln\frac{d_0^2}{d_f^2} = 2\ln\frac{d_0}{d_f} = 2\ln\frac{8.00}{6.10} = 2\times0.2712 = 0.542$$

#### Why the uniform-deformation formulas fail here

The formulas $\sigma_T = \sigma(1+\varepsilon)$ and $\varepsilon_T = \ln(1+\varepsilon)$ of Slide 38 come from constant volume, $A_0 l_0 = A l$, applied to a gauge length that deforms **uniformly**, so that one strain $\varepsilon$ describes every cross-section: from $A_0 l_0 = A l$, $A = A_0 l_0/l = A_0/(1+\varepsilon)$ and $\sigma_T = F/A = (F/A_0)(1+\varepsilon) = \sigma(1+\varepsilon)$. After the maximum load the strain concentrates in the neck: the average strain of the gauge length (0.14) is much smaller than the local strain at the fracture surface. Using them anyway gives

$$\sigma_f\,(1 + 0.140) = 354.1\ \text{MPa}\times1.140 = 403.7\ \text{MPa} \qquad \ln(1 + 0.140) = 0.131$$

against 609.1 MPa and 0.542 from the measured neck: the area ratio of the neck is $A_0/A_f = 1.720$, not $1 + \varepsilon = 1.140$. That is why the slide switches to $F_i/A_i$ and $\ln(A_0/A)$ after necking [Session 11 Slide 38].

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
chunks.x:
- **Physical meaning.** The engineering curve falls after the maximum (427.7 to 354.1 MPa) only because it divides by the original area; the metal in the neck is still hardening, and at fracture it carries 609.1 MPa. The slide states $\sigma_{\text{real}} > \sigma_{\text{eng}}$ and $\varepsilon_{\text{real}} < \varepsilon_{\text{eng}}$ [Session 11 Slide 37]. The stress inequality holds here (609.1 > 354.1 MPa). The strain inequality is written for the uniform deformation of the gauge length, where $\ln(1+\varepsilon) < \varepsilon$ (0.131 < 0.140); the 0.542 found above is not a counterexample, because it is the local strain of the neck, while 0.14 is the average over the whole gauge length.
- **Control checks.** $\sigma_f < \sigma_{TS} < \sigma_{T,f}$; $0 < RA < 100$ %; if the specimen had broken without necking ($d_f \to d_0$), $RA \to 0$ and $\sigma_{T,f} \to \sigma_f$, the behaviour of a brittle material.
- **Dimensions.** $F/A$ is N/m² = Pa; %EL and %RA are ratios of lengths and of areas, and $\ln(A_0/A_f)$ is the logarithm of a pure number, so both strains are dimensionless.
- **Common exam mistake.** Dividing the fracture load by the original area and calling it the true fracture stress, or computing %RA with the diameters instead of their squares ($1 - 6.10/8.00 = 23.8$ %, wrong).

chunks.t: Ductility and true fracture stress of an aluminium alloy from the broken specimen
Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.h: Bank P15 — Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its curve
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the January 2014 final (resilience; true stress and strain at a point of the curve). Here every datum is read from a drawn curve, and the two formulas the final applies directly are derived: the modulus of resilience as an integral with Barrow's rule, the true strain as an integral and the true stress from constant volume. Method: Session 11, Slides 9, 12, 28, 30, 35, 37-38. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x: The figure shows the engineering stress-strain curve of a steel, drawn to fracture (left), and the start of the same test enlarged (right). The marked points are: A on the straight part, Y where the dashed line parallel to the straight part from $\varepsilon = 0.002$ meets the curve, B on the rising part, U at the maximum and F at fracture.

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x:
#### Data

Values read from the figure: A, B and Y have dashed projections that end on a printed axis value; U lies on the 0.15 and 600 gridlines; F is at (0.25, 500) and is not needed.

| Point | What it is | Strain $\varepsilon$ | Stress $\sigma$ (MPa) | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A | point of the straight part (right panel) | 0.0015 | 310 | $3.10\times10^{8}$ Pa |
| Y | crossing with the 0.2 % offset line (right panel) | read below | 450 | $4.50\times10^{8}$ Pa |
| B | rising part, before the maximum (left panel) | 0.08 | 560 | $5.60\times10^{8}$ Pa |
| U | maximum of the curve (left panel) | 0.15 | 600 | $6.00\times10^{8}$ Pa |

#### Model

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x:
- Hooke's law $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ on the straight part; $E$ is its slope [Session 11 Slide 12].
- Conventional yield strength at the crossing with the line parallel to the elastic one from $\varepsilon = 0.002$ [Session 11 Slide 28].
- Modulus of resilience: energy per unit volume up to yielding, $U_r = \int_0^{\varepsilon_y}\sigma\,d\varepsilon$ [Session 11 Slide 35].
- True stress $\sigma_T = F/A_i$ and true strain $\varepsilon_T = \int_{l_0}^{l} dl/l$ [Session 11 Slide 37]; before necking the volume is constant, $A_0 l_0 = A_i l_i$ [Session 11 Slide 38].
- Hypothesis for $U_r$: as on Slide 35, the elastic region is taken as linear up to $\sigma_y$ (the small rounding of the curve between about 380 and 450 MPa is neglected).

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x: The slope of the straight part comes from one point of it and the origin. The resilience is the area under the elastic line from zero to the yield strain: write it as an integral of $E\varepsilon$.

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x:
#### Modulus of elasticity from point A

The straight part passes through the origin and through A, and Hooke's law says its slope is $E$ [Session 11 Slide 12]:

$$E = \frac{\sigma_A - 0}{\varepsilon_A - 0} = \frac{310\ \text{MPa}}{0.0015} = 206\,667\ \text{MPa} = 206.7\ \text{GPa}$$

This agrees with the steel value of the slide's table, 207 GPa [Session 11 Slide 17].

#### Yield strength from point Y

The yield strength is the stress at the crossing of the curve with the offset line [Session 11 Slide 28]; the horizontal projection of Y ends at 450 on the stress axis:

$$\sigma_y = 450\ \text{MPa}$$

Check of the reading: on the offset line $\sigma = E(\varepsilon - 0.002)$, so the strain of Y must be $\varepsilon_Y = 0.002 + \sigma_y/E = 0.002 + 450/206\,667 = 0.004177$, which is where Y sits in the right panel (just to the right of the 0.004 gridline).

#### Elastic strain at the yield strength

Treating the elastic region as linear up to $\sigma_y$ (Slide 35) and isolating the strain from Hooke's law $\sigma_y = E\,\varepsilon_y$:

$$\varepsilon_y = \frac{\sigma_y}{E} = \frac{450\ \text{MPa}}{206\,667\ \text{MPa}} = 0.002177$$

#### Modulus of resilience as the area under the elastic line

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x:
The resilience is the energy absorbed per unit volume while the material deforms elastically, the area under the curve up to the yield point [Session 11 Slide 35]. In the elastic region $\sigma = E\varepsilon$, so

$$U_r = \int_0^{\varepsilon_y}\sigma\,d\varepsilon = \int_0^{\varepsilon_y}E\,\varepsilon\,d\varepsilon$$

$E$ is a constant and leaves the integral; an antiderivative of $\varepsilon$ is $\varepsilon^2/2$ (its derivative is $2\varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon$). Barrow's rule with the limits substituted:

$$U_r = E\left[\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\right]_0^{\varepsilon_y} = E\left(\frac{\varepsilon_y^2}{2} - \frac{0^2}{2}\right) = \frac{E\,\varepsilon_y^2}{2}$$

Replacing $\varepsilon_y = \sigma_y/E$: $U_r = \dfrac{E}{2}\,\dfrac{\sigma_y^2}{E^2} = \dfrac{\sigma_y^2}{2E}$, the formula of the slide, which is also the area of the triangle $\tfrac12\sigma_y\varepsilon_y$.

#### Numerical value

$$U_r = \frac{\sigma_y^2}{2E} = \frac{(450\ \text{MPa})^2}{2\times206\,667\ \text{MPa}} = \frac{202\,500}{413\,333}\ \text{MPa} = 0.490\ \text{MPa}$$

Since $1\ \text{MPa} = 10^6\ \text{N/m}^2 = 10^6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m/m}^3 = 1\ \text{MJ/m}^3$, each cubic metre of this steel stores 0.490 MJ of recoverable elastic energy before it yields. Check with the triangle: $\tfrac12\times450\ \text{MPa}\times0.002177 = 0.490$ MPa.

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x: Write the true strain as the integral of $dl/l$, and use constant volume, $A_0 l_0 = A l$, to replace the instantaneous area by the length.

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x:
- $\varepsilon_{T,B} = \ln(1.08) = 0.0770$
- $\sigma_{T,B} = 560 \times 1.08 = 604.8$ MPa
- Valid only up to U ($\varepsilon = 0.15$), where necking starts

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x:
#### True strain as a sum of small increments

The true strain adds each small elongation $dl$ divided by the length $l$ the specimen has at that moment [Session 11 Slide 37]:

$$\varepsilon_T = \int_{l_0}^{l}\frac{dl}{l}$$

An antiderivative of $1/l$ is $\ln l$. Barrow's rule with the limits substituted:

$$\varepsilon_T = \left[\ln l\right]_{l_0}^{l} = \ln l - \ln l_0 = \ln\frac{l}{l_0}$$

Since $\varepsilon = (l - l_0)/l_0$, the ratio is $l/l_0 = (l_0 + l - l_0)/l_0 = 1 + \varepsilon$, and

$$\varepsilon_T = \ln(1 + \varepsilon)$$

#### True stress from constant volume

Plastic deformation does not change the volume, and before necking the specimen deforms uniformly, so the volume of the gauge length is the same at every instant [Session 11 Slide 38]:

$$A_0\,l_0 = A_i\,l_i$$

Isolating the instantaneous area: $A_i = A_0\,l_0/l_i$. The true stress is the load over that area [Session 11 Slide 37]:

$$\sigma_T = \frac{F}{A_i} = \frac{F}{A_0\,l_0/l_i} = \frac{F}{A_0}\cdot\frac{l_i}{l_0} = \sigma\,(1 + \varepsilon)$$

using again $l_i/l_0 = 1 + \varepsilon$.

#### Values at point B

Point B is read at $\varepsilon_B = 0.08$, $\sigma_B = 560$ MPa:

$$\varepsilon_{T,B} = \ln(1 + 0.08) = \ln 1.08 = 0.0770$$

$$\sigma_{T,B} = \sigma_B\,(1 + \varepsilon_B) = 560\ \text{MPa}\times1.08 = 604.8\ \text{MPa}$$

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x:
As Slide 37 predicts, $\sigma_T > \sigma$ (604.8 > 560 MPa) and $\varepsilon_T < \varepsilon$ (0.0770 < 0.08). The cross-section at B has shrunk by the factor $A_i/A_0 = 1/1.08 = 0.926$.

#### Why not after point U

Point U is the maximum of the curve, the tensile strength (600 MPa), and necking follows it [Session 11 Slide 30]. From U on the deformation concentrates in the neck: the gauge length no longer has one area, $A_0 l_0 = A_i l_i$ with a single $A_i$ fails, and $\sigma(1+\varepsilon)$ and $\ln(1+\varepsilon)$ no longer describe the neck. After necking the slide uses the measured area, $\sigma_T = F_i/A_i$ and $\varepsilon_T = \ln(A_0/A) = 2\ln(D_0/D)$ [Session 11 Slide 38], so the diameter of the neck would have to be measured (for example at F).

chunks.t: Resilience and true stress of a steel read from its stress-strain curve
chunks.x:
- **Physical meaning.** $U_r = 0.490$ MJ/m³ is small next to the area under the whole curve (the toughness: a mean stress of about 530 MPa over a strain of 0.25 gives roughly $530\ \text{MPa}\times0.25 \approx 130$ MJ/m³): a structural steel absorbs almost all its energy plastically. A spring material needs high $\sigma_y$ and low $E$ [Session 11 Slide 35].
- **Limiting case.** For small strains $\ln(1+\varepsilon) \approx \varepsilon$ and $1+\varepsilon \approx 1$: at A ($\varepsilon = 0.0015$) the true stress exceeds the engineering one by 0.15 % and the true strain is smaller by about 0.075 %; at B the stresses differ by 8 % and the strains by about 3.8 % (0.0770 against 0.08). The distinction matters only in the plastic range.
- **Dimensions.** $\int\sigma\,d\varepsilon$ is Pa × (dimensionless) = Pa = J/m³; $\sigma_y^2/E$ is Pa²/Pa = Pa; $\ln(l/l_0)$ is the logarithm of a pure number; $\sigma(1+\varepsilon)$ is Pa.
- **Common exam mistake.** Taking $\varepsilon_y = 0.002$ or $\varepsilon_Y = 0.004177$ (the strain of the crossing, which includes the plastic offset) in the resilience: $U_r$ uses only the elastic strain $\sigma_y/E$.
