Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.h: Bank P16 — Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the magnesium tensile tests of the finals of January 2013 and January 2014, but worked backwards: the report gives the results and the student must recover the loads and the lengths and diameters the machine and the calliper would have measured. Each definition of the slides is solved for the measurement instead of the property. Method: Session 11, Slides 9, 12, 28, 30, 32, 33, 37-38. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.x: The raw data sheet of a tensile test on a round magnesium alloy specimen (initial diameter 9.00 mm, initial gauge length 45.00 mm) has been lost. The report only keeps the results: modulus of elasticity 45 GPa, yield strength (0.2 % offset) 170 MPa, tensile strength 255 MPa reached at an engineering strain of 0.080, elongation after fracture 11.0 % and reduction in area 13.0 %.

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Initial diameter | $d_0$ | 9.00 mm | $9.00\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Initial gauge length | $l_0$ | 45.00 mm | $4.500\times10^{-2}$ m |
| Modulus of elasticity | $E$ | 45 GPa | $4.5\times10^{10}$ Pa $= 45\,000$ MPa |
| Yield strength (0.2 % offset) | $\sigma_y$ | 170 MPa | $1.70\times10^{8}$ Pa |
| Tensile strength | $\sigma_{TS}$ | 255 MPa | $2.55\times10^{8}$ Pa |
| Engineering strain at the maximum load | $\varepsilon_u$ | 0.080 | (dimensionless) |
| Elongation after fracture | $EL$ | 11.0 % | 0.110 |
| Reduction in area | $RA$ | 13.0 % | 0.130 |

Initial area, with the conversion written out:

$$A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(9.00\ \text{mm})^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\times81.00\ \text{mm}^2}{4} = 63.62\ \text{mm}^2 = 6.362\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2$$

A stress in MPa times an area in mm² gives N, because $1\ \text{MPa} = 1\ \text{N/mm}^2$.

#### Model

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.x:
- $\sigma = F/A_0$ and $\varepsilon = (l - l_0)/l_0$ [Session 11 Slide 9]; Hooke's law $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ [Session 11 Slide 12].
- 0.2 % offset: the yield point lies on the line $\sigma = E(\varepsilon - 0.002)$ [Session 11 Slide 28].
- $EL\,(\%) = \dfrac{l_f - l_0}{l_0}\times100$ [Session 11 Slide 32] and $RA\,(\%) = \dfrac{A_0 - A_f}{A_0}\times100$ [Session 11 Slide 33].
- Constant volume before necking, $A_0 l_0 = A_i l_i$, and $\sigma_T = F/A_i$ [Session 11 Slides 37-38].
- Hypothesis: the deformation is uniform up to the maximum load, where necking starts [Session 11 Slide 30].

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.x:
#### Loads from the stresses

The engineering stress is $\sigma = F/A_0$ [Session 11 Slide 9]; multiplying both sides by $A_0$ isolates the load, $F = \sigma A_0$:

$$F_y = \sigma_y\,A_0 = 170\ \text{N/mm}^2\times63.62\ \text{mm}^2 = 10\,815\ \text{N}$$

$$F_{\max} = \sigma_{TS}\,A_0 = 255\ \text{N/mm}^2\times63.62\ \text{mm}^2 = 16\,222\ \text{N}$$

#### Strain at the yield point from the offset line

The conventional yield point is where the curve meets the line parallel to the elastic one from $\varepsilon = 0.002$ [Session 11 Slide 28], so its coordinates satisfy $\sigma_y = E(\varepsilon_Y - 0.002)$. Dividing by $E$ and then adding 0.002 to both sides:

$$\varepsilon_Y - 0.002 = \frac{\sigma_y}{E} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \varepsilon_Y = 0.002 + \frac{\sigma_y}{E} = 0.002 + \frac{170\ \text{MPa}}{45\,000\ \text{MPa}} = 0.002 + 0.003778 = 0.005778$$

The total strain at that point is the plastic offset plus the elastic part, as the figure shows; the total strain before fracture is always $\varepsilon_t = \varepsilon_e + \varepsilon_p$ [Session 11 Slide 32].

#### Gauge length at the yield point

From $\varepsilon = (l - l_0)/l_0$, multiplying by $l_0$ and adding $l_0$: $l = l_0\,(1 + \varepsilon)$.

$$l_y = l_0\,(1 + \varepsilon_Y) = 45.00\ \text{mm}\times1.005778 = 45.260\ \text{mm}$$

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.x: The extensometer read an elongation of 0.260 mm. A student who places the yield point on the elastic line ($\varepsilon = 0.003778$) would rebuild 45.170 mm, missing the 0.090 mm of plastic offset.

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.x: Solve the definitions of %EL and %RA for $l_f$ and $A_f$. At the maximum load the deformation is still uniform, so constant volume gives the area from the length.

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.x:
#### Gauge length after fracture from %EL

From $EL = (l_f - l_0)/l_0$ (as a fraction, 0.110), multiplying by $l_0$ and adding $l_0$:

$$l_f = l_0\,(1 + EL) = 45.00\ \text{mm}\times(1 + 0.110) = 49.95\ \text{mm}$$

This is the distance between the marks with the two halves fitted together, after the elastic recovery [Session 11 Slide 32].

#### Neck diameter from %RA

From $RA = (A_0 - A_f)/A_0$ (0.130 as a fraction), multiplying by $A_0$ and isolating $A_f$:

$$A_f = A_0\,(1 - RA) = 63.62\ \text{mm}^2\times(1 - 0.130) = 63.62\ \text{mm}^2\times0.870 = 55.35\ \text{mm}^2$$

The area of a circle is $\pi d^2/4$, so $d_f = \sqrt{4A_f/\pi}$; the factor $\pi/4$ cancels against that of $A_0$, which gives directly

$$d_f = d_0\,\sqrt{1 - RA} = 9.00\ \text{mm}\times\sqrt{0.870} = 9.00\ \text{mm}\times0.9327 = 8.39\ \text{mm}$$

#### Diameter at the maximum load from constant volume

Up to the maximum load the deformation is uniform and the volume of the gauge length does not change [Session 11 Slide 38]: $A_0 l_0 = A_u l_u$. Isolating the area and writing $l_u/l_0 = 1 + \varepsilon_u$:

$$A_u = \frac{A_0\,l_0}{l_u} = \frac{A_0}{1 + \varepsilon_u} = \frac{63.62\ \text{mm}^2}{1.080} = 58.90\ \text{mm}^2$$

and, with $A \propto d^2$, $d_u = d_0/\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon_u} = 9.00\ \text{mm}/\sqrt{1.080} = 8.66$ mm.

#### True stress at the maximum load

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.x:
The true stress is the load over the instantaneous area [Session 11 Slide 37]:

$$\sigma_{T,u} = \frac{F_{\max}}{A_u} = \frac{16\,222\ \text{N}}{58.90\ \text{mm}^2} = 275.4\ \text{MPa}$$

the same as $\sigma_{TS}(1 + \varepsilon_u) = 255\ \text{MPa}\times1.080 = 275.4$ MPa, as it must be, since both come from constant volume.

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
chunks.x:
- **Consistency of the report.** The neck diameter after fracture (8.39 mm) is smaller than the uniform diameter at the maximum load (8.66 mm): the neck kept thinning after the maximum, as it must [Session 11 Slide 30]. And $l_f = 49.95$ mm is longer than the length at the maximum, $45.00\times1.080 = 48.60$ mm, because the neck added plastic elongation even though the elastic part was recovered.
- **Order of magnitude.** $E = 45$ GPa is the magnesium value of the slide's table [Session 11 Slide 17]; magnesium is hcp, with 6 slip systems against 12 for fcc and bcc [Session 11 Slide 25]. **Extension** (not on the slides): fewer slip systems usually mean less ductility, which fits the small %RA of 13 %.
- **Limiting case.** If $RA \to 0$ (no neck), $d_f \to d_0$; if $\varepsilon_u \to 0$, $d_u \to d_0$ and $\sigma_T \to \sigma$.
- **Dimensions.** $F = \sigma A_0$ is Pa·m² = N; $l_0(1 + \varepsilon)$ is m; $d_0\sqrt{1 - RA}$ is m; $F/A_u$ is Pa.
- **Common exam mistake.** Getting the diameter after fracture as $d_0(1 - RA)$ = 7.83 mm: %RA is a reduction of the area, so the diameter scales with the square root.

chunks.t: Rebuilding the raw measurements of a magnesium alloy tensile test from its report
Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
chunks.h: Bank P17 — Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the final of January 2017 (question 5). Method: Session 11, Slides 9, 10, 12 and 19. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
chunks.x: A tie rod of the engine mount of a light aircraft is a solid cylinder of a nickel alloy, 8.0 mm in diameter and 350 mm long. In service it is pulled along its axis by a force of 9.5 kN. The alloy has a Young's modulus of 207 GPa (the value of nickel in the table of the slides), a yield strength of 280 MPa and a Poisson's ratio of 0.31.

chunks.t: Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value given | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Initial diameter | $d_0$ | 8.0 mm | $8.0\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Initial length | $l_0$ | 350 mm | 0.350 m |
| Axial force | $F$ | 9.5 kN | $9.5\times10^{3}$ N |
| Young's modulus | $E$ | 207 GPa | $207\times10^{9}$ Pa |
| Yield strength | $\sigma_y$ | 280 MPa | $280\times10^{6}$ Pa |
| Poisson's ratio | $\nu$ | 0.31 | dimensionless |

#### Model

- Engineering stress and strain: $\sigma = F/A_0$ and $\varepsilon = (l - l_0)/l_0 = \Delta l/l_0$ [Session 11, Slide 9].
- Elastic zone $\sigma < \sigma_y$, plastic zone $\sigma > \sigma_y$ [Session 11, Slide 10].
- Hooke's law in the elastic zone, $\sigma = E\,\varepsilon$ [Session 11, Slide 12].
- Poisson's ratio, $\nu = -\varepsilon_{\text{transverse}}/\varepsilon_{\text{longitudinal}}$ [Session 11, Slide 19].
- Hypotheses: uniform uniaxial stress over the cross-section, isotropic material, no change of $A_0$ used in the stress (engineering stress).

chunks.t: Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
chunks.x:
- $A_0 = 5.027\times10^{-5}$ m²
- $\sigma = 189.0$ MPa $< \sigma_y = 280$ MPa: elastic, no plastic deformation
- Ratio $\sigma_y/\sigma = 1.48$

chunks.t: Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
chunks.x:
#### Area of the cross-section, with the diameter in metres

The stress needs the initial area of the circular section. The diameter is first converted to metres, $d_0 = 8.0\ \text{mm} = 8.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}$, and then:

$$A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(8.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m})^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\times 6.4\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2}{4} = 5.027\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2$$

#### Engineering stress produced by the force

The force is converted to newtons, $F = 9.5\ \text{kN} = 9.5\times10^{3}\ \text{N}$. The engineering stress is the force over the initial area [Session 11, Slide 9]:

$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A_0} = \frac{9.5\times10^{3}\ \text{N}}{5.027\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2} = 1.890\times10^{8}\ \text{Pa} = 189.0\ \text{MPa}$$

#### Compare the stress with the yield strength

The rod deforms plastically only if the stress exceeds the yield strength [Session 11, Slide 10]. Here

$$\sigma = 189.0\ \text{MPa} < \sigma_y = 280\ \text{MPa}$$

so the rod stays in the elastic zone: **it does not deform plastically**, and all its deformation is recovered when the load is removed. The yield strength is $280/189.0 = 1.48$ times the applied stress.

chunks.t: Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
chunks.x: The rod is elastic, so Hooke's law gives the axial strain; Poisson's ratio gives the transverse strain, which has the opposite sign.

chunks.t: Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
chunks.x:
#### Axial strain from Hooke's law

Part (a) showed that the rod is elastic, so Hooke's law applies [Session 11, Slide 12]. Isolating the strain from $\sigma = E\,\varepsilon_z$ (divide both sides by $E$):

$$\varepsilon_z = \frac{\sigma}{E} = \frac{189.0\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}}{207\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}} = 9.130\times10^{-4}$$

#### Length under the load

From the definition $\varepsilon_z = \Delta l/l_0$ [Session 11, Slide 9], multiplying both sides by $l_0$ gives the elongation:

$$\Delta l = \varepsilon_z\,l_0 = 9.130\times10^{-4}\times 350\ \text{mm} = 0.3196\ \text{mm}$$

$$l = l_0 + \Delta l = 350\ \text{mm} + 0.3196\ \text{mm} = 350.320\ \text{mm}$$

#### Transverse strain from Poisson's ratio

A longitudinal elastic stretch comes with a transverse contraction [Session 11, Slide 19]. From $\nu = -\varepsilon_x/\varepsilon_z$, multiplying both sides by $-\varepsilon_z$:

$$\varepsilon_x = -\nu\,\varepsilon_z = -0.31\times 9.130\times10^{-4} = -2.830\times10^{-4}$$

#### Diameter under the load

The transverse strain is the relative change of the diameter, $\varepsilon_x = \Delta d/d_0$, so

$$\Delta d = \varepsilon_x\,d_0 = -2.830\times10^{-4}\times 8.0\ \text{mm} = -2.264\times10^{-3}\ \text{mm}$$

$$d = d_0 + \Delta d = 8.0\ \text{mm} - 0.002264\ \text{mm} = 7.9977\ \text{mm}$$

The diameter shrinks by about 2.3 µm while the length grows by about 0.32 mm.

chunks.t: Nickel alloy tie rod under a tensile load
chunks.x:
- The rod works at 189 MPa, two thirds of its yield strength, so the whole deformation is elastic and is recovered on unloading. If the same force acted on a rod of 6.0 mm, the stress would rise by $(8/6)^2$ to 336 MPa and the rod would yield: the check of part (a) must always come before Hooke's law.
- Control case: with $\nu = 0$ the diameter would not change; with $\nu = 0.5$ (incompressible, Slide 19) the contraction would be $-4.57\times10^{-4}$, larger than the one found. The value 0.31 lies in the range 0.25 to 0.4 of metals in the slide.
- SI check: $\sigma = F/A_0$ in N/m² = Pa; $\varepsilon = \sigma/E$ in Pa/Pa, dimensionless; $\Delta l = \varepsilon\,l_0$ and $\Delta d = \varepsilon_x d_0$ in metres.
- Common mistake: using the radius in place of the diameter in $\pi d_0^2/4$, or forgetting the minus sign of the transverse strain and giving a diameter that grows under tension.

Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.h: Bank P18 — Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the final of January 2016 (question 5); the alloys are hypothetical. Method: Session 11, Slides 9, 12, 19 and 29. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x:
A cylindrical control rod of an aircraft must be 250 mm long and 12 mm in diameter, and it carries an axial tensile load of 18 kN. The designer sets three requirements: (1) no yielding with a safety factor $N = 2$; (2) the diameter may not shrink by more than 10 µm under the load; (3) the rod may not weigh more than 150 g. Four alloys are available:

| Alloy | $E$ (GPa) | $\sigma_y$ (MPa) | $\nu$ | $\rho$ (g/cm³) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A, aluminium alloy | 69 | 300 | 0.33 | 2.7 |
| B, titanium alloy | 107 | 850 | 0.34 | 4.5 |
| C, steel | 207 | 480 | 0.30 | 7.8 |
| D, magnesium alloy | 45 | 220 | 0.29 | 1.8 |

chunks.t: Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value given | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Length | $l_0$ | 250 mm | 0.250 m |
| Diameter | $d_0$ | 12 mm | $12\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Axial force | $F$ | 18 kN | $18\times10^{3}$ N |
| Safety factor | $N$ | 2 | dimensionless |
| Largest diameter loss | $\lvert\Delta d\rvert_{\max}$ | 10 µm | $10\times10^{-6}$ m $= 10\times10^{-3}$ mm |
| Largest mass | $m_{\max}$ | 150 g | 0.150 kg |

Moduli in pascals: $1\ \text{GPa} = 10^{9}\ \text{Pa}$, $1\ \text{MPa} = 10^{6}\ \text{Pa}$. Densities: $1\ \text{g/cm}^3 = 10^{3}\ \text{kg/m}^3$, so for example $\rho_A = 2.7\ \text{g/cm}^3 = 2700\ \text{kg/m}^3$.

#### Model

- Engineering stress $\sigma = F/A_0$ [Session 11, Slide 9].
- Working stress $\sigma_w = \sigma_y/N$: the design keeps $\sigma \le \sigma_w$ [Session 11, Slide 29].
- Hooke's law $\sigma = E\,\varepsilon_z$ in the elastic zone [Session 11, Slide 12] and Poisson's ratio $\nu = -\varepsilon_x/\varepsilon_z$ [Session 11, Slide 19].
- Mass $m = \rho\,V$ with $V = A_0\,l_0$ for a cylinder (geometry).
- Hypotheses: uniform uniaxial stress; the dimensions are set, so the stress is the same for the four alloys; the deformation is elastic in every alloy that passes requirement (1).

chunks.t: Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x:
- $A_0 = 1.131\times10^{-4}$ m², $\sigma = 159.2$ MPa
- Required $\sigma_y \ge 318.3$ MPa: A (300) and D (220) are rejected; B and C pass

chunks.t: Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x:
#### Stress in the rod, the same for every alloy

The diameter in metres is $d_0 = 12\times10^{-3}$ m, so the initial area is

$$A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(12\times10^{-3}\ \text{m})^2}{4} = 1.131\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$$

and with $F = 18\ \text{kN} = 18\times10^{3}$ N the engineering stress is [Session 11, Slide 9]

$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A_0} = \frac{18\times10^{3}\ \text{N}}{1.131\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2} = 1.592\times10^{8}\ \text{Pa} = 159.2\ \text{MPa}$$

#### Turn the safety factor into a minimum yield strength

The rod is safe when the stress does not exceed the working stress, $\sigma \le \sigma_w = \sigma_y/N$ [Session 11, Slide 29]. Multiplying both sides by $N$ isolates the yield strength the alloy needs:

$$\sigma_y \ge N\,\sigma = 2\times 159.2\ \text{MPa} = 318.3\ \text{MPa}$$

#### Screen the four alloys

| Alloy | $\sigma_y$ (MPa) | $\sigma_y \ge 318.3$ MPa? |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| A | 300 | no, rejected (it would work with $N = 300/159.2 = 1.88$) |
| B | 850 | yes |
| C | 480 | yes |
| D | 220 | no, rejected ($N = 220/159.2 = 1.38$) |

Only **B and C** meet the requirement of no yielding with $N = 2$. Alloy A would not yield (300 > 159.2 MPa), but its margin is below the one demanded.

chunks.t: Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x: The stress is below the yield strength of B and C, so Hooke's law and Poisson's ratio give the diameter change. The volume is the same for every alloy.

chunks.t: Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x:
- $\Delta d_B = -6.07$ µm, $\Delta d_C = -2.77$ µm: both within 10 µm
- $V = 28.27$ cm³; $m_B = 127.2$ g, $m_C = 220.5$ g: C is rejected by mass
- Chosen: alloy B (titanium), elongation $\Delta l_B = 0.372$ mm

chunks.t: Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x:
#### Diameter change from Hooke's law and Poisson's ratio

B and C are elastic at 159.2 MPa (part a). Hooke's law gives $\varepsilon_z = \sigma/E$ [Session 11, Slide 12]; Poisson's ratio gives $\varepsilon_x = -\nu\,\varepsilon_z$ [Session 11, Slide 19]; and $\Delta d = \varepsilon_x\,d_0$. Putting the three together, line by line:

$$\Delta d = \varepsilon_x\,d_0 = -\nu\,\varepsilon_z\,d_0 = -\nu\,\frac{\sigma}{E}\,d_0$$

For B, with $E = 107\times10^{9}$ Pa and $d_0 = 12$ mm:

$$\Delta d_B = -0.34\times\frac{159.2\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}}{107\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}}\times 12\ \text{mm} = -0.34\times 1.487\times10^{-3}\times 12\ \text{mm} = -6.07\times10^{-3}\ \text{mm} = -6.07\ \mu\text{m}$$

For C, with $E = 207\times10^{9}$ Pa:

$$\Delta d_C = -0.30\times\frac{159.2\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}}{207\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}}\times 12\ \text{mm} = -0.30\times 7.689\times10^{-4}\times 12\ \text{mm} = -2.77\ \mu\text{m}$$

Both losses are smaller than 10 µm, so B and C meet requirement (2).

#### Mass of the rod

The volume of the cylinder is the same for every alloy:

$$V = A_0\,l_0 = 1.131\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\times 0.250\ \text{m} = 2.827\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^3 = 28.27\ \text{cm}^3$$

using $1\ \text{m}^3 = 10^{6}\ \text{cm}^3$. With $m = \rho V$:

$$m_B = 4.5\ \text{g/cm}^3\times 28.27\ \text{cm}^3 = 127.2\ \text{g} \le 150\ \text{g}$$

chunks.t: Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x:
$$m_C = 7.8\ \text{g/cm}^3\times 28.27\ \text{cm}^3 = 220.5\ \text{g} > 150\ \text{g}$$

Steel C is rejected by the mass limit.

#### Choice and summary of the rejections

| Alloy | Requirement (1), $\sigma_y \ge 318.3$ MPa | Requirement (2), $\lvert\Delta d\rvert \le 10$ µm | Requirement (3), $m \le 150$ g | Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A | fails (300 MPa) | 9.13 µm | 76.3 g | rejected by (1) |
| B | 850 MPa | 6.07 µm | 127.2 g | **chosen** |
| C | 480 MPa | 2.77 µm | fails (220.5 g) | rejected by (3) |
| D | fails (220 MPa) | fails (12.31 µm) | 50.9 g | rejected by (1) and (2) |

The values of A and D in columns (2) and (3) are given only for completeness (computed with the same formulas). The rod is made of the **titanium alloy B**. Its elongation under the load is

$$\Delta l_B = \frac{\sigma}{E_B}\,l_0 = \frac{159.2\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}}{107\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}}\times 250\ \text{mm} = 0.372\ \text{mm}$$

chunks.t: Choosing the alloy of a light control rod
chunks.x:
- The three requirements pull in different directions: steel is stiff and strong but heavy, the light alloys are too weak for $N = 2$, and the titanium alloy wins on strength per unit density. **Extension** (not on the slides): the specific strength $\sigma_y/\rho$ is the yield strength divided by the density; with the table it is about 111 (A), 189 (B), 61.5 (C) and 122 (D) MPa per g/cm³, so B is clearly ahead. On the specific modulus $E/\rho$ B is actually the lowest of the four (23.8 against 25.0 to 26.5 GPa per g/cm³): here stiffness is not the deciding property.
- D fails twice: a low yield strength and a low modulus (a large elastic strain, hence a large diameter loss). A low $E$ makes $\lvert\Delta d\rvert$ grow as $\nu/E$.
- Limiting check: the diameter loss of B, 6.07 µm, is $5\times10^{-4}$ of the diameter, a typical elastic strain of a metal, far below 1 %.
- SI check: $\nu\,\sigma\,d_0/E$ has units Pa·m/Pa = m; $\rho\,V$ in (kg/m³)·m³ = kg.
- Common mistake: rejecting A because "it yields". It does not yield at 159.2 MPa; it is rejected because its safety factor would be 1.88 < 2.

chunks.h: Bank P19 — Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the final of June 2017 (question 5). Method: Session 11, Slides 9, 10, 12, 21 and 32. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x: A cylindrical specimen of an aluminium alloy, 12.0 mm in diameter and with a gauge length of 50.0 mm, is pulled in a tensile machine up to a load of 40 kN. At that load the engineering strain measured on the gauge length is 0.035. The load is then removed completely, and later the same specimen is loaded again to 30 kN. Data of the alloy: $E = 69$ GPa, $\sigma_y = 275$ MPa (0.2 % offset).

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value given | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Initial diameter | $d_0$ | 12.0 mm | $12.0\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Gauge length | $l_0$ | 50.0 mm | $50.0\times10^{-3}$ m |
| Maximum load | $F_B$ | 40 kN | $40\times10^{3}$ N |
| Total strain at $F_B$ | $\varepsilon_B$ | 0.035 | dimensionless |
| Reloading force | $F_R$ | 30 kN | $30\times10^{3}$ N |
| Young's modulus | $E$ | 69 GPa | $69\times10^{9}$ Pa |
| Yield strength | $\sigma_y$ | 275 MPa | $275\times10^{6}$ Pa |

#### Model

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x:
- Engineering stress $\sigma = F/A_0$ and strain $\varepsilon = (l - l_0)/l_0$ [Session 11, Slide 9]; elastic zone for $\sigma < \sigma_y$, plastic for $\sigma > \sigma_y$ [Session 11, Slide 10].
- Hooke's law $\sigma = E\,\varepsilon$ for the elastic part [Session 11, Slide 12].
- Beyond yield the total strain is the sum of an elastic and a plastic part, $\varepsilon_t = \varepsilon_e + \varepsilon_p$; on unloading the elastic part is recovered along a line parallel to the elastic line and the plastic part remains [Session 11, Slide 32].
- **Extension** (idealisation, not stated on the slides): on reloading, the unloaded specimen follows the unloading line elastically up to the previous maximum stress before it yields again. The slides only state that cold work raises the yield strength [Session 12, Slide 5].
- Yielding is drawn, as an idealisation, at the end of the straight elastic line; the real 0.2 % offset value of 275 MPa lies on the curve at a strain of about 0.0060.
- Hypotheses: uniform uniaxial stress; the engineering stress uses the initial area $A_0$; the unloading is elastic with the same modulus $E$; the elastic reloading of part (c) rests on the idealisation marked **extension** above.

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x: Compare the stress with the yield strength. The strain at 40 kN is measured, so Hooke's law is not needed for the length.

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x:
#### Stress at the maximum load

With $d_0 = 12.0\times10^{-3}$ m:

$$A_0 = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{4} = \frac{\pi\,(12.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m})^2}{4} = 1.131\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$$

and with $F_B = 40\ \text{kN} = 40\times10^{3}$ N [Session 11, Slide 9]:

$$\sigma_B = \frac{F_B}{A_0} = \frac{40\times10^{3}\ \text{N}}{1.131\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2} = 3.537\times10^{8}\ \text{Pa} = 353.7\ \text{MPa}$$

#### Elastic or plastic

$\sigma_B = 353.7\ \text{MPa} > \sigma_y = 275\ \text{MPa}$, so the specimen is in the plastic zone [Session 11, Slide 10]. Hooke's law does not hold up to this point: the measured strain 0.035 is much larger than the elastic strain at yield, $\sigma_y/E = 275\times10^{6}/69\times10^{9} = 3.986\times10^{-3}$.

#### Length under the load

The strain under load is given, so the length comes straight from the definition $\varepsilon_B = (l_B - l_0)/l_0$. Multiplying by $l_0$ and adding $l_0$ to both sides:

$$l_B = l_0\,(1 + \varepsilon_B) = 50.0\ \text{mm}\times(1 + 0.035) = 51.750\ \text{mm}$$

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x: On unloading only the elastic part of the strain is recovered, along a line of slope $E$ that starts at the stress reached, not at the yield strength.

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x:
- Recovered elastic strain $\varepsilon_e = 5.126\times10^{-3}$
- Permanent strain $\varepsilon_p = 0.02987$
- Final length $l_P = 51.494$ mm (the specimen shortens by 0.256 mm on unloading)

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x:
#### Split the total strain into its elastic and plastic parts

At point B of the curve the total strain is $\varepsilon_B = \varepsilon_e + \varepsilon_p$ [Session 11, Slide 32]. Unloading removes the stress from $\sigma_B$ to 0 along a straight line parallel to the elastic line, of slope $E$ [Session 11, Slide 32]. The strain recovered is therefore Hooke's law applied to the stress drop $\sigma_B - 0$:

$$\varepsilon_e = \frac{\sigma_B}{E} = \frac{353.7\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}}{69\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}} = 5.126\times10^{-3}$$

#### Permanent strain

Isolating the plastic part from $\varepsilon_B = \varepsilon_e + \varepsilon_p$ (subtract $\varepsilon_e$ from both sides):

$$\varepsilon_p = \varepsilon_B - \varepsilon_e = 0.035 - 5.126\times10^{-3} = 0.02987$$

#### Final length after unloading

The permanent strain is measured on the initial gauge length, so

$$l_P = l_0\,(1 + \varepsilon_p) = 50.0\ \text{mm}\times(1 + 0.02987) = 51.494\ \text{mm}$$

The specimen shortens on unloading by $l_B - l_P = 51.750 - 51.494 = 0.256$ mm, which is $\varepsilon_e\,l_0 = 5.126\times10^{-3}\times 50.0$ mm.

#### Loading and unloading path

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x: O to Y is the elastic line, with yielding idealised at its end (the 0.2 % offset value lies a little further along the curve); Y to B is the plastic loading up to 353.7 MPa at $\varepsilon = 0.035$; B to P is the unloading, parallel to OY, ending at the permanent strain 0.0299.

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x: Compare the new stress with the highest stress the specimen has already carried. Measure the strain from the original gauge length.

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x:
- $\sigma_R = 265.3$ MPa $< \sigma_B = 353.7$ MPa: the reloading runs back up the line PB, elastically
- $\varepsilon_R = 0.03372$, $l_R = 51.686$ mm

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x:
#### Is the reloading elastic?

Extension: reloading to the previous maximum
The idealisation used here is not stated on the slides: a specimen unloaded from B climbs back along the unloading line PB elastically and yields again only when the stress reaches the previous maximum, 353.7 MPa. The slides only say that cold work raises the yield strength [Session 12, Slide 5].

With that idealisation, the reloading is elastic if the new stress stays below 353.7 MPa. The new stress is

$$\sigma_R = \frac{F_R}{A_0} = \frac{30\times10^{3}\ \text{N}}{1.131\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2} = 265.3\ \text{MPa} < 353.7\ \text{MPa}$$

so the specimen is elastic on the line PB (point R of the figure), even though 265.3 MPa is close to the original $\sigma_y = 275$ MPa.

#### Strain and length at R

The strain at R is the permanent strain plus the elastic strain of Hooke's law for $\sigma_R$:

$$\varepsilon_R = \varepsilon_p + \frac{\sigma_R}{E} = 0.02987 + \frac{265.3\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}}{69\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}} = 0.02987 + 3.844\times10^{-3} = 0.03372$$

$$l_R = l_0\,(1 + \varepsilon_R) = 50.0\ \text{mm}\times 1.03372 = 51.686\ \text{mm}$$

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded
chunks.x:
- The elastic recovery, 0.256 mm, is only about 1/7 of the total elongation of 1.750 mm: in a ductile metal loaded well past yield most of the strain is permanent.
- Control cases: had the load stayed below $\sigma_y$, $\varepsilon_p = 0$ and the specimen would return to 50.0 mm; at R, setting $F_R = 0$ gives back $l_P$, and $F_R = 40$ kN gives back $l_B$, because $\varepsilon_p + \sigma_B/E = 0.035$.
- SI check: $\sigma/E$ is Pa/Pa, dimensionless, and it adds to $\varepsilon_p$, also dimensionless; $l = l_0(1+\varepsilon)$ is in metres.
- Common mistake: recovering $\sigma_y/E$ instead of $\sigma_B/E$ on unloading (that gives 51.551 mm), or computing the length under load with Hooke's law in the plastic zone.

chunks.t: Aluminium alloy specimen loaded beyond yield and unloaded

chunks.h: Bank P20 — Minimum diameter of a titanium hanger rod
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the finals of June 2015 (question 3) and January 2015 (question 8). Method: Session 11, Slides 9, 12, 29 and 35. Every result is recomputed by tools/materials_bank/verify_mt2.py.

chunks.t: Minimum diameter of a titanium hanger rod
chunks.x: In an engine test cell, a mass of 2400 kg hangs from a solid cylindrical rod of a titanium alloy, 1.20 m long. The alloy has $E = 107$ GPa and $\sigma_y = 880$ MPa, and the design uses a safety factor $N = 2.5$. Take $g = 9.81$ m/s².

chunks.t: Minimum diameter of a titanium hanger rod
chunks.x:
#### Data

| Quantity | Symbol | Value given | In SI |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Hanging mass | $m$ | 2400 kg | 2400 kg |
| Rod length | $l_0$ | 1.20 m | 1.20 m $= 1200$ mm |
| Young's modulus | $E$ | 107 GPa | $107\times10^{9}$ Pa |
| Yield strength | $\sigma_y$ | 880 MPa | $880\times10^{6}$ Pa |
| Safety factor | $N$ | 2.5 | dimensionless |
| Gravity | $g$ | 9.81 m/s² | 9.81 m/s² |

#### Model

- Weight of the mass $F = m\,g$ (it is the axial force on the rod at rest).
- Engineering stress $\sigma = F/A_0$ and strain $\varepsilon = \Delta l/l_0$ [Session 11, Slide 9].
- Working stress $\sigma_w = \sigma_y/N$ [Session 11, Slide 29].
- Hooke's law $\sigma = E\,\varepsilon$ [Session 11, Slide 12].
- Modulus of resilience $U_r = \int_0^{\varepsilon_y}\sigma\,d\varepsilon$ [Session 11, Slide 35].
- Hypotheses: uniform uniaxial stress; the weight of the rod is neglected against 2400 kg; linear elastic behaviour up to $\sigma_y$.

chunks.t: Minimum diameter of a titanium hanger rod
chunks.x:
#### Load on the rod

The rod holds the mass at rest, so the axial force is its weight:

$$F = m\,g = 2400\ \text{kg}\times 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 = 23\,544\ \text{N}$$

#### Largest stress allowed

The design keeps the stress at or below the working stress [Session 11, Slide 29]:

$$\sigma_w = \frac{\sigma_y}{N} = \frac{880\ \text{MPa}}{2.5} = 352\ \text{MPa} = 352\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}$$

#### Minimum area and diameter

The condition is $\sigma = F/A_0 \le \sigma_w$. Multiplying both sides by $A_0$ and dividing by $\sigma_w$ isolates the area:

$$A_0 \ge \frac{F}{\sigma_w} = \frac{23\,544\ \text{N}}{352\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}} = 6.689\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2$$

From $A_0 = \pi d_0^2/4$: multiply by 4, divide by $\pi$ and take the square root:

$$d_{\min} = \sqrt{\frac{4A_{\min}}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{4\times 6.689\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2}{\pi}} = \sqrt{8.516\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2} = 9.228\times10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 9.23\ \text{mm}$$

chunks.t: Minimum diameter of a titanium hanger rod
chunks.x:
- $A_0 = 7.854\times10^{-5}$ m², $\sigma = 299.8$ MPa
- $N_{\text{real}} = 2.94$
- $\varepsilon = 2.802\times10^{-3}$, $\Delta l = 3.36$ mm

chunks.t: Minimum diameter of a titanium hanger rod
chunks.x:
#### Stress with the 10 mm rod

$$A_0 = \frac{\pi\,(10\times10^{-3}\ \text{m})^2}{4} = 7.854\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2 \qquad \sigma = \frac{F}{A_0} = \frac{23\,544\ \text{N}}{7.854\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2} = 299.8\ \text{MPa}$$

#### Real safety factor

From $\sigma_w = \sigma_y/N$ with the working stress equal to the actual stress, isolating $N$:

$$N_{\text{real}} = \frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma} = \frac{880\ \text{MPa}}{299.8\ \text{MPa}} = 2.94 \ge 2.5$$

#### Elongation

The rod is elastic ($\sigma < \sigma_y$), so Hooke's law gives the strain [Session 11, Slide 12], and $\Delta l = \varepsilon\,l_0$ the elongation:

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E} = \frac{299.8\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}}{107\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}} = 2.802\times10^{-3} \qquad \Delta l = 2.802\times10^{-3}\times 1200\ \text{mm} = 3.36\ \text{mm}$$

chunks.t: Minimum diameter of a titanium hanger rod
chunks.x:
#### Definition and upper limit

The modulus of resilience is the elastic energy per unit volume stored up to the yield point, the area under the curve from 0 to $\varepsilon_y$ [Session 11, Slide 35]. The upper limit follows from Hooke's law at the yield point, $\sigma_y = E\,\varepsilon_y$, divided by $E$:

$$\varepsilon_y = \frac{\sigma_y}{E} = \frac{880\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa}}{107\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}} = 8.224\times10^{-3}$$

#### Integrate with Barrow's rule

In the elastic range $\sigma = E\,\varepsilon$ with $E$ constant, so $E$ leaves the integral. The antiderivative of $\varepsilon$ is $\varepsilon^2/2$, and Barrow's rule substitutes the limits:

$$U_r = \int_0^{\varepsilon_y}\sigma\,d\varepsilon = \int_0^{\varepsilon_y}E\,\varepsilon\,d\varepsilon = E\left[\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\right]_0^{\varepsilon_y} = E\left(\frac{\varepsilon_y^2}{2} - \frac{0^2}{2}\right) = \frac{E\,\varepsilon_y^2}{2}$$

Replacing $\varepsilon_y = \sigma_y/E$:

$$U_r = \frac{E}{2}\,\frac{\sigma_y^2}{E^2} = \frac{\sigma_y^2}{2E}$$

#### Value

$$U_r = \frac{(880\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa})^2}{2\times 107\times10^{9}\ \text{Pa}} = \frac{7.744\times10^{17}\ \text{Pa}^2}{2.14\times10^{11}\ \text{Pa}} = 3.619\times10^{6}\ \text{J/m}^3 = 3.619\ \text{MPa}$$

chunks.t: Minimum diameter of a titanium hanger rod
chunks.x:
- Rounding the diameter up from 9.23 mm to 10 mm raises the safety factor from 2.5 to 2.94: the area grows with the square of the diameter, $(10/9.228)^2 = 1.174$.
- Control case: with $N = 1$ the minimum diameter would be $9.228\sqrt{1/2.5} = 5.84$ mm, the rod that just reaches yield; the diameter scales as $\sqrt{N}$.
- The resilience 3.62 MJ/m³ is high because $\sigma_y$ is high and $E$ moderate, the property Slide 35 asks of spring alloys. At the working load each cubic metre of the 10 mm rod stores only $\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma\varepsilon = 0.420$ MJ/m³, about 1/8.6 of $U_r$, since the energy goes with $\sigma^2$.
- SI check: $F/\sigma_w$ in N/Pa = m²; $\sigma_y^2/E$ in Pa²/Pa = Pa = N/m² = J/m³, an energy per volume.
- Common mistake: using the mass in kg as the force (forgetting $g$), or the yield strength in place of the working stress, which gives 5.84 mm and no margin.
