Session 13, Slide 29: $\sigma = \sigma_0\exp(-E_g/2kT)$, so $\sigma_2/\sigma_1 = \exp\left[\frac{E_g}{2k}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)\right] = \exp\left[\frac{1.11}{2\cdot8.62\times10^{-5}}\cdot0.00050\right] = \exp(3.22) = 25.0$.

- a) The ratio was inverted: $\sigma(400)/\sigma(500) = 0.0400$.
- b) The exponent was reported and the exponential was not evaluated: $\ln(\sigma_2/\sigma_1) = 3.22$.
- d) The factor 2 of $2kT$ was dropped: $\sigma\propto\exp(-E_g/kT)$ gives $\exp(6.44) = 625$.

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.h: Q56.3 Wavelength that crosses the gap
chunks.x:
- id: B56-Q3
- concept_id: u6-photon-gap-calc
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 1240/1.5

A material for photovoltaic cells has $E_g = 1.5$ eV. Taking $hc = 1240$ eV·nm, determine the longest wavelength of light that can excite an electron across its band gap:

a) 413 nm
b) 827 nm
c) 1650 nm
d) 1860 nm

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 46: a photon excites an electron from the valence to the conduction band only if $hc/\lambda \ge E_g$, so $\lambda_{max} = hc/E_g = 1240/1.5 = 827$ nm (near infrared). The value $hc = 1240$ eV·nm is a constant given in the statement (**extension**: it is not in the slides); the gap of 1.5 eV is the one of the slide for solar light.

- a) The photon energy was set to twice the gap: $1240/(2\cdot1.5) = 413$ nm.
- c) Half of the gap was used, as in the factor $E_g/2$ of $\exp(-E_g/2kT)$: $1240/0.75 = 1653$ nm, rounded to 1650 nm.
- d) The two numbers were multiplied instead of divided: $1240\cdot1.5 = 1860$ nm.

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.h: Q56.4 Two semiconductors with the same donors
chunks.x:
- id: B56-Q4
- concept_id: u6-gap-from-curves
- format: diagram-reading
- asks: figure-reading

From the shown plot of $\ln\sigma$ against $1/T$ for two n-type semiconductors A and B with the same donor concentration, indicate which one has the larger band gap and why:

a) A, as its intrinsic range starts at a higher temperature with a steeper slope
b) B, as its intrinsic range starts at a lower temperature with a smaller slope
c) Both equal, as their flat ranges are at the same height
d) B, as its intrinsic slope is less steep, being $-2k/E_g$

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 43: the slope of the intrinsic range is $-E_g/2k$, so the steeper line (A) has the larger gap, and a larger gap makes the electrons cross it only at a higher temperature (smaller $1/T$), which is where A leaves the flat exhaustion range.

- b) The two features of the figure were read right but the conclusion was inverted: a smaller slope and a lower onset temperature belong to the smaller gap.
- c) The height of the flat range is set by the donor concentration, which is the same; the band gap is read from the intrinsic range.
- d) The slope was taken as $-2k/E_g$: it is $-E_g/2k$, proportional to the gap.

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.h: Q56.5 Conductivity in the exhaustion range
chunks.x:
- id: B56-Q5
- concept_id: u6-exhaustion-mobility
- format: cause-effect
- asks: cause

In the exhaustion range of an n-type semiconductor, the conductivity decreases slightly with temperature because:

a) Electrons return to the donor level as the temperature rises
b) The carrier number is constant while the thermal disorder lowers the mobility
c) Holes generated across the gap cancel part of the electron current
d) Donor atoms leave the lattice and so the carrier number falls

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 44: at moderate to high temperature all the donors are already ionised, so the number of carriers stays constant while the disordering effect of temperature lowers the mobility; with $\sigma = n|q_e|\mu_e$, $\sigma$ decreases slightly.

- a) The freeze-out behaviour of low temperatures was applied: the electrons leave the donors as $T$ rises, they do not return to them.
- c) Holes created across the gap add to $\sigma$ (intrinsic range); they do not cancel the electron current.
- d) The impurity atoms stay in the lattice, so the number of ionised donors cannot fall.

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.h: Q56.6 First semiconductor to become intrinsic
chunks.x:
- id: B56-Q6
- concept_id: u6-intrinsic-onset-gap
- format: identify
- asks: comparison

Four n-type samples have the same donor concentration. From the band gaps of the table, indicate which one starts to behave as an intrinsic semiconductor at the lowest temperature:

| Material | $E_g$ (eV) |
| :--- | :--- |
| Si | 1.11 |
| Ge | 0.67 |
| GaAs | 1.42 |
| InSb | 0.17 |

a) Germanium
b) Silicon
c) Gallium arsenide
d) Indium antimonide

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slides 33 and 43: the intrinsic range starts when the electrons excited across the gap, $\propto\exp(-E_g/2kT)$, outnumber those of the donors; the smaller the gap, the lower the temperature at which this happens. InSb has the smallest gap (0.17 eV).

- a) Germanium has the second smallest gap (0.67 eV), not the smallest.
- b) Silicon, the best-known elemental semiconductor, has a larger gap (1.11 eV) than Ge and InSb.
- c) The largest gap was chosen, which gives the highest onset temperature, not the lowest.

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
- id: B56-Q7
- concept_id: u6-pn-junction-pairs
- format: identify
- asks: application

Which one of the following pairs of doped crystals, when joined, forms a p-n junction?

a) Silicon with boron and silicon with phosphorus
b) Germanium with antimony and germanium with arsenic
c) Silicon with aluminium and silicon with indium
d) Silicon with phosphorus and pure silicon

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slides 36, 37 and 45: a p-n junction is the interface between p-type and n-type material. Boron (group IIIA) gives p-type silicon and phosphorus (group VA) gives n-type silicon.

- b) Antimony and arsenic are both group VA donors, so both crystals are n-type.
- c) Aluminium and indium are both group IIIA acceptors, so both crystals are p-type.
- d) Pure silicon is intrinsic, not p-type, so the interface is between an n-type and an intrinsic crystal.

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.h: Q56.8 LED materials with a larger gap than GaP
chunks.x:
- id: B56-Q8
- concept_id: u6-led-gap-comparison
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: classification

Among the LED materials of the slide, the two whose band gap is larger than that of the green GaP are:

a) AlGaAs and ZnSe
b) AlGaAs and diamond
c) SiC and diamond
d) AlGaAs and SiC

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 47: the band gap increases down the list, and the emitted wavelength falls with it: AlGaAs (red and infrared) lies above GaP (green), while SiC (blue) and diamond (ultraviolet) lie below, so both have a larger gap.

- a) AlGaAs has the smaller gap (red and infrared) and ZnSe the larger one; one of the two is wrong.
- b) AlGaAs emits red and infrared light, which needs a gap smaller than that of GaP.
- d) SiC is right, but AlGaAs again has the smaller gap.

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.h: Q56.9 Resistance of a germanium thermistor
chunks.x:
- id: B56-Q9
- concept_id: u6-thermistor-resistance
- format: cause-effect
- asks: effect

With an increase in temperature, the electrical resistance of a thermistor made of intrinsic germanium:

a) Rises, as the mobility of the carriers falls
b) Rises, as the number of carriers falls
c) Falls, as the mobility of the carriers rises
d) Falls, as more electron-hole pairs are generated

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slides 29 and 48: in an intrinsic semiconductor $n = p = n_i \propto \exp(-E_g/2kT)$ grows with $T$ and this effect masks the loss of mobility, so $\sigma$ rises by orders of magnitude (chart of Slide 48) and the resistance falls. This large change is what a thermistor uses.

- a) The behaviour of a metal was applied: there the mobility falls and the conductivity decreases slightly (aluminium in the chart).
- b) The trend of the carrier number was inverted: it increases with temperature.
- c) Right trend with a wrong cause: the thermal disorder lowers the mobility, it does not raise it.

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
- id: B56-Q10
- concept_id: u6-transistor-function
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: definition

Which one of the following semiconductor devices can be used to amplify electrical signals?

a) The light emitting diode
b) The thermistor
c) The photovoltaic cell
d) The transistor

chunks.t: Extrinsic conductivity against temperature and devices
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 49: a transistor is a semiconductor device that can be used to amplify electrical signals.

- a) The LED emits monochromatic light when it is directly polarised (Slide 47).
- b) The thermistor uses the change of conductivity with temperature (Slide 48).
- c) The photovoltaic cell uses the excitation of electrons by light of energy near $E_g$ (Slide 46).

chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten test questions written for the bank in the style of Part I of Assessment Test II (four options, one right answer; +0.5 right, -0.15 wrong). Content: Session 13, Slides 51-60.

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.h: Q57.1 Dipole moment of a pair of charges
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q1
- concept_id: u6-dipole-moment-charge-distance
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 3.2e-19*0.12e-9

A dipole is formed by two charges, $+q$ and $-q$ with $q = 3.2\times10^{-19}$ C, separated by a distance of 0.12 nm. Determine its dipole moment:

a) $1.92\times10^{-29}$ C·m
b) $3.84\times10^{-29}$ C·m
c) $7.68\times10^{-29}$ C·m
d) $3.84\times10^{-30}$ C·m

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 51: the dipole moment is $p = q\cdot d$, with $q$ the dipole charge and $d$ the separation between its positive and negative ends: $p = 3.2\times10^{-19}\cdot0.12\times10^{-9} = 3.84\times10^{-29}$ C·m.

- a) The charge of a single electron, $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, was used instead of the stated $q$: $1.6\times10^{-19}\cdot0.12\times10^{-9} = 1.92\times10^{-29}$.
- c) The two charges were added, $2q\cdot d$: in $p = q\,d$ the charge $q$ is the magnitude of one end of the dipole.
- d) The nanometre was converted as $10^{-10}$ m (an ångström): the separation is ten times too small.

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.h: Q57.2 Capacitor of circular plates with a PET film
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q2
- concept_id: u6-capacitor-circular-plates
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 3.2*8.85e-12*3.141592653589793*0.015**2/0.2e-3*1e12

A capacitor has two circular plates of 3.0 cm diameter separated by a PET film 0.20 mm thick ($\varepsilon_r = 3.2$, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m). Determine its capacitance:

a) 31.3 pF
b) 0.100 pF
c) 400 pF
d) 100 pF

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slides 52 and 57: $C = \varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0 A/d$ with $A = \pi(D/2)^2 = \pi(0.015)^2 = 7.07\times10^{-4}$ m² and $d = 0.20\times10^{-3}$ m: $C = 3.2\cdot8.85\times10^{-12}\cdot7.07\times10^{-4}/0.20\times10^{-3} = 1.00\times10^{-10}$ F $= 100$ pF.

- a) The dielectric constant was left out: $C_0 = \varepsilon_0 A/d = 31.3$ pF is the value with vacuum between the plates.
- b) The separation was left in mm ($d = 0.20$ taken as metres): the result is $10^{3}$ times too small.
- c) The diameter was used as the radius, $A = \pi D^2$: the area is four times too large.

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.h: Q57.3 Capacitance ratio from the permittivity table
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q3
- concept_id: u6-permittivity-table-ratio
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 700/6.0

The table gives the relative permittivity of several materials:

| Material | $\varepsilon_r$ |
| --- | --- |
| BaTiO₃ | 4000 |
| KNbO₃ | 700 |
| Rochelle salt | 170 |
| Al₂O₃ | 10 |
| Porcelain | 6.0 |
| PET | 3.2 |

Two capacitors have identical plates and separation, one filled with KNbO₃ and the other with porcelain. Determine the ratio $C_{KNbO_3}/C_{porcelain}$:

a) 117
b) 28.3
c) 667
d) 1.67

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slides 52 and 57: with the same $A$ and $d$, $C = \varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0 A/d$ is proportional to $\varepsilon_r$, so $C_{KNbO_3}/C_{porcelain} = 700/6.0 = 117$.

- b) The value of Rochelle salt was used in place of KNbO₃: $170/6.0 = 28.3$.
- c) The value of BaTiO₃, the first row of the table, was used: $4000/6.0 = 667$.
- d) The value of Al₂O₃ was used for the porcelain-to-KNbO₃ pair: $10/6.0 = 1.67$.

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.h: Q57.4 Plate area needed for the same capacitance
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q4
- concept_id: u6-permittivity-plate-area-order
- format: ordering
- asks: comparison

Three capacitors must have the same capacitance and the same plate separation, using PET, Rochelle salt or Al₂O₃ as dielectric ($\varepsilon_r$ = 3.2, 170 and 10, respectively). Ranked from the smallest to the largest plate area required, they are:

a) PET, Al₂O₃, Rochelle salt
b) Al₂O₃, Rochelle salt, PET
c) Rochelle salt, Al₂O₃, PET
d) Rochelle salt, PET, Al₂O₃

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slides 52 and 57: from $C = \varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0 A/d$, a fixed $C$ and $d$ give $A = Cd/(\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0)$, so the area is inversely proportional to $\varepsilon_r$: the largest $\varepsilon_r$ (Rochelle salt, 170) needs the smallest area and the smallest (PET, 3.2) the largest.

- a) The order was inverted: it ranks by increasing $\varepsilon_r$, which is the order of increasing capacitance, not of increasing area required.
- b) The first two were swapped: Al₂O₃ ($\varepsilon_r = 10$) cannot need less area than Rochelle salt (170).
- d) The last two were swapped: PET ($\varepsilon_r = 3.2$) needs more area than Al₂O₃ (10).

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q5
- concept_id: u6-insulator-against-dielectric
- format: true-statement
- asks: comparison

Which one of the following statements correctly contrasts an electrical insulator with a dielectric for capacitors?

a) The insulator needs a low permittivity, the dielectric needs intense dipoles that line up easily
b) The insulator needs a high permittivity, the dielectric needs intense dipoles that line up easily
c) The insulator needs a low permittivity, the dielectric needs a low permittivity too
d) The insulator needs intense dipoles that line up easily, the dielectric needs a high resistivity

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slides 52 and 54: an insulator separates conductors and should have a low permittivity, to avoid polarisation; a dielectric between the plates of a capacitor increases its capacitance and needs intense dipoles that line up easily with the electric field.

- b) The requirement of the capacitor was attributed to the insulator: a high permittivity means a strong polarisation, which an insulator must avoid.
- c) The dielectric was treated as an insulator: a low permittivity would give a capacitor with hardly any extra capacitance.
- d) The roles were swapped: easily aligned dipoles characterise the dielectric, and a high resistivity (to avoid current leaks) is a requirement of the insulator.

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.h: Q57.6 Maximum voltage across an insulating sheet
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q6
- concept_id: u6-dielectric-strength-voltage
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 14*2.4

An insulating sheet 2.4 mm thick has a dielectric strength of 14 kV/mm. Determine the maximum voltage it can hold across its thickness without electrical breakdown:

a) 0.171 kV
b) 16.4 kV
c) 33.6 kV
d) 5.83 kV

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 53: $E_{break} = U_{break}/d$, so $U_{break} = E_{break}\,d = 14\ \text{kV/mm}\cdot2.4\ \text{mm} = 33.6$ kV.

- a) The ratio was inverted, $d/E_{break} = 2.4/14$: the units of the result would not be kV.
- b) The strength and the thickness were added, $14 + 2.4 = 16.4$, instead of multiplied.
- d) The strength was divided by the thickness, $E_{break}/d = 14/2.4$, instead of multiplied by it.

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.h: Q57.7 Changes that do not raise the dielectric loss
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q7
- concept_id: u6-loss-factor-factors
- format: false-statement
- asks: cause

A capacitor works in an alternating current circuit. Which one of the following changes will NOT increase the electrical energy lost as heat in its dielectric?

a) Operating the capacitor at a higher temperature
b) Letting the dielectric absorb moisture
c) Raising the frequency of the current
d) Lowering the frequency of the current

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 53: the loss factor $\tan\delta$, the electrical energy lost as heat by friction among dipoles that try to reorient, increases with moisture, temperature and the frequency of the current; lowering the frequency therefore does not raise it.

- a) Temperature is one of the three factors listed on the slide: the loss factor rises with it.
- b) Moisture is also listed: a wet dielectric loses more energy, not less.
- c) A higher frequency makes the dipoles try to reorient more often, so the friction losses increase.

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q8
- concept_id: u6-ferroelectric-loop-area-energy
- format: diagram-reading
- asks: figure-reading

The shown polarisation against electric field loops belong to two ferroelectrics with the same remanent polarisation. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

a) Material 2 needs more energy to reorient its dipoles, as its loop is narrower
b) Material 1 needs more energy to reorient its dipoles, as its loop encloses more area
c) Material 1 has the larger remanent polarisation, as its loop is wider
d) Both need the same energy to reorient their dipoles, as they share the same remanent polarisation

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 56: the area under the hysteresis curve is related to the energy required to change the orientation of the dipoles; loop 1 is much wider and encloses a larger area than loop 2, so material 1 needs more energy per cycle.

- a) The reading of the width was inverted: a narrow loop encloses a small area and a small energy.
- c) Both loops cross the polarisation axis at the same height, so the remanent polarisation is equal; the width of the loop measures the coercive field, not $P_r$.
- d) The energy depends on the whole area of the loop, which differs, not on the remanent polarisation alone.

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.h: Q57.9 Barium titanate on both sides of the Curie temperature
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q9
- concept_id: u6-curie-temperature-barium-titanate
- format: true-statement
- asks: application

Two BaTiO₃ samples, one at 80 °C and the other at 150 °C, are examined. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

a) The 80 °C sample is cubic and unpolarised, and the 150 °C sample is tetragonal and polarised
b) The 80 °C sample is tetragonal and polarised, and the 150 °C sample is cubic and unpolarised
c) The 80 °C sample is tetragonal and polarised, and the 150 °C sample is tetragonal and unpolarised
d) Both are ferroelectric, as the Curie temperatures of ferroelectrics lie between $-200$ and 640 °C

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slide 56: BaTiO₃ has $T_c = 120$ °C; under 120 °C its structure is tetragonal and it keeps permanent dipoles, and above 120 °C it is cubic, the permanent dipoles disappear and the material becomes a common dielectric.

- a) The two structures were swapped between the temperatures: the tetragonal, polarised form belongs to the lower one.
- c) The loss of the dipoles was kept but not the change of structure: above 120 °C the crystal becomes cubic.
- d) The typical range of Curie temperatures of ferroelectrics ($-200$ to 640 °C) was read as a condition for being ferroelectric: each material has its own $T_c$, 120 °C for BaTiO₃, and above it the sample is no longer ferroelectric.

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.h: Q57.10 Devices that use the reverse piezoelectric effect
chunks.x:
- id: B57-Q10
- concept_id: u6-piezoelectric-reverse-devices
- format: identify
- asks: classification

In which pair are both devices based on the reverse piezoelectric effect, an electric field that changes the dimensions of the material?

a) A lighter and a microphone
b) A microphone and a hydrophone
c) A speaker transducer and an inkjet printer
d) A speaker transducer and a hydrophone

chunks.t: Dielectrics, ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics applied
chunks.x:
Session 13, Slides 58-60: in the reverse effect an external electric field alters the dipoles and deforms the crystal structure, giving a dimensional change; the transducer of a speaker (voltage to motion) and the actuator of an inkjet printer (voltage pulse to a change of volume) work this way.

- a) Both devices turn a mechanical action into an electric signal (a shock gives a spark, sound pressure gives a voltage): the direct effect.
- b) Microphones and hydrophones sense pressure waves and generate a voltage from the stress: the direct effect, although both appear in the same list of Slide 60.
- d) The speaker is right but the hydrophone was taken as an emitter: it detects the pressure of sound in water, a direct effect.

Practice item, not an official exercise
Ten test questions written for the bank in the style of Part I of Assessment Test II (four options, one right answer; +0.5 right, -0.15 wrong). Content: Session 15, Slides 3-13.

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.1 Moment of a mole of chromium atoms
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q1
- concept_id: u7-moment-per-mole-3d-table
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 5*9.27e-24*6.022e23

The table gives the net magnetic moment of an atom of some 3d elements:

| Element | Sc | Ti | V | Cr | Mn | Fe | Co | Ni | Cu |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Moment ($\mu_B$) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 0 |

Determine the total moment of one mole of chromium atoms with all their moments aligned, with $\mu_B = 9.27\times10^{-24}$ A·m² and $N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}$ atoms/mol:

a) 16.7 A·m²
b) $4.64\times10^{-23}$ A·m²
c) 27.9 A·m²
d) 22.3 A·m²

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slide 3: the moment of the atom is the sum of its electron moments, 5 $\mu_B$ for Cr, so the mole gives $5\cdot9.27\times10^{-24}\cdot6.022\times10^{23} = 27.9$ A·m².

- a) The row of Co (3 $\mu_B$) was read instead of that of Cr: $3\cdot9.27\times10^{-24}\cdot6.022\times10^{23} = 16.7$.
- b) The moment of a single atom, $5\mu_B$, was given: the number of atoms in the mole was not applied.
- d) The row of Fe (4 $\mu_B$) was read instead of that of Cr: $4\cdot9.27\times10^{-24}\cdot6.022\times10^{23} = 22.3$.

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.2 Why iron has less moment than manganese
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q2
- concept_id: u7-iron-manganese-moment-pairing
- format: complete-sentence
- asks: cause

An Fe atom has one 3d electron more than a Mn atom, but its moment is 4 $\mu_B$ against 5 $\mu_B$ for Mn, because the sixth 3d electron:

a) takes the spin opposite to the other five, which cancels one moment
b) has no spin moment, which reduces the five moments of Mn by one
c) moves into the 4s shell, which removes one of the 3d moments
d) raises the orbital moment, which opposes the spin moments

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slide 3: the moment of an atom is the sum of the moments of its electrons; the five 3d orbitals of Mn hold five parallel spins (5 $\mu_B$), and the sixth electron of Fe must pair with one of them with the opposite spin, so one moment is cancelled and $5 - 1 = 4$ $\mu_B$ remain.

- b) A paired electron was treated as spinless: every electron carries a spin moment $\pm\mu_B$, and this one has the opposite sign.
- c) The sixth electron stays in the 3d shell, as the table of the slide shows; a move to 4s would not cancel an existing moment.
- d) The orbital contribution was invoked: the moments of the table come from the spin of the 3d electrons, and the pairing of spins is what lowers the sum.

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.3 Induction in a material with a given susceptibility
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q3
- concept_id: u7-induction-from-susceptibility
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 1.257e-6*(1+4.0)*1.2e3*1e3

A material has a magnetic susceptibility $\chi_m = 4.0$ and is placed in a field $H = 1.2\times10^{3}$ A/m. Determine the induction $B$ inside it, with $\mu_0 = 1.257\times10^{-6}$ H/m:

a) 6.03 mT
b) 7.54 mT
c) 1.51 mT
d) $-4.53$ mT

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slide 4: $M = \chi_m H$ and $B = \mu_0 H + \mu_0 M = \mu_0(1+\chi_m)H = \mu_r\mu_0 H$, with $\mu_r = 1+\chi_m = 5.0$: $B = 1.257\times10^{-6}\cdot5.0\cdot1.2\times10^{3} = 7.54\times10^{-3}$ T.

- a) The relative permeability was taken equal to the susceptibility, $\mu_r = \chi_m = 4.0$.
- c) The contribution of the magnetization was left out: $\mu_0 H = 1.51$ mT is the induction in vacuum.
- d) A sign slip, $\mu_r = 1-\chi_m = -3.0$: with $\chi_m > 0$ the material strengthens the field, so $B > \mu_0 H$.

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.4 Classifying three materials from their susceptibility
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q4
- concept_id: u7-classify-by-susceptibility-table
- format: diagram-reading
- asks: classification

Three materials have the susceptibilities $\chi_m$ shown:

| Material | A | B | C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\chi_m$ | $+3.0\times10^{-4}$ | $+5.0\times10^{5}$ | $-1.2\times10^{-5}$ |

Which option classifies A, B and C, in that order?

a) Paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, paramagnetic
b) Diamagnetic, ferromagnetic, paramagnetic
c) Paramagnetic, paramagnetic, diamagnetic
d) Paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, diamagnetic

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slides 5, 6, 8 and 9: a paramagnetic material has $10^{-5} \le \chi_m < 10^{-2}$ (A), a ferromagnetic one has a very large $\chi_m$, up to $10^{6}$ (B), and a diamagnetic one has $\chi_m < 0$ (C).

- a) Only the size of $|\chi_m|$ was used for C ($1.2\times10^{-5}$ is of paramagnetic size): its negative sign makes it diamagnetic.
- b) The meaning of the sign was inverted: a small positive $\chi_m$ is paramagnetic and a negative one diamagnetic.
- c) Every positive susceptibility was called paramagnetic: B, with $\chi_m$ up to $10^{6}$, is ferromagnetic.

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.5 Diamagnetic material on a B against mu0 H plot
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q5
- concept_id: u7-induction-line-types
- format: diagram-reading
- asks: figure-reading

In the schematic plot of the induction $B$ against $\mu_0H$, the dashed line is the induction in vacuum. Which line corresponds to a diamagnetic material?

a) Line 1
b) Line 2
c) Line 3
d) The dashed line

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slides 6 and 8: for a diamagnetic material $B < B_0 = \mu_0H$ ($\mu_r < 1$, $\chi_m < 0$), so its line lies below the dashed vacuum line: line 2. Line 1 ($B > B_0$) is a paramagnetic material and line 3, with a much larger slope, a ferromagnetic one.

- a) The trend was inverted: line 1 lies above the vacuum line, which is the paramagnetic behaviour ($B > \mu_0H$).
- c) The strongest response was read as diamagnetic: line 3 has $B \gg \mu_0H$, as a ferromagnetic material.
- d) Diamagnetism was taken as no response: on the vacuum line $B = \mu_0H$ the dipoles would add nothing, whereas the induced dipoles of a diamagnet oppose the field.

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.6 Ferro-, antiferro- and ferrimagnetic examples
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q6
- concept_id: u7-examples-of-each-magnetism
- format: identify
- asks: classification

Which one of the following lists gives, in this order, a ferromagnetic, an antiferromagnetic and a ferrimagnetic material?

a) Co, MnO, a garnet M₃Fe₅O₁₂
b) Ni, a ferrite AB₂O₄, MnO
c) Al, Cr, a garnet M₃Fe₅O₁₂
d) Fe, Cu, a ferrite AB₂O₄

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slides 9-11: Fe, Ni and Co are ferromagnetic; Cr, Mn and MnO are antiferromagnetic; the ceramics ferrites (AB₂O₄), garnets (M₃Fe₅O₁₂) and AB₁₂O₁₉ are ferrimagnetic. Co, MnO and a garnet follow the asked order.

- b) The second and third materials were swapped: the ferrite is the ferrimagnetic ceramic and MnO the antiferromagnetic oxide.
- c) Aluminium was taken as ferromagnetic: it is paramagnetic (Slide 8).
- d) Copper was taken as antiferromagnetic: it is diamagnetic (Slide 6).

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.7 Types with oriented dipoles without a field
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q7
- concept_id: u7-oriented-dipoles-zero-field
- format: identify
- asks: classification

Which group lists only types of magnetism whose dipoles are oriented in the absence of an applied field?

a) Ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic and paramagnetic
b) Paramagnetic, ferrimagnetic and diamagnetic
c) Ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic
d) Antiferromagnetic, ferrimagnetic and diamagnetic

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slide 13 (summary): the dipoles are oriented in the absence of a field in ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic materials; in paramagnetic materials they are oriented only in the presence of a field, and diamagnetic materials have no permanent dipoles, only induced ones.

- a) The permanent dipoles of a paramagnet were taken as oriented: without a field they point at random (Slide 8).
- b) Paramagnetic and diamagnetic were included: neither has oriented dipoles at zero field; only the ferrimagnetic one belongs to the group.
- d) The induced dipoles of a diamagnet were counted: they exist only while a field acts (Slide 6).

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.8 Net moment of two electrons
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q8
- concept_id: u7-orbital-spin-moment-sum
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 2 + (-1) + 1 + 1

Two electrons of an atom have orbital quantum numbers $m_l = +2$ and $m_l = -1$, and both have a spin moment of $+\mu_B$. Determine the net magnetic moment of the two electrons, in Bohr magnetons:

a) 5 $\mu_B$
b) 1 $\mu_B$
c) 2 $\mu_B$
d) 3 $\mu_B$

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slide 3: the orbital moment of each electron is $m_l\mu_B$ and its spin moment $\pm\mu_B$, and the moment of the atom is the sum of those of all its electrons: $(+2) + (-1) + (+1) + (+1) = 3$ $\mu_B$.

- a) The orbital contributions were added as magnitudes, $2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5$, without the sign of $m_l = -1$.
- b) Only the orbital moments were summed, $2 - 1 = 1$: the spin moments also count.
- c) Only the spin moments were summed, $1 + 1 = 2$: the orbital moments also count.

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.9 Titanium and gold in the same field
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q9
- concept_id: u7-titanium-gold-induction
- format: true-statement
- asks: application

A titanium rod and a gold rod are placed, one after the other, in the same field $H$. Which one of the following statements compares their induction $B$ with $\mu_0H$?

a) Both rods have an induction slightly above $\mu_0H$
b) Titanium has an induction slightly below $\mu_0H$ and gold slightly above
c) Titanium has an induction slightly above $\mu_0H$ and gold slightly below
d) Both rods have an induction slightly below $\mu_0H$

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slides 6 and 8: titanium is paramagnetic ($\mu_r > 1$, $B > B_0 = \mu_0H$, a small addition) and gold is diamagnetic ($\mu_r < 1$, $B < B_0$, a small reduction).

- a) Gold was treated as paramagnetic, as if every metal strengthened the field.
- b) The two behaviours were swapped between the metals: titanium is the paramagnetic one.
- d) Titanium was treated as diamagnetic, as if every metal weakened the field.

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.h: Q58.10 Magnetization of a ferromagnet against a paramagnet
chunks.x:
- id: B58-Q10
- concept_id: u7-susceptibility-ratio-ferro-para
- format: numeric
- asks: calculation
- calc: 2.0e5/3.0e-4

In the same field $H$, a ferromagnetic material with $\chi_m = 2.0\times10^{5}$ and a paramagnetic one with $\chi_m = 3.0\times10^{-4}$ are magnetized. Determine the ratio $M_{ferro}/M_{para}$:

a) $6.67\times10^{8}$
b) $1.50\times10^{-9}$
c) $6.67\times10^{5}$
d) $6.67\times10^{9}$

chunks.t: Magnetic moments, fields and types of magnetism applied
chunks.x:
Session 15, Slides 4, 8 and 9: $M = \chi_m H$ with the same $H$, so $M_{ferro}/M_{para} = \chi_{ferro}/\chi_{para} = 2.0\times10^{5}/3.0\times10^{-4} = 6.67\times10^{8}$.

- b) The ratio was inverted, $\chi_{para}/\chi_{ferro}$.
- c) The exponent of the paramagnetic susceptibility was read as $10^{-1}$ instead of $10^{-4}$: $2.0\times10^{5}/0.30$.
- d) The exponent of the paramagnetic susceptibility was read as $10^{-5}$ instead of $10^{-4}$: $2.0\times10^{5}/3.0\times10^{-5}$.
