chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: **Central idea:** the electrical behaviour of a solid is decided by how its electrons fill the energy bands that the atoms form when they come together. A half-filled (or overlapping) band gives a **conductor**; a full valence band separated by a small gap $E_g$ from an empty conduction band gives a **semiconductor**; a large gap gives an **insulator**. In every case the conductivity is carriers times charge times mobility, $\sigma = n\,\lvert q\rvert\,\mu$, and the whole topic is about what controls $n$ (temperature, doping, band gap) and $\mu$ (collisions with vibrations, impurities and defects). Insulators that can be polarised (dielectrics, ferroelectrics, piezoelectrics) close the unit.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: This page follows the single official session of Topic 6 (Session 13) slide by slide. Slide 1 is the title and agenda (band structure and electrical properties; conducting materials, metallic and non-metallic; semiconducting materials, intrinsic and extrinsic of types n and p; insulating and dielectric materials). Slides 9, 24 and 50 repeat this agenda as section dividers. Every section names the slides it comes from. Figures that appear on the slides are copied from them as PNG crops, and each caption names its slide. The few drawings that have no figure on the slides (the conductivity scale built from the table of Slide 5, the bar of Ohm's law, the band-gap trends and the cubic BaTiO3 cell) are drawn for this page, and their captions say so. The questions printed on the slides (Q1 to Q5 and Q10) are problems 1 to 5 and 10 of the official sheet, and they are solved on the problems page of this topic.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 1. Learning objectives and classification of materials [Session 13 Slides 2, 5]
chunks.x:
The slides set three objectives [Session 13 Slide 2]:

- Know the **classification of the materials** according to their electrical and magnetic properties.
- Understand how the **structure and composition** of a material determine its response to an electric field and to a magnetic field.
- Understand the **influence of the temperature** on the electrical and magnetic properties.

Materials are classified by their electrical conductivity $\sigma$, measured in $(\Omega\cdot\text{m})^{-1}$ [Session 13 Slide 5]:

| Class | Conductivity $\sigma$ in $(\Omega\cdot\text{m})^{-1}$ | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Insulators | $10^{-20}$ to $10^{-10}$ | Polyethylene (PVC coating on the slide) |
| Semiconductors | $10^{-6}$ to $10^{4}$ | Si, Ge (microprocessors) |
| Conductors | about $10^{7}$ | Metals (copper wire) |

Counting from the smallest to the largest value of the table, the scale spans about 27 orders of magnitude (the author's count, not printed on the slide).

The reciprocal of the conductivity is the **resistivity** $\rho = 1/\sigma$, in $\Omega\cdot\text{m}$ [Session 13 Slide 13].

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 2.1 From atomic levels to bands [Session 13 Slide 3]
chunks.x: An isolated atom has discrete energy levels. When atoms come within close proximity, their orbitals interact and **each atomic level splits**: two atoms give two levels, a few atoms give a few close levels, and a large number of atoms (a solid) gives so many levels, so close in energy, that they form a **continuous energy band**. The slide plots the electron energy against the interatomic separation for an aggregate of atoms, with the core-level electrons staying almost unchanged and the outer levels broadening into bands. Between bands a **band gap** $E_g$ may remain, where no electron states exist.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 2.2 Valence band, conduction band and gap [Session 13 Slide 4]
chunks.x:
The electron energy band structure of a solid is given by its **interatomic separation**: the bands broaden as the atoms approach and the solid sits at the **equilibrium interatomic distance**, where the bands have the width and the gap shown in the figure. Two bands matter:

- **Valence band:** the outermost band occupied with electrons (the valence electrons).
- **Conduction band:** the band located immediately above the valence band.
- **Band gap** $E_g$: the energy range between them where there are no states.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
A material conducts when electrons can find **empty states just above the filled ones**, so that a small excitation (an electric field) lets them move. There are two ways [Session 13 Slide 6]:

- **A1) Half-filled valence band.** There is only one $s$ electron per atom (Na, Cu, Al in the slide's caption), so the valence band is half filled: filled states below the Fermi energy $E_f$ and empty states above it in the same band.
- **A2) Overlapping bands.** In Mg the filled $3s$ band overlaps the empty $3p$ band, so the two bands together are only partly filled.

The slide lists the electron configurations used to decide this:

| Element | Atomic number | Configuration |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| Mg | 12 | $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2$ |
| Al | 13 | $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^1$ |
| Cu | 29 | $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^{10}\,4s^1$ |

Printed configuration of aluminium
The slide's table gives aluminium as $3s^2\,3p^1$ (one electron in the $3p$ level), while its caption says that Na, Cu and Al have a half-filled band "since there is only one $s$ electron". The table is kept as printed; Na is not in the table.

For a metal, the occupancy of the electron states changes by an electron excitation as in the figure: before the excitation the states are filled up to $E_f$, and after it an electron has been promoted to an empty state just above $E_f$ [Session 13 Slide 7].

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
- In a **semiconductor** the filled valence band is separated from the empty conduction band by a relatively **narrow** gap, $E_g < 2$ eV (pure silicon: $E_g = 1.1$ eV; pure germanium: $E_g = 0.67$ eV).
- In an **insulator** the gap is relatively **large**, $E_g > 2$ eV (pure diamond: $E_g = 6$ to $7$ eV).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
The macroscopic law is Ohm's law, $I = V/R$, with $I$ the electric current (A), $V$ the potential difference (V) and $R$ the resistance ($\Omega$). The charge can be carried in two ways: by **ionic conductivity** (aqueous electrolytes, some ceramics) or by **electrical (electronic) conductivity** (metals). In a conductive metal there is a cloud of electrons around the nuclei (the positive ions).

For a bar of length $l$ and cross-section $A$ the microscopic form is $\mathbf J = \sigma\mathbf E$. Writing $E = V/l$ and $J = I/A$ in it gives $V = (l/\sigma A)\,I$, so $R = \rho\,l/A$ (derived here: the slide only writes $I = V/R$; this is the link with the geometry of the specimens of the sheet).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
When a uniform electric field $E$ is applied, the electrons accelerate. Newton's second law for one electron of charge $q_e$ ($1.6\times10^{-19}$ C) and mass $m_e$ ($9.109\times10^{-31}$ kg) is

$$F = q_e E = m_e a \quad\Rightarrow\quad a = \frac{q_e E}{m_e}$$

Printed units
The slides write the field $E$ in V/m² (and in A/m² on Slide 12). The field strength is in **V/m** (volt per metre); the units printed are typographical slips and V/m is used here.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 4.3 Collisions, drift velocity and mobility [Session 13 Slide 11]
chunks.x:
If the electrons only accelerated, the current would grow without limit. For a given $E$ the current $I$ is constant, so the speed of the electrons is constant: there are "friction forces", due to **collisions** with the ions, that counteract the acceleration. This is the origin of the **resistivity**. Between collisions the drift velocity grows linearly with time; at each collision it falls back (sawtooth of the figure), so the **average drift velocity** $v_d$ is the average speed of the electrons in the direction of the force generated by the field:

$$v_d = \frac{\tau\,\lvert q_e\rvert\,E}{m_e} = \mu\,E \qquad\text{with}\qquad \mu = \frac{\tau\,\lvert q_e\rvert}{m_e}$$

$\tau$ is the **relaxation time** (the mean time between collisions) and $\mu$ is the **electron mobility**, in m²/(V·s).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 4.4 Current density, conductivity and resistivity [Session 13 Slides 12-13]
chunks.x:
For a material with $n$ free conducting electrons per unit volume, the current density is the charge that crosses a unit area per second:

$$J = n\,\lvert q_e\rvert\,v_d = n\,\lvert q_e\rvert\,\mu\,E \qquad\text{and, since}\quad J = \sigma E:\qquad \sigma = n\,\lvert q_e\rvert\,\mu$$

In metals the carriers are the non-bonded electrons, so the conductivity depends on **the number of electrons per unit volume and on their mobility**. The resistivity is $\rho = 1/\sigma$, in $\Omega\cdot\text{m}$. The slide adds that the resistivity grows with the **disorder in the metal structure** and with the **number of collisions between the non-bonded electrons and the metallic ions** [Session 13 Slide 13].

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
The total resistivity of a metal is the sum of a thermal part and a residual part:

$$\rho_{total} = \rho_T + \rho_r$$

$\rho_T$ is the **thermal resistivity**, produced by the vibrations of the lattice, and $\rho_r$ is the **residual resistivity**, produced by impurities and defects (next section). The slide's plot of resistivity against temperature shows $\rho_r$ as a constant floor (the curve tends to it at low temperature) and $\rho_T$ as the temperature component added on top.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
The thermal resistivity grows linearly with the temperature:

$$\rho_T = \rho_0\,(1 + \alpha_T\,\Delta T)$$

$\rho_0$ is the resistivity at 0 °C (in $\Omega\cdot\text{m}$) and $\alpha_T$ is the temperature coefficient of resistivity (in ${}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$). Because $\rho_0$ is the value at 0 °C, $\Delta T$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius. The slide's table:

| Metal | Resistivity at 0 °C in $\mu\Omega\cdot\text{cm}$ | $\alpha_T$ in ${}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$ |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Aluminium | 2.7 | 0.0039 |
| Copper | 1.6 | 0.0039 |
| Gold | 2.3 | 0.0034 |
| Iron | 9 | 0.0045 |
| Silver | 1.47 | 0.0038 |

The second chart of the slide shows the effect of temperature on the resistivity of selected metals (Fe, Rb, Os, Co, Na, Ir, Rh, Mg, Au, Cu, Ag): almost straight lines above about −100 °C.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 5.3 Question 1: equal resistivity of silver and aluminium [Session 13 Slide 15]
chunks.x: Q1 asks at which temperature a silver wire has the same resistivity as an aluminium wire at 45 °C, with $\rho_0 = 1.47\times10^{-6}$ and $2.70\times10^{-6}\ \Omega\cdot\text{cm}$ and $\alpha_T = 0.0038$ and $0.0039\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$ for silver and aluminium. The slide first evaluates the aluminium resistivity with the law above, $\rho_{Al,45} = 2.7\times10^{-6}(1 + 0.0039\cdot45) = 3.173\times10^{-6}\ \Omega\cdot\text{cm}$, and then solves the law for the temperature of silver, $T = (\rho_T - \rho_{0,Ag})/(\rho_{0,Ag}\,\alpha_{T,Ag}) = 304.86\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}$. This is problem 1 of the sheet, and its page redoes the calculation with the units in SI and the unrounded intermediate value (the key of the sheet is 305 °C).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 6. Residual resistivity: impurities and defects [Session 13 Slides 16-17]
chunks.x:
The residual resistivity $\rho_r$ does not depend on temperature. It depends on [Session 13 Slide 16]:

- the **concentration and type of impurities or alloying elements** (impurity resistivity $\rho_i$), and
- the **structural imperfections** (deformation resistivity $\rho_d$): dislocations, grain boundaries and similar.

So $\rho_r = \rho_i + \rho_d$ and, with Matthiessen's rule, $\rho_{total} = \rho_T + \rho_i + \rho_d$. $\rho_r$ **increases with the degree of distortion of the metal lattice**: a foreign atom, a large one or a small one, disturbs the periodicity around it. The slide's chart shows how small additions of various elements raise the room-temperature resistivity of copper: for each element the resistivity grows linearly with the weight percent of impurity, with a slope that depends on the element (the steepest are P, Fe, Si and As; Ni, Pb and Ag are the gentlest among those plotted).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: A conduction electron moves through a **perfect crystal** without scattering. In a crystal **heated to a high temperature** the atoms vibrate and displace from their sites, and in a crystal containing **atomic-level defects** (foreign atoms, vacancies, dislocations) the periodicity is broken too. In both cases the electron is scattered, which reduces its mobility and therefore the conductivity. The chart of the slide shows copper with different nickel contents and deformed copper: the curves are parallel, separated by the constant residual terms $\rho_i$ and $\rho_d$, while the temperature component $\rho_T$ is the same.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
**All hardening methods cause, to a greater or lesser extent, a decrease of the conductivity**, [Session 13 Slide 18]. The reason, in the author's reading (not printed on the slide), is that every hardening method of Topic 5 works by putting obstacles in the way of the dislocations, and the same obstacles scatter the electrons. The slide plots yield strength and conductivity against the percent of cold work and against the percent of zinc (a solid solution):

- **Cold work:** the yield strength rises strongly, while the conductivity falls only slightly (the chart compares with the zinc case, where it falls much more).
- **Zinc in solution:** the yield strength rises moderately but the conductivity falls sharply.

Q2 on Slide 19 asks what happens to the conductivity and the tensile strength of an aluminium alloy wire when it is alloyed with copper, when its working temperature is lowered, when its grain size is increased, when intermetallic precipitates are formed and when it is cold worked, and which strategy gives the lightest wire with the same strength and conductivity. It is problem 2 of the sheet.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: A few thermoset polymers, when they are specifically manufactured, can become conductive. Their advantages against metals are **flexibility and easy formability**. The main mechanism for transmitting the charge is the movement of **delocalised electrons**: an exchange reaction of electrons between neighbouring redox sites.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
Graphene is a single layer of a hexagonal lattice formed by hexagons with an atom at each vertex (graphite is a stack of these layers). It has a huge $\pi$ cloud with delocalised electrons that can move all over the surface at a speed higher than in any other material (about $1000$ km/s). The slide compares

| Material | Conductivity in $(\Omega\cdot\text{m})^{-1}$ |
| :--- | ---: |
| Graphene | $0.96\times10^{8}$ |
| Cu | $0.60\times10^{8}$ |
| Si | $4.5\times10^{-4}$ |

Printed symbol
The slide writes these values with the symbol $\rho$, but the unit $(\Omega\cdot\text{m})^{-1}$ is the unit of conductivity, so they are $\sigma$.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
Ceramics are traditionally insulators, but some advanced ceramics are good electrical conductors. The main mechanism for transmitting the charge is

- **Electronic:** movement of electrons due to impurities with a different valence, or rare-earth elements. Uses: resistors, electrodes or heating elements.
- **Ionic:** movement of anions or cations through vacancies or interstitial voids at high temperatures. Uses: gas sensors, fuel cells or batteries. The slide shows two pictures: the movement of ions or, equivalently, the movement of vacancies, and the movement of small interstitial cations ($r_i < r_{atom}$), and a solid oxide fuel cell (anode, electrolyte with oxygen ions, cathode).

Q3 on Slide 23 compares the effect of vacancies, interstitial cations, interstitial anions, temperature, disorder of the lattice and doping with other valences on an ionic ceramic and on a metal. It is problem 3 of the sheet.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
Semiconductors are materials whose electrical conductivity is approximately midway between the values for good conductors and insulators. In the energy-band model the electronic band structure consists of a **full valence band and an empty conduction band, separated by an energy gap** $E_g < 2$ eV [Session 13 Slide 25]. The materials are mediocre conductors, but their conductivity is **easily controllable**, and this became useful in the twentieth century with the manufacture of materials of extremely high chemical and structural purity.

Two types depending on the origin of the carriers [Session 13 Slide 26]:

- **Intrinsic semiconductors:** the conductivity is determined by the inherent properties of the pure material (elemental silicon and germanium).
- **Extrinsic semiconductors:** the electrical properties are given by adding **dopants** with a number of valence electrons different from the solvent. They are generally substitutional solid solutions with low impurity concentrations (100 to 1000 ppm). The extra charge carriers are of two kinds, **type n** and **type p**.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 10.1 Excitation and the two kinds of carriers [Session 13 Slides 27-28]
chunks.x:
In an intrinsic semiconductor an electric or thermal excitation makes an electron pass from the valence band to the conduction band. This generates a **hole** in the valence band, and **both the free electron and the hole** are charge carriers. In the covalent crystal a bonding valence electron cannot move unless it receives enough energy to leave its bonding position; once a critical amount of energy has been supplied, it becomes a free conduction electron and leaves a **positively charged hole** in the lattice.

There are two types of carriers: **electrons** in the conduction band (charge $-1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, density $n_e$) and **holes** in the valence band (charge $+1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, density $n_H$). The conductivity is the sum of both contributions:

$$\sigma = n_e\,\lvert q_e\rvert\,\mu_e + n_H\,\lvert q_H\rvert\,\mu_H = n\,\lvert q_e\rvert\,(\mu_e + \mu_H) \qquad\text{since}\quad n_e = n_H = n,\ \ \lvert q_e\rvert = \lvert q_H\rvert$$

$\mu_e$ and $\mu_H$ are the mobilities of electrons and holes, and $\lvert q_e\rvert$ is the absolute value of the electron or hole charge. In an intrinsic semiconductor $\mu_e > \mu_H$ [Session 13 Slide 33].

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
For an intrinsic semiconductor **both $n$ and $p$ increase with temperature**:

$$n_i \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT}\right)$$

$k$ is Boltzmann's constant (the sheet gives $k_B = 8.62\times10^{-5}$ eV/K), $T$ the temperature in kelvin and $E_g$ the band gap; $n_i = n = p$ is the number of excited electrons (and holes) per unit volume. Since $\sigma \propto n_i$,

$$\sigma = \sigma_0\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT}\right) \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \ln\sigma = \ln\sigma_0 - \frac{E_g}{2kT}$$

Plotted as $\ln\sigma$ against $1/T$ the law is a straight line of slope $-E_g/2k$, as the slide's chart shows. Temperature also disorders the crystal and lowers the mobility, **but this effect is masked by the increase in the number of carriers** [Session 13 Slide 29]. Compare with a metal, where $n$ is fixed and only the mobility changes, so that $\sigma$ falls with temperature.

Q4 on Slide 30 asks to justify the different effect of a temperature increase on a metal and on an intrinsic semiconductor. It is problem 4 of the sheet, and problems 7 (germanium at 75 °C) and 8 (carrier concentrations of silicon) apply the formulas of this section.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
The elemental semiconductors are the pure elements of **group IVA**, silicon and germanium, bonded by **covalent bonds**. As the atom size increases, $E_g$ decreases, and the conductivity of the intrinsic semiconductor increases. The figure of the slide shows the bands of Si and Ge at $0$ K (no electrons in the conduction band, gap printed as $1.09$ eV for Si and $0.72$ eV for Ge) and at $300$ K, when a few electrons have crossed the gap. The data table of the slide:

| Property | Silicon | Germanium |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Energy gap, eV | 1.1 | 0.67 |
| Electron mobility $\mu_n$, m²/(V·s) | 0.135 | 0.39 |
| Hole mobility $\mu_p$, m²/(V·s) | 0.048 | 0.19 |
| Intrinsic carrier density $n_i$, carriers/m³ | $1.5\times10^{16}$ | $2.4\times10^{19}$ |
| Intrinsic resistivity $\rho$, $\Omega\cdot$m | 2300 | 0.46 |
| Density, g/m³ | $2.33\times10^{6}$ | $5.32\times10^{6}$ |

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
Compounds of elements of groups IIIA and VA (GaAs, InSb) and of groups IIB and VIA (CdS, ZnTe) are also intrinsic semiconductors. Going from the group-14 elemental semiconductors (purely covalent) to the 13-15 and then to the 12-16 compounds, **the covalent character decreases and the ionic character increases**: $E_g$ **increases** and, for an intrinsic semiconductor, $\sigma$ **decreases**. The slide also classifies semiconductors as simple (Si, Ge) and compound (III-V: GaAs, InP, GaN; II-VI: ZnS, ZnSe; IV-IV: SiC, SiGe).

The conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor is determined by $n$: the number of charge carriers is small, but the high chemical and structural purity favours high mobilities. The table of the slide (it prints slightly different Si and Ge mobilities from the previous one):

| Material | $E_g$ in eV | $\sigma$ in $(\Omega\cdot\text{m})^{-1}$ | $\mu_e$ in m²/(V·s) | $\mu_H$ in m²/(V·s) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Si | 1.11 | $4\times10^{-4}$ | 0.14 | 0.05 |
| Ge | 0.67 | 2.2 | 0.38 | 0.18 |
| GaP | 2.25 | n/a | 0.03 | 0.015 |
| GaAs | 1.42 | $10^{-6}$ | 0.85 | 0.04 |
| InSb | 0.17 | $2\times10^{4}$ | 7.7 | 0.07 |
| CdS | 2.40 | n/a | 0.03 | n/a |
| ZnTe | 2.26 | n/a | 0.03 | 0.01 |

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: Q10 on Slides 34 and 41 asks to order semiconductors by conductivity at the same temperature and to explain the criterion; Slide 34 poses AlP, GaAs and InSb, and Slide 41 the doped pairs (Ge with As or Sb, Si with B or In). It is problem 10 of the sheet.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
Extrinsic semiconductors are the most usual type: the dopants add charge carriers, raise the conductivity and make it possible to manufacture devices with special properties (transistors and others). Two types, depending on the doping atoms:

- **Type n:** dopant with **more valence electrons** than the host.
- **Type p:** dopant with **fewer valence electrons** than the host.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
The impurity atoms have more valence electrons than the atoms of the network, so they behave as **electron donors** (group VA: P, As, Sb; the periodic-table fragment of Slide 35 also lists N). In silicon ($4$ valence electrons) a phosphorus atom ($5$ valence electrons) uses four of them in the covalent bonds and has **one excess electron**, loosely bound to it. This electron needs only a small energy to jump into the conduction band. In band language the donor atoms create a **donor level** $E_d$ inside the gap, very close to the conduction band, so the excitation energy is $\Delta E = E_c - E_d$, small compared with $E_g$. The distance from the donor level to the conduction band determines $n_e$. The electrons in the conduction band are the **majority carriers**, $n_e \gg n_H$, and

$$\sigma \approx n_e\,\lvert q_e\rvert\,\mu_e$$

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
The impurity atoms have fewer valence electrons than the atoms of the network, so they behave as **acceptors** (B, Al, Ga and In of group IIIA; in silicon, boron has $3$ valence electrons). There is a bond with a missing electron: an **excess of holes**. The acceptor creates an **acceptor level** $E_a$ in the gap, just above the top of the valence band, so a small energy $\Delta E = E_a - E_v$ lifts an electron from the valence band into the acceptor level, leaving a hole in the valence band. The holes moving through the valence band are the majority carriers, $p \gg n$, and

$$\sigma \cong p\,\lvert q_e\rvert\,\mu_H$$

Printed group
Slide 37 writes "B, Al, Ga (group VA)", but the table printed on the same slide places B, Al, Ga and In in group 3A (IIIA); group VA is the one of the donors. The acceptors are IIIA.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 12.4 Excitation and majority and minority carriers [Session 13 Slide 38]
chunks.x:
In a donor semiconductor the excitation lifts an electron from the donor state to the conduction band, generating a free electron. In an acceptor semiconductor the excitation lifts an electron from the valence band into the acceptor level, generating a hole in the valence band. The slide ends with the table of carrier names:

| Semiconductor | Majority-carrier concentration | Minority-carrier concentration |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| n-type | $n_n$ (electrons in n-type material) | $p_n$ (holes in n-type material) |
| p-type | $p_p$ (holes in p-type material) | $n_p$ (electrons in p-type material) |

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: Q5 asks whether silicon doped with antimony, germanium doped with arsenic and silicon doped with gallium (substitutional solid solutions) are n-type or p-type and whether the impurities act as donors or acceptors. The version of the sheet changes the second case to silicon doped with arsenic. It is problem 5 of the sheet, and problem 6 (phosphorus in silicon) applies $\sigma \approx n_e\lvert q_e\rvert\mu_e$.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
The slide gives the donor and acceptor energy gaps (in electron volts) when silicon and germanium are doped, that is, the energy $E_c - E_d$ or $E_a - E_v$ that an electron needs, and the maximum solid solubility of each dopant:

| Dopant | Si: $E_d$ | Si: $E_a$ | Ge: $E_d$ | Ge: $E_a$ |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| P | 0.045 | | 0.0120 | |
| As | 0.049 | | 0.0127 | |
| Sb | 0.039 | | 0.0096 | |
| B | | 0.045 | | 0.0104 |
| Al | | 0.057 | | 0.0102 |
| Ga | | 0.065 | | 0.0108 |
| In | | 0.160 | | 0.0112 |

The arrows of the slide say that, as the ionic radius of the dopant increases, the conductivity increases for the donors (P, As, Sb: Si and Ge) and decreases for the acceptors (B, Al, Ga, In), in agreement with the table, where the acceptor energies grow with the size (B $<$ Al $<$ Ga $<$ In). The author's rule of thumb for comparing dopants (not printed on the slide) is to compare $E_d$ or $E_a$: the smaller the energy, the more carriers at a given temperature. The lower table of the slide gives the maximum solid solubility of the dopants, in atoms/m³:

chunks.x:
| Host | Dopant | Group | Maximum solubility in atoms/m³ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | ---: |

| Si | Al | IIIA | $20\times10^{24}$ |

Slide 41 repeats the same two tables with the second part of Q10: germanium with 5 ppm of As or of Sb, silicon with 10 ppm of B or of In (the slide prints the germanium pair twice).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: In extrinsic semiconductors also $\mu_e > \mu_H$ (the ratio $\mu_e/\mu_H$ is $2.81$ for Si and $2.05$ for Ge). **The distortion of the crystal structure caused by the doping is negligible, so $\sigma$ is controlled by the number of charge carriers.** The chart shows the room-temperature electron and hole mobilities of silicon against the dopant concentration: both are almost constant (about $0.13$ and $0.05$ m²/(V·s)) up to about $10^{21}$ m⁻³ and fall for high doping (electrons about $0.10$ m²/(V·s) at $10^{22}$ m⁻³ and below $0.01$ m²/(V·s) at $10^{25}$ m⁻³; read from the chart).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 14. Extrinsic semiconductors: effect of temperature [Session 13 Slides 43-44]
chunks.x:
At **low temperature** the number of ionised impurities per unit volume determines $\sigma$. As $T$ increases, the number of ionised atoms increases and so does $\sigma$: this is the **extrinsic range**, whose slope in the $\ln\sigma$ against $1/T$ plot depends on the type of semiconductor. For the n-type and p-type the slide writes

$$\sigma = \sigma_0\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_c - E_d}{2kT}\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sigma = \sigma_0\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_a - E_v}{2kT}\right)$$

so $\ln\sigma = \ln\sigma_0 - \dfrac{E_c-E_d}{2kT}$ for the n-type and the same with $E_a - E_v$ for the p-type: the slope of the line is $-(E_c-E_d)/2k$ (n-type) or $-(E_a-E_v)/2k$ (p-type).

Printed energy for the p-type
Slide 43 prints $E_a - E_c$ for the p-type. The ionisation energy of an acceptor is the distance from the acceptor level to the top of the valence band, $E_a - E_v$ (Slide 37), and that is the form used here.

Slope label of the chart
The chart on the right of Slide 43 labels the extrinsic slope as $-(E_c - E_d)/k$, without the factor 2 that the equations on the left of the same slide carry, $-(E_c - E_d)/2k$. The factor 2 is the one that follows from $\sigma \propto \exp[-(E_c - E_d)/2kT]$, and it is the one used on this page.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 14. Extrinsic semiconductors: effect of temperature [Session 13 Slides 43-44]
chunks.x: At **intermediate temperature** all the impurities have been ionised and $\sigma$ is almost constant: the **exhaustion range** for the n-type (all the donor electrons have been lost) and the **saturation range** for the p-type (all the atoms are ionised). At **high temperature** the intrinsic generation across the gap takes over, with slope $-E_g/2k$: the **intrinsic range** [Session 13 Slide 43]. Slide 44 summarises it: at low and moderate $T$ the material behaves as an extrinsic conductor and $\sigma$ is governed by the number of ionised atoms; at high $T$ the conductivity slightly decreases, because the number of carriers stays constant and the disordering effect of the temperature (lower mobility) becomes visible; at very high $T$ the material behaves as an intrinsic conductor.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
A **p-n junction** is a boundary or interface between two types of semiconductor material, p-type and n-type, inside a single crystal. It is the basis of the diode, the photovoltaic cell and the LED of the next sections (the slide links two videos, listed at the end of this page).

The slide draws the junction in three steps: the carriers on both sides, the **depletion layer** (fixed negative charge on the p side and positive on the n side, with the internal electric field) and the **band diagram** with the diffusion potential $V_{bi}$ between the two sides.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: Electrons jump from the valence to the conduction band due to **thermal excitation**, due to **intense electric fields** or due to **exposure to radiation of a given wavelength**. **Photoconductivity** is the phenomenon in which a material becomes more conductive due to the absorption of electromagnetic radiation, such as visible light, whose photon energy must be at least $E_g$. The same effect used to generate electricity gives the **photovoltaic cells**; solar light has $E_g \sim 1.5$ eV. The slide's absorption figure marks that silicon absorbs photons above $1.1$ eV, gallium arsenide above $1.43$ eV and aluminium gallium arsenide above $1.7$ eV, while photons of lower energy go through.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
A **light-emitting diode** is a semiconductor doped to create a p-n junction that emits **monochromatic light** when it is directly polarised (forward bias): electrons from the n side and holes from the p side recombine at the junction and release the energy $E_g$ as a photon. The **colour depends on the distance between the valence and the conduction band**, as in the slide's table (the band gap increases from top to bottom and the wavelength increases from bottom to top):

| Material | Radiation |
| :--- | :--- |
| AlGaAs | red and infra-red |
| GaN | green |
| GaP | green |
| ZnSe | blue |
| InGaN | blue |
| SiC | blue |
| Diamond | ultra-violet |

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: **Thermistors** are devices based on the change of the electrical conductivity of semiconductors with temperature. The chart compares aluminium, whose conductivity decreases with temperature (reducing mobility), with germanium, whose conductivity increases by several orders of magnitude between $0$ and 400 °C (increasing charge carriers).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: A **transistor** is a semiconductor device that can be used to amplify electrical signals. The slide shows the downscaling of the transistor and of its interconnects through the generations of $180$ nm (1999), $130$ nm (2001), $90$ nm (2003), $65$ nm (2005) and $45$ nm (2007), down to prototypes of $30$ nm and $20$ nm, with micrographs and a plot of the size against the year (source: Intel).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
An electrically insulating material (large $E_g$) that exhibits, or can be made to exhibit, a **dipolar structure** is a dielectric. The **dipole moment** of two charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by a distance $d$ is

$$p = q\cdot d$$

Without field the dipoles of the material are randomly oriented and the net polarisation is zero (unpolarised); an applied electric field **polarises** the material by aligning the dipoles, and opposite charges appear on the faces next to the plates.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
Highly resistive materials have two applications, depending on their response to the electric field:

- **Insulators** insulate conductors from each other and from a metal mass: high $E_g$.
- **Dielectric materials** are placed between the plates of a capacitor and increase its capacitance: intense dipoles that easily line up with the electric field.

The capacitance of two parallel plates of area $A$ separated by a distance $d$ is

$$C = \varepsilon_r\,\varepsilon_0\,\frac{A}{d} \qquad\text{and}\qquad C = \varepsilon_r\,C_0 \quad\text{with}\quad C_0 = \varepsilon_0\frac{A}{d}$$

$\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m is the permittivity of vacuum, $\varepsilon_r$ the dielectric constant (relative permittivity) and $C_0$ the capacitance with vacuum between the plates. The dielectric polarises, so the net charge at its surfaces ($-Q'$ and $+Q'$) lets the plates store more charge, $Q_0 + Q'$, for the same voltage.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 16.3 Loss factor and dielectric strength [Session 13 Slide 53]
chunks.x:
Capacitors are normally used in alternating-current circuits, so the **dipoles must realign fast** when the field changes. The **loss factor** $\tan\delta$ is the amount of electrical energy lost, as heat, by a capacitor in an alternating circuit, due to the friction among dipoles when they try to reorient. It **increases with moisture, temperature and the frequency of the current**, and these also lower the resistivity.

The **dielectric strength** is the maximum electric field that the dielectric can sustain without electrical breakdown:

$$E_{break} = \frac{U_{break}}{d}$$

$U_{break}$ is the breakdown voltage and $d$ the separation between the conductors (in mm on the slide).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.h: 16.4 What an insulator should have [Session 13 Slide 54]
chunks.x:
| Requirement | Why |
| :--- | :--- |
| High resistivity $\rho$ | to avoid current leaks |
| High dielectric strength $E_{break}$ | to avoid breakdowns of the insulation |
| Small loss factor $\tan\delta$ | (no reason printed; see the loss factor above: energy lost as heat) |
| Low permittivity $\varepsilon$ | to avoid polarisation |

| Alumina insulators | $>10^{12}$ | 250 | 9.8 | ... | 9 | ... | 0.0008-0.009 |
| Soda-lime glass | ... | ... | ... | ... | 7.2 | ... | 0.009 |
| Fused silica | ... | 8 | ... | ... | 3.8 | ... | 0.00004 |

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x: Ferroelectric materials have **permanent dipoles** that can remain aligned in the absence of an electric field: they show **spontaneous polarisation** with no external field. If a ferroelectric is slowly cooled to a temperature below the critical temperature in the presence of a strong electric field, the anions are displaced towards the positive side of the field and the cations towards the negative side, which produces a permanent electric dipole (the slide draws a perovskite cell with $\text{Ti}^{4+}$ or $\text{Zr}^{4+}$ at the centre, $\text{O}^{2-}$ at the faces and $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ at the corners, non-polarised and polarised, for $T < T_{Curie}$).

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
The electric-field hysteresis cycles are similar to those of ferromagnetic materials with the magnetic field: the polarisation $P$ (or $D$) against the field $E$ shows a saturation polarisation, a **remanent polarisation** $P_r$ that stays when the field is removed, a non-remanent part, and a coercive field $E_c$ that must be applied in the opposite direction to bring $P$ to zero. The **area under the hysteresis curve** is related to the energy required to change the orientation of the dipoles.

The **Curie temperature** $T_c$ is the temperature above which the material loses its ferroelectric properties and becomes a plain dielectric; typically $-200\,{}^{\circ}\text{C} < T_c < 640\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}$. Example: BaTiO₃ has $T_c = 120\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}$. Below 120 °C the structure is **tetragonal**; above 120 °C the crystal structure of BaTiO₃ is **cubic** and the permanent dipoles disappear.

The slide gives the dimensions of the cell, 0.403 nm for the vertical edge and 0.398 nm for the horizontal ones, and the displacements of the ions in the tetragonal phase (0.006 nm and 0.009 nm).

$\varepsilon_r(\text{ferroelectric}) \gg \varepsilon_r(\text{common dielectric})$, so ferroelectrics give **small and very efficient capacitors** (for example, for computer memories). Since $C = \varepsilon_r C_0$, a capacitor with BaTiO₃ stores about $4000$ times the charge of the same capacitor with vacuum.

chunks.t: Topic 6 - Electrical Properties
chunks.x:
**Piezoelectric materials** are ferroelectric materials that can be polarised when an external mechanical stress is applied. They occur in ceramics whose crystal structure has a **low degree of symmetry** [Session 13 Slide 58]. Two effects:

| Direct piezoelectric effect | Reverse piezoelectric effect (electrostriction) |
| :--- | :--- |
| External stress | External electric field |
| $\downarrow$ crystalline structure deformation | $\downarrow$ dipole alteration |
| $\downarrow$ dipole alteration | $\downarrow$ crystalline structure deformation |
| Electric field (voltage) generation | Dimensional change of the material |

They are used to transform electrical energy into mechanical energy and vice versa [Session 13 Slide 59], for example in **lighters** (a mechanical shock converted into a spark), **transducers in speakers**, **inkjet printers** (a piezoelectric actuator pushes the ink droplet out of the nozzle with a pulsed voltage), and **microphones and hydrophones** [Session 13 Slide 60].

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x: **Central idea:** every magnetic property comes from the magnetic moments of electrons, and the type of magnetism depends on whether those moments exist in the atom, whether they are permanent, and how neighbouring moments are arranged: induced and opposite (diamagnetic), permanent and random (paramagnetic), parallel (ferromagnetic), antiparallel and equal (antiferromagnetic) or antiparallel and unequal (ferrimagnetic). In the ferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic materials the moments group into domains, and the motion of the domain walls sets the shape of the hysteresis loop, so a material is a soft magnet or a hard one. The thermal properties follow from what heat does to the lattice: it raises the vibrational energy (heat capacity), it increases the mean interatomic distance (thermal expansion), it is carried by electrons and phonons (thermal conductivity), and when expansion is restrained or uneven it creates stresses (thermal stress and thermal shock).

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x: This page follows the single official session of Topic 7 (Session 15) slide by slide. Part I covers the magnetic properties (Slides 1 to 32) and Part II the thermal properties (Slides 33 to 48). Every section names the slides it comes from. Figures that appear on the slides are copied from them as PNG crops, and each caption names its slide; the two drawings that are not on the slides (the asymmetric potential well and the thermal-shock stress profile) are extensions and their captions say so. Anything that is not printed on the slides is marked as an extension. The photographs of the slides (uses of magnets, levitation, trains, thermocouples) are not reproduced. Problems 11 and 12 of the sheet `Problems T6andT7` are the magnetic problems of this topic, and they are solved on the problems page of this topic.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x: Slide 1 is the title and the agenda of the magnetic part: introduction, basic concepts, types of magnetism, magnetic domains, hysteresis cycles, and superconductivity and magnetism. Slide 2 lists the uses of magnetic materials with pictures: the compass, ferrofluids, permanent magnets, and the magnetic coverings used in stealth technologies.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 2. Origin of the magnetic behaviour [Session 15 Slide 3]
chunks.x:
**Magnetism** is the phenomenon by which materials induce forces of attraction or repulsion over other materials, and it has its origin in the movement of electrically charged particles [Session 15 Slide 3]. The macroscopic magnetic properties of a material are a consequence of the magnetic moments associated with its individual electrons. Each electron has two contributions:

- **Orbital magnetic moment** $= m_l\,\mu_B$, from its motion around the nucleus.
- **Spin magnetic moment** $= \pm\mu_B$, from its spin (two possible directions).

Here $m_l$ is the magnetic quantum number of the electron (the slide writes "magnetic quantum moment") and $\mu_B$ is the **Bohr magneton**:

$$\mu_B = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2$$

The magnetic moment of an atom is the sum of the magnetic moments of all its electrons. If the net moment of the atom is not null, the atom behaves like a **magnetic dipole**. The slide tabulates the moment of the 3d transition elements from the electronic structure of their 3d shell, which counts its unpaired spins (the 4s electrons are not counted, and the moment of an atom is not the moment per atom of the solid metal: compare Fe, Co and Ni here with the values of Section 4.3):

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 2. Origin of the magnetic behaviour [Session 15 Slide 3]
chunks.x:
| Element | Sc | Ti | V | Cr | Mn | Fe | Co | Ni | Cu |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Atomic number | 21 | 22 | 23 | 24 | 25 | 26 | 27 | 28 | 29 |
| Moment in $\mu_B$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 0 |

Definition of the Bohr magneton
The slide gives only the value of $\mu_B$. The definition $\mu_B = e\hbar/2m_e$ is an extension, and it reproduces the value above.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 3. Basic concepts: field, induction, magnetization [Session 15 Slide 4]
chunks.x:
Slide 4 defines the quantities of the magnetic response of a material in SI units. Some later slides also print other units: gauss (Slide 23), emu/cm³ and Oe (Slide 24), cal (Slides 35 and 41) and Btu (Slide 43).

- $H$ is the **magnetic field strength**, in A/m.
- $B$ is the **magnetic induction**, also called magnetic flux density (the slides also write "inductance"), in Wb/m² or tesla.
- $\mu$ is the **permeability** of the medium through which $H$ passes and in which $B$ is measured, in H/m (or Wb/(A·m)).
- $M$ is the **magnetization** (the magnetic moment per unit volume), in A/m.
- $\chi_m$ is the **magnetic susceptibility** (dimensionless).

$$B = \mu H \qquad\text{and in vacuum}\qquad B = \mu_0 H \qquad\text{with}\quad \mu_0 = 1.257\times10^{-6}\ \text{H/m}$$

$$\mu_r = \frac{\mu}{\mu_0} \qquad B = \mu H = \mu_0 H + \mu_0 M \qquad M = \chi_m H$$

The relative permeability $\mu_r$ is the ratio of the permeability of the material to that of vacuum. Substituting $M = \chi_m H$ in $B = \mu_0 H + \mu_0 M$ gives $B = \mu_0 (1 + \chi_m) H$, and comparing with $B = \mu_r\mu_0 H$,

$$\mu_r = 1 + \chi_m \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \chi_m = \mu_r - 1$$

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 3. Basic concepts: field, induction, magnetization [Session 15 Slide 4]
chunks.x:
(derived here from the two printed relations). The figure of the slide plots the induction against the field: in vacuum $B = \mu_0 H$, and in a material the line differs by the term $\mu_0 M$, which is the contribution of the material (higher for $M > 0$, lower for the diamagnetic $M < 0$).

Dimensional check
$[\mu_0 H] = (\text{H/m})(\text{A/m}) = \text{V}\cdot\text{s/m}^2 = \text{T}$, the unit of $B$. $\chi_m$ and $\mu_r$ have no units, because $M$ and $H$ are both in A/m.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
Slide 5 gives the overview. Materials are grouped by the value of $\mu_r$: the **ferromagnetic** and **ferrimagnetic** ones have $\mu_r \gg 1$ and $\chi \approx 10^5$ to $10^6$, while the **paramagnetic** and **diamagnetic** ones have $\mu_r$ close to 1 and a susceptibility of about $10^{-5}$ in absolute value. The **antiferromagnetic** materials are non-magnetizable. The chart of the slide plots the induction against the applied field with the line of vacuum ($\chi = 0$) as reference [Session 15 Slide 5]:

- (1) Diamagnetic ($\chi \sim -10^{-5}$): Al₂O₃, Cu, Au, Si, Ag, Zn. The line lies below that of vacuum.
- (2) Paramagnetic: Al, Cr, Mo, Na, Ti, Zr. The line lies slightly above that of vacuum.
- (3) Ferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic ($\chi$ as large as $10^6$): Fe₃O₄, NiFe₂O₄, ferrite ($\alpha$), Co, Ni, Gd. The line is far above, with $B \cong \mu_0 M$ for $H \ll M$.

Printed sign of the diamagnetic susceptibility
The text of Slide 5 writes the diamagnetic susceptibility as $\chi \approx 10^{-5}$ without the sign, while the chart on the same slide and Slide 6 give $\chi_m < 0$. The sign is negative.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
Chromium in two lists
Cr is listed as paramagnetic on Slide 5 and as antiferromagnetic on Slide 10. Slide 23 resolves it: its Néel temperature is 310 K, so it is antiferromagnetic below 310 K and paramagnetic above. By the same table MnO (116 K) and α-Mn (100 K) are paramagnetic at room temperature (this reading is an extension).

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
In a diamagnetic material there are no dipoles in the absence of an external field. In the presence of a field, dipoles are induced that are aligned **opposite** to the field direction. The external field induces a change in the speed of the orbital movement of the electrons, so the effect is **not permanent**: it exists only while the field is applied. The induced moment is very small and opposite to the applied field [Session 15 Slide 6]:

$$\mu_r < 1 \qquad \chi_m < 0 \qquad B_{dia} \cong \mu_0 H \qquad B_{dia} < B_0$$

where $B_0 = \mu_0 H$ is the induction in vacuum.

Examples on the slide: gold, silver and copper.

Slide 7 is titled "The frog incident" and only prints the link of a video (listed at the end of Part I). The slide does not describe it. The title points to the well-known demonstration of the diamagnetic levitation of a living frog in a very strong magnetic field; this reading is outside the slide.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
A paramagnetic material has atoms with **permanent** magnetic dipoles that are **randomly oriented**, so the material has no permanent net magnetization. When an external field is applied the dipoles turn and align with its direction. The induced field is relatively small and its effect is **added** to the applied field [Session 15 Slide 8]:

$$\mu_r > 1 \qquad 10^{-5} \le \chi_m < 10^{-2} \qquad B_{para} \cong \mu_0 H \qquad B_{para} > B_0$$

Examples on the slide: aluminium and titanium.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
A ferromagnetic material has magnetic dipoles **permanently oriented** (parallel) in the absence of an external field, so it shows a large permanent magnetization (within each domain: Section 5 explains why a piece that was never magnetized has no net magnetization). The slide states that the permanent magnetic moment of ferromagnetic materials is due fundamentally to the **spin** magnetic moments, with a small contribution from the orbital moments [Session 15 Slide 9]. The susceptibility is very large, up to $10^6$:

$$\chi_m \gg 1 \quad (\text{up to } 10^6) \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad M \gg H \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad B \cong \mu_0 M$$

The slide tabulates the magnetic moment at 0 K of the ferromagnetic metals:

| Metal | Fe | Co | Ni | Gd |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Magnetic moment in $\mu_B$ | 2.22 | 1.72 | 0.60 | 7.12 |

The examples of the slide are iron, nickel and cobalt; gadolinium appears in this table and in the table of Curie temperatures (Section 9).

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x: In an antiferromagnetic material the permanent magnetic dipoles are oriented in an **antiparallel** way, so the solid as a whole has no net magnetic moment. The examples are Cr, Mn and MnO. The slide shows the antiparallel alignment of the spin moments of the Mn²⁺ ions in manganese oxide, with the O²⁻ ions in between [Session 15 Slide 10].

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
Ferrimagnetism is present in **ceramic** materials with permanent dipoles of **different intensity** aligned in an antiparallel way, so a net moment remains. The ferrimagnetic ceramics are the **ferrites** (compounds of formula AB₂O₄), the **garnets** (M₃Fe₅O₁₂) and the compounds AB₁₂O₁₉ [Session 15 Slide 11]. The slide shows the arrangement of the cations in the oxygen lattice (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ in octahedral sites, Fe³⁺ in tetrahedral sites) and the net spin magnetic moment of each cation:

| Cation | Fe³⁺ | Fe²⁺ | Mn²⁺ | Co²⁺ | Ni²⁺ | Cu²⁺ |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Net spin moment in $\mu_B$ | 5 | 4 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 1 |

**Magnetite, Fe₃O₄ (extension, built from the table above).** Magnetite is the ferrite Fe³⁺(Fe²⁺Fe³⁺)O₄: one Fe³⁺ ion in a tetrahedral site and one Fe²⁺ and one Fe³⁺ ion in octahedral sites per formula unit. The two Fe³⁺ moments are antiparallel and cancel, $5\,\mu_B - 5\,\mu_B = 0$, so the net moment per formula unit is that of the Fe²⁺ ion, $4\,\mu_B$.

Slide 12 lists commercial ferrite compositions (MgFe₂O₄, Mg-Zn, MnFe₂O₄, Mn-Fe, Mn-Zn, NiFe₂O₄ and the lithium ferrite) and commercial garnet compositions (yttrium iron garnet Y₃Fe₅O₁₂ and its aluminium, chromium, lanthanum and praseodymium variants), with the comments on which site each substituting ion prefers.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 4.6 Summary of the types of magnetism [Session 15 Slide 13]
chunks.x:
Slide 13 draws the dipoles of the five types and groups them by when they are oriented: ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic materials have **oriented dipoles in the absence of a magnetic field**; paramagnetic materials have dipoles **oriented only in the presence of a field**; diamagnetic materials have **no permanent dipoles, only induced dipoles**. Together with the previous slides:

| Type | Dipoles | $\mu_r$ and $\chi_m$ | Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Diamagnetic | induced, opposite to $H$, not permanent | $\mu_r < 1$, $\chi_m < 0$ (about $-10^{-5}$) | Au, Ag, Cu, Si, Zn, Al₂O₃ |
| Paramagnetic | permanent, random, aligned by $H$ | $\mu_r > 1$, $10^{-5} \le \chi_m < 10^{-2}$ | Al, Ti, Cr, Mo, Na, Zr |
| Ferromagnetic | permanent, parallel without a field | $\mu_r \gg 1$, $\chi_m$ up to $10^6$ | Fe, Co, Ni, Gd |
| Antiferromagnetic | permanent, antiparallel and equal | no net moment, non-magnetizable | Cr, Mn, MnO |
| Ferrimagnetic | permanent, antiparallel and unequal | $\mu_r \gg 1$, $\chi_m$ about $10^5$ to $10^6$ | ferrites, garnets, Fe₃O₄ |

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 5. Magnetic domains and Bloch walls [Session 15 Slides 14-15]
chunks.x:
A **magnetic domain** is a three-dimensional region of a ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic material with uniform magnetization. Because of the domains, a ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic material that has never been exposed to a magnetic field has a null net magnetization [Session 15 Slide 14].

A **Bloch wall** is a narrow transition region at the boundary between magnetic domains, over which the magnetization changes progressively from its value in one domain to its value in the next. The sizes given on the slide are:

| Feature | Size |
| :--- | :--- |
| Domain | about 10 to 100 μm |
| Bloch wall | about 100 nm (approximately 300 atoms) |

The domains are usually smaller than the grains: a small grain can be a single domain, and a larger grain contains several. The slide shows the domain pattern of an iron (001) single crystal film.

Slide 15 gives the reason for the domains: the magnetic domain structure is generated **spontaneously to decrease the magnetostatic energy** of the material. A single domain has a high magnetostatic energy (the stray field closes through the air around it); two domains have a lower one, four domains a lower one still, and the closure domains of the last panel have zero magnetostatic energy [Session 15 Slide 15].

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
When a magnetic field is applied to a magnetic material the magnetization increases slowly at first, then more rapidly as the domains begin to grow, and later it slows down because the domains must eventually **rotate** to reach saturation [Session 15 Slide 16]. The stages of the slide are:

1. **Random distribution of domains** (demagnetized state, $H = 0$).
2. **Growth of the favourable domains** and shrinkage of the unfavourable ones.
3. **More growth** of the favourable domains.
4. **Rotation of domains** towards the field direction.
5. **Saturation.**

The two permeabilities of the slide are the slopes of the curve: $\mu_i$ is the **initial permeability** (slope at the start) and $\mu_{max}$ is the **maximum permeability** (the line from the origin tangent to the curve, that is, the largest value of $B/H$); the permeability varies with $H$. The slide's axis reads "magnetization $M$ or inductance $B$": strictly these slopes are permeabilities on the $B$ curve. The **saturation magnetization** $M_s$ is the magnetization that results when all the magnetic dipoles of the solid are aligned with the external field; the corresponding induction is the saturation flux density $B_s$.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
The slide draws the loop with the domains at each point. When the field is reduced from saturation, the magnetization does not follow the initial curve back, because the domains do not return to their random arrangement (the author's reading of the sketches). The loop of $B$ against $H$ defines two quantities:

- $B_r$ is the **remanence**: the induction that remains when the field is brought back to zero.
- $H_c$ is the **coercivity**: the reverse field needed to bring the induction to zero. It is a measure of the opposition to a change in orientation of the dipoles: the slide writes it as 1/(how easy it is to change the orientation of the dipoles).

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 7.2 Soft and hard magnetic materials [Session 15 Slide 18]
chunks.x:
The materials are classified by the shape of their loop, with the limit $H_c = 10\,000$ A/m [Session 15 Slide 18]:

| | Soft magnetic materials | Hard magnetic materials |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Bloch walls | easy to move | difficult to move |
| Properties | high initial permeability, low $H_c$ | high remanence, high $B_s$ and $H_c$, low $\mu_i$ |
| Use | materials under alternating fields, to increase $B$ and produce fast flux changes in coils and circuits with minimum energy losses | permanent magnets, because of their high resistance to demagnetization |

Saturation of soft and hard materials
Slide 18 lists a high $B_s$ for the hard materials, and Slide 19 asks for a high saturation magnetization in the soft ones. The data favour the soft side: on the chart of Slide 19 CoFe and Fe reach about 2 T or more against about 1.5 T for NdFeB, and on Slide 24 soft $B_{max}$ goes up to 2.30 T against 1.23 T for the best hard $\mu_0 M_r$. Both statements are kept as printed; the loops above are the ones of Slide 18.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
The slide matches each type of loop with its use [Session 15 Slide 19]:

- **Permanent magnets:** hard magnetic materials, with high resistance to demagnetization (high remanence, high coercive field).
- **Materials under alternating electrical fields** (cores of electromagnets, transformers, generators and electric motors, to increase the magnetic flux in coils and circuits): soft magnetic materials, to minimize energy losses, with high saturation magnetization, small coercive field and high permeability.
- **Magnetic memories** in computers, magnetic amplifiers and pulse transformers (data storage): materials with a **rectangular** hysteresis loop, with low remanence, low saturation magnetization and low coercive field (soft magnetic materials modified by a thermal treatment in the presence of a magnetic field).

The slide also plots the saturation magnetization against the coercivity of many materials, from the soft ferrites and iron alloys at low coercivity to the hard ferrites and rare-earth magnets at about $10^5$ A/m and above, with the regions labelled soft, semihard and hard. A second figure compares three loops: the soft magnet for electrical applications, the hard magnet for permanent magnets and the square loop for computer applications.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
Rectangular loop as printed
Slide 19 prints "low remanance" for the rectangular loop. A rectangular loop has $B_r$ close to $B_s$, so "low" can only mean low in absolute value, not low relative to $B_s$. The recording powders of Slide 24 also have $H_c$ of 22 to 240 kA/m, above the 10 kA/m limit of soft materials, so the slide's description does not fit them.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 8. Factors that control the hysteresis cycle [Session 15 Slides 20-22]
chunks.x:
The shape of the loop depends on [Session 15 Slide 20]:

- **The material's composition:** the number and intensity of its dipoles, and the type of magnetism of the material.
- **Processing:** its microstructure (grain size, pores, impurities, etc.) and the presence of strains due to mechanical deformations.
- **Working conditions:** working temperature, radiation and electrical currents.

The **coercivity** is a strongly microstructure-dependent property (crystallographic direction, grain boundaries, pores, shape of the particles), while the **saturation magnetization** is constant for a material of a given composition (at a given temperature, as the next paragraph shows).

**Microstructure** [Session 15 Slide 21]. The Bloch walls move more easily in larger grains, and obstacles stop them:

| Change | Effect on the Bloch walls | Effect on the loop |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Larger grain size | mobility increases | $\mu$ increases, $H_c$ and $B_r$ decrease |
| More inclusions, dislocations, pores, etc. | mobility decreases (a particle pins the wall) | $\mu$ decreases, $H_c$ and $B_r$ increase |

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 8. Factors that control the hysteresis cycle [Session 15 Slides 20-22]
chunks.x: **Temperature** [Session 15 Slide 22]. When the temperature rises the mobility of the dipoles rises. The maximum alignment reached when the field is applied is lower, so $M_s$ is reduced, and it is harder to keep the dipoles aligned when the field disappears, so $B_r$ and $H_c$ are reduced (the loop shrinks, as in the slide's figure for low, moderate and high temperature). When $T > T_c$ the dipoles can still align with $H$, but when $H$ disappears their alignments become random, and the material becomes **paramagnetic**.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 9. Curie and Néel temperatures, typical properties [Session 15 Slides 23-24]
chunks.x:
Thermal agitation tends to misalign the dipoles [Session 15 Slide 23].

- The **Curie temperature** $T_c$ is the temperature at which the saturation magnetization abruptly falls to 0. For $T > T_c$ ferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic materials become paramagnetic.
- The **Néel temperature** is the temperature at which an antiferromagnetic material becomes paramagnetic: the thermal energy becomes large enough to destroy the macroscopic magnetic ordering of the material.

| Ferromagnetic material | Fe | Co | Ni | Gd |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $T_c$ in K | 1043 | 1404 | 631 | 289 |

| Antiferromagnetic material | α-Mn | MnO | Cr | NiO |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Néel temperature in K | 100 | 116 | 310 | 523 |

The slide plots the saturation magnetization of pure iron and of magnetite against the temperature: both fall to zero, iron at about 770 °C (1043 K) and Fe₃O₄ at about 580 °C.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 9. Curie and Néel temperatures, typical properties [Session 15 Slides 23-24]
chunks.x: Slide 24 reproduces three tables of typical properties: selected **soft** magnetic materials (initial and maximum relative permeability, coercivity $H_c$, retentivity $B_r$, $B_{max}$ and resistivity: ingot iron, low-carbon steel, Fe-Si alloys, Fe-Ni alloys, Supermendur, metallic glasses, MnZn and NiZn ferrites), selected **hard** (permanent) magnetic materials (Fe-Co, Alnico-5, barium ferrite, SmCo₅, Nd₂Fe₁₄B, with $\mu_0 M_r$, $\mu_0 H_c$ and $(BH)_{max}$) and typical magnetic recording powders.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 10.1 Zero resistivity and critical temperature [Session 15 Slide 25]
chunks.x:
The electrical resistivity of a **superconductor** becomes **zero** below some critical temperature $T_c$. Superconductors can be pure metals and alloys, ceramics (typically with copper oxide) and organic compounds (based, for example, on Se or S). $T_c$ ranges between 0.01 and 165 K (the text of the slide; its chart marks 163 K), which is the practical limitation, and it is usually lower for metals than for ceramics. This $T_c$ is the critical temperature of a superconductor, not the Curie temperature of Section 9, and likewise $H_c$ below is the critical field, not the coercivity. The slide gives the critical temperatures (read from the slide):

| Material | $T_c$ in K | Material | $T_c$ in K |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: |
| Al | 1.20 | Nb₃Sn | 18.05 |
| Hg | 4.15 | Nb₃Al | 17.5 |
| Mo | 0.92 | V₃Ga | 16.5 |
| Nb | 9.26 | La₃In | 10.4 |
| Pb | 7.19 | LaBaCuO | 35 |
| Ta | 4.48 | YBCO | 90 |
| Ti | 0.39 | Tl₂Ba₂Ca₂Cu₃O₁₀ | 125 |
| Zn | 0.88 | Hg₁₂Tl₃Ba₃₀Ca₃₀Cu₄₅O₁₂₅ | 138 |

The slide also plots the resistivity against the temperature (the superconductor drops to zero at $T_c$, the normal metal tends to a residual value) and the history of the record $T_c$: the discovery of superconductivity (1911), the heavy-fermion superconductors (1979), the high-$T_c$ cuprates (1986) and the iron-based high-$T_c$ superconductors (2006).

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 10.2 Critical field and critical current density [Session 15 Slide 26]
chunks.x: At temperatures below $T_c$ the superconducting state stops when a sufficiently large magnetic field ($H_c$) or current density ($J_c$) is applied, and $H_c$ and $J_c$ **decrease with increasing temperature**. The **superconducting envelope** is the surface in the $(T, H, J)$ space that bounds the superconducting state; the slide shows it for Nb₃Sn, with $B_{c2} = 24.5$ T, $T_c = 18$ K and $J_c = 10^7$ A/cm² ($= 10^{11}$ A/m²).

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
The **Meissner-Ochsenfeld effect** is the expulsion of the magnetic field from a material when it is in the superconducting state. Above $T_c$ the field lines go through the material; below $T_c$ they are pushed around it, and the material becomes diamagnetic. Superconductors in the Meissner state exhibit **perfect diamagnetism** (superdiamagnetism): the total magnetic field is very close to zero deep inside. A permanent magnet **levitates** above a superconductor cooled by liquid nitrogen: the slide's drawing shows the repulsion of the Meissner effect, an attraction from the trapped magnetic flux, and gravity [Session 15 Slide 27].

Printed words
Slide 27 writes "semiconductor state" and "Oschsenfeld". The effect belongs to the superconducting state, and the name is Meissner-Ochsenfeld.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.h: 10.4 Type I and Type II superconductors [Session 15 Slides 28-29]
chunks.x:
- **Type I (soft superconductors):** sharp transition to the normal state, at a very low $H_c$, so they have low practical interest. They are pure metals: Sn, Al, Pb and Hg [Session 15 Slide 28].
- **Type II (hard superconductors):** gradual transition to the normal state as $H$ grows. The lowest critical field $H_{c1}$ can be 100 times lower than the highest critical field $H_{c2}$, and they have a high resistance against the destruction of superconductivity by magnetic fields. They are alloys (Nb-Zr, Nb-Ti), intermetallics (Nb₃Sn) and ceramics (YBaCuO). The flux lines begin to penetrate the material at $H_{c1}$, and at $H_{c2}$ the penetration is complete; for fields between the two the material is in a **mixed state**, with normal and superconducting regions [Session 15 Slide 29].

Printed words
Slides 28 and 29 write "Type I semiconductors" and "Type II semiconductors" for the lists of materials. They are superconductors.

chunks.t: Topic 7 - Magnetic and Thermal Properties
chunks.x:
The **Josephson** or tunnel effect occurs when a current flows through two superconductors separated by a very thin insulating layer, the **tunnel junction** (an oxide layer of about 3 nm) [Session 15 Slide 31]. The Josephson current goes through the junction even though there is no potential difference; a d.c. voltage applied through the junction causes a radio-frequency current oscillation (and an RF voltage causes a d.c. current); and its value is very sensitive to the magnetic field. It has many applications.

The applications of superconductors on Slide 32 are levitated transport, the powerful superconducting electromagnets of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), RF and microwave filters (for mobile-phone base stations and for military receivers), the Large Hadron Collider and other particle accelerators, and very low-loss filters based on ceramic superconductors for wireless communications [Session 15 Slide 32].
